title: Board Burst Strength or Puncture Resistance
html:
A board bursting-strength result does not establish its resistance to a projecting hard feature pushing through it. Distributed loading and localized penetration are different failure questions, even when both concern the same material.

For a Regular Slotted Shipping Cartons: Size Around the Inner Pack, show the projecting item or support that creates the local contact. Request evidence for that question separately from board bursting or carton compression; the concept does not establish puncture resistance.

For a gift brand comparing outer-carton proposals, identify the contact event that worries you before treating a reported strength value as relevant evidence. Neither material result, by itself, proves the protection of a complete packed shipment.

No board, load, penetration or transport result is measured in the hypothetical example below.

Pressure Loading and Pointed Contact Act Differently

Pressure applied over an area distributes the loading across that area. The board can deflect and develop stresses within the loaded region and its support arrangement. A pointed or projecting contact introduces a more localized interaction.

The relevant public standards retain that distinction. ISO 2759:2014 identifies a board bursting assessment based on increasing hydraulic pressure. ISO 3036:2025 identifies puncture resistance assessed with a pendulum device.

Those public descriptions establish different test questions; they do not provide the complete paid procedures or an actual packaging result.

A label such as “strong board” does not erase the difference between the loading areas, tool/contact shape and response being assessed.

Local Penetration Involves the Contact and the Material Around It

When a hard feature presses against a limited region, the interaction depends on more than a pressure value from another arrangement. The shape and direction of contact, how the board is supported and the construction around that location matter.

An edge or projection inside the pack can raise a different contact question from an external object meeting the carton. A holder that changes where the product can move can also change the interaction presented to the board.

These are relevant inputs, not findings that either event will occur. The existence of a projecting feature does not establish a puncture or quantify a required resistance.

It does explain why a distributed-load specimen result cannot automatically resolve the concern. The requested evidence needs to address the actual mechanism and remain connected to the evaluated construction.

A Hypothetical Ornament Creates a Separate Evidence Gap

Imagine a gift brand comparing outer-carton board proposals for an ornament with a projecting rigid feature. Each quotation supplies bursting-strength information, but neither identifies relevant puncture evidence.

No pressure numbers, penetration values or supplier reports are assigned to this example. The question is whether the offered information answers the particular product-contact concern.

The burst information may remain useful for its own stated board comparison. It cannot be converted into a puncture result by renaming the metric or choosing the larger number.

The brand also needs to keep the complete packed arrangement visible: the ornament, holder, carton and the way movement or contact could reach the board. A material specimen does not reproduce all of those features.

The unresolved conclusion is therefore not “both cartons fail.” It is that the separate penetration question and the complete package’s behavior remain unestablished from the burst figures alone.

Method, Direction and Support Remain Part of Each Result

Before comparing like results, identify the board construction, applicable method, preparation and relevant direction. Keep the support and loading arrangement that give the result its meaning.

A revised grade, thickness or layered construction can change that basis. A number for another material should not become the result for the board actually being offered.

The same caution applies when results concern different mechanisms. There is no universal conversion from a bursting pressure to puncture performance, nor a generic safety factor that creates a shipment acceptance result from either.

The buyer does not need to improvise a puncturing tool or destructive test. The responsible supplier or technical evaluator should identify the appropriate evidence and limits for the actual proposal.

Keep These Questions Separate From Crush and Whole-Package Protection

The edge-crush and box-compression guide separates board edge loading from assembled-container compression. Bursting and penetration introduce other loading arrangements, not alternate names for ECT or BCT.

The packed-system protection guide considers the product, internal packing and outer container together. That complete system is still the relevant level when the brand’s question concerns protection during distribution.

The distribution-test scope guide can help describe that configuration. It does not turn a material test into a successful transport result.

A favourable material finding can be an input to technical consideration while the assembled-system requirement remains open.

Request the Evidence for the Contact Being Considered

For the hypothetical ornament, separate the board’s distributed-pressure question from the concern about a hard feature meeting a local region. Then identify whether the available evidence covers either or both, and what remains to establish for the complete pack.

Packrivo can coordinate construction details and supplier questions. It does not test bursting or puncture resistance, establish a transport rating or certify an actual carton through project coordination.

A bursting result and a puncture result describe different loading questions. Keep the contact mechanism visible before selecting a material comparison or claiming product protection.

Source scope: Public ISO catalogue abstracts accessed 11 October 2026. ISO 2759:2014 is edition 4, published July 2014 and confirmed 18 March 2025. ISO 3036:2025 is edition 2, published March 2025. Their complete paid methods were not obtained. No test pressure, penetration result, performance conversion, board rating or actual shipment outcome is established.

Match the board document to the contact event

The invented ornament family keeps product O-H and board B-H identified while distinguishing three questions: a distributed-pressure material record, local projection contact and the packed-system configuration. None contains a result.

Reference Question Next evidence
DOC-B Board bursting property Actual method, construction and scoped result
LOC-P Projection Q-H toward local board region P1 Relevant contact/support and penetration evidence
PACK-A Holder H-H within carton C-H Complete arrangement and intended distribution scope
PACK-B Proposed holder H2-H New movement/contact configuration; no assumed remedy

Locate Q-H and P1 on the same packed drawing, including whether the concern begins inside or outside the carton. The projection’s existence does not prove that it reaches the board. Leave movement, contact and penetration blank when unobserved.

If a revised holder changes that route, preserve PACK-A and add PACK-B. A relocation proposal can change which board region is relevant; it does not by itself establish that puncture is prevented or that a higher burst value is needed.

Retain a burst document for its actual material question rather than converting it to a local-contact result. No universal conversion, safety factor, improvised tool or destructive buyer test is supplied. The technical source should identify applicable material and complete-system evidence.

Download the burst strength versus puncture resistance record (.csv). HYPOTHETICAL rows are invented examples. Use ACTUAL_BLANK for permitted project inputs; replace that row label only when recording actual facts. Empty evidence, observation and date fields mean unknown or not performed, never acceptance. Keep checkpoints and revisions separate.

Bring the located projection, holder revision and document scope through the linked enquiry route before treating a board-strength quotation as product protection. Packrivo coordinates independent suppliers. These records establish no supplier offer, service availability or MOQ exception; its published baseline is 500 pieces per product/design.

title: Shrink Film Percentage and Force on a Gift Set
html:
A film’s free-shrink percentage does not, by itself, predict the force it will exert against a gift set that restrains its contraction. Dimensional change without the item’s restraint and force under restraint are different mechanical questions.

Use Packaging Test Reports: Match the Ordered Configuration to keep the specimen, method and constrained state attached to any shrink-film evidence. A free-shrink percentage and force against the actual gift set answer different questions; neither can replace the other in a supplier comparison.

For a brand considering shrink wrapping, identify whether the unresolved requirement concerns the film’s change of size, its contact with the package or the response of the complete loaded set. A larger shrink percentage is not automatically a tighter, better-protected or suitable package.

No film, heating process, force or wrapped-gift result is evaluated in this article.

Free Shrink Describes an Unrestrained Dimensional Response

Some manufacturing histories leave orientation and internal stresses in a heat-shrinkable film. Heating can release a tendency for the material to contract, with the response depending on the particular film and conditions.

The public explanation of ASTM D2732-14(2025) concerns unrestrained linear thermal shrinkage. That is a dimension-change assessment under its stated conditions, not a test of the force received by a particular object inside the film.

A percentage therefore needs its direction and thermal basis. A film can behave differently along different material directions, and a value under one condition cannot silently represent every process or temperature.

The buyer should also distinguish an unrestrained specimen from a finished wrapping. Contact with the item changes the constraints, so the film may no longer be able to take the same dimensional path.

Restraint Makes the Interaction a Force Question

When an object limits contraction, the response includes forces at the constrained arrangement rather than only a free change in length. The actual restraint and available movement matter.

ASTM D2838-18(2026) identifies shrink-tension and related force/stress questions in its public scope. It distinguishes restraint arrangements and notes that actual packaging is not generally identical to an ideal totally restrained state.

That boundary is important. Neither a freely shrinking strip nor one particular laboratory restraint automatically reproduces the contact around a finished gift set.

The same free-shrink percentage can leave the relevant force response unresolved. A dimensional ratio has no universal conversion into the load at a box corner, label or fragile component.

A Hypothetical Two-Candle Gift Set Has Several Constraints

Imagine a brand considering a shrink-film proposal around a rigid gift box containing two glass candle jars. The material information identifies free-shrink characteristics, but the brand is also concerned about interaction with the box corners and the loaded presentation.

This is a proposed comparison, not a recommendation to heat or shrink-wrap a real candle container. No film grade or process compatibility has been established.

The wrapping can encounter corners, flat faces, unsupported film spans and transitions around the set. Those locations do not necessarily impose the same restraint or contact geometry.

A free-shrink description could inform the dimensional tendency of the specified material under its stated basis. It does not identify the force received at those different locations or prove that the loaded presentation remains suitable.

The immediate evidence gap is therefore specific: what information relates the offered film and proposed process to the actual wrapping constraints and contact question?

Choosing a greater percentage from a different material sheet would not answer that gap. It might change the construction or thermal behavior while leaving the application force unknown.

Appearance and Contact Loading Are Related but Separate Requirements

A visually close wrap does not measure its contact loading. The film can appear to fit a shape while the relevant package response remains unestablished.

Likewise, a material force characterization does not alone approve the complete wrapped appearance, label position or loaded product condition. The intended construction and use need to remain part of those decisions.

The tapered-container label guide concerns a flat label’s fit on a tapered receiving shape. A thermal shrink response is a different mechanism; successful label geometry cannot be relabeled as shrink-force evidence.

The film-and-varnish construction guide identifies surface layers in a packaging proposal. An independent shrink wrap is not automatically equivalent to a film laminated onto paperboard.

Retain Film Direction, Construction and Thermal Conditions

For a relevant material result, identify the film and direction, its thickness, the evaluation condition and the restraint arrangement. If a comparison changes those inputs, the meaning of the result changes as well.

This article does not provide a heating temperature, dwell time or machine speed. A process setting copied from a specimen method or another material cannot establish compatibility with the actual package and contents.

It also does not predict a shrink-force curve or a peak force from a generic percentage. Such a graph without relevant data would create an unmeasured result, not explain the remaining requirement.

The appropriate supplier or technical party must determine which material and application evidence can address the proposed construction.

Choose Evidence for the Actual Wrapping Job

First decide what is being asked: the film’s unrestrained size change, its force under a particular constraint, or the finished wrapping’s behavior around the gift. Keep the separate purposes visible when comparing information.

Where only a free-shrink value is available, contact loading remains an open question. Where a relevant restraint result is available, the actual package and process still need a suitable basis before any acceptance or heating recommendation.

Packrivo can coordinate film identity, construction and supplier questions. It does not operate a shrink line, measure contact forces or certify thermal suitability through project coordination.

Free shrink tells how a specimen can change dimensions under its stated conditions. It does not independently tell how much force a restrained gift set receives.

Source scope: Public ASTM catalogue material accessed 11 October 2026. D2732-14(2025) is the active reapproval updated 12 December 2025; D2838-18(2026) is the active reapproval updated 22 April 2026. Full paid methods were not obtained. No shrink percentage, heating condition, measured force, wrapped sample or product-contact suitability is established.

Locate free spans and constrained contacts on the same wrap

A single hypothetical film proposal F-H can meet a corner C1, a flat face F1 and an unsupported span U1 around one gift-set outline. This map identifies local questions without assigning a shrink percentage, heating condition or force.

Region Proposed relationship Evidence gap
C1 Film meeting a box corner Actual contact/constraint and local response
F1 Film beside a flat face Actual contact and available movement
U1 Film across unsupported region Local geometry and possible free movement
SPEC-H Separate unrestrained specimen record Direction, material and thermal basis; not application force

A region label does not classify the entire wrap as totally restrained. Contact can vary around one assembly, and its state can change during a proposed process. Leave actual contact and movement blank unless the responsible evidence establishes them.

Keep film identity, material direction and process reference with every document. A free-shrink percentage can populate only its dimensional-response record; it cannot fill the C1 force cell. A restrained-specimen result also needs an applicability review before describing the gift set.

This is a construction and evidence map, not permission to heat the package or its contents. No temperature, dwell, machine speed, force curve, thermal compatibility or material recommendation follows from the illustration.

Download the shrink film force versus shrink percentage record (.csv). HYPOTHETICAL rows are invented examples. Use ACTUAL_BLANK for permitted project inputs; replace that row label only when recording actual facts. Empty evidence, observation and date fields mean unknown or not performed, never acceptance. Keep checkpoints and revisions separate.

Bring the film identity and region-specific contact questions through the original enquiry route so dimensional and force evidence retain their separate meanings. Packrivo coordinates independent suppliers. These records establish no supplier offer, service availability or MOQ exception; its published baseline is 500 pieces per product/design.

title: Counter Display Stability as Stock Is Removed
html:
A counter display standing as intended when full has not, through that observation alone, established its behavior with a different remaining stock arrangement. Removing or repositioning products can change the loaded centre of mass and the way a disturbance acts on the display.

For a gift brand, separate the base and loaded mass distribution from capacity, front-wall access and artwork. Those factors help define the tipping question; they do not provide a measured stability rating or prove that any particular display will fall.

The example below is hypothetical. No display, product weight, force or tipping threshold has been measured.

The Support Footprint Sets the Relevant Edges

For an ideal unsupported-by-anything-else object on a level surface, gravity acts through its centre of mass. The relationship between that line of action and the base of support matters when considering rotation about a base edge.

OpenStax’s stability explanation connects the centre-of-gravity position with the base of support. Its general statics discussion also distinguishes an equilibrium state from the conditions under which displacement changes that state.

The relevant footprint is the actual contact and support arrangement, not necessarily the largest artwork outline or the width of an overhanging header.

A wide-looking panel can sit on a narrower support. A supported or attached display can also have additional constraints that an isolated free-standing model does not include. Those differences have to remain visible before applying a simple explanation to a real fixture.

A Disturbance Introduces a Turning Effect

In a simplified static model, a horizontal force acting above the counter can create a turning effect about a base edge. The loaded weight can provide an opposing effect when its line of action is appropriately inside that edge.

The general moment-balance basis is described in OpenStax’s conditions for static equilibrium. The location of the force matters alongside its size.

For that idealized comparison, write the possible overturning moment as F × h, with h the perpendicular distance for the horizontal force. The opposing weight moment is W × d, with d the inward horizontal distance of the weight’s line of action from the selected base edge.

These symbolic relationships are not an acceptance calculation for a paperboard display. Their comparison assumes an appropriate rigid, stationary model and excludes unestablished effects such as prior sliding, flexible deformation or additional supports.

No numerical force or safe product arrangement follows without the relevant actual basis.

A Partially Emptied Display Can Have a Different Mass Distribution

Imagine a hypothetical counter display with products at a lower and an upper level. Staff or customers remove some of the lower products while others remain above.

Depending on the assumed product masses and positions, the loaded centre of mass can change. The total weight also changes. The footprint can remain the same while the force-and-moment relationship is different.

This does not establish that fewer products always make a display less stable. Removing a particular product can shift the distribution in different ways, and no values are assigned to the example.

It also does not establish that the remaining arrangement tips. The relevant conclusion is narrower: the original full-state observation does not answer the changed-state question by itself.

If an intended pickup or replenishment action adds a horizontal or eccentric force, that action introduces another condition beyond the remaining products’ static positions. It should not disappear inside a generic description of “the same display.”

Access and Stability Ask Different Questions

The front-wall access guide considers how a customer reaches and removes the sale-ready unit. A workable grip route does not establish the loaded display’s response to the forces introduced by that action.

The replenishment-pattern guide identifies different stock and refill arrangements. Those arrangements can also provide inputs to the mass-distribution question, without turning the refill record into stability evidence.

The same distinction applies to a clear neighboring-product path. Avoiding a collision is useful, but it does not supply a tipping threshold for the fixture.

Sliding, Deformation and Additional Support Remain Separate Possibilities

An actual display can slide or deform rather than behave as a rigid body rotating about a selected edge. Counter contact, structure and any intended attachment can affect which response is relevant.

Thus the position of a drawn centre-of-mass point cannot, on its own, certify the entire display. The point also is not measured merely because an illustration places a dot inside the base.

The static model explains why footprint, mass position and force application matter. It does not replace evidence for the actual constructed fixture and intended use.

Compare the Stock States That Change the Mechanical Question

For a proposed counter display, identify the support footprint, the intended full and remaining product positions, and the actions that can introduce relevant forces. Keep those inputs connected to the construction being offered.

If the available evidence covers only a full stationary arrangement, retain the limits when considering a different stock state or pickup action. The responsible technical party should determine any appropriate evaluation and acceptance basis.

Packrivo can coordinate layout, construction and supplier questions. It does not certify retail-fixture stability or prescribe a safe force or loaded arrangement through project coordination.

A display’s capacity and front profile do not define its tipping behavior. The relevant comparison retains the support footprint, loaded centre of mass and the action being considered.

Source scope: Public OpenStax stability and static-equilibrium material accessed 11 October 2026. It supports general mechanics, not a counter-display conformity standard. The F × h and W × d expressions are ideal symbolic moments only; no actual masses, dimensions, forces, friction, restraint or fixture performance is established.

Name the remaining stock state without predicting its balance

An invented two-level fixture D-H uses position IDs U1, U2, L1 and L2. The state register distinguishes which units remain, which move and which action is considered. Product masses and centre-of-mass coordinates are unknown.

State Occupied positions Staff action Unresolved mechanical question
ST-A U1 U2 L1 L2 None assumed Complete full-state support and response
ST-B U1 U2 L2 L1 removed Changed mass distribution
ST-C U2 L2 U1 removed after ST-B Another remaining arrangement
ACT-H State must be named Pickup or refill as separate action Applied action, contact and support scope

A count of three units does not specify ST-B unless their positions are recorded. If staff move L2 toward the front, give that a new state reference instead of treating the layout as unchanged.

Keep actual counter contact and any intended attachment with the fixture revision. The support footprint is not inferred from the header width. Sliding, flexible deformation and rotation are different possible responses, none of which this state map predicts.

Do not place a computed-looking centre-of-mass dot on an unevaluated layout. The original symbolic F×h and W×d explanation remains useful within its assumptions, but this register supplies no force, moment, tipping limit or safer stock arrangement.

Download the counter display tipping stability record (.csv). HYPOTHETICAL rows are invented examples. Use ACTUAL_BLANK for permitted project inputs; replace that row label only when recording actual facts. Empty evidence, observation and date fields mean unknown or not performed, never acceptance. Keep checkpoints and revisions separate.

Bring the occupied-position map and actual support arrangement through the existing enquiry route before extending full-state evidence to a depleted display. Packrivo coordinates independent suppliers. These records establish no supplier offer, service availability or MOQ exception; its published baseline is 500 pieces per product/design.

title: Peel Adhesion or Static Shear for Packaging Tape
html:
A tape’s resistance to being peeled away does not establish how long it will remain in place under a sustained load parallel to its bonded surface. Peel and static shear describe different demands on a pressure-sensitive bond.

For Pressure-Sensitive Paper Sealing Tape Fits the Carton and Dispensing Method, identify whether the proposed carton joint loads the tape in peeling, sustained shear or another route. The product concept does not supply test values or establish suitability for the actual carton surface and storage conditions.

For a gift-box sleeve, identify the load the joint must resist during use before selecting the relevant evidence. A useful peel result can leave a sustained-holding requirement unanswered, and the reverse substitution is no more reliable.

The example below is hypothetical. No tape, adhesive, force threshold or holding time has been evaluated.

Peeling Advances a Separation Front

During a peel action, separation can progress along the bonded area from a free edge. The tape backing bends and the relation between the applied action and the moving bond front matters.

That arrangement differs from asking whether a bonded area remains in place while a load acts mainly parallel to the receiving surface. Naming both results “adhesion” does not make their loading histories equivalent.

The public description of ASTM D3330/D3330M-04(2025) identifies peel-adhesion assessment for pressure-sensitive tape. Its stated specimen and geometry belong to that result; a peel value is not a universal functional strength score for every use of the tape.

It does not follow that a tape which is difficult to peel is the appropriate choice for a particular sleeve joint. The use requirement and the actual receiving surface still need a relevant basis.

Static Shear Introduces Sustained In-Plane Loading

For a mainly shear-loaded joint, the imposed load acts along the bonded interface rather than deliberately lifting a free edge through a peel route. When that load is maintained, elapsed exposure becomes part of the question about remaining adhered or retaining position.

ASTM D3654/D3654M-06(2024) describes sustained parallel loading in its public scope. It includes relevant surface-specific packaging contexts, while a standard-panel result does not automatically establish behavior on another receiving construction.

The actual tape backing, adhesive, bonded area, substrate and conditions remain important. No universal conversion changes a peel value into a shear holding time.

This article also does not propose a hanging-weight procedure. The public scope distinguishes the question; it does not provide the full paid method or an acceptance condition for the sleeve.

One Hypothetical Sleeve Joint Can Have Two Jobs

Imagine a paperboard sleeve whose overlap is secured with pressure-sensitive tape. During its intended storage, the overlap is assumed to remain under a mainly in-plane load. When someone deliberately opens it, a free edge may be pulled through a peel action.

The first job is maintaining the secured overlap under the relevant sustained loading. The second is the response during the intended opening. Neither event has been performed in this example.

Suppose a supplier can provide a favorable peel-adhesion result on an identified surface. That information could help with a suitable peel comparison. It would not establish the duration for which the sleeve joint resists its different storage load.

If a relevant shear result were available instead, it would not establish clean removal, the required peel action or the appearance of the paperboard after opening.

The useful conclusion is to keep the two requirements separate. It is not to select the tape with the highest number in an unrelated report.

Real Joint Geometry Can Introduce Mixed Loading

The mainly in-plane example is a simplification. A curved sleeve, eccentric load, lifted corner or flexible receiving panel can introduce a peel component alongside shear.

Thus calling a joint “an overlap” does not prove that its bond experiences only shear. The actual load path and geometry have to be identified before a particular specimen result is treated as representative.

The opposite limitation applies to an opening demonstration. Observing a moving edge does not reconstruct every sustained load that the joint experienced beforehand.

Where the two stages or components matter, the technical party should establish which evidence addresses each one. A single unexplained adhesion figure cannot select between them.

Surface and Time Belong to the Result’s Meaning

A tape result retains the receiving construction and conditions it covers. A bare test panel is not automatically equivalent to printed, coated or wrapped paperboard, and an initial bond observation does not describe an unspecified later exposure.

These qualifications do not make the data useless. They identify the limits within which the data can inform the actual joint decision.

The label-removal observation guide concerns residue and surface condition after the intended removal. That endpoint differs from maintaining the bond during a sustained shear load.

The liner-release guide separates release from the liner from adhesion to the final package. Neither a release value nor easy dispensing establishes peel or sustained shear performance on the sleeve.

Choose Evidence for the Load the Bond Must Actually Resist

For a proposed packaging joint, describe its construction and identify whether the unresolved function concerns a moving peel front, sustained parallel loading or a mixture of modes. Keep the opening and storage stages distinct when both matter.

The supplier or qualified technical party can then identify relevant evidence and an appropriate acceptance basis. No holding duration, strength threshold or safe load follows from the comparisons in this article.

Packrivo can coordinate the surface, construction and use questions. It does not test or certify adhesive holding performance through project coordination.

Peel and static shear are different loading questions. A result becomes relevant when its load, surface and exposure match the job the bond must perform.

Source scope: Public ASTM catalogue information accessed 11 October 2026. The official entries identify D3330/D3330M-04(2025), updated 14 August 2025, and D3654/D3654M-06(2024), updated 29 October 2024, as active. The generic D3654 endpoint failed while its exact reapproval page was accessible. Full paid procedures were not obtained, and no actual adhesive, holding time, package result or peel-to-shear conversion is established.

Split the storage job from the deliberate opening job

One hypothetical pressure-sensitive overlap J-H can have two intended stages. A document for a peel action and a document for sustained in-plane loading belong in different rows, even when the tape reference is unchanged.

Job Proposed demand Evidence request
HOLD-H Maintain overlap under sustained mainly in-plane load Actual substrate, area, exposure and applicable shear scope
OPEN-H Deliberate opening with a moving peel front Actual peel arrangement and relevant result
END-H Paperboard condition after opening Separate residue and appearance observation

Keep the finished receiving surface S-H beside the tape backing and adhesive identity. A standard-panel result must not silently become a result on printed or coated S-H. The method name alone does not establish that applicability.

Record a holding duration only when an actual scoped document supplies it. Do not turn a peel quantity into time, choose a generic hanging weight or set a buyer-created threshold. The register is for matching evidence to the joint’s job, not performing a method.

A revision that changes a free edge or overlap curvature can change the load mode while leaving the tape grade unchanged. Preserve the geometry revision and keep clean removal, holding and intended opening as separate acceptance questions.

title: Gift Bag Balance: Contents and Handle Support
html:
A gift can fit inside a paper bag yet produce a different hanging arrangement when it is placed away from the centre. Fitting through the mouth and balancing while suspended are different questions.

The loaded system’s mass distribution and its handle support affect force and moment balance. An off-centre item does not automatically prove a misplaced handle, and it does not provide a carrying-capacity finding or a predictable tilt angle.

The examples here are hypothetical. No bag, handle, load, angle or strength has been measured.

Weight Acts Through the Loaded System’s Centre of Mass

For a stationary suspended system, support forces have to balance its weight, while the overall turning effects also have to balance. OpenStax’s statics explanation treats these as separate equilibrium conditions: net force and net external torque are zero in the stated static situation.

The location of a force matters to its turning effect. OpenStax’s torque chapter explains that the perpendicular lever arm is part of that relationship, not just the magnitude of the force.

For a bag and gift, the relevant centre of mass belongs to the whole loaded arrangement. Moving an item within the bag can change it even when the item and total weight remain the same.

The point is not that every off-centre load makes a bag tilt. It is that the support arrangement must accommodate a different distribution of turning effects and forces.

Two Support Locations Can Share the Load Differently

In an idealized arrangement with two separated vertical supports, a weight located between them can be balanced by different shares of upward support. Moving that weight changes the moment relationship, so an unchanged total weight does not establish equal loading at both supports.

This simplified model describes force balance, not the detailed behavior of a paper carrier. It assumes identifiable support locations and a suitable stationary arrangement, without assigning actual reaction forces.

A real bag has flexible handles and walls. It can deform, the grip can change, and the gift can contact or move within the base. These changes affect the actual load route and the final suspended arrangement.

If the bag or contents rotate or rearrange, the geometry used for a static model changes as well. A drawing of two arrows and a weight cannot calculate a final hanging angle without the relevant construction and constraints.

A Hypothetical Candle Position Changes the Question

Imagine a glass candle carton placed in a paper gift bag. In one proposal it is near the centre of the base; in another it sits nearer the left side. The bag, carton and added tissue are otherwise assumed unchanged.

This is a conceptual comparison, not an observed carrying trial or a real customer configuration.

Moving the carton can change the centre of mass of the loaded system relative to its supports. That can change the support loading or how the flexible arrangement settles when lifted. It does not establish that the left-hand proposal will tilt by a particular amount or cause a particular joint to fail.

Nor does it prove that the centred proposal is safe to carry. Balance is one question; strength, grip access and complete loaded use remain separate requirements.

The useful observation to preserve is the proposed item’s position and the actual support arrangement. A comment such as “the handle looks uneven” may otherwise conceal a change in contents, grip or base geometry.

Where the Hand Supports the Handles Also Matters

The handle attachment locations on the bag are not necessarily the same as the support locations imposed by the hand. Handle length, flexibility and the way the handles are brought together can affect the route from the loaded bag to the grip.

A comparison that changes the grip while also changing the gift position is not an isolated test of one variable. Likewise, taking out tissue or moving a second component to make lifting easier changes the loaded arrangement being considered.

The bag-handle joint guide identifies attachments and hidden joining work. Those details remain necessary, but identifying a joint does not establish moment balance or actual support loads.

The gift-bag loading-clearance guide addresses the route by which the gift enters the bag. That geometry should not be relabeled as evidence that the same package hangs as intended afterward.

Balance and Carrying Strength Are Not Interchangeable

A system can have a balanced stationary arrangement while a component remains unsuitable for its actual load. Conversely, a component may remain attached while the loaded bag changes posture.

Those statements describe different possible questions, not failures observed in this example. The geometry and force balance help locate the use configuration that strength evidence would need to represent; they do not generate that evidence.

Movement introduces another boundary. Starting, stopping or swinging a carried bag is not the same as a stationary equilibrium model. Static explanation should not be used as a complete handling or carrying qualification.

Compare the Loaded Arrangement That Matters to the Customer

For an actual proposal, keep the complete gift position, support geometry and intended grip identifiable. Consider whether a changed posture is consistent with a changed loaded arrangement before attributing it to an artwork or handle-position error.

If a carrying requirement is intended, the responsible supplier or technical party needs an appropriate basis for the actual complete configuration and use. No weight allowance or safe carrying claim follows from the centre-of-mass explanation alone.

Packrivo can coordinate the dimensions, construction and supplier questions. It does not perform or certify a carrying test through project coordination.

A bag that contains the gift and a loaded bag that hangs as intended are different propositions. Preserve the product position and support arrangement before deciding what an uneven posture means.

Source scope: OpenStax’s public College Physics 2e statics and torque explanations were accessed 11 October 2026. They describe general equilibrium, not a paper-bag standard or measured carrier. No actual support load, tilt, joint strength, movement response or carrying performance is established.

Keep gift-position and grip changes in separate comparisons

The invented carrier family below changes either the gift location or the grip route. Bag B-H, joint J-H, gift G-H and tissue T-H remain identified throughout. No hanging posture, reaction force or carrying capacity is calculated.

Configuration Gift position Grip route Comparison purpose
B-A POS-C GR-H Reference complete arrangement
B-B POS-L GR-H Gift position only
B-C POS-C GR2-H Grip route only
Any tissue move New tissue position Record if grip changes New configuration rather than hidden adjustment

Use a top-view position reference and an inside view of the complete contents. A visible carton shift does not measure the whole system’s centre of mass; tissue, accessories and the carrier itself remain part of that system.

The hand’s support route need not coincide with the handle attachment. Record how the handles are brought together, without treating this as a handling instruction or a claim about equal support loads. Comparing B-B with B-C combines two different variables.

Keep a stationary hanging observation separate from starting, stopping or swinging use. A level-looking bag does not demonstrate joint strength. Actual carrying evidence must identify the complete configuration and intended use; the worksheet leaves those outcomes blank.

Download the gift bag load balance record (.csv). HYPOTHETICAL rows are invented examples. Use ACTUAL_BLANK for permitted project inputs; replace that row label only when recording actual facts. Empty evidence, observation and date fields mean unknown or not performed, never acceptance. Keep checkpoints and revisions separate.

Bring the complete contents-position and grip references through the linked enquiry route before attributing a hanging observation to a handle defect. Packrivo coordinates independent suppliers. These records establish no supplier offer, service availability or MOQ exception; its published baseline is 500 pieces per product/design.

title: An RGB Colour Can Be Valid on Screen but Outside the Printing Gamut
html:
A saturated colour can be valid in a screen image and still fall outside the colours reproducible under a specified printing condition. That is a gamut question, not proof that the printer has failed to match an achievable target.

For a gift brand, identify the intended print condition before treating an RGB choice as a production colour. If the target is outside that condition’s gamut, conversion or a design/process decision is needed; copying the same numbers does not create the missing colour capability.

No device profile, actual packaging colour or measured colour difference is assigned to the hypothetical example below.

A Gamut Is a Range, Not a Guarantee Attached to a Colour Name

A device or output condition has a range of colours it can represent. A display and a particular ink/substrate process can have different ranges. Their data also use different colour-system descriptions.

Adobe’s current out-of-gamut guidance explains that some RGB colours cannot be reproduced accurately in a selected CMYK output. The warning is evaluated against a proof profile, so the intended output basis matters.

It does not establish one universal gamut for every screen or every print process. Nor should a generic diagram imply that all possible RGB and CMYK gamuts have the same boundary or a fixed nesting relationship.

An RGB triplet without its relevant colour-space context is not an ink recipe. Even a properly described digital colour needs a relationship to the proposed physical output before the brand can treat it as a printable target.

Conversion Can Map a Colour Without Preserving Its Exact Appearance

When an out-of-range colour is converted into a destination space, it has to be represented by an available destination colour according to the conversion choices. Completing that conversion does not mean that the original appearance has become physically available.

The result can change the look of a saturated design area or the relationships among neighbouring colours. The Adobe colour-management explanation describes the role of profiles in translating between device colour spaces; profile-based translation does not repair every source-image or production problem.

A conversion can therefore be technically completed while the brand still needs to decide whether the changed design is acceptable. That is a design decision, not merely a file-format success.

The software’s warning overlay also is not the appearance of the printed colour. Its highlight identifies a potential output-range issue within the chosen proof setup; it does not constitute a physical printed sample.

A Hypothetical Saturated Blue Reveals the Choice

Imagine a brand selecting a vivid blue for a gift-box panel on screen. The specified print condition’s profile indicates that the chosen colour lies outside its gamut.

This is an assumed scenario, not a profile analysis performed on a real Packrivo job. It provides no numerical difference or prediction of the final blue.

One possible decision is to adjust the design toward an achievable colour that preserves the intended relationship with the other areas. Another is to investigate a different output construction or ink approach with the printing provider.

Neither option should be described as automatically restoring the original screen appearance. A proposed spot ink, new substrate or other process change needs its own evidence and commercial scope; a new name alone does not establish the colour that will result.

The brand should also decide what matters most in the affected area. Retaining the exact digital saturation, preserving a colour relationship or selecting an achievable physical brand target are related but different priorities.

Without that decision, repeatedly requesting “the same RGB” can leave the printer trying to satisfy an output condition that has never been established as capable of it.

Out-of-Gamut and Out-of-Tolerance Are Different Findings

An out-of-gamut question concerns whether the specified output can reproduce the target colour within its available range. An out-of-tolerance finding concerns a particular evaluated result compared with an applicable target and criterion.

A physically achievable colour can still be printed differently from its intended reference. Conversely, a well-controlled process cannot be assumed to reproduce a colour outside its stated capability simply by using a tighter tolerance.

The physical colour-reference guide explains how to establish the appearance comparison on the intended material and finish. That remains useful after the output-range decision; it should not be substituted for deciding whether the starting target is achievable under that output.

Changing the colour-difference formula also does not expand the printing gamut. It changes the interpretation of specified colour data, rather than creating a new ink/substrate capability.

Preserve the Intended Output in the Next Design Discussion

For an actual proposal, identify the selected output condition and suitable profile with the responsible printing party. Keep any gamut warning, conversion and proposed design revision tied to that basis, rather than treating a generic CMYK label as complete context.

Then use appropriate output and physical evidence to decide the revised appearance. A screen preview can help locate a problem or compare design directions without becoming an approved print colour.

Packrivo can coordinate the artwork, material and supplier questions. It does not certify a press gamut, provide an actual profile analysis or guarantee colour reproduction through project coordination.

A valid screen colour and a reproducible print colour are different propositions. Establish the destination condition before deciding how an out-of-range target should change.

Source scope: Adobe’s public out-of-gamut page was accessed 11 October 2026 and is updated 6 October 2026; its colour-management explanation was also available. These software principles do not establish a particular packaging press, substrate or profile. No gamut volume, RGB/CMYK recipe, Delta E result or real colour sample has been measured.

A second output should retain its original source identity

Compare three proposed file paths without analysing a real colour. SOURCE_MASTER is the retained RGB source. OUT_A is a proposed conversion for output condition P_A; OUT_B is another proposed conversion from the same source for P_B. A later OUT_A-to-P_B conversion has a different input from SOURCE_MASTER-to-P_B.

Hypothetical configuration Named object Relationship Input or next scope
DIRECT_A OUT_A proposed source SOURCE_MASTER_RGB
DIRECT_A OUT_A proposed output condition P_A
DIRECT_B OUT_B proposed source SOURCE_MASTER_RGB
DIRECT_B OUT_B proposed output condition P_B
RECONVERTED_FROM_A RECONVERTED_FROM_A proposed source OUT_A
RECONVERTED_FROM_A RECONVERTED_FROM_A proposed output condition P_B
DIRECT_B_VS_RECON SOURCE_MASTER_RGB different from OUT_A
RECONVERTED_FROM_A SECOND_CONVERSION does not guarantee ORIGINAL_APPEARANCE_RECOVERY

LINEAGE TECHNICAL_EXPORT not a MEASURED_PHYSICAL_MATCH

If the first conversion remapped information, converting its result again cannot simply be called recovery of the original RGB appearance. Retain the master and output lineage so the responsible printer can identify which source and destination were actually used. This model supplies no actual profile, conversion intent or loss amount.

P_A and P_B name different proposed output conditions, not universal CMYK gamuts. Neither path establishes which colours are in range or what the physical print will look like. A technically completed export or soft proof is not a measured match.

The useful buyer decision is which exact source/output relationship the revised proof should cover. Request the appropriate source-based comparison and physical approval evidence rather than repeatedly renaming a converted file. Changing the output construction or profile also reopens its commercial and appearance scope; no ink capability or colour tolerance is created by the filename.

ACTUAL_BLANK is a separate empty starting row; enter permitted project evidence before using an actual record. A blank means unknown.

Use the Packaging Color Approval With a Physical Reference for its separate question. Use the Printing on Uncoated Paper: Review the Proposed Stock for its separate question.

Software conversion and soft proof do not establish a physical match, one global CMYK gamut or universal colour tolerance. The added configurations and calculations are hypothetical, with actual evidence and decisions pending.

title: Print Trapping and Packaging Registration Gaps
html:
A fine white line between two printed colour areas does not necessarily mean that the artwork contains a missing object. When separately printed colours shift relative to each other, a boundary intended to meet exactly can expose the substrate. Trapping introduces a controlled overlap to reduce that particular gap risk.

For a gift brand, the useful decision is whether a reported boundary problem concerns missing artwork, registration or the selected prepress compensation. Expanding every shape without that distinction can change the intended edge while leaving the underlying question unresolved.

The illustrations below are hypothetical. No actual press, registration tolerance or trap width is specified.

A Butt Boundary Depends on the Colours Meeting as Intended

Imagine a pale block beside a dark blue field on a folding-carton panel. In the intended composition, their edges meet without a white line between them.

If those areas depend on separate output separations, a relative displacement can change the printed boundary. A shift in one direction can open a gap; a shift in another can introduce overlap. The source file and the physical printed relationship are therefore different stages of the observation.

A gap that was already present in the intended artwork would be a different problem. Trapping is not a substitute for restoring a genuinely missing design object or correcting the file’s intended geometry.

Adobe’s current trap-preset guidance describes slight overlaps at adjoining colour boundaries as a way to compensate for press misregistration. It also directs the choice of settings to the selected prepress workflow rather than a universal number.

The principle is local: manage a particular boundary where relative printing displacement could reveal an unwanted sliver of substrate.

An Overlap Provides a Limited Geometric Reserve

In a simplified one-dimensional illustration, the two printed areas are made to overlap slightly across their intended meeting line. If a relative displacement tends to pull their edges apart, some overlap can remain instead of immediately exposing the substrate.

That reserve is finite. A displacement beyond what the particular compensation covers can still leave a visible gap. Adding an overlap does not establish perfect registration or eliminate every possible boundary problem.

The overlap can also affect the appearance of the edge where colours meet. Its visible effect depends on the inks, substrate, geometry and output. A drawing of two coloured rectangles does not predict the resulting physical edge colour.

This explains why the relevant question is not “should all objects be bigger?” It is which boundary needs compensation, in which output context, and how that compensation preserves the intended design.

The Direction and Objects of Compensation Matter

Different adjacent colours and print arrangements can call for different treatment. One side of a boundary can be extended or another adjusted within a prepress decision; indiscriminately spreading every object is not the same operation.

Adobe’s trap-options explanation ties those controls to ink and press conditions. Its software defaults and ranges are not instructions for this hypothetical carton or every packaging process.

Overprint is another related but distinct instruction. It concerns how an object interacts with underlying printing, rather than proving that a chosen local trap is suitable. An unchanged composite preview also may not answer how the final separations and output workflow handle the boundary.

Some colour relationships need no added trapping under the agreed process. The presence of two neighbouring shapes alone does not establish that every boundary should receive the same adjustment.

A Hypothetical White Sliver Needs Its Location Preserved

Suppose a brand sees a white sliver where the pale block meets the blue field in an illustrative printed candidate. The first useful comparison is the intended boundary against the output and physical observation.

If the intended file already includes a white separation, the design question comes first. If the shapes meet in the intended file but the printed areas do not, registration and the output treatment become relevant investigation questions.

If a trap was specified, the printer still needs to establish whether the selected output used it as intended and whether it was suitable for that particular boundary. None of those findings follows merely from seeing a white line.

This is not a diagnosis of an actual job. It identifies competing explanations and prevents a global artwork expansion from being treated as the automatic remedy.

The brand can keep the reported location, the intended objects and the selected output version together. That gives the designer and printer a specific boundary to resolve, without inventing a press setting or promising that compensation alone will fix it.

Locate the boundary before asking for a trap change

Name the two objects and the output version containing them. Keep a view of the intended file beside the located printed observation. If the design deliberately separates the objects, that is a different request from a print whose intended butt boundary has opened.

Boundary record Unresolved fact Focused response
A 1 / B 1 intended relationship Butt boundary or deliberate gap in the approved design? Artwork owner identifies intended geometry
Printed candidate P 1 Does the visible sliver reproduce that geometry? Printer locates observation on identified output
Proposed compensation Was the relevant trap applied and is it suitable? Prepress provider confirms process-specific treatment

Leave numeric width and ink behavior unassigned until the responsible prepress source supplies them. A revised trapping choice should remain tied to the output file and the named boundary. It does not change the approved color target, close every finish-mask issue or replace a representative print review.

Download this article’s project record (CSV). The record includes field definitions, labeled teaching examples and a blank project row. Add source evidence and the details of your actual project.

For a sourcing discussion, send the intended adjacent objects, located output view and the prepress question. Packrivo coordinates supplier questions; the responsible technical or commercial parties confirm the actual method, configuration and terms.

Keep Boundary Compensation Separate From Other Colour Decisions

The spot-plate review guide concerns which output channels belong to a job. A correct plate list does not, by itself, establish the registration treatment between their printed areas.

Likewise, approving an ink colour does not establish that adjoining objects meet cleanly in a particular print. Trapping addresses the boundary relationship, not the colour’s full reproducibility, a finish mask or a complete print-quality result.

For an actual package, the designer and prepress provider should determine the suitable compensation within the agreed output process. Packrivo can coordinate the intended design and supplier questions, but does not prescribe trap widths, control a press or certify registration through project coordination.

A trap is a deliberate, limited overlap at a relevant boundary. Establish the intended geometry and output before treating a white line as missing artwork or enlarging the design.

Source scope: Adobe’s two linked public English-language InDesign guidance pages were accessed on 16 October 2026. Update labels may differ by regional page; no common publication or update date is asserted here. Their explanations support the compensation principle and workflow dependence; software settings are not a packaging specification. No actual print, measured registration displacement, trap dimension or completed production result is established.

title: Barcode Bar-Width Reduction and Correct Source Data
html:
A barcode can encode the intended data while printing changes the widths of its bars and spaces. Source-data validation and printed geometry are separate questions.

For a gift brand placing an EAN/UPC symbol on packaging, the printing process may need a properly determined bar-width adjustment. A designer should not invent that adjustment from a screen image or apply one universal reduction to every printer and stock.

Keep the data decision separate from the geometry decision

The barcode source-data guide ties the generated asset to its responsible data owner. That chain matters even when the printed bars are imperfect.

Conversely, correct decoded content does not demonstrate that the printed element widths meet the relevant requirements. A read on one device is a limited observation and cannot replace suitable verification.

Before discussing a printing correction, preserve the identity of the intended symbol and its approved data. Changing an identifier is not a solution to bar growth. Editing the human-readable text beside an unchanged symbol also cannot correct either encoded data or printed geometry.

This article contains no real identifier, scannable symbol or production barcode asset.

Bar growth also consumes neighbouring space

Consider an invented one-dimensional pattern with a black bar of width w and a neighbouring white space of width s. Assume, only for this simple geometric example, that each adjacent black boundary advances into the space by the same positive amount d.

If a bar’s two boundaries both move outward by d, its width becomes w + 2d. If the two bars beside a space each advance into it by d, that space becomes s – 2d, while it remains open.

The assumed change therefore affects both black and white elements. Comparing the black bars alone can miss the narrowing spaces between them.

These expressions are original idealized geometry, not a model calibrated to any printing process. The assumption excludes uneven edges, directional distortion and other defects. It cannot predict a verifier grade or establish a suitable adjustment.

No numeric value for d is assigned. If the boundaries no longer leave an open space, the simple separated-element picture also ceases to describe that state.

Process compensation needs process evidence

GS1’s current General Specifications, Release 26.0, ratified January 2026, discusses barcode master-image production in section 5.12.4.2. Its EAN/UPC wet-ink context distinguishes bar gain from bar loss and describes bar-width adjustment determined for the particular reproduction conditions.

Where gain calls for a narrower master-image bar, the adjustment is described as bar-width reduction. The less common opposite correction addresses loss. The relevant selection also relates to the chosen X-dimension.

Those distinctions do not provide a reduction setting for this brand. The printer and barcode specialist need applicable production evidence rather than an arbitrary percentage chosen to make the screen version look thin.

Keep compensation within the responsible generation and printing workflow. Repeatedly shrinking the whole barcode image changes more than bar boundaries and is not equivalent to a controlled bar-width adjustment.

A nominally identical file can enter a different process

Suppose an invented gift sleeve retains the same approved data and placement, but the printer proposes a different stock or printing route. The data chain may remain unchanged while the earlier geometry compensation needs review.

A compensation determined for another press and substrate cannot be assumed correct because both outputs carry the same product identifier. The new production conditions require the responsible provider’s assessment.

Similarly, a proof and the production run may represent different reproduction conditions. Identify what the proof can demonstrate and keep any remaining production-quality question open.

This hypothetical change has no measured bar gain, required adjustment or verification result. It locates the reason to ask whether the earlier process evidence remains applicable.

Request process evidence without changing approved barcode data

A useful response identifies the affected generated asset, production route and proposed compensation together. Keep the exact approved data with its owner; the public worksheet uses only fictional references and deliberately contains no identifier or scannable symbol.

For an invented stock change from SUB-A to SUB-B, retain the previous compensation as history and mark applicability to SUB-B unconfirmed. Ask the printer or barcode specialist for the relevant production assessment and the correctly generated replacement asset if an adjustment is required. Do not enter a guessed numeric d or copy an arbitrary reduction percentage into the worksheet. The symbolic w+2 d and s−2 d expressions explain why both elements matter; they are not compensation settings.

Download this article’s project record (CSV). It includes field definitions, clearly hypothetical teaching rows and a blank actual-project row. Keep actual source evidence and unresolved fields with the record.

For a sourcing discussion, send the affected artwork reference, substrate/process change and the provider evidence still missing. Packrivo coordinates supplier questions; the responsible technical or commercial parties confirm the actual method, configuration and terms.

Keep Quiet Zones and finished placement in their own scope

Bar-width adjustment does not reserve an adequate clear margin around the symbol. Nor does it prevent a fold, seam or coating from affecting the finished presentation.

The finished retail-barcode proof guide addresses those package relationships. Retain them alongside the geometry question rather than treating one correctly adjusted element as approval of the complete printed symbol.

Ask the printer to identify the proposed process compensation and the evidence appropriate to the actual output. Ask the identifier owner to retain the approved data. Ask the relevant verification provider to assess the intended printed candidate within the applicable scope.

Packrivo can coordinate those inputs. It does not supply a universal bar-width-reduction recipe or certify a symbol from an illustrative diagram.

Source scope: Checked 11 October 2026. GS1 Release 26.0 section 5.12.4.2 was available through the official GS1 Austria PDF’s indexed public text. Direct reading returned a tool content-length restriction; the entire 579-page document was not read. The geometry is hypothetical and unscaled, with no actual bar gain, valid symbol, reduction setting or grade.

title: Two Regular Print Patterns Can Create a New Visible Pattern
html:
An unwanted ripple in a printed image is not always missing image resolution. Two regular structures can interact and produce a larger visible pattern that was absent from either structure alone. This is a moire concern.

For packaging with fine stripes, textiles or a previously screened image, the useful question is whether regular detail in the artwork interacts with the reproduction screen. Increasing a file’s pixel count without identifying that relationship may leave the concern unresolved.

Separate the intended pattern from the reproduction pattern

A design may intentionally contain repeated fine lines or dots. A screened printing process also introduces a structure used to reproduce tone. Their spacing and orientation can interact.

The resulting larger pattern is different from the individual lines or dots the designer intended. An apparently broad band can arise from the changing alignment of finer structures across an area.

This explains a possible mechanism, not the cause of every visible band. Actual print evidence can involve other defects, while digital resampling and screen display can introduce their own pattern concerns.

Identify where the observation was made: a source image, a resized screen preview, a PDF or an actual print. These are different stages, and a pattern visible at one stage cannot automatically be assigned to the press.

Follow an invented striped-panel example

Suppose a gift-box lid uses a fine diagonal stripe background. The designer’s intended repeated structure is part of the artwork. The printer proposes a reproduction process with its own regular screen.

Imagine placing two transparent regular line patterns over one another. Small changes in their relative angle or spacing can change the larger pattern you see. That tabletop analogy makes the interaction visible without defining a production screen setting.

An accompanying AI illustration is only an invented overlay. It is not the actual lid artwork, a simulated press result or proof that the chosen process will produce moire.

The appropriate next discussion concerns the actual stripe pattern at final size and the printer’s reproduction method. A printer may propose changes to the artwork or production treatment, but the accepted solution needs evidence for that specific combination.

A previously screened image can bring a pattern with it

A scanned printed picture may retain the earlier reproduction pattern. Sending that picture through another regular screening stage can introduce a second structure rather than starting from an unscreened original.

Where authorized, obtaining the original image can therefore answer a different need from enlarging the scanned version. A file can have many pixels while still carrying an unwanted regular source pattern.

Adobe’s public Bitmap conversion guidance explains halftone-screen settings and warns about moire when a screened image is printed using a halftone printer. This is a versioned software explanation, not a universal packaging-screen prescription.

Its discussion of screen frequency and angle also shows why those properties deserve separate identities. Do not copy a familiar angle or frequency into a packaging brief without the selected printer’s requirements.

Resolution and screening remain different questions

The placed-image resolution guide relates available pixels to printed size. That calculation remains useful, but it does not identify interference between regular patterns.

A source can have adequate effective resolution for a stated workflow and still contain problematic periodic detail. Conversely, a soft image may have a resolution concern without the repeated structure needed for this moire mechanism.

Ask the designer to preserve the final-size crop in the comparison. Changing the physical scale changes the pattern spacing presented to the reproduction process. A cropped view enlarged to another size is not an unchanged pattern condition.

If a screen preview changes as the reviewer zooms, record that observation instead of interpreting one screenshot as a physical print result. The output comparison needs the appropriate specimen and scope.

Give the printer a located interaction to assess

Provide the actual file, the affected area and the intended placement size. Identify whether the source already contains a reproduction screen or deliberate repeated artwork. Ask what evidence addresses that combination under the proposed printing conditions.

The packaging PDF preflight guide helps define technical file checks. A clean general preflight report does not establish that every pattern will reproduce as intended; the chosen profile may not examine this interaction.

When a correction is proposed, retain the new source and final-size comparison. Avoid treating a higher pixel count, a different filename or a clean PDF export as proof that the visible concern is resolved.

Packrivo can coordinate the affected artwork and printer’s questions. The actual design and reproduction combination determines the evidence needed. No screen angle, line frequency or print approval is specified by this conceptual example.

Source scope: Checked 11 October 2026. Adobe’s public Bitmap conversion page was updated 23 February 2026. The cited explanation concerns its software and halftone interaction; it does not prescribe press settings for the invented lid. No actual artwork, screen, print or moire correction was evaluated here.

Fine intervals can share a much larger alignment period

Use abstract length units, not millimetres, pixels or line-screen settings. Pattern A has marks every 5 units and pattern B every 6 units, both starting at zero. Their first positive shared alignment is 30 units: six A intervals and five B intervals. This is an integer-spacing model, not a simulated press result.

ALIGNMENT_MODEL BOTH_PATTERNS start at COMMON_ZERO

The example explains why a larger repeated relationship can arise from finer repeated structures. It does not predict a visible moire period for a particular image, viewing system or printing process. Actual angle, screening, sampling and final-size artwork remain unspecified.

Increasing file pixel count does not change those declared source intervals by itself. If a proposal rescales or replaces the original pattern, that is a different input, and its physical placement must be retained in the comparison. A zoom-dependent screen observation also remains a screen observation.

Adobe’s Bitmap guidance warns of possible rescreening moire in its stated context; it does not say every pair of patterns must show it. No 45° or other universal angle is prescribed here. Ask the designer and printer which source structure, output treatment and final-size evidence address the actual concern before calling it resolved.
