The ISO 12040:1997 catalogue entry identifies a standard for assessing the lightfastness of prints and printing inks using filtered xenon-arc light. ISO lists the March 1997 edition as published and last reviewed and confirmed in 2022.

Its public catalogue information establishes that print lightfastness has a distinct technical assessment framework. The complete method is not freely available from that listing, and the listing alone does not provide testing conditions, approval thresholds or predictions for retail packaging.

For a proposed display sleeve, a responsible printing or material specialist should establish whether suitable exposure evidence exists for the relevant print system and construction.

An ink-related result obtained on another substrate cannot automatically establish the behaviour of a finished sleeve with a different coating or lamination. A result for an uncoated laboratory print does not necessarily answer what happens to a finished, converted package.

The exposure conditions and the criterion used to evaluate colour change also matter. A controlled accelerated-exposure result is evidence under its declared conditions, not an automatic conversion into months or years of acceptable appearance in a particular shop.

The brand’s practical requirement should come first: does the sleeve need to maintain a close colour relationship with another package throughout an extended display period, or is the principal requirement its appearance during initial presentation and unboxing?

Those two uses may justify different sourcing discussions. Neither creates a universal acceptable fading percentage or required lightfastness grade.

Initial Colour Accuracy Cannot Substitute for Exposure Durability

A printer can supply a candidate that matches the physical reference closely at the initial review stage. That is useful evidence for the initial appearance decision.

It does not establish that the printed colour will remain within the same visual relationship after exposure.

Likewise, choosing a tighter Delta E tolerance does not establish the future durability of the colourant. A colour-difference calculation compares specified colour data; it does not, by itself, describe how those data may change after light exposure.

This is why the physical colour reference approval process and an exposure-durability review have different purposes. The first establishes what the printed package should look like when assessed against its agreed reference. The second considers whether that intended appearance is suitable for the package’s expected exposure history.

A similar distinction applies to uneven appearance on a newly formed printed panel. That question belongs to the formed solid-panel review before any exposure-related explanation is assumed.

If a gift sleeve will be displayed for extended periods, the brand can ask the proposed printer to identify the ink, substrate and finish combination and explain what relevant durability evidence can be provided. The brand can also reconsider the intended display arrangement where sustained colour appearance matters.

Reducing exposure may reduce an exposure-related risk, but no particular UV filter, laminate, pigment family or display adjustment should be treated as an unconditional guarantee.

The Buying Decision Depends on the Expected Display

A candle carton opened shortly after delivery and a decorative gift package kept in a shop window may have very different exposure histories.

Both need an acceptable initial print appearance. Only the second necessarily raises a prominent question about appearance over sustained display, although exposure may matter in other distribution and use environments as well.

When a print looks different after display, return the relevant physical pieces to the same agreed viewing condition before deciding what the observation means.

If the difference disappears, the immediate problem may concern viewing conditions rather than a lasting change to the print.

If a difference persists, retain the possibility of exposure-induced change while keeping alternative material, production, storage and surface explanations open. A specialist assessment may be necessary where identifying the mechanism matters to the decision.

Packrivo can help coordinate sourcing questions about proposed ink systems, substrates, finishes, display expectations and evidence from a printing partner. Packrivo does not claim to perform lightfastness testing or certify a package’s display lifetime. Any specific technical method, result or acceptance requirement must be established by the responsible parties.

A colour approved under a viewing light is an initial appearance decision. A colour expected to withstand continuing exposure is a separate material-durability decision.

Record both histories before treating a retained piece as the baseline

For invented specimens S1 and R1 from nominal print batch PB-H, plan S1 for display and R1 for retention away from that display light. Later comparison C1 puts both under the same agreed light L1. No initial equality, exposure history or physical difference has actually been verified.

Record Planned identity/state Open evidence
Initial PB-H S1 and R1 Actual initial comparability
S1 Display history Light, storage, handling and surface history
R1 Retained history Conditions and possible aging; not assumed unchanged
C1 Both together under L1 Actual difference and relevant viewing conditions

Keep print construction, ink/substrate/finish, initial references and both actual histories attached. A retained label is a role, not proof that the specimen never aged. If the pieces were different at the beginning, a later mismatch cannot be attributed to display exposure alone.

The neutral symbols depict no fading or measured color difference. Use the same agreed viewing condition for the later physical comparison while keeping alternative production, handling and material explanations open. The CSV supplies no exposure hours, lux dose, Delta E, grade, accelerated-test conversion or acceptable display lifetime. A persistent difference would prompt the appropriate print/material investigation, not automatically a darker reprint.

Download the packaging print lightfastness record (.csv). HYPOTHETICAL rows are invented examples. Use ACTUAL_BLANK for permitted project inputs; replace that row label only when recording actual facts. Empty evidence, observation and date fields mean unknown or not performed, never acceptance. Keep checkpoints and revisions separate.

Send actual initial references, both specimen histories and the same-light comparison before seeking construction-specific durability evidence. Packrivo coordinates independent suppliers. These records establish no supplier offer, service availability or MOQ exception; its published baseline is 500 pieces per product/design.

title: Thin Packaging Pieces Can Cling Without an Adhesive Joint
html:
When a loose piece of packaging film follows another sheet during separation, the problem is not necessarily adhesive tack. Contact and separation can leave insulating surfaces electrically charged, allowing electrostatic attraction to influence lightweight pieces even when no adhesive joint was intended.

For a jewellery, candle or gift brand, the first decision is whether the disputed contact actually contains an adhesive interface. If it does not, requesting a stronger or weaker adhesive may address a mechanism that was never present.

Electrostatic attraction is one plausible explanation. Cling alone does not prove that either sheet is charged, identify a charge polarity or rule out ink/coating blocking, unintended adhesive contact or a mechanical snag.

Electrostatic Attraction Does Not Require an Adhesive Film

Many flexible packaging films are electrical insulators. Charge generated through contact, friction and separation may remain on their surfaces rather than dissipating immediately.

Simco-Ion’s web-handling and converting overview identifies friction and material separation as sources of electrostatic charge. It also describes sheet attraction, sticking and handling difficulties during converting.

A lightweight piece may move toward or remain close to another surface under electrostatic attraction. The force is electrical rather than the result of a deliberately applied pressure-sensitive or curing adhesive.

This distinction is not merely theoretical. Simco-Ion’s separate static-charging explanation describes industrial electrostatic pinning, in which controlled charge is used to hold materials together temporarily.

Controlled industrial pinning and unwanted cling during packaging handling are different situations. The manufacturer’s description demonstrates a possible physical mechanism, not a measured explanation for an unidentified packaging pair.

Nor does attraction establish that the two surfaces carry equal and opposite charges.

A charged surface can attract an initially neutral material through electrical polarization. OpenStax’s University Physics Volume 2, Section 5.2 explains how the charge distribution within a neutral material can shift in response to a nearby charged object.

Therefore, observing two films attract does not justify assigning a positive charge to one and a negative charge to the other.

The actual materials, charge state and competing physical interactions remain unknown until appropriately investigated.

Sticking, Blocking and Snagging Are Different Physical Questions

Several mechanisms can produce a similar complaint: two packaging pieces are difficult to separate, or one follows the other unexpectedly.

Electrostatic attraction involves electrical forces between surfaces. An adhesive coating is not required. The separation and handling history of the actual material pair become relevant, but the movement itself does not confirm charge.

Ink or coating blocking involves adjacent finished surfaces sticking together through an ink or coating film. This can occur in printing and coating operations, particularly where the material has not reached an appropriate setting or drying state for subsequent contact and stacking.

A corresponding printed deposit may suggest ink setoff. Sheets sticking through a coating film can instead raise a blocking question. Absence of a visible coloured deposit does not, by itself, exclude coating-related adhesion.

Adhesive contact involves a specified or unintended adhesive interface. A pressure-sensitive label, exposed tape edge or other adhesive-bearing construction needs its actual contacting faces identified.

If an adhesive is intentionally present, its contact and release behaviour require review. If the drawing specifies no adhesive at the disputed face, the buyer should not assume that changing adhesive tack is the correct response.

Mechanical snagging involves physical interference. A film edge may catch under a fold, overlap or cut feature and travel with the adjacent piece.

That can resemble cling even though the reason is geometric restraint rather than electrostatic attraction.

The important distinction is not how the complaint is casually described. It is whether the parts are being held by an electrical force, a coating or adhesive film, or a physical obstruction.

More than one mechanism may be present.

A Hypothetical Loose Film Liner Follows Another Sheet

Consider an entirely hypothetical gift-packaging project involving a loose, thin protective film liner placed against another flat packaging sheet.

The converter confirms that the disputed contacting faces have no intended adhesive layer or adhesive joint.

During separation, the loose liner follows the neighbouring sheet instead of falling away immediately.

This is an invented observation for explanation only. No actual film was handled, no charge was measured and no separation force was recorded.

Electrostatic attraction is a plausible mechanism. The materials have been in contact and are separating, a situation in which charge generation can occur.

Because the loose liner is lightweight, electrical attraction could be relevant to its movement without forming an adhesive bond.

But the described movement remains insufficient for diagnosis.

It does not establish that charge was generated by the particular materials, that either surface carried a particular polarity, or that electrostatic attraction was the dominant force.

The original construction also needs review for possible coatings, exposed adhesive from an adjacent feature or a cut edge that could catch during separation.

Confirming that no adhesive was specified is not equivalent to proving that every other surface interaction is absent.

Suppose the next proposed liner uses a different film or surface finish. Even if the following motion changes, that observation cannot automatically be attributed to electrostatics. The modified material may also differ in flexibility, coating, surface interaction or handling behaviour.

No effective neutralization treatment, improved material or successful correction is assumed in this example.

The Original Interface Determines the Next Investigation

A useful supplier investigation begins with the particular two faces that were together.

For the hypothetical liner, the buyer needs the film construction and the opposing sheet construction identified, including which surfaces actually meet. The converter should clarify whether those faces carry printing, coating, release treatment or an intended adhesive.

The separation sequence matters as well.

Identify whether the liner follows another sheet as the faces part, whether an edge remains physically engaged, and whether any deposited material, tacky region or surface change is visible.

These observations help route the technical question. They are not substitutes for charge measurement or material analysis.

Where the faces are unbonded and no specific mechanical catch or coating-related explanation has been established, the converter can review whether electrostatic charging during the actual cutting, stacking, handling or separation process warrants further investigation.

If ink or coating blocking is suspected, the relevant printing or coating process becomes the next subject of review.

If an adhesive-bearing face is actually involved, investigate that specified construction. For example, separating a pressure-sensitive label from its backing is a different question, addressed in the label-liner release guide.

If a component catches at an identified physical feature, the investigation should focus on the geometry and movement of that contact. A sliding tray catching an internal seam, for instance, belongs to the separate sleeve seam travel investigation.

The next comparison should retain identifiable material faces and handling conditions. If the material, coating, orientation or separation process changes, identify the changed configuration rather than treating the result as proof of one mechanism.

No universal humidity setting, static-control device or adhesive substitution follows from the original cling observation. Any appropriate technical assessment or proposed process treatment requires the responsible converter or specialist to establish its scope for the actual materials.

Decide Whether an Adhesive Change Is Relevant at All

The practical outcome is a better-directed supplier question.

For two thin packaging pieces with no intended adhesive interface, unexpected following or sticking should not automatically become a request to adjust adhesive strength.

Electrostatic attraction is a credible physical possibility, but not a diagnosis. Ink/coating blocking, actual adhesive contact and mechanical snagging must remain separate explanations until the relevant evidence distinguishes them.

Packrivo can coordinate the packaging construction details, sourcing questions and subsequent sample-review discussion. It does not measure electrostatic charge, certify material performance or guarantee a treatment.

Before changing adhesive, establish whether the pieces were ever supposed to be joined by adhesive. That decision prevents an unbonded film-handling question from being sent down the wrong technical route.

Source and scope note — checked October 10, 2026: Both cited Simco-Ion pages were accessible and do not display a confirmed publication date. They are commercial explanations of industrial static charging and converting applications, not test evidence for the hypothetical liner. OpenStax’s University Physics Volume 2 was originally published October 6, 2016 and supports the general physical explanation of attraction through polarization. No actual sample, surface charge, adhesive interface or neutralization treatment was tested for this article.

Keep the nominal faces separate from a nearby adhesive edge

Keep the same invented loose film L1 and opposing sheet S1 in two path records. Their nominal contacting faces have no intended adhesive. FACE_ONLY30 separates those faces away from nearby tape edge A1. EDGE_PATH30 proposes a path passing near an exposed adhesive-bearing edge A1. Whether L1 actually touches it is unknown; no sticking result is drawn or recorded.

Hypothetical configuration Named object Relationship Input or next scope
FACE_ONLY30 L1 nominal unbonded face with S1
FACE_ONLY30 L1 proposed path AWAY_FROM_ADJACENT_A1
FACE_ONLY30 L1_S1_CONTACTING_FACES assumed NO_INTENDED_ADHESIVE
EDGE_PATH30 L1 nominal unbonded face with S1
EDGE_PATH30 L1 proposed path NEAR_EXPOSED_A1_CONTACT_UNKNOWN
EDGE_PATH30 L1_S1_CONTACTING_FACES assumed NO_INTENDED_ADHESIVE
EDGE_PATH30 A1 is ADJACENT_ADHESIVE_BEARING_EDGE
EDGE_PATH30 L1_A1_CONTACT remains UNKNOWN_NOT_SHOWN_STICKING
CONTACT30 NO_DESIGNED_L1_S1_ADHESIVE does not prove NO_ADJACENT_ADHESIVE_ENCOUNTER
CONTACT30 FOLLOWING_MOTION does not assign STATIC_POLARITY_OR_EXCLUDE_BLOCKING_SNAGGING

The absence of a designed adhesive joint between L1 and S1 does not establish that every possible travel path avoids other adhesive-bearing features. An actual contact at A1 would concern a different interface from the unbonded flat faces. Ask for the located path and component construction rather than changing an unspecified adhesive on the nominal face.

If no A1 contact is established, the observation still does not prove electrostatics. Coating interaction, mechanical engagement and electrical attraction remain different questions. The purpose of the path map is to state which interface an offered explanation concerns, not to identify charge from appearance. An intended-face drawing alone cannot settle an undocumented edge encounter.

Preserve available handling evidence without rubbing, charging, heating or treating a sample to manufacture an explanation. A changed path may also change overlap or restraint, so a difference after revision is not automatically an electrical diagnosis. The converter or relevant specialist must define any actual investigation. Industrial pinning demonstrates a possible mechanism, not the cause of this hypothetical pair or a suitable treatment.

Download the loose film contact path adjacent adhesive edge record (.csv). It includes the original table fields and scenarios alongside the added relationships. HYPOTHETICAL rows are editorial examples or required review scopes, not actual records. Actual quantity, configuration, component and file identities, materials, process, specification, copy, method, condition, observation, owner, decision, evidence and dates are blank. ACTUAL_BLANK is a separate empty starting row; enter permitted project evidence before using an actual record. A blank means unknown.

Use the Label Liner Release vs Adhesion: Review Both Interfaces for its separate question.

Source scope checked 17 October 2026: Simco-Ion industrial charging/converting explanations and OpenStax polarization support possible attraction without an adhesive film or opposite net charges on both pieces. They do not diagnose cling, prove permanent adhesion or prescribe humidity, meters, neutralizers or adhesive changes. The added configurations and calculations are hypothetical, with actual evidence and decisions pending.

Discuss this packaging specification with Packrivo. We coordinate independent suppliers. MOQ: 500 pieces per product/design; illustrative quantities are not production offers. Confirm materials, samples, price and timing for your project.

title: Sliding Gift Boxes: Starting and Moving Resistance
html:
A sliding gift box that takes a firm first pull but then moves smoothly presents a different question from one that becomes harder to move halfway through its travel. The first pattern may involve resistance before sliding begins. The second may involve sliding friction, changing contact pressure or a local obstruction.

Neither pattern can be explained by visible clearance alone.

For a jewellery drawer, candle presentation sleeve or small gift tray, the useful first distinction is between starting resistance and resistance during movement. Identify the surfaces actually meeting, how they are pressed together and when the difficulty occurs before requesting a larger sleeve or an anti-scuff finish.

Starting resistance is not the same as sliding resistance

When two surfaces are pressed together but are not moving relative to each other, static friction can oppose an attempted movement. That resistance responds to the applied force up to a limiting value.

Once the surfaces slide relative to each other, kinetic friction becomes relevant.

An elementary friction model expresses the distinction using two relationships:

  • Static friction before movement: fₛ ≤ μₛN

  • Kinetic friction during sliding: fₖ ≈ μₖN

Here, N represents the normal contact force pressing the two surfaces together. The coefficients μₛ and μₖ describe the relevant contact pair under stated conditions. The limiting static resistance in the simple model is μₛN; static friction does not remain at that maximum throughout every stationary moment.

The kinetic relationship is also an approximation for interfaces whose friction behaves simply, not a universal description of every surface.

OpenStax’s University Physics Volume 1, Section 6.2, published September 19, 2016, explains these relationships as an empirical model.

The equations establish an important distinction for packaging buyers: a friction coefficient is not itself a pull force. Resistance depends on both the contacting surfaces and the normal forces acting between them.

For a drawer sleeve, the normal force pressing a sidewall against the tray is not necessarily equal to the weight of the product inside. Wall deformation, assembly fit and support conditions can also affect that contact.

Nor should a buyer assume that starting friction always exceeds sliding friction for every material pair and movement condition. A higher starting resistance followed by easier travel is one possible behavior, not a guaranteed feature of every package.

Friction belongs to a contact pair under stated conditions

A finish cannot be described as having one universally applicable friction value.

Consider the inside lining of a paperboard sleeve meeting the printed wrap of its tray. That is a different contact pair from a plastic film sliding against itself. Changing either face can change the interaction.

The public scope of ASTM D1894-24, Standard Test Method for Static and Kinetic Coefficients of Friction of Plastic Film and Sheeting, distinguishes starting and sliding friction for plastic film and sheeting against itself or another specified substance under stated conditions.

Its publicly accessible significance-and-use information also identifies motion conditions, surface condition and material age as factors relevant to some film and sheet measurements.

Westpak’s material-analysis service description likewise lists starting and sliding coefficients separately for plastic film and sheeting.

These sources support treating the two measurements as different quantities. They do not establish a standard opening-force test for a completed rigid paperboard drawer.

A film coefficient supplied for one pairing should therefore not be treated as the opening force of a finished sleeve-and-tray assembly. Even when a relevant surface measurement is available, the assembly may have multiple contacts, changing normal forces, deformation and other sources of resistance.

A meaningful comparison must identify which finished faces touch, their condition, the loading arrangement and the movement conditions. A different coating, board construction or opposing face changes the comparison rather than simply changing a material name.

A sleeve can change its contact pressure during travel

A drawer is not necessarily a rigid block moving across one unchanging flat surface.

A paperboard sleeve can flex when a loaded tray enters or leaves it. A sidewall may press against the tray wrap in one position and release some of that contact farther along the opening path. The loaded tray itself may change shape or alignment.

These are possible mechanical responses, not established characteristics of a particular Packrivo package.

The distinction matters because visible space and normal contact force describe different things.

A nominal gap at the sleeve mouth does not establish the contact conditions farther inside. Similarly, finding that one measured dimension has sufficient clearance does not prove that the assembled drawer will move with little resistance.

If two surfaces do not touch, their interface cannot contribute sliding friction at that location. But a clear-looking region does not rule out contact at an adjacent wall, folded edge or seam.

The mechanical questions are different:

A contact surface may resist the first movement without a hard geometric obstruction. An internal overlap may cause a localized catch only after the drawer reaches it. A flexible wall may progressively increase contact pressure while the tray moves.

All three can produce a complaint that the drawer feels tight, but they do not justify the same design change.

Packrivo’s sleeve seam travel guide addresses the separate task of locating possible seam interference. A contact-location observation is useful, but it does not by itself determine friction coefficients or quantify sliding resistance.

A hypothetical starting peak does not establish the cause

Consider an entirely hypothetical jewellery drawer containing a pendant on a fitted holder and an information card.

The tray has a ribbon pull, and the finished sleeve and tray are assembled in their intended orientation.

Imagine that a properly supported opening action produces the following qualitative response:

At first, the tray remains stationary while the applied pull increases. There is a relatively high resistance immediately before movement begins. Once the tray starts moving, the resistance falls to a lower, fairly even level through the remaining travel.

This is an invented, schematic force pattern. It is not a measurement, an estimated force, a Packrivo test or a claim that the package will behave this way.

A friction-dominated start is one possible explanation for such a pattern. Contact that has remained stationary can resist the initial movement differently from contact that is already sliding.

But the shape alone does not prove that explanation.

A mechanical catch, temporary deformation or another release event could also produce an apparent starting peak. A force trace without the matching movement and contact context is not a definitive diagnosis.

Now imagine a different response from the same hypothetical packaging format.

The drawer begins moving easily but becomes harder to pull near the middle, then moves more freely after passing that region.

That pattern raises questions about changing contact geometry, sleeve deformation or a localized obstruction. It should not automatically be labelled high static friction, because the tray was already moving when the difficulty developed.

The two hypothetical responses have different decision implications. One directs attention toward the contact pair and conditions immediately before movement. The other directs attention toward what changes along the travel path.

Neither response supports a universal opening-force limit, a particular friction coefficient or an automatic material substitution.

Separate the starting grip from the force needed to start sliding

Before interpreting resistance, establish whether the buyer is actually observing resistance of the moving assembly.

A ribbon that is difficult to grasp can make a box feel hard to open even when the tray itself is not particularly resistant. A flexible pull may change the hand position or loading direction. An attachment may move or deform before the tray starts sliding.

Those are pull-design and attachment questions.

The drawer-pull attachment guide addresses the availability of the starting grip, the hidden attachment and the loaded opening action.

Once the intended grip and attachment are understood, the remaining question is whether resistance comes from the tray-to-sleeve interaction and how it changes between starting and continued movement.

This separation avoids treating a ribbon revision as proof that sleeve friction has changed. It also avoids blaming the ribbon simply because the first movement requires more effort.

Match the next investigation to the movement pattern

For a complaint concentrated at the first movement, the useful technical request is to review the identified tray-to-sleeve contact pair and the conditions under which movement begins.

That includes the finished contacting surfaces, loaded configuration, assembly orientation, starting condition and intended pull direction. If quantitative opening resistance matters, the responsible technical party must define an appropriate assembled-package evaluation rather than transferring a flat-film coefficient into an unsupported drawer-force prediction.

For resistance concentrated partway through travel, investigate what changes at that position. A seam, folded edge, shifted holder or flexing wall can alter the local contact condition. Enlarging the complete sleeve before identifying the interface may change the overall fit without addressing the specific mechanism.

For a visible mark noticed after sliding, keep the appearance observation separate from the force question. The surface-scuff observation guide addresses how to document a mark and its preceding action. A scuff does not reveal the resistance that occurred or prove that an anti-scuff finish will reduce opening effort.

If two material or construction proposals are to be compared, the basis must remain identifiable. The loaded contents, finished geometry, supported opening orientation, pull direction, starting dwell and movement conditions all affect what a comparison means.

Where geometry or loading changes along with the surface, the result represents a changed assembly, not a friction-only comparison.

A supplier may propose a suitable way to evaluate starting and travelling resistance on the actual package. The measurement method, relevant conditions and functional criteria still require project-specific agreement. This article does not prescribe an improvised ASTM test or a numerical pass threshold.

Decide whether the problem begins at rest or develops in motion

The practical decision is not simply whether the drawer feels tight.

If the intended grip is unavailable or its attachment is unresolved, address that construction first.

If the grip works and the loaded tray shows difficulty mainly before movement, investigate starting resistance and the contacting surfaces under their actual conditions.

If resistance increases after movement begins, examine changing contact, deformation and local interference along the travel path.

Only then can a proposed clearance or surface change be connected to a defined problem.

Packrivo can coordinate these distinctions within the packaging brief, supplier questions and sample-review discussion. It does not establish friction performance, certify a material or guarantee a particular opening effort.

Starting a drawer and keeping it moving are separate friction questions. A sensible packaging decision preserves that distinction before changing the structure or finish.

Source and scope note — checked October 10, 2026: ASTM D1894-24 is the active edition; its public catalogue lists December 16, 2024 as the last-update date. Only the publicly available scope and significance-and-use material were consulted, not the paid seven-page method. Westpak’s accessible material-analysis and coefficient-of-friction service pages have no confirmed publication date. OpenStax’s University Physics Volume 1 was published September 19, 2016 and provides the general approximate friction model. None of these sources supplies a measured force, friction coefficient or acceptance criterion for the hypothetical paperboard drawer described here.

Attach the observation to the movement stage

For invented sleeve S-H and tray T-H, use T0 before motion, T1 first movement, T2 mid travel and T3 exit as record headings. They are planned checkpoints, not an observed opening sequence. The icons depict position only, without a loaded specimen or a force trace.

Stage Located question Do not infer
T0 before motion Starting grip, support and contact A friction coefficient from feel
T1 first movement What first moves or deforms? Starting peak proves one cause
T2 mid travel Where does the interaction change? All moving resistance is static friction
T3 exit Final contacts and support Free exit proves every earlier stage accepted

If difficulty begins after motion, retain the actual position and contact question rather than labelling the whole event high starting friction. If the pull changes shape before the tray moves, keep that attachment/grip observation separate. These are routing questions, not diagnoses.

Define the actual loaded configuration, supported action, contact pair, conditions and any quantitative method with the responsible party. Do not import a plastic-film coefficient into a paperboard drawer-force field. The CSV leaves force in newtons, position in millimetres, method and observations blank; no universal force limit, elapsed-time rule or successful operation is invented.

Download the sliding gift box friction record (.csv). HYPOTHETICAL rows are invented examples. Use ACTUAL_BLANK for permitted project inputs; replace that row label only when recording actual facts. Empty evidence, observation and date fields mean unknown or not performed, never acceptance. Keep checkpoints and revisions separate.

Send the located stage, actual loaded contact configuration and supported action before requesting a surface, clearance or quantitative evaluation change. Packrivo coordinates independent suppliers. These records establish no supplier offer, service availability or MOQ exception; its published baseline is 500 pieces per product/design.

title: Care Card Paper Opacity and Reverse Show-Through
html:
If a dark graphic printed on the back of a care card appears as a faint shadow through its pale front, the answer is not necessarily darker front artwork or a different white paper.

For an Informational insert card, send both printed faces, the proposed paper grade and the actual backing used during the review. The product concept does not establish opacity or remove the need to compare the finished two-sided proof.

The first question is whether the proposed sheet hides its reverse-side printing well enough for the way the card will be used.

Reverse-side show-through can be an optical effect. The ink may remain on the side where it was printed while its image still affects what someone sees from the other side. A screen proof cannot establish how much of that image will be visible through the actual paper.

For a jewellery, candle or gift brand choosing a two-sided card, that distinction changes the decision: review the paper’s opacity, the relationship between front and back artwork, and the backing against which the finished card will be seen before changing the front colour.

Reverse-Side Printing Can Be Visible Without Ink Reaching the Front

Paper is not necessarily a complete optical barrier.

When a printed sheet is viewed under reflected light, some light can enter and scatter within the paper. The printing and background on its far side can influence the light returning toward the viewer.

If the sheet does not sufficiently conceal a dense reverse-side graphic, a faint version of that graphic may become visible through a lighter area on the front.

This is optical show-through. It does not, by itself, demonstrate that ink has travelled through the sheet.

That matters because three different mechanisms can produce superficially similar complaints.

Optical show-through concerns the visibility of printing through the paper even when the printed ink remains on its intended side.

Ink strike-through involves ink penetrating the paper structure sufficiently to affect its opposite side. This is a physical ink-and-substrate question, not simply a lack of optical hiding.

Setoff involves ink transferring by contact to another sheet or surface. An image on the back of an adjacent sheet after stacking therefore raises a different question from seeing a graphic through the same sheet.

A visible shadow cannot establish which mechanism occurred. If ink penetration or surface transfer is suspected, the printer needs to investigate the physical evidence and the relevant printing process rather than classify the problem from a photograph alone.

For a proposed card that shows a faint outline aligned with its own reverse artwork, however, opacity is a legitimate question to investigate before assuming a wet-ink defect.

Whiteness and Opacity Describe Different Paper Properties

A sheet can look bright and clean without concealing everything printed behind it.

Holmen’s General Technical Information separates opacity from CIE whiteness, ISO brightness and colour.

Its opacity section describes a measurement principle that compares reflectance from one sheet over a black background with reflectance from an opaque stack of paperboard samples. The result is expressed as a percentage.

The principle concerns how much the material hides what is behind it.

Whiteness describes the visual impression of a near-white surface. ISO brightness concerns blue-region reflectance. Neither measurement is interchangeable with opacity.

This means choosing a paper simply because its sample looks whiter does not establish that it will better conceal reverse-side printing.

It also means a supplier’s opacity figure should not be treated as a completed readability assessment for a particular care card.

The public description of ISO 2471:2008 identifies a diffuse-reflectance method for determining paper-backing opacity. The fourth edition was published in December 2008 and was last confirmed in 2023.

The public scope permits certain papers containing fluorescent whitening agents when the specified ultraviolet adjustment is made. It excludes coloured papers or boards incorporating fluorescent dyes or pigments.

Those distinctions matter when interpreting an actual supplier’s reported method. The public abstract does not give a universal minimum opacity for two-sided care cards, and the paid full standard was not consulted for this article.

A higher opacity value under a specified comparable method may be useful when assessing material alternatives. It still cannot guarantee that a dense reverse graphic will be unobtrusive behind the particular pale area of a finished card.

Reverse Artwork and Intended Backing Affect Visibility

A material’s opacity is only part of the finished appearance.

Consider a care card with a large dark brand mark on the reverse and a nearly unprinted ivory area on the front.

The dark mark creates a stronger visual contrast behind that pale area than a small, lightly printed line might create.

Moving or reducing the reverse mark could change the visible interference without changing the paper. Alternatively, retaining that artwork might make a different paper proposal worth investigating.

Neither change is automatically the right choice.

The backing also matters.

A care card displayed flat against the inside of a gift-box lid may not look identical to the same card held alone during unboxing. A light backing, dark backing or neighbouring material can change the amount and contrast of light returned toward the viewer.

An opaque stack of sheets is not equivalent to a single loose care card.

Before comparing samples, decide which presentation actually matters. If the customer will remove and read the card in their hand, a favourable appearance while it rests on a pale box lining cannot settle the loose-card question.

If the card is permanently mounted, the actual backing belongs in the proposed construction and its appearance review.

The useful target is not an abstract demand for perfectly opaque paper. It is sufficient concealment of the actual reverse artwork under the viewing conditions that matter to the finished product.

A Hypothetical Two-Sided Care Card

Suppose a small gift brand is developing a near-white care card.

The front contains a short set of care instructions, surrounded by generous pale space. The reverse has a dense, dark rectangular brand mark.

In the artwork file, the rectangle sits almost directly behind the palest part of the front design.

A screen proof shows each side clearly. It may confirm the artwork placement, but it cannot reproduce the optical interaction of two printed faces separated by a real paper sheet.

The brand requests a physical duplex proof using the proposed grade.

For illustration only, suppose the printer supplies that proof and the brand observes the following:

When the card is held loose under the intended reading light, a faint rectangular shape is visible in the pale front area. When the same card rests on its intended light-coloured packaging backing, the shape is less distracting.

These are invented observations for this example, not reported test results.

The brand now has a defined design question.

If customers normally receive the card loose, the favourable backed appearance does not resolve the problem. The brand still needs to judge the card in the loose viewing condition.

If the reverse rectangle can move away from the pale front area without compromising the design, the printer could prepare a comparable duplex proof with that layout change.

Keeping the proposed paper grade and front artwork unchanged would help the team investigate the effect of the reverse artwork arrangement.

If the rectangle must remain in its current position, the next useful request may instead be an alternative paper grade with relevant opacity documentation and another complete duplex proof.

A front-only print on the same proposed stock could also provide a useful visual reference. It would not replace the duplex proof, but it could help clarify how the reverse printing changes the front appearance.

None of these comparisons is an ISO opacity measurement or a diagnosis of ink penetration.

Their practical value is that the buyer can distinguish a possible artwork-layout solution from a material-selection question instead of changing several variables at once.

Choose the Change That Addresses the Visible Problem

A paper change, artwork change and backing change are different responses.

If the problem is concentrated where one dense reverse graphic overlaps a pale front panel, reconsidering that overlap may be more relevant than changing every front colour.

If the reverse design and card format must stay unchanged, a paper with different documented opacity may be worth comparing. The material supplier or printer must confirm the proposed grade, its relevant properties and its suitability for the printing process.

If the design depends on a particular backing, review the full printed arrangement against that backing. Do not assume the same appearance when the card is removed.

If the printer finds physical ink on a surface where it should not be, the investigation moves beyond opacity toward ink penetration or contact transfer, depending on the evidence.

These choices do not establish a universal preferred grammage, coating or opacity percentage. Increasing paper weight, choosing a brighter white or introducing a finish without examining the actual result would substitute a material assumption for the unresolved visual question.

The decision should be expressed through the intended finished appearance: the required front information remains readable, and reverse-side artwork does not create objectionable interference in the specified viewing arrangement.

Compare one variable in a care-card opacity review

Give the front artwork, reverse artwork and proposed grade separate references. A front-only reference, duplex proof held loose and the same duplex proof on the intended backing answer different questions. Keep the actual light, orientation and viewing arrangement with each observation.

Planned comparison Keep unchanged Question it isolates
Front-only versus duplex Grade, front artwork and viewing arrangement Does the reverse image affect this front view?
Loose versus intended backing Same duplex candidate and light Does the backing change the visible interference?
Revised reverse layout Grade and front artwork Does moving the dark object resolve the located overlap?

These are proposed comparisons, not completed findings. If the printer identifies actual deposited ink on the wrong face or on another sheet, retain that physical evidence separately. An opacity document and this visual record cannot diagnose strike-through or setoff from a photograph alone.

Download this article’s project record (CSV). The record includes field definitions, labeled teaching examples and a blank project row. Add source evidence and the details of your actual project.

For a sourcing discussion, send the two artwork faces, proposed paper grade and the actual backing/viewing question. Packrivo coordinates supplier questions; the responsible technical or commercial parties confirm the actual method, configuration and terms.

Review the Complete Two-Sided Card Before Changing Its Colour

A physical duplex proof answers something a screen image and a blank paper sample cannot: how the chosen front and reverse artwork appear together through one actual sheet.

The review should preserve the distinction between the optical visibility of reverse printing and evidence of ink physically moving to another location.

Packrivo’s guide to reviewing artwork on proposed uncoated paper covers broader artwork-element and substrate-proof questions. The narrower question here is whether the same sheet adequately conceals the reverse artwork in its intended use.

Packrivo can coordinate questions about proposed paper grades, duplex artwork, supplier documentation and the scope of physical proofs. Any technical measurements, process diagnosis or material acceptance criteria must be established with the responsible printer or material specialist.

A brighter-looking care card is not necessarily a more opaque one. Resolve the reverse-side visibility question before revising the front design to hide a symptom.

Source review: 10 October 2026. Holmen’s online technical collection is undated and describes its paperboard product context. ISO 2471:2008 is the fourth edition, published in December 2008 and confirmed in 2023. Its public description was reviewed; the paid eight-page standard was not read. Neither source establishes a measured result or universal acceptance limit for the hypothetical care card.

title: A Case GTIN and a Logistic-Unit SSCC Identify Different Kinds of Thing
html:
A case GTIN identifies a defined trade-item class. An SSCC identifies an individual logistic unit established for transport or storage. The two identifiers answer different questions, even when the goods and packaging look identical.

In a GS1 logistics workflow, two separately handled units containing the same case type need different SSCCs. Repeating the case GTIN on both units does not identify them individually. Nor does scanning an SSCC, by itself, reveal everything packed inside.

The GS1 System Architecture, version 12.0.0 (October 2024) explicitly distinguishes a trade-item class identified by a GTIN from a physical logistic unit identified by an SSCC. Its Identify, Capture and Share model also separates identification from the information associated with an identifier.

A case type can repeat across different logistic units

Consider a wholly hypothetical candle gift-box order.

TypeT is a defined, orderable case type containing six empty candle presentation boxes. Assume that TypeT has an appropriately assigned case-level GTIN. TypeT is a fictional name, not a GS1 identifier.

The packing operation creates two separate transport units:

  • UnitU1 contains four cases of TypeT.

  • UnitU2 also contains four cases of TypeT.

Both units contain the same trade-item class in the same quantity. The individual TypeT cases may legitimately carry the same case-level GTIN.

But UnitU1 and UnitU2 are different physical logistic units. Under an applicable GS1 logistic-label workflow, each needs its own unique SSCC.

If someone prints the same TypeT GTIN as the only identifying barcode for both transport units, reading that barcode cannot distinguish UnitU1 from UnitU2. The result identifies the case type, not which particular logistics unit was handled.

This does not make the repeated GTIN incorrect. GTIN reuse across physical examples of the same defined trade-item class is normal. The error is expecting that class identifier to perform the SSCC’s individual-unit role.

There is a further distinction: GS1 can identify a particular trade-item instance through a GTIN combined with a serial number. That compound trade-item identifier is still conceptually different from an SSCC identifying a logistic unit.

One physical case can have two identification roles

An outer case is not automatically either a trade item or a logistic unit exclusively.

A defined case may be ordered and invoiced as a trade item. The same physical case may also be the individual unit managed during transport. When both roles apply, its GTIN and SSCC identify different aspects of that physical object.

The GS1 Logistic Label Guideline, release 1.3 (ratified July 2019) explains that cartons and outer cases can carry GTIN barcodes without being GS1 Logistic Labels. A GS1 Logistic Label, by contrast, requires an SSCC.

The distinction matters when reviewing artwork. An existing case GTIN barcode is not evidence that the case has also received a unique logistic-unit identity.

It does not follow that every parcel, decorative gift box or courier shipping carton must receive an SSCC. The requirement described here belongs to the applicable GS1 logistic-identification process, not to all packaging in commerce.

An SSCC identifies the unit without describing its complete contents

A unique identifier is a key to information, not necessarily a container for all that information.

In the hypothetical example, the trade-item data associated with TypeT defines the case class. That shared definition may be used whenever TypeT appears.

The information about UnitU1 and UnitU2 has a different scope. It concerns two particular physical loads.

The packing information would associate the SSCC identifying UnitU1 with its four TypeT cases, and separately associate UnitU2’s different SSCC with its four TypeT cases. The two associations can describe identical quantities without becoming the same unit record.

This is the practical distinction between the three GS1 functions:

Identify provides the relevant class or unit key. Capture enables a system to read that key and any other data correctly encoded in the carrier. Share makes associated business information available through an agreed information system or exchange.

A GS1 barcode can carry permitted information beyond its identification key. But reading an SSCC does not create missing packing information, infer an unrecorded component revision or establish that a shipment record is accurate.

For the receiving partner to associate a physical unit with its declared contents, the necessary data must already have been captured and made available. Depending on the agreed workflow, this may involve trade-item master data, a despatch advice or another linked business-information system.

The GS1 System Architecture distinguishes master data, transaction data and visibility data. It also identifies content descriptions as examples of information that can be associated with an SSCC.

That association is the information boundary. The physical identifier enables a relationship to be found; the corresponding data and working integration must supply the meaning.

Homogeneous and mixed units need different content-information treatment

The GS1 Logistic Label Guideline makes a further distinction that prevents a case GTIN from being used indiscriminately on every transport label.

In the original hypothetical example, UnitU1 is homogeneous: it contains only TypeT cases. It is assumed not to be a separately traded item itself.

For this type of logistic unit, the guideline allows the contents to be described using Application Identifier (02) for the GTIN of the contained trade item, together with AI (37) for the count. The logistics label still requires the unit’s SSCC under AI (00).

Thus, the label can communicate both a unique logistic-unit identity and relevant information about its homogeneous contents. The contents GTIN does not replace the SSCC.

Now consider a different hypothetical packing plan.

UnitU2 contains TypeT cases together with TypeV cases, where TypeV represents another fictional trade-item class. Assume this mixed logistic unit is not itself a trade item.

This is a heterogeneous unit. Section 4 of the guideline advises that GTIN and related trade-item information should not be included on the GS1 Logistic Label for such a unit. Instead, it strongly encourages electronic information exchange linked to the SSCC.

The SSCC identifies UnitU2, while the linked contents information distinguishes its TypeT and TypeV cases and their actual quantities.

Printing only TypeT’s GTIN as though it described the whole mixed unit would misrepresent the situation. A scan of UnitU2’s SSCC alone would not reconstruct its mixed-case breakdown.

There is also a separate scenario in which the logistic unit is itself a trade item. The guideline permits AI (01) to specify that trade item’s GTIN. It explicitly prohibits using AI (01) GTIN and AI (02) CONTENT together on the same logistic label.

These are distinctions about what the identifiers and data fields mean, not a complete label-design specification. The applicable current GS1 General Specifications and trading-partner requirements still govern implementation.

Keep case artwork, logistic-unit identity and shared contents data separate

Before adapting a repeated case-label design for an actual shipping process, establish what that design already identifies.

If the printed GTIN belongs to the defined case trade item, it identifies that case class. It cannot be treated as a substitute for assigning individual SSCCs where the GS1 logistics workflow requires them.

The physical logistic units must be separately identifiable, and each unit’s actual contents must be associated with its identity using the agreed packing and information-sharing process. The receiving party also needs a way to use that association. A readable barcode does not demonstrate that those steps happened.

This is different from recording which component artwork revision or lot was packed in a carton. Packrivo’s carton-to-component-version manifest addresses those internal physical-content references. Its master-carton label reconciliation guide addresses discrepancies between printed label information and packed units.

Those records can support a broader logistics workflow, but neither converts a GTIN into an SSCC or establishes an electronic exchange with a receiving partner.

For a small jewellery, candle or gift brand, the useful decision is not simply which barcode image to copy onto another carton. It is whether the packaging is being identified as a defined trade item, an individual logistic unit or both—and how the information about each physical unit will be made available after its identity is captured.

Packrivo can help coordinate the relevant packaging, artwork and sourcing questions. Actual GS1 identifier allocation, label implementation and trading-partner acceptance remain separate responsibilities.

Source scope: The publicly accessible GS1 System Architecture version 12.0.0 (October 2024) and GS1 Logistic Label Guideline release 1.3 (July 2019) were reviewed on 10 October 2026. All named units and case types are fictional. No identifiers were allocated, barcodes tested, actual goods tracked or electronic transactions performed.

A split needs child-unit records as well as reconciled case counts

Extend TypeT with a fictional split event. PARENT30 contains four TypeT cases; each TypeT case contains six empty presentation boxes under the original trade-item premise. The proposed split creates CHILD_A30 with two cases and CHILD_B30 with two cases. Each child therefore holds twelve empty boxes, and the pair reconciles to four cases and twenty-four boxes.

Hypothetical configuration Named object Relationship Input or next scope
SPLIT30 TYPET_EMPTY_BOXES assumed input 6 boxes/case
PARENT30 TYPET assumed input 4 cases/unit
PARENT30 EMPTY_BOXES calculated from PARENT_CASES*TYPE_CONTENT; 24 boxes/unit
CHILD_A30 TYPET assumed input 2 cases/unit
CHILD_A30 EMPTY_BOXES calculated from CHILD_A30_CASES*TYPE_CONTENT; 12 boxes/unit
CHILD_A30 CHILD_A30 requires OWN_APPROPRIATE_PHYSICAL_UNIT_IDENTITY_ASSIGNMENT_PENDING
CHILD_A30 CHILD_A30 requires OWN_LINKED_ACTUAL_CONTENTS_RECORD
CHILD_B30 TYPET assumed input 2 cases/unit
CHILD_B30 EMPTY_BOXES calculated from CHILD_B30_CASES*TYPE_CONTENT; 12 boxes/unit
CHILD_B30 CHILD_B30 requires OWN_APPROPRIATE_PHYSICAL_UNIT_IDENTITY_ASSIGNMENT_PENDING
CHILD_B30 CHILD_B30 requires OWN_LINKED_ACTUAL_CONTENTS_RECORD
SPLIT30 RECONCILED_CASES calculated from CHILD_A30_CASES+CHILD_B30_CASES; 4 cases
SPLIT30 RECONCILED_EMPTY_BOXES calculated from CHILD_A30_BOXES+CHILD_B30_BOXES; 24 boxes
SPLIT30 TYPET_CLASS remains SAME_BY_PREMISE
SPLIT30 PARENT_UNIT_ID not copied as BOTH_CHILD_UNIQUE_UNIT_IDENTITIES
SPLIT30 BALANCED_COUNT does not prove ACTUAL_PACK_SCAN_OR_RECEIVER_DATA_AVAILABILITY
SOURCE30 GENSPEC26_JAN2026 not equivalent to 27JAN_LAST_MODIFIED_OR_ALL_GSCN_REVIEW

The TypeT class does not change merely because its cases move into different physical groupings. The unit records do change. Within the applicable GS1 logistics workflow, do not copy one parent-unit identifier onto both children and expect the receiver to distinguish them. The responsible identifier owner must establish the appropriate child identities and contents associations under the actual current rules; this worksheet allocates no SSCC or GTIN.

Keep the parent history, split event and each child’s contents relationship visible instead of overwriting the parent with the latest total. A balanced 2 + 2 count does not prove that the receiving partner obtained either child record, that a label scans, or that the physical packing matches it. Data availability and actual capture remain separate from arithmetic.

One physical carton can have both trade-item and logistic-unit roles. This split example does not remove that possibility or impose SSCCs on every courier carton. The reviewed General Specifications archive lists 26.0.0 published January 2026; 27 January is a directory last-modified field, not a verified publication or effective date. The full large PDF and all dynamic GSCN notices were not reviewed, so no absence of later changes is claimed.

Download the GS1 logistic unit split parent child contents identity record (.csv). It includes the original table fields and scenarios alongside the added relationships. HYPOTHETICAL rows are editorial examples or required review scopes, not actual records. Actual quantity, configuration, component and file identities, materials, process, specification, copy, method, condition, observation, owner, decision, evidence and dates are blank. ACTUAL_BLANK is a separate empty starting row; enter permitted project evidence before using an actual record. A blank means unknown.

Use the Shipping-Carton IDs Need the Packaging Versions Inside Them for its separate question.

Additional official reference: GS1 General Specifications archive, GS1 standards directory and last-modified fields, GS1 approved-change notices entry. The archive lists a January 2026 publication month; 27 January directory modification is a different field. All GSCN notices and the full General Specifications PDF were not reviewed.

Source scope checked 17 October 2026: GS1 Architecture 12.0.0 published 18 October 2024 and Logistic Label 1.3 July 2019 support class/unit and identify/capture/share distinctions. General Specifications 26.0.0 is January 2026; directory 27 January last-modified is different. Full General Specifications and all GSCNs were not read. No real allocation, label implementation, scan or data exchange was approved. The added configurations and calculations are hypothetical, with actual evidence and decisions pending.

Discuss this packaging specification with Packrivo. We coordinate independent suppliers. MOQ: 500 pieces per product/design; illustrative quantities are not production offers. Confirm materials, samples, price and timing for your project.

title: QR Code Data, Error Correction and Print Size
html:
A QR code can become harder to print and read when more data or stronger error correction pushes it into a larger symbol version, but the packaging artwork keeps the same reserved area. The number of small squares, called modules, increases. If the available space cannot grow, each module must become smaller.

That is the trade-off to examine before approving a QR code on a jewelry care card, candle label or gift-box sleeve. Higher error correction may help restore damaged encoded data, but it does not guarantee that smaller printed modules will remain readable.

The useful decision is whether to simplify the encoded data, allocate more space or reconsider the correction setting and print constraints. Simply choosing the highest correction level and scaling the artwork down can work against the intended result.

QR Capacity Changes in Version Steps

A standard QR Code has numbered versions. Version 1 contains 21 × 21 modules, Version 2 contains 25 × 25, and Version 4 contains 33 × 33. Each version increases the count by four modules per side.

DENSO WAVE’s explanation of QR Code versions identifies three factors that determine capacity: the amount of information, the character mode and the selected error-correction level.

Character mode matters because the same number of visible characters does not always require the same encoded capacity. QR Codes support modes including numeric, alphanumeric and byte data. Mixed content may require different encoding arrangements.

For example, the length of a website address alone does not determine its version. Lowercase letters and other characters in an ordinary URL cannot automatically be treated as an all-uppercase QR alphanumeric payload. The actual encoding method matters.

Capacity also changes in steps, not continuously. Adding a few characters to a payload that still fits the current version does not add another row of modules. But crossing that version’s capacity limit requires a different solution, often a higher version.

The manufacturer’s Version 1–10 capacity table illustrates how correction level affects the limit. At Version 2, Level M accommodates up to 38 purely alphanumeric characters, whereas Level H accommodates up to 20. Those figures apply to the stated character mode, not indiscriminately to website URLs.

Increasing correction from M to H can therefore require a larger version when the same payload no longer fits. It does not mean that every change to H automatically increases the version.

A Fixed Print Area Determines the Module Pitch

The symbol itself is not the entire space needed on the packaging.

DENSO WAVE’s code-area guidance requires a clear margin, called a quiet zone, four modules wide on every side. Therefore, the reserved square must accommodate the symbol’s modules plus eight additional module widths: four on the left and four on the right, with the same arrangement vertically.

For a square allocation:

Module pitch = reserved side length ÷ (symbol modules per side + 8)

Module pitch is the width of one module, not the diameter of a printed dot or a guaranteed readable dimension.

Consider a deliberately hypothetical gift-card layout with a 22 mm × 22 mm reserved square, including all quiet zones. Compare two assumed symbol versions:

Version 2 model

  • Symbol: 25 modules per side

  • With quiet zones: 25 + 8 = 33 module pitches

  • Module pitch: 22 ÷ 33 ≈ 0.667 mm

Version 4 model

  • Symbol: 33 modules per side

  • With quiet zones: 33 + 8 = 41 module pitches

  • Module pitch: 22 ÷ 41 ≈ 0.537 mm

In the same reserved square, the Version 4 model has a module pitch approximately 19.5% smaller than the Version 2 model.

These versions are assumed solely to compare geometry. No specific URL has been encoded, no actual QR artwork has been generated, and neither result establishes a minimum readable pitch.

There is another way to examine the trade-off.

If the designer wants to preserve the hypothetical Version 2 pitch of approximately 0.667 mm while moving to Version 4, the reserved side would need to become approximately:

41 × (22 ÷ 33) = 27.33 mm

That is an increase from 22 mm to approximately 27.33 mm per side, including quiet zones.

It is a geometric comparison, not a recommendation that 27.33 mm will work with a particular printer, label stock, finish or smartphone.

The design question is now visible: does the artwork have room to grow, or must something about the data and symbol specification change?

Error Correction Restores Codewords, Not Arbitrary Printed Areas

QR Code error correction uses additional information to help recover encoded data when part of a symbol is damaged.

DENSO WAVE describes four correction levels: L, M, Q and H. Its technical explanation of error correction uses Reed–Solomon error correction and defines the restoration rates in terms of total codewords. One QR Code codeword contains eight bits.

The manufacturer’s published QR Code overview gives approximate restoration rates of 7%, 15%, 25% and 30% of codewords for Levels L, M, Q and H respectively.

These percentages are not permissions to obscure equivalent percentages of the printed square.

For example, Level Q’s approximately 25% restoration figure does not establish that a logo can safely cover 25% of a QR code’s area. The spatial position of damage, its effect on encoded information and interference with features required to locate and interpret the symbol are different questions. The quiet zone is not expendable correction capacity.

The same distinction matters for a code printed on a small packaging surface. More correction information may improve the ability to recover damaged codewords. But if the chosen configuration also forces a higher version inside the same area, the resulting smaller modules introduce another printing and reading constraint.

Whether that trade-off is acceptable must be determined for the actual encoded symbol and intended printed application. The correction percentage alone cannot decide it.

Change the Data, Area or Correction Decision Before Shrinking the Symbol

Suppose a small gift brand has already allocated a fixed square to a QR code that will lead to product-care information.

The first design question is whether the entire proposed payload needs to be encoded.

A long destination containing optional tracking parameters may consume more capacity than a shorter, controlled address that still reaches the intended content. Simplifying the encoded address could help the code remain in a lower version, although removing characters does not guarantee a version change.

The brand must still preserve the destination’s usefulness and maintainability. The separate Packrivo guide to QR code placement, links and long-term maintenance covers those customer-facing and website responsibilities.

If the necessary payload cannot be reduced, the next question is whether the reserved square can grow. Increasing the available area allows a given version to use larger modules while retaining its four-module quiet zones.

If the allocated area cannot grow, review whether the proposed error-correction level matches the intended environment. Do not select Level H merely because it sounds safest, or lower the level merely to make the artwork smaller. Either choice changes the balance between data capacity and correction capability.

A smaller module pitch may still be proposed, but it remains a print-and-reading question requiring evidence from the intended application.

These options are not interchangeable. Shortening data is useful for module size only if it permits a relevant version reduction. Changing correction settings helps the geometry only if it changes the required version. Enlarging the print allocation directly changes the space available per module.

Keep a QR print-size record with the actual encoding result

The two numerical versions above are assumed examples. In an actual project, ask the responsible generating service for the resulting version after it encodes the exact approved payload and correction level. A shorter displayed URL or a higher correction setting does not independently identify that version.

Record symbol modules, quiet-zone modules on each side and the entire reserved square separately. If the actual candidate uses N modules per side, the four-module margins give N+8 pitches across the reserved width. Retain the actual generated file and a print-review request; this worksheet supplies no barcode artwork or default pass. Ask the printer and technical reviewer to assess the finished candidate rather than using the mesh sketch as a production asset.

Download this article’s project record (CSV). The record includes field definitions, labeled teaching examples and a blank project row. Add source evidence and the details of your actual project.

For a sourcing discussion, send the intended code area, actual payload-owner reference and the unresolved print review. Packrivo coordinates supplier questions; the responsible technical or commercial parties confirm the actual method, configuration and terms.

Keep Geometry Separate from Printed-QR Performance

Before the artwork is finalized, identify the actual encoded data, selected mode or modes, correction level, resulting version and reserved area. Use those values to calculate the proposed module pitch, including quiet zones.

Then discuss the candidate with the responsible printer or technical provider in relation to the actual substrate, print process, finish and intended scanning conditions.

A numerical fit within the artwork is not proof of printed readability. Neither is a successful screen scan a substitute for examining the finished printed candidate.

For an application involving retail identification rather than an ordinary consumer-information link, the requirements must be reviewed separately. Packrivo’s finished retail-barcode proof guide addresses that different review task.

For small packaging projects, the immediate improvement is to avoid treating QR code size as an isolated artwork adjustment. Establish what needs to be encoded, understand the version that results and calculate the module geometry before deciding whether the allocated area is suitable.

Packrivo can help organize packaging dimensions, proposed artwork constraints and outstanding supplier questions through its packaging brief. Actual code generation, printing feasibility and reading performance need their own appropriate technical review.

Source/access note — DENSO WAVE public educational pages were checked 10 October 2026 and are undated. Paid ISO/IEC 18004 was not obtained. The 22 mm calculations are hypothetical arithmetic, not printed or scanned QR evidence.

title: NFC Packaging Near Foil, Metal and Jewellery
html:
A visible NFC tag is not necessarily a readable NFC tag. If a gift box includes conductive foil, metallic components or jewellery close to the proposed tag, the completed package may present a different reading environment from the plain card on which the tag was first demonstrated.

Before approving the location, decide whether the tag will operate next to metal in the package’s intended use. A position on nonmetal material and a tag construction designed for metal-adjacent use are different candidates. Neither should be assumed to work in the finished package without relevant evidence.

This distinction matters for small jewellery, candle and gift brands considering NFC-enabled care cards, gift boxes or product information touchpoints. The issue is not simply whether a customer can see or reach the printed NFC symbol.

NFC Reading Depends on Magnetic Coupling

A QR code is read optically by a camera. An NFC tag communicates through a different physical mechanism.

In a typical 13.56 MHz HF/NFC system, the reader and tag contain antennas that couple through an alternating magnetic field. A passive tag draws energy from that field to operate and communicate. The orientation, antenna characteristics and surrounding materials can affect the interaction.

STMicroelectronics explains this magnetic coupling in its AN2866 application note on 13.56 MHz tag antennas, Rev. 6, September 2025.

For packaging, the important consequence is that the magnetic environment extends beyond the visible NFC mark.

A tag may be printed or attached on the outside of a lid while a conductive layer sits behind it. A metal jewellery item may occupy the space beneath that lid. The customer still has an unobstructed surface to tap, but the tag antenna is no longer necessarily operating in the same environment as it did on an isolated card.

The printed position describes where the customer is invited to tap. It does not, by itself, establish how the antenna will behave.

Nearby Metal Can Change the Antenna’s Electrical Behaviour

An alternating magnetic field can induce circulating electrical currents, called eddy currents, in nearby conductive material.

Those currents generate their own magnetic fields and can oppose part of the field responsible for coupling between the reader and tag. Conductive material can also introduce losses and change the effective electrical characteristics of an antenna.

One possible consequence is detuning: the antenna no longer responds optimally at its intended operating frequency in the new environment.

NXP’s NFC Antenna Design Made Easy, published 12 October 2021, discusses antenna geometry and metal proximity, including ferrite-backed configurations.

A more specific historical illustration appears in NXP’s AN11535, Measurement and tuning of a NFC and Reader IC antenna with a MiniVNA, Rev. 1.1, 3 November 2014.

In section 6, NXP placed an aluminium plate near a particular reader-antenna setup. The documented return-loss minimum moved to approximately 14.8 MHz rather than the intended 13.56 MHz region. The note attributes the change in antenna inductance to eddy currents associated with the metal plate.

That experiment demonstrates a real detuning mechanism. It does not measure a packaging label, predict the behaviour of thin decorative foil or establish the reading distance of a passive tag inside a gift box. Its particular circuit adjustments are not instructions for a packaging buyer.

The behaviour of an actual package depends on the materials, conductor geometry, antenna construction and relative positions involved. A metallic-looking finish is not sufficient evidence that it contains a conductive layer, and a confirmed conductive foil does not automatically mean that an NFC tag will fail.

The relevant question is whether the proposed material arrangement changes the NFC operating conditions enough to require a different tag construction or location.

A Plain Card and a Filled Gift Box Are Different Configurations

Consider a hypothetical jewellery brand developing an NFC touchpoint for a gift box.

The brand initially considers attaching a particular passive NFC tag to a plain, nonmetal card. This provides a starting construction for discussing tag size and location.

The same tag candidate is then considered for two other packaging arrangements.

In the first arrangement, the NFC location sits beside or over a decorative layer that the supplier has confirmed contains conductive foil. The foil belongs to the actual packaging structure, not merely to a metallic-looking digital artwork preview.

In the second arrangement, the tag sits on the outside of a closed gift-box lid, with metal jewellery inside the box near the tag’s position.

These arrangements create different questions.

On the plain card, there is no identified nearby conductive packaging layer. With confirmed foil, the review must consider the foil’s actual position and extent relative to the antenna. With the filled box, the orientation and location of the jewellery also become relevant.

The metal jewellery is not necessarily positioned directly behind the entire tag antenna. Its shape and location could differ between products and packing arrangements. Those differences must not be collapsed into the assumption that every piece of jewellery has the same influence.

No phone scan, reading distance, detuning value or failure is assumed in this example. The example identifies three physical configurations, not three measured outcomes.

A result obtained on the first configuration would describe that configuration. It would not automatically approve the other two.

This is why the final contents matter even when the tag itself remains visible.

Placement and Tag Construction Offer Different Design Responses

If a confirmed conductive layer or metal item is close to the proposed tag, the brand has two broad design directions to discuss.

One is to change the tag’s location.

Moving the tag onto a nonmetal region may change its relationship to the conductive material. For example, the brand might consider a separate unfoiled card, a different lid region or another accessible part of the assembled package.

However, nonmetal mounting surface does not necessarily mean metal-free surroundings. Jewellery, a candle tin or a metal closure may still be nearby once the package is assembled. The proposed position must be considered in its actual use arrangement.

The other direction is to review a tag construction intended for metal-adjacent applications.

Certain NFC configurations incorporate ferrite material between the antenna and nearby metal to manage magnetic-field interaction. NXP discusses ferrite-backed antenna options, while STMicroelectronics illustrates ferrite-protected NFC touchpoints in its NFC Touchpoints design guidance.
