A supplier-designed ferrite-backed tag is not equivalent to adding an arbitrary sheet, choosing a universal spacer thickness or assuming that the same inlay will work on every metallic substrate.

The complete proposed construction matters: tag antenna, backing material, adhesive, finished substrate, nearby conductor and the intended phone approach.

For a packaging buyer, the decision is not how to retune an electronic circuit personally. It is whether the original label candidate remains appropriate or whether the project requires a different placement or a vendor-designed metal-adjacent construction.

Both choices remain candidates until reviewed in the relevant finished arrangement.

The Final Material Stack Matters More Than the Artwork Preview

Packaging artwork may accurately show the front of a finished NFC label without showing what lies beneath or behind its antenna.

An engineering review therefore needs a physical description of the proposed assembly.

For a foil-finished lid, that description should identify the actual foil process and conductive material where confirmed, the location of the NFC antenna rather than only the printed tap symbol, and the layers separating the tag from the conductor.

For a jewellery-filled box, it must also describe where the metal product sits when the recipient is expected to tap the package.

This information helps the tag vendor evaluate the intended configuration rather than an idealised blank card.

STMicroelectronics’ AN2866 specifically identifies the tag’s surrounding environment, including metal surfaces, as a factor affecting antenna tuning. Its guidance also explains why the final label material can influence the resulting frequency.

The electrical relationship is therefore not confined to visible decorative artwork. An adhesive layer, tag support material or altered construction can matter even when the customer-facing design remains unchanged.

Packrivo’s separate guide to mapping foil against folds and glue areas addresses the physical relationship between finishing artwork and the folding or joining structure. An NFC review adds a separate electrical question: where is the actual tag antenna relative to nearby conductive material?

Passing one review cannot substitute for the other.

Evaluate the Package in the State the Customer Will Use

STMicroelectronics’ NFC Touchpoints guidance distinguishes a tag evaluated in free air from one evaluated in situ, meaning in its installed environment. It recommends checking the actual final product and touchpoint with different phones.

That distinction is especially important when a gift box changes state during packing or use.

If the intended interaction is tapping a closed box before opening it, evidence from an empty open box would not cover the final filled, closed arrangement. If the tag is instead on a care card intended to be removed and tapped separately, that use state presents another configuration.

The brand should define the intended interaction first, then obtain relevant evidence for the tag construction and package state that will actually be used.

For the hypothetical jewellery box, useful vendor review would compare the proposed tag in the assembled foil-finished and jewellery-filled arrangement, using the intended tapping face and relevant phone types and orientations. The brand and responsible technical supplier would need to agree what constitutes an acceptable user interaction before interpreting the observations.

A successful tap under one recorded condition does not establish reliable operation with every phone, every filling arrangement or every future packaging change.

Likewise, an unsuccessful tap does not establish metal as the sole cause. Tag configuration, positioning, reader behaviour and other factors may also require investigation.

Keep the NFC Decision Separate From the Digital Destination

The electromagnetic review concerns whether a phone can communicate with the tag in the intended package.

What happens after the communication succeeds is another decision.

A tag might be intended to open product care information, a gift message or another brand-controlled page. The destination still needs appropriate content, ownership and maintenance.

Packrivo’s QR code placement and link-maintenance guide addresses those website and information responsibilities for printed optical codes. Those questions remain relevant to a digital customer experience, but QR code readability cannot be used as evidence that an NFC antenna will function next to metal.

Nor does a functioning NFC tap, by itself, establish product authenticity, secure authentication or permission to collect customer information. Those would require separate decisions and appropriate technical evidence.

Decide the Metal-Adjacent Configuration Before Approval

An NFC feature on gift packaging should not be approved solely because the tag was readable on an isolated card or its printed mark remains accessible on the final design.

Where conductive foil, metal closures or metal product contents could affect the antenna, the packaging decision is to identify the actual operating environment and choose a corresponding placement or tag construction for review.

That approach does not predict failure. It prevents evidence from one physical configuration being transferred to another without justification.

For projects considering NFC-enabled packaging, Packrivo’s packaging enquiry can be used to describe the intended tag position, finish and packed contents so the relevant sourcing and supplier questions can be coordinated. NFC antenna design, performance evaluation and any technical acceptance remain matters for appropriately qualified tag vendors and reviewers.

Source/access note — Sources checked 10 October 2026. ST AN2866 Rev.6 is dated September 2025; NXP AN11535 Rev.1.1 is dated 3 November 2014 and its metal-plate illustration concerns a reader experiment, not this passive packaging tag. Public technical sources explain mechanisms, not an actual scan result or vendor guarantee.

Keep each intended NFC use state in its own row

Track invented TAG-H at C0 on a plain nonmetal card, C1 on an empty open box and C2 on a filled closed box. These are different installed contexts, not a controlled metal-only experiment. Neither scan success nor failure is assumed for any row.

Configuration State to identify Evidence that cannot be borrowed
C0 Loose plain card Does not approve installed box
C1 Empty/open box and actual tag position Does not cover filled/closed state
C2 Filled/closed, contents and finish nearby Needs relevant final-use observation
Digital/security Destination and intended function RF communication is not authentication or consent

Identify the antenna location and actual surrounding materials rather than inferring conductivity from a metallic-looking illustration. The cutaway marks proposed nearby material positions, not an approved foil wrap, spacing or physical package. Changes in location, phone approach and contents must remain recorded.

Ask the qualified tag vendor to define the relevant construction and evaluation for the intended state. A future C0 read cannot fill C2's outcome; a future C2 failure would not prove metal alone caused it. Actual phone, orientation, read observation and technical acceptance are blank. No arbitrary shield, spacer thickness, tuning change, read distance or reliability probability is prescribed.

Download the NFC packaging near metal record (.csv). HYPOTHETICAL rows are invented examples. Use ACTUAL_BLANK for permitted project inputs; replace that row label only when recording actual facts. Empty evidence, observation and date fields mean unknown or not performed, never acceptance. Keep checkpoints and revisions separate.

Send the final intended tapping state, actual materials, tag construction and contents for vendor-led configuration review. Packrivo coordinates independent suppliers. These records establish no supplier offer, service availability or MOQ exception; its published baseline is 500 pieces per product/design.

title: A Carton Can Keep Deforming While Its Applied Load Stays Constant
html:
A shipping carton can continue to deform even when the weight pressing down on it stays the same. Its first response to compression does not necessarily describe what happens during a longer period of stacked storage.

That time-dependent deformation is called creep. A peak box compression test (BCT) result cannot, by itself, establish how a complete packed carton will behave under sustained loading. A storage decision needs evidence covering the relevant load, duration, packed configuration and conditions—not a stack-height estimate obtained by dividing a peak compression number by carton mass.

The First Shortening Is Not the Whole Deformation

When a vertical load is first applied to a carton, the structure responds. Corrugated walls may deflect, contact points may settle, and any supporting contents or internal packaging may participate in carrying the load.

Some movement can occur as soon as the load is applied. Further deformation may develop while that same load remains in place.

The second part is the important distinction. In creep, deformation changes with elapsed time under sustained loading. The load does not have to increase for the carton to continue changing shape.

Original research by Martin Holmvall on containerboards and stacked corrugated boxes, first published online in September 2021 and appearing in a 2022 journal issue, examines this time-dependent behavior and the variation in loading lifetimes. Separately, Westpak’s educational explanation of creep describes changes in cushioning-material thickness under persistent compressive loading.

These sources address different material and structural scopes. A measured cushioning-material response must not be presented as a measured shipping-carton response.

For a complete carton, deformation may also alter how its walls, corners, fittings and contents share the applied load. An unchanged external force does not guarantee that the internal load distribution remains unchanged.

A carton that appears satisfactory immediately after stacking therefore has not yet demonstrated its response throughout the intended storage period.

Peak Compression and Constant Loading Ask Different Questions

A reported peak BCT result generally identifies the maximum compressive force reached during the stated compression test. It is useful evidence about resistance under that test’s loading arrangement.

Sustained loading asks something else: what happens when a specified force remains applied as time passes?

The distinction is reflected in the published standards.

ASTM D642-25 addresses compressive resistance testing of shipping containers, components and unit loads. Its public description directs constant-load testing questions to ASTM D4577-19(2023).

ASTM D4577’s published scope addresses vertically applied constant loads maintained for a specified period or until failure. It can concern empty or filled containers, including palletized or unitized configurations.

Even if two loading histories briefly reach a similar force, they are not equivalent. A compression event records a response along one loading history. A fixed-load exposure introduces elapsed time as an essential part of the question.

This is why dividing a peak BCT value by the mass of an individual carton cannot determine a safe number of stacked layers.

Force and mass are different quantities. Even after correctly expressing the mass as weight force, the resulting comparison still does not describe time-dependent deformation, contact conditions, contents, environmental exposure or variation between cartons.

There is no universal conversion from a peak compression result to a guaranteed stacking duration.

A Hypothetical Carton That Settles at the Start

Imagine a candle gift brand considering stacked storage of complete shipping cartons. Each carton contains the intended retail candle boxes, internal holders and closures.

For this hypothetical comparison, suppose a responsible technical evaluation applies the same agreed vertical force to cartons of the proposed packed configuration.

Both cartons show an initial settling response.

That starting observation does not reveal whether they will behave alike afterward.

One carton might undergo relatively little additional change within the observation period. Another might continue shortening or develop visible distortion. The rate of deformation might also change as exposure continues.

These are possible outcomes, not invented test findings. No force, displacement, duration, material performance or failure time has been measured or assigned to either carton.

The only defensible conclusion from the shared starting observation is that both responded initially to the applied load.

Their later behavior remains unknown until suitable time-dependent evidence exists.

A record showing that a carton supported a load at the beginning cannot establish that it will maintain an acceptable condition throughout an unspecified period.

A Deformation Curve Needs an Elapsed-Time Axis

For a relevant constant-load evaluation, a useful record distinguishes the applied force from the deformation that occurs while that force is maintained.

Consider a graph with elapsed time along the horizontal axis and carton shortening along the vertical axis.

The beginning identifies the response when the load is first applied. Any subsequent measured shortening during the maintained-load interval provides evidence about continuing deformation.

The curve may not have a constant slope. Its rate of change can vary, and a short observed segment does not justify a straight-line prediction into an unobserved period.

Three interpretations matter:

  • Further shortening under the maintained load: deformation has continued after the initial response. Its measured extent and rate belong to the observed interval.

  • Little additional change during the recorded interval: the carton changed little in that interval. This does not prove that deformation will never resume or that indefinite stacking is acceptable.

  • An evaluation ending before failure: the record may establish observations through the stated endpoint. It does not establish an unmeasured failure time.

The associated carton condition matters alongside the dimensional trace. Wall distortion, changes around corners, closure behavior and the condition of the packed contents can be relevant to the intended acceptance question.

A single initial photograph, final photograph or peak force cannot reconstruct that entire history.

The original corrugated-box research also addresses variation in creep lifetime. Its findings reinforce the distinction between a particular observed result and a prediction for other cartons or conditions; they do not provide a universal lifetime formula for a buyer’s proposed package.

Duration Belongs in the Storage Decision

A complete packed carton can have different load paths from an empty carton. Internal holders, products, closures and the surfaces supporting the carton can affect the assembled system’s behavior.

The intended application also matters. Storage may involve an extended stationary load, while distribution can introduce changes in handling, support, loading and environmental conditions.

Evidence from one fixed-load exposure does not automatically represent every part of that broader history.

Before treating a report as relevant to a proposed stored stack, the responsible reviewer needs to establish what was actually loaded, how the force was applied, how long it remained applied, what conditions were present and what was observed over time.

An evaluation that ended at a specified duration without observed failure answers a bounded question. It does not establish an unlimited safe storage period, nor does it automatically validate another loading arrangement.

For buyers, the useful technical question is:

For this complete packed-carton configuration, what evidence describes deformation and package condition under the proposed sustained load throughout the relevant exposure period?

If the available answer is only a peak BCT number, the time-dependent storage question remains unresolved.

The existing distribution-test scope guide provides a place to define the complete packed system and distribution objective. The test-report configuration guide helps connect reported evidence to the configuration actually evaluated.

Packrivo can coordinate packaging specifications and supplier questions. The appropriate technical parties must determine the evaluation method, evidence and acceptance requirements. No tested stacking capacity or safe storage duration is established here.

Keep a Peak Result Separate From a Storage Claim

A carton may initially resist compression and still undergo further deformation while the same load remains applied.

A peak compression result answers a resistance question within its stated test. A sustained-load record addresses behavior across an observed period. Neither result should be extended beyond its demonstrated scope without a technically supported basis.

For a proposed stacked arrangement, retain the difference between initial resistance, observed time-dependent behavior and an actual acceptance decision.

Until the complete loaded system has relevant evidence for its intended exposure, safe stack height and storage duration remain unestablished.

Source scope: Public information accessed 10 October 2026. ASTM D4577-19(2023) is the active 2023 reapproval; ASTM D642-25 is the active compression-test edition. The full paid ASTM procedures were not obtained. Westpak’s undated educational page addresses material creep and does not provide a carton-specific result. Holmvall’s original research concerns studied containerboards and corrugated boxes, not Packrivo packaging. This article is an interpretation guide, not a testing procedure or authorization to stack products.

Keep the unloaded reference when separating initial and later shortening

Use invented readings to define the origin of a shortening record. A hypothetical complete carton has 300 N maintained at START30 and LATER30. Relative to its original unloaded height, total shortening is 2 mm at START30 and 4 mm at LATER30. The checkpoint names supply no elapsed hours, test method or actual observations.

Hypothetical configuration Named object Relationship Input or next scope
START30 MAINTAINED_FORCE assumed input 300 N
START30 SHORTENING_FROM_UNLOADED_REFERENCE assumed input 2 mm
LATER30 MAINTAINED_FORCE assumed input 300 N
LATER30 SHORTENING_FROM_UNLOADED_REFERENCE assumed input 4 mm
LATER30 SHORTENING_AFTER_START calculated from LATER30_TOTAL-START30_TOTAL; 2 mm
CARTON30 TOTAL_SHORTENING uses reference ORIGINAL_UNLOADED_HEIGHT
CARTON30 LATER30_TOTAL4 is not all POST_START_CREEP
CARTON30 SYMBOLIC_CHECKPOINTS do not supply ELAPSED_TIME_RATE_FAILURETIME_OR_SAFE_STACK
CARTON30 ILLUSTRATIVE_SPECIMEN is COMPLETE_CARTON_NOT_FOAM_MATERIAL

Additional shortening after START30 is 4 − 2 =2 mm. Calling all 4 mm post-start creep would include the initial response in the later increment. Conversely, resetting the displayed origin to zero at START30 without retaining the original 2 mm would hide how far the carton had already changed. Keep total shortening and post-start change as different fields connected to their own reference.

The example does not establish a creep rate: no interval was supplied. It also gives no failure time, safe stack height or allowable distortion. If the intended decision concerns storage, the responsible reviewer still needs actual elapsed time, complete packed configuration, maintained load, environment and package condition. A later endpoint cannot justify straight-line extrapolation into an unobserved period.

This reference check complements matching a report to an order. A genuine constant-load report can still be misread if its displacement origin is omitted; a peak compression record cannot fill that history. Ask what was zeroed, when load was established and what each displacement refers to. The 300 N assumption is arithmetic context, never a suggested loading procedure.

Download the carton creep initial shortening reference subtraction record (.csv). It includes the original table fields and scenarios alongside the added relationships. HYPOTHETICAL rows are editorial examples or required review scopes, not actual records. Actual quantity, configuration, component and file identities, materials, process, specification, copy, method, condition, observation, owner, decision, evidence and dates are blank. ACTUAL_BLANK is a separate empty starting row; enter permitted project evidence before using an actual record. A blank means unknown.

Use the Packaging Test Reports: Match the Ordered Configuration for its separate question.

Source scope checked 17 October 2026: Holmvall research was online-first 28 September 2021 and published in a 2022 journal issue; the earlier source study obtained publisher text after an access error. ASTM D642-25 and D4577-19(2023) public scopes differ; paid methods were not acquired. Westpak material creep is not a complete carton model or lifetime guarantee. The added configurations and calculations are hypothetical, with actual evidence and decisions pending.

Discuss this packaging specification with Packrivo. We coordinate independent suppliers. MOQ: 500 pieces per product/design; illustrative quantities are not production offers. Confirm materials, samples, price and timing for your project.

title: Label Edge Lift on Curved Candle Jars
html:
A label lifting at the edge of a curved candle jar does not automatically need a stronger adhesive. The pressure-sensitive adhesive must first establish intimate contact with the finished container surface. At the same time, the label facestock may resist being held in a curved shape.

These two effects work together. A construction can have an adhesive suitable for the surface but a facestock that places too much restoring demand on the bond. Another construction may bend easily yet fail to establish sufficient contact with the actual finish.

For a small jewellery, candle or gift brand, the useful next question is not simply which adhesive is stronger. It is whether the proposed change improves contact, reduces the facestock’s tendency to spring back, changes the area being covered, or addresses more than one of those problems.

Adhesive Contact Depends on the Finished Surface

A pressure-sensitive adhesive needs intimate contact with the material receiving it. The visible label area is not necessarily the area where effective adhesive contact has formed.

A smooth-looking container may have a coating or another finish that changes how the adhesive interacts with its surface. Texture can also matter. If an adhesive does not conform sufficiently to a textured surface, some regions may make contact while others remain separated.

3M’s material-bonding guidance explains that wet-out—the adhesive establishing intimate contact with the substrate—is necessary for bonding. Surface energy and cleanliness influence that contact.

Its separate surface-science explanation adds an important qualification: roughness can increase the available surface area, but excessive roughness can also prevent an adhesive from flowing into contact with it.

This means neither a nominally large label area nor a general description such as “glass jar” is enough to establish compatibility.

For an actual packaging proposal, the receiving surface is the finished surface the adhesive meets—not merely the underlying container material. The label construction and application conditions must be considered against that surface.

Wet-out is also not a complete performance verdict. Establishing contact is necessary, but the resulting bond must still withstand the demands placed on it.

A Bent Facestock Can Keep Pulling Against the Bond

A label has a physical structure beyond its adhesive.

When a relatively stiff facestock is bent around a container, it may tend to return toward its original flatter shape. The adhesive must retain the label against that restoring tendency.

This is often called facestock memory or spring-back.

Avery Dennison’s discussion of neck-label detachment explains how paper construction can create a memory effect when labels are applied to curved surfaces. It also notes that inks, varnishes and embellishments can influence stiffness and label behaviour.

The principle is relevant to considering other curved packaging surfaces, but Avery Dennison’s discussion specifically concerns bottle-neck labels. It does not establish a universal material choice for candle jars or gift packaging.

A tighter curve generally asks the same facestock to bend more sharply. Whether that creates a practical edge-lift problem depends on the complete construction, the actual curved area and the adhesive bond.

This also explains why changing only the adhesive may miss the problem.

If the facestock continues to impose substantial restoring demand, an adhesive change addresses the holding side of the relationship without necessarily reducing the demand itself.

Conversely, a more conformable facestock may reduce the bending problem but cannot compensate automatically for poor adhesive contact with the receiving surface.

Avery Dennison’s 2019 Small Diameter Portfolio discusses combinations of flexible facestocks and compatible adhesives. It also identifies stiffness, ink and varnish coverage, and label overlap as factors affecting performance.

That historical product brochure supports reviewing the construction as a combination. It does not establish present availability or an approved construction for this article’s example.

A Label Can Fit the Container Shape Without Staying Attached

Geometric fit and adhesive contact are related but different questions.

A label outline may follow the boundaries of a curved container correctly. Its artwork may appear level, and its upper and lower edges may occupy the intended area.

That establishes a possible geometric fit. It does not show that the adhesive has formed sufficient contact or that the facestock will remain conformed to the curve.

Likewise, a correctly shaped paper mockup cannot reproduce the contact behaviour of an adhesive-coated label or the bending behaviour of its finished facestock.

This distinction becomes important when reviewing a proposed fix.

If the flat outline is unsuitable for a tapered or irregular container, changing its shape or coverage may be necessary. If the outline already fits the intended band, another shape adjustment alone may not resolve edge lift caused by inadequate contact or spring-back.

A brand should avoid using the success of one question—artwork alignment or outline fit—as evidence that the other has been answered.

Compare Paper and Film as Complete Construction Candidates

Consider a hypothetical candle brand with one identified curved container and an already-defined label band.

The brand wants to retain the same artwork. A converter is considering two conceptual alternatives:

  • Candidate P: A relatively stiff paper facestock.

  • Candidate F: A more conformable film facestock.

Neither candidate has been manufactured, applied or tested for this example. No adhesion reading, successful construction or material superiority is assumed.

For Candidate P, the buyer needs to consider how readily the paper can remain curved over the intended band. If its tendency to flatten is substantial, the adhesive may face continuing demand at the label boundaries.

For Candidate F, greater conformability could reduce that mechanical demand. But the film proposal still needs an appropriate adhesive, surface compatibility, printing and finishing construction, and application method.

The film is not automatically the better label. Paper constructions also differ in flexibility, and films do not all behave alike.

The useful comparison separates two questions.

First, can the adhesive establish suitable contact?

Review the actual finished container, its relevant surface condition, and the converter’s proposed adhesive and application instructions. A facestock change does not establish that the adhesive will wet out the surface.

Second, what bending demand does the facestock impose?

Compare how the proposed complete constructions accommodate the identified curvature, including any printing, coating or embellishment that could affect their behaviour.

Where technically feasible, comparing facestocks while retaining other defined variables can help clarify the material difference. If the proposed paper and film require different adhesives or other construction changes, they must instead be evaluated as different complete constructions. An observed difference cannot then be attributed to the facestock alone.

A visible lifted edge would not, by itself, establish which mechanism caused it.

A construction that appears to conform initially may still require an agreed observation under its intended conditions. An edge that remains attached during one brief observation does not establish performance throughout storage, handling or use.

The next candidate should be selected through a defined construction comparison, not through an assumed result.

Select the Next Change According to the Unresolved Mechanism

The same visible defect can lead to different design questions.

If the principal concern is contact with the receiving finish, the next comparison should address the surface–adhesive combination and the intended application conditions. Changing the facestock alone would not explain how the adhesive meets that surface.

If the principal concern is bending demand, the converter can consider a more conformable facestock or a different finished construction. Simply requesting greater tack does not reduce the facestock’s tendency to return toward flatness.

If the label spans a curved transition, raised feature or unsuitable contact region, reconsider its position or coverage. Reducing coverage or changing geometry may alter the problem, provided the required information and intended appearance remain accommodated.

If both poor contact and spring-back are plausible, the next proposal may need to change the adhesive and facestock together. This is a combined-construction comparison, not evidence that either individual change would have succeeded.

These choices are alternative technical directions, not diagnoses from photographs.

The actual observations, construction details and review conditions must determine which explanation deserves further examination.

Review the Applied Construction Rather Than an Adhesive Name

Before comparing the next candidates, identify the finished container version and the intended label band.

The converter should explain the proposed facestock, adhesive, relevant finishes and dimensions. The application owner should confirm how the actual labels will be applied and which conditions the comparison will cover.

A useful review should distinguish contact-related concerns from possible facestock-return effects as far as the available evidence permits. It should also describe where any visible lifting occurs and what the observation does—and does not—establish.

For the broader surface and application inputs, see Packrivo’s label adhesion and surface-use guide.

If the unresolved question concerns the flat outline on a tapered container, use the separate tapered-container label geometry guide. That shape decision does not replace review of the finished pressure-sensitive construction.

If the problem occurs while the label separates from its backing rather than after application to the container, liner release needs its own review.

Packrivo can coordinate the packaging brief and supplier questions. It does not establish a label’s physical performance through project coordination alone.

The practical outcome is a better-directed next comparison: improve actual surface contact, reduce facestock bending demand, revise coverage, or review a combined construction.

A stronger adhesive is only a meaningful answer when it addresses the actual unresolved mechanism.

Source/access note — Sources checked 10 October 2026. 3M and Avery Dennison public pages are undated. The 2019 Small Diameter Portfolio is historical product guidance, not a verified exact publication day, present availability or a tested candle-jar construction.

Identify the changed inputs before attributing an improvement

Use invented reference A with paper facestock P1 and adhesive AD1. Proposal B changes both to film F2 and AD2. A conditional C would retain P1 with AD2 only if the vendor can actually provide a suitable construction. No candidate has been made, applied or observed.

Candidate Facestock Adhesive Comparison meaning
A P1 paper AD1 Reference proposal
B F2 film AD2 Two changed inputs
C, conditional P1 paper AD2 Adhesive question only if other relevant fields held
All Actual print/finish to identify Receiving finish V1 to identify No diagnosis or material winner

If B later looks different from A, that comparison cannot isolate facestock as the cause when adhesive also changed. C is a proposed way to ask a narrower question, not evidence of compatibility or supplier availability. Other relevant variables still need matching.

Keep V1's finished surface, application conditions, artwork/finish and observation stage with each candidate. Record visible edge position and timing before assigning poor contact or spring-back as the cause. The diagram's contact and bending icons show questions rather than actual wet-out, force or microscopy. No label outline or liner-release approval substitutes for this applied-construction record.

Download the label edge lifting curved jars record (.csv). HYPOTHETICAL rows are invented examples. Use ACTUAL_BLANK for permitted project inputs; replace that row label only when recording actual facts. Empty evidence, observation and date fields mean unknown or not performed, never acceptance. Keep checkpoints and revisions separate.

Send every changed construction field and the actual finished surface before requesting a matched comparison or cause review. Packrivo coordinates independent suppliers. These records establish no supplier offer, service availability or MOQ exception; its published baseline is 500 pieces per product/design.

title: Sealed Air Cushions Can Respond Differently When Pressure, Volume or Temperature Is Constrained
html:
A sealed air cushion does not necessarily keep the same pressure, shape or contact with the packed product throughout shipping. Its response depends partly on which conditions are constrained.

When a trapped gas warms, its absolute pressure increases if its volume is fixed. If its absolute pressure stays constant and it can expand freely, its volume increases instead. A flexible air pillow inside a shipping carton may follow neither limiting case exactly.

For a jewellery, candle or gift brand, the important distinction is that an air pillow looking fully inflated at pack-out does not establish how it will support the contents under different transport conditions.

The gas relationship depends on what remains fixed

NASA’s public educational explanation of the equation of state describes the ideal-gas relationship:

P × V = n × R × T

Here:

  • P is the gas’s absolute pressure.

  • V is the volume occupied by the gas.

  • n is the amount of gas.

  • R is the universal gas constant.

  • T is absolute temperature in kelvin (K).

If the amount of gas remains constant, the relationship between two states can be written:

P₂V₂ / P₁V₁ = T₂ / T₁

This does not mean pressure and volume each change by the temperature ratio. Their product changes according to that ratio.

One more distinction matters for inflatable packaging: the pressure in this equation is absolute internal pressure, not simply the pressure above the surrounding atmosphere.

The difference between internal and surrounding pressure matters to the forces acting on a flexible film. It is not interchangeable with the absolute pressure used in the gas equation.

The relationship is an idealized model. It does not describe the mechanical behavior of the bag film, its seals or its contact with surrounding packaging.

The same temperature change produces two different limiting results

Consider a completely hypothetical quantity of gas initially at 300 K and later at 330 K.

Assume the gas amount does not change and ideal-gas behavior applies. These temperatures are mathematical inputs, not measurements or predicted shipping conditions.

A sealed rigid volume changes pressure

First, suppose the gas is enclosed in a perfectly rigid chamber whose volume cannot change.

Because volume and gas amount stay fixed:

P₂ / P₁ = T₂ / T₁ = 330 / 300 = 1.10

The final absolute pressure is 1.10 times the initial absolute pressure, an increase of 10%.

The calculation does not say the gauge pressure increases by 10%, and it does not supply a pressure in psi or kPa. Those results would require additional information.

A rigid chamber is a limiting illustration, not a description of an ordinary flexible packaging pillow.

Gas at fixed absolute pressure changes volume

Now suppose the same idealized amount of gas can expand while its absolute internal pressure is held constant.

Then:

V₂ / V₁ = T₂ / T₁ = 330 / 300 = 1.10

The final gas volume is 1.10 times the initial volume.

This is a 10% increase in gas volume under the stated assumptions. It is not necessarily a 10% increase in pillow length, height or thickness.

The two results describe alternative constraints, not simultaneous predictions for the same package.

In the rigid case, volume remains unchanged. In the fixed-pressure case, pressure remains unchanged. When both pressure and volume can change, the gas equation alone cannot determine either final value.

A flexible pillow responds to its film and surrounding carton

A shipping air pillow is neither a rigid container nor an imaginary gas chamber that expands without resistance.

Its response involves the flexibility of the film, the seams, the initial inflated shape and the space available inside the closed carton.

Imagine a flexible pillow warming while sealed.

If it has room to change shape, some of the gas-state change may appear as increased volume. If the carton restricts expansion, the pillow cannot follow the freely expanding illustration.

Its internal pressure and the forces acting on its film and contact surfaces may change instead.

Neither result can be quantified from the ideal-gas relationship without knowing the relevant mechanical constraints.

Surrounding air pressure introduces another distinction.

If surrounding pressure decreases, the difference between the pillow’s internal pressure and its surroundings may increase. A flexible pillow may expand if its film and available space permit.

If its volume is rigidly fixed and temperature and gas amount remain unchanged, a change in surrounding pressure alone would not change its calculated internal absolute pressure. It would change the pressure difference across the enclosure.

A real pillow can change volume, so its internal pressure may also change as the system responds.

Similarly, an increase in surrounding pressure may encourage a flexible pillow to occupy less volume, depending on its internal state and mechanical constraints.

None of these possibilities establishes a particular change in size, seal loading or protection during an actual shipment.

Gas loss creates a further limitation. If air escapes through a seal or film, the trapped gas amount is no longer constant. The simple fixed-gas-amount comparison no longer describes the complete change.

Two similar-looking gift packs can have different constraints

Consider a hypothetical small gift brand using a sealed air pillow to fill space beside a smooth-sided gift box inside an outer shipping carton.

The brand considers two layouts.

In the first layout, the pillow occupies part of a relatively open void. It has some room to change shape without immediately pressing against every surrounding surface.

In the second layout, a visually similar pillow is confined between the gift box and the outer carton’s closed wall. Its available expansion space is much more restricted.

Both pillows might look similarly inflated before final closure.

That appearance does not mean their pressure and volume would respond identically if the environmental conditions changed.

The first pillow may have greater freedom to change its shape and contact position. The second has a stronger geometric constraint, so it cannot be represented by the same free-expansion assumption.

But this comparison does not establish which pack is safer.

The more restrained pillow might exert different contact forces. The less restrained pillow might move or lose a useful contact position. The actual responses depend on the package, bag construction and conditions.

No hypothetical gas calculation demonstrates whether either layout will adequately protect the gift.

The example explains why the closed-carton geometry matters to the gas-state interpretation, rather than merely whether the pillow initially looks full.

Inflatable void fill is not automatically verified impact cushioning

UPS’s public US packaging guidance describes inflatable air bags as void-fill material for lightweight items without sharp corners or edges.

It also warns that extreme hot or cold temperatures can affect their ability to provide adequate product protection.

That guidance does not specify a universal inflation pressure, permitted temperature range, safe product weight or performance result for a particular air-pillow construction.

An air pillow used to occupy empty space is not automatically a verified shock-cushioning system.

For a glass candle container, delicate jewellery component or other fragile product, the distinction remains especially important. Preventing obvious movement is not equivalent to establishing resistance to the impacts that may occur during transport.

Nor can the gas equation determine whether a visibly smaller or softer pillow necessarily provides worse protection.

The complete packaging arrangement matters. Packrivo’s mailer-box protection guide addresses the separate question of reviewing the outer carton, inserts, cushioning, contents and closure as one system.

Identify the actual constraint before interpreting the air cushion

A buyer reviewing an inflatable-packaging proposal can make a more useful decision by distinguishing three situations.

If the claimed behavior assumes fixed volume, establish what physically prevents the pillow from changing volume in the fully closed package. A close-fitting carton is not automatically a perfectly rigid gas chamber.

If the claimed behavior assumes constant absolute pressure, establish whether the pillow actually has freedom to expand and what film resistance, contact or surrounding-pressure conditions might prevent that assumption.

If neither condition is established, the ideal-gas equation identifies a relationship between possible gas states, not a unique final pressure or volume.

A proposal also needs to distinguish an effectively sealed gas quantity from a product whose gas retention is unknown. Actual leakage would change the amount of gas available.

For a relevant shipping proposal, the missing physical information may include the pillow construction, remaining space after carton closure, surrounding contact surfaces and anticipated environmental conditions along the intended route.

If the proposed benefit is protection from transport impacts rather than simply occupying a void, appropriate evidence for the actual packed system remains a separate question.

Packrivo can coordinate these sourcing and project questions, but an equation, supplier photograph or nominal inflated appearance cannot substitute for package-specific performance evidence.

The useful conclusion is therefore not a universal inflation setting. It is knowing which pressure–volume assumptions the proposed package permits, which remain unverified and why its initial appearance cannot settle the transport-protection decision.

Source/access note — Sources were checked on 10 October 2026. NASA provides a public general ideal-gas explanation; the undated UPS US guidance concerns inflatable void fill. Neither supplies actual pillow pressure, dimensions or protection results for these hypothetical arrangements.

A small starting pressure difference changes the percentage comparison

Extend the original ideal-gas explanation with explicit, invented pressure baselines. INITIAL30 is a perfectly rigid chamber at 300 K, holding a fixed amount of ideal gas at 102 kPa absolute while its surroundings are 100 kPa absolute. The pressure difference is 102 − 100 = 2 kPa. This is a limiting calculation, not an inflation instruction or a flexible-pillow specification.

Hypothetical configuration Named object Relationship Input or next scope
INITIAL30 ABSOLUTE_TEMPERATURE assumed input 300 K
INITIAL30 OUTSIDE_ABSOLUTE_PRESSURE assumed input 100 kPa
INITIAL30 INSIDE_ABSOLUTE_PRESSURE assumed input 102 kPa
INITIAL30 INSIDE_MINUS_OUTSIDE calculated from INITIAL30_IN-INITIAL30_OUT; 2 kPa
INITIAL30 INITIAL30 assumes IDEAL_RIGID_FIXED_GAS_AMOUNT_AND_VOLUME
WARM30 ABSOLUTE_TEMPERATURE assumed input 330 K
WARM30 OUTSIDE_ABSOLUTE_PRESSURE assumed input 100 kPa
WARM30 INSIDE_ABSOLUTE_PRESSURE calculated from INITIAL30_IN*WARM30_T/INITIAL30_T; 112.2 kPa
WARM30 INSIDE_MINUS_OUTSIDE calculated from WARM30_IN-WARM30_OUT; 12.2 kPa
WARM30 WARM30 assumes IDEAL_RIGID_FIXED_GAS_AMOUNT_AND_VOLUME
LOWER_OUTSIDE30 ABSOLUTE_TEMPERATURE assumed input 300 K
LOWER_OUTSIDE30 OUTSIDE_ABSOLUTE_PRESSURE assumed input 90 kPa
LOWER_OUTSIDE30 INSIDE_ABSOLUTE_PRESSURE assumed input 102 kPa
LOWER_OUTSIDE30 INSIDE_MINUS_OUTSIDE calculated from LOWER_OUTSIDE30_IN-LOWER_OUTSIDE30_OUT; 12 kPa
LOWER_OUTSIDE30 LOWER_OUTSIDE30 assumes IDEAL_RIGID_FIXED_GAS_AMOUNT_AND_VOLUME
WARM30 PRESSURE_RATIO calculated from WARM30_IN/INITIAL30_IN; 1.1 ratio
WARM30 DIFFERENCE_RATIO calculated from WARM30_DIFF/INITIAL30_DIFF; 6.1 ratio
GAS30 WARM30_VS_LOWER_OUTSIDE30 are DIFFERENT_CHANGED_VARIABLE_BRANCHES
GAS30 IDEAL_GAS_ARITHMETIC does not establish FILM_SEAL_LEAK_STRESS_OR_PROTECTION

WARM30 holds gas amount and volume unchanged and raises the assumed temperature to 330 K. Its absolute internal pressure becomes 102 × 330 ÷ 300 = 112.2 kPa. If outside pressure remains 100 kPa, the difference becomes 12.2 kPa. Absolute pressure has a 1.10 ratio, but the pressure difference has a 6.10 ratio against its small initial 2 kPa baseline. Applying the 10% absolute increase to that difference would give the wrong answer.

A different branch, LOWER_OUTSIDE30, keeps the initial 300 K gas state and rigid volume but changes outside pressure to 90 kPa absolute. Internal absolute pressure stays 102 kPa under those assumptions; the difference becomes 12 kPa. Do not combine this branch with WARM30 silently. Each row states which variable changed and which remained constrained.

A real film, seam, contact arrangement or gas loss can make neither rigid branch representative. The arithmetic calculates no membrane stress, leak, burst, contact load or protection. Keep absolute pressure for the gas relation and the inside-minus-outside difference for its separate role, then ask the responsible source which actual mechanical constraints are known. UPS void-fill guidance does not validate these invented states for shipping.

Download the air cushion absolute pressure gauge difference baseline record (.csv). It includes the original table fields and scenarios alongside the added relationships. HYPOTHETICAL rows are editorial examples or required review scopes, not actual records. Actual quantity, configuration, component and file identities, materials, process, specification, copy, method, condition, observation, owner, decision, evidence and dates are blank. ACTUAL_BLANK is a separate empty starting row; enter permitted project evidence before using an actual record. A blank means unknown.

Use the Mailer Box Shipping Protection: Review the Packed System for its separate question.

Source scope checked 17 October 2026: NASA’s ideal-gas equation is conditional on gas amount, absolute temperature/pressure and stated constraints. UPS US void-fill advice for lightweight items without sharp edges and its temperature cautions are not actual air-pillow performance, inflation limits or transport approval. The added configurations and calculations are hypothetical, with actual evidence and decisions pending.

Discuss this packaging specification with Packrivo. We coordinate independent suppliers. MOQ: 500 pieces per product/design; illustrative quantities are not production offers. Confirm materials, samples, price and timing for your project.

title: Film WVTR and Moisture Paths in a Finished Pouch
html:
A water-vapour transmission rate (WVTR) measured on flat packaging film does not establish how well a finished pouch controls moisture exchange.

If both water vapour and oxygen are part of the requirement, use OTR and WVTR Measure Different Barrier Questions to keep the two document requests separate. Neither flat-film rate establishes the performance of the proposed finished pouch and its closure.

Water vapour can pass through an intact film wall. It may also enter or leave through an opening, an imperfect closure or another path in the assembled package. A test of one route does not automatically measure the other.

For a small jewellery, candle or gift brand considering protective pouches, the decision is whether the intended claim needs evidence about the film material, the finished pouch and closure, or both. A photograph showing water droplets beading on the surface cannot settle that decision.

Water vapour can take two different routes

Consider a polymer pouch surrounding printed care cards.

The first possible route is directly through its intact film wall.

Water-vapour molecules can move through a barrier material even when it has no visible hole. The rate depends on the material and the conditions under which transmission occurs. A film does not have to become visibly wet for water vapour to pass through it.

The second possible route is around the barrier wall.

A pouch opening, an incomplete seal, a gap at a closure or a damaged area can provide another pathway between the pouch interior and its surroundings. Depending on the actual construction and environmental conditions, that pathway may permit moisture transport or the exchange of moisture-bearing air.

The distinction matters because a film can have a comparatively low measured WVTR while the pouch made from it still has an unresolved opening.

Conversely, closing the opening does not eliminate vapour transmission through the film itself.

Neither statement assigns a measured transmission rate to a particular pouch. They identify two physical routes that must not be confused.

Flat-film WVTR measures the material under defined conditions

ASTM F1249-25 describes a method for determining water-vapour transmission through flexible barrier materials using a modulated infrared sensor.

Its published scope covers films and sheets up to 3 mm thick, including specified single-layer and multilayer materials. The method distinguishes water-vapour transmission rate, permeance and, for homogeneous materials, a permeability coefficient.

A reported film WVTR, commonly expressed in grams per square metre per day, describes transmission relative to the area of the tested material and the measurement period. It is not automatically a rate for the entire assembled pouch.

The temperature, humidity conditions, actual film construction and measurement method matter when interpreting or comparing results.

A lower WVTR from one film test can indicate lower measured transmission through that tested material under the stated conditions. It does not establish the relative performance of two finished pouches if their openings, seams or other constructions differ.

The ASTM scope also cautions that WVTR cannot always be assumed to vary inversely with thickness or directly with the water-vapour partial-pressure difference.

That prevents a tempting shortcut: a buyer should not simply halve a reported WVTR because a proposed film is twice as thick, or transfer a reported value to different humidity conditions through an assumed constant relationship.

Those calculations would require technical justification that the supplied number alone does not provide.

An undefined pouch opening leaves the care-card question unanswered

Imagine a hypothetical gift brand considering a translucent polymer pouch for near-white printed care cards.

The supplier provides a flat-film WVTR result. The brand also receives an illustration showing water droplets on the outside of the film.

However, the proposed pouch opening is not yet defined.

One possible design would be filled with the cards and then closed with a heat seal. Another would use a reusable fold-over opening.

These are invented design alternatives, not tested products. Neither has a measured package transmission rate.

The film data could be identical for both proposals because the wall material is the same.

But the opening presents a different physical question.

In the heat-sealed proposal, the brand would need to know how the intended finished seal is formed and whether the actual sealed construction has been assessed.

In the fold-over proposal, the brand would need to understand the remaining opening and the way the pouch is actually used.

Even where a design has an apparently continuous closure, that appearance alone cannot establish its moisture-barrier performance.

The missing information is not another decimal place in the flat-film result. It is the definition and assessment of the assembled enclosure.

The film report may still help the brand compare potential wall materials. It cannot decide whether either finished pouch will maintain a particular internal relative humidity or protect the cards for a stated period.

The cards and enclosed air also begin with their own moisture conditions. No initial moisture measurements or subsequent internal humidity measurements exist in this hypothetical example.

It would therefore be unjustified to describe either pouch as keeping its contents dry, maintaining a specified humidity or providing a particular storage life.

Water beading is not evidence of humidity retention

Water beading concerns the visible behaviour of liquid water on a surface.

WVTR concerns the movement of water vapour through a material under specified conditions.

Those are different observations.

A photograph of droplets remaining rounded on polymer film does not reveal the film’s WVTR. It does not measure moisture movement through a closure or establish what happens to the humidity inside the pouch.

Even a convincing water-beading demonstration on the central panel leaves the opening and other possible pathways unexamined.

Likewise, a measured WVTR does not by itself establish that the pouch resists liquid water at its seams or closure.

The brand should not translate either observation into a general waterproof or humidity-protection promise.

The protective claim determines which evidence is needed

If the immediate purchasing decision concerns only the film material, comparable flat-film WVTR evidence may be relevant.

The buyer can use that evidence to assess the offered material within the conditions and measurement scope stated in the report. That decision does not extend automatically to an assembled pouch.

If the intended claim concerns a closed pouch as a protective enclosure, the relevant question expands to the finished construction.

The actual opening, sealing arrangement, seams and intended use need to be defined before a qualified reviewer can determine what finished-package assessment would answer the claim.

AMETEK MOCON’s package-cartridge information illustrates the measurement distinction.

The manufacturer separately describes cartridges for film samples, flexible pouches, complete packages and closures. Its package adaptor is described as accommodating complete packages and closures, while a dedicated flexible-pouch fixture uses a different mounting arrangement.

These are examples of measurement capabilities, not test results for the proposed care-card pouch. The reviewer must still establish whether a particular method and mounting arrangement assess the intended closure and relevant vapour pathways.

A finished-package test may answer a different question from a flat-film test. It does not automatically establish internal humidity or storage duration under every intended use condition.

When the brand must support both its film selection and a finished-pouch protective statement, both levels of evidence may be needed.

That distinction gives the sourcing discussion a useful direction.

The brand can first describe the pouch’s intended function and opening arrangement through a packaging supplier brief. Once a physical construction exists, the packaging sample review guide can help organize a separate examination of the assembled pack. Neither document replaces a suitable moisture-performance assessment.

Packrivo coordinates packaging sourcing and project questions; it does not establish film permeability, seal integrity or humidity-retention performance through its own testing.

The practical purchasing decision is to keep the wall-material claim separate from the finished-enclosure claim.

A flat-film WVTR may justify further consideration of the film. Only relevant evidence addressing the assembled pouch and its intended use can support an appropriately bounded finished-package moisture-protection statement.

Source review: 10 October 2026. ASTM F1249-25 was listed as active, with its catalogue last updated on 10 November 2025. Only the publicly accessible catalogue description and scope were reviewed, not the paid complete standard. The AMETEK MOCON product page was undated; its fixture descriptions do not verify any particular pouch’s performance. No material sample, measured WVTR, assembled pouch, closure or humidity-retention result was examined for this article.

Keep each finished closure outside the flat-film result field

Imagine document F-H is offered for film FL-H, while P-A proposes a heat-sealed pouch and P-B a fold-over pouch using that film identity. This record supplies no numerical WVTR or actual document. The offered wall-material evidence and the two finished-construction questions remain separate.

Record Intended object Evidence question
F-H / FL-H Flat film and stated conditions Exact material, method, temperature/humidity basis
P-A Proposed heat-sealed construction Actual complete closure and mounting/evaluation scope
P-B Proposed fold-over construction Actual opening and intended use
Protective wording Finished package claim Evidence for relevant assembly and conditions

A shared film reference does not justify copying one finished-pouch outcome into the other. The same intended care-card contents also need their initial condition identified; the diagram does not establish moisture content or internal humidity.

The smooth band and fold are generic proposal symbols, not seal-integrity evidence. Keep actual value/unit and test conditions in the material row, and ask what the finished-package assessment includes at seams and closure. No film value, liquid-water bead or closed-looking seam supplies a humidity-retention or storage-life result here. All rates, observations, methods for the complete packages and wording decisions stay blank.

Download the film WVTR versus finished pouch record (.csv). HYPOTHETICAL rows are invented examples. Use ACTUAL_BLANK for permitted project inputs; replace that row label only when recording actual facts. Empty evidence, observation and date fields mean unknown or not performed, never acceptance. Keep checkpoints and revisions separate.

Send the exact film report and each actual finished-pouch/closure definition, then ask for the evidence level required by the intended claim. Packrivo coordinates independent suppliers. These records establish no supplier offer, service availability or MOQ exception; its published baseline is 500 pieces per product/design.

title: Pallet Stacking: Column and Interlocking Load Paths
html:
A pallet pattern should do more than fit the maximum number of cartons into a rectangle. It must also support the cartons above, preserve support at the pallet deck and allow the complete load to be restrained during handling.

Use the Regular Slotted Shipping Cartons: Size Around the Inner Pack as a structural reference when identifying the cartons in the proposed pallet pattern. Obtain the actual carton dimensions, condition and loading evidence; the concept does not provide a stacking-strength rating.

Straight column stacking and interlocking layers address different parts of this problem. Aligned columns generally preserve a clearer vertical load path. Interlocking arrangements can help resist movement between layers under suitable conditions, but they change where upper cartons bear on those below.

Neither pattern is automatically safe. A useful packaging proposal shows the actual carton arrangement, pallet construction, loaded weight, layer contacts and intended restraints before anyone decides whether the complete load is suitable for a particular journey.

Column stacking preserves a clearer vertical load path

In a column-stacked arrangement, each carton sits directly above a carton in the previous layer. The vertical edges and corners remain aligned from one layer to the next.

This alignment matters because a corrugated shipping carton is not a solid block. Its erected walls, corners, panels and closures form a structure that responds to the loads applied to it.

When identical cartons are stacked directly above one another, the upper carton can transfer load towards corresponding structural regions below. Moving an upper carton across a lower carton’s panel or joint changes that contact relationship.

FedEx Freight’s US LTL packing guidance, accessed 10 October 2026, recommends column stacking to improve top-to-bottom compression strength. It also describes load-protector pads between tiers as a way to improve stability.

This is a general carrier recommendation, not a compression rating for a particular carton.

A column arrangement can still move sideways if the cartons are inadequately restrained. It can also perform poorly when the pallet deck fails to support important parts of the bottom layer.

Column alignment answers a vertical-support question. It does not independently establish that the entire pallet is stable.

Interlocking layers change the contact between cartons

An interlocking arrangement changes the positions or orientations of cartons between layers. Instead of every upper carton sitting directly above the same footprint, some cartons can span joints between cartons below.

This may help limit relative movement in a suitably designed load. However, it also changes the vertical support points.

Consider an upper shipping carton whose corner sits over the top panel of a lower carton rather than over the corresponding lower corner. The load is no longer being introduced at the same structural location as it would be in a column stack.

Whether that difference is acceptable depends on the real carton construction, contents, contact surfaces, load and handling conditions. A top-view pattern cannot quantify the effect.

FedEx’s US pallet guidance, accessed 10 October 2026, describes interlocking as a possible stability improvement when carton contents are rigid. It also advises maintaining appropriate corner-to-corner and edge-to-edge contact.

That rigid-content condition matters. Cartons holding glass candles, lightweight empty gift boxes or jewellery packaging components may have very different internal support arrangements. Their outer dimensions alone do not establish whether the contents provide suitable support.

A historical UPS Air Freight Packaging Pointers guide from 2005 favours corner-aligned column stacking and also identifies interlocking as a possible stability improvement when the contents are rigid. Its rigid-content condition and appropriate corner-to-corner and edge-to-edge support matter; the guidance is not a blanket contrast with FedEx’s conditional advice. This older source is historical context, not a current acceptance rule for every UPS service.

These recommendations should not be reduced to a universal winner. The buyer needs to ask two separate questions: how does vertical load pass through this arrangement, and how will the cartons be kept together during handling?

Twelve cartons fit the hypothetical footprint on paper

Consider an entirely hypothetical planning example.

A brand proposes a pallet with a nominal footprint of 1200 × 1000 mm. Each finished, closed shipping carton has a proposed outside footprint of 400 × 250 mm.

For an aligned layout:

  • Three cartons along the 1200 mm direction occupy 3 × 400 = 1200 mm.
  • Four cartons along the 1000 mm direction occupy 4 × 250 = 1000 mm.
  • The resulting rectangular layer contains 3 × 4 = 12 cartons.

The area calculation agrees. Each carton occupies a nominal 0.10 m², and twelve occupy 1.20 m², equal to the nominal pallet footprint.

That is a geometric planning result, not evidence of a feasible loaded pallet.

The layout has zero nominal clearance. It does not account for differences between nominal and actual usable pallet-deck dimensions, dimensional variation in finished cartons, bulging, tape or other projections, or the practical positioning of cartons during loading.

Even a small change in the finished footprint can prevent the proposed arrangement from fitting as drawn.

Turning every carton through 90 degrees does not automatically preserve the twelve-carton grid. In that uniform rotated orientation, each carton occupies 250 mm along the 1200 mm direction and 400 mm along the 1000 mm direction. Neither pallet dimension divides evenly by its corresponding carton dimension.

A mixed-orientation layout might be proposed, but it must be drawn and checked carton by carton. It cannot inherit the aligned layout’s count simply because the total carton area is unchanged.

Most importantly, twelve cartons in one layer says nothing about the permissible number of layers, total payload or safe stacking height.

The bottom layer must meet the actual pallet deck

A pallet’s nominal outside dimensions do not describe every support surface beneath the cartons.

Wooden pallets may have spaces between their top deck boards. Different pallet constructions also distribute support differently. A carton can be fully inside the pallet perimeter while one of its bottom corners lies over a gap.

The position of each carton therefore matters relative to the actual deck boards, not just the pallet’s rectangular outline.

The packing reviewer should overlay the bottom-layer layout onto the deck-board arrangement. This reveals where carton corners and edges are supported and where the proposed base might bridge unsupported spaces.

FedEx’s pallet guidance describes bottom load-protector pads as a means of providing a more level surface and helping prevent cartons from entering gaps between boards.

Such a pad is not automatically a structural solution. Its proposed material, construction and effect on the loaded system still need evaluation.

Avoid cartons extending beyond the pallet perimeter. Also avoid treating a visually neat, flush edge as proof that the base is properly supported.

A stable unit needs more than an efficient layer pattern

Even well-aligned cartons need a way to remain together as one handling unit.

A palletized load may encounter lifting, changes in direction, vibration, braking, temporary storage and contact with other freight. These conditions create demands that are different from a static top-down load.

Interlayer sheets, load protectors, edge boards, stretch film and banding have different roles. For example, a tier sheet may change contact between layers, while suitable restraint can help prevent cartons from separating or shifting relative to the pallet.

The proposed securing method must be assessed as part of the actual load, including how the restraint connects the cartons to the pallet.

FedEx Freight’s current packing guidance distinguishes stacking methods from securing materials, including edge boards, banding and stretch wrap. These are related but separate design decisions.

Adding more wrapping does not automatically restore lost carton support. Likewise, a correctly aligned column pattern does not replace the need to evaluate the restraint system.

Neither a wrapping specification nor a safe stacking height can be inferred from the twelve-carton footprint calculation.

Compare complete pallet candidates at the layer interfaces

Return to the hypothetical 1200 × 1000 mm pallet.

Candidate A uses the aligned 3 × 4 arrangement. Its nominal count is twelve cartons per layer, and corresponding carton footprints align between consecutive layers.

This gives a clear starting arrangement for reviewing vertical contacts. But the reviewer still needs the actual carton height and mass, intended number of layers, pallet-deck construction, support conditions and proposed restraint system.

Candidate B uses an alternative rotated or interlocking arrangement. Before treating it as a competing solution, the packing party must resolve its complete geometry. The carton count, gaps, orientation and support relationships cannot be assumed from Candidate A.

For Candidate B, a layer-interface view should show whether upper carton edges and corners bear over supported regions of the lower layer or cross joints and panels differently.

Compare the two candidates using the same actual filled-carton specification and intended handling conditions. Otherwise, changes to the cartons or contents could be mistaken for effects of the layer pattern.

A useful comparison package contains a dimensioned top view of every distinct layer and a side section showing the proposed vertical arrangement. It also identifies the contact between layers, carton orientation, deck boards and gaps, pallet perimeter, load distribution, proposed restraint materials and complete loaded dimensions and mass.

Mark estimated values as estimates. Unknown carton strength, content rigidity, actual weight and handling conditions remain open questions rather than values to infer from the drawing.

The meaningful output is not a preferred pattern in isolation. It is a complete candidate unit load that a responsible packing, engineering or freight reviewer can evaluate.

The intended transport service determines the next evaluation

Different distribution routes can expose the same pallet to different handling and stacking conditions.

A pallet intended for warehouse storage, domestic less-than-truckload transport, air freight or an international shipment may need different checks. Carrier rules also depend on the actual service, contents, dimensions, weight and handling arrangement.

Use the selected carrier’s applicable current terms and packing guidance rather than treating one general article as approval for all services.

If the technical reviewer cannot yet establish whether the cartons can support the proposed load, or whether the restraints will keep the unit stable, the buyer should leave the pattern unresolved and obtain the necessary project-specific assessment.

For a small jewellery, candle or gift brand, the immediate purchasing decision is therefore straightforward: compare layer patterns by vertical support, deck support and restraint as one loaded system, not by cartons per layer alone.

Packrivo can help organise the packaging specifications and coordinate the questions through a packaging enquiry. The packing party, qualified technical reviewers and relevant carrier remain responsible for evaluating the actual arrangement and its intended transport conditions.

Source scope: FedEx and FedEx Freight’s undated US carrier guidance was accessed on 10 October 2026. The UPS reference is historical, dating to 2005. No actual pallet, carton, restraint system or transport performance was tested or verified for this article.

Access boundary: the relevant UPS page-8 wording was checked through the official indexed document excerpt. Direct PDF access failed in this review, so this article does not claim a fresh visual review of the complete historical PDF or access to a current UPS acceptance standard.

Recheck the declared grid when finished carton dimensions change

Extend the nominal 1200 x 1000 mm example with a separate invented finished footprint of 401 x 251 mm. The declared 3 x 4 grid would occupy 1203 x 1004 mm, exceeding that nominal rectangle by 3 and 4 mm. This is hypothetical geometry, not a standard tolerance, measured carton or safe pallet decision.

Case Declared3x4 extent Nominal rectangle comparison What remains open
400x 250 mm input 1200x 1000 mm Zero nominal margin Actual deck, contacts and restraint
401x 251 mm input 1203x 1004 mm 3 mm /4 mm excess Cannot retain this declared grid as fitting
Layer/deck/restraint Three separate views No alternative count calculated Complete unit-load technical review

Do not round the second footprint back to the first or infer that some different mixed pattern must hold twelve. Any alternative needs its own complete layer geometry. These assumed one-millimetre changes are not a supplier tolerance or a prediction of bulging.

The figure illustrates contact locations, not equal carton counts or a complete interlocking plan. Overlay actual bottom corners on the actual deck-board/gap map and obtain the restraint route separately. A footprint calculation supplies no payload, number of layers or stack height. The CSV leaves actual support and technical decisions blank; no drawing authorizes loading a shipment.

Download the column versus interlocking pallet stacking record (.csv). HYPOTHETICAL rows are invented examples. Use ACTUAL_BLANK for permitted project inputs; replace that row label only when recording actual facts. Empty evidence, observation and date fields mean unknown or not performed, never acceptance. Keep checkpoints and revisions separate.

Send every actual layer drawing, finished measurements, deck overlay and proposed restraint as one unit-load review package. Packrivo coordinates independent suppliers. These records establish no supplier offer, service availability or MOQ exception; its published baseline is 500 pieces per product/design.

title: Wet-Ink Setoff and Surface Abrasion Need Different Print Investigations
html:
A printed image appearing on the back of another sheet and a pale mark on a finished packaging sleeve should not automatically receive the same treatment. The first observation may point to ink transfer while printed sheets were stacked. The second may point to mechanical contact during converting, assembly or use.

For a small jewellery, candle or gift brand, the practical decision is where to begin the investigation. Preserve the contacting sheet pair when an ink-shaped transfer appears before converting. When a formed sleeve develops a visible surface mark during tray movement, establish the contact path before requesting an anti-scuff finish.

Neither appearance proves its cause. Both require evidence from the relevant production stage.

Wet-Ink Setoff Involves Transfer Between Adjacent Sheets

In sheetfed printing, wet-ink setoff occurs when ink transfers from a printed surface to an adjacent sheet before or during the ink-setting and drying process.

Sappi’s Sheetfed Ink Setoff technical guide, Version 001, © 2012, describes ink transfer onto the backside of a neighbouring sheet. It distinguishes relatively light transfer from blocking, in which sheets become stuck together by an ink or coating film under pressure.

That distinction matters when reviewing a printed care card.

Suppose a dark artwork shape is visible on the back of the next sheet in a pile. If the deposited mark corresponds to the printed image on the contacting sheet, wet-ink setoff becomes a relevant possibility.

The physical relationship between the sheets is more informative than the description "the print rubbed off."

Look for the original contacting faces, the position of the mark relative to the artwork and the stage at which it was first observed. An image merely visible through the original paper is not the same observation as ink deposited onto a separate sheet.

A matching pattern alone does not establish when the transfer occurred or which production condition caused it.

Sappi identifies ink-setting behaviour, substrate compatibility, sheet separation, pressure and handling among the considerations in conventional sheetfed work. The same guide cautions that ink feeling dry to the touch may not be fully polymerised.

The buyer should therefore request the printer’s process-specific review rather than prescribe a universal drying interval, press adjustment or protective coating.

Surface Abrasion Involves Mechanical Contact and Movement

A surface mark created through rubbing involves a different physical question: what contacted the printed surface, and what movement or pressure occurred?

Sappi’s separate Ink Chalk and Scuff technical guide, Version 001, © 2012, describes ink scuffing as dry pigment transfer through abrasive mechanical contact. It discusses ink-film resilience, paper surface characteristics and mechanical action as relevant factors.

A pale line on a printed sleeve could be consistent with local surface wear. It might involve pigment loss, a change in finish appearance or damage to another surface layer. The line alone cannot identify which layer changed.

The location and direction of the mark become important.

A narrow line along the travel path of an internal tray presents a different investigation from a matching ink image transferred between flat sheets in a stack. The printer and converter may need to consider the tray’s contact points, sleeve construction, printed surface and the stage at which the mark was first present.

Mechanical marking can also occur during finishing or handling before the package is assembled. A mark found on a formed sleeve should not automatically be attributed to the consumer’s opening action.

Two Hypothetical Packaging Observations Lead to Different Questions

Consider two independent, hypothetical examples. They are teaching scenarios, not Packrivo production cases or measured test results.

Example A: A Care Card Transfers an Image Before Converting

A gift brand receives evidence of printed care-card sheets before cutting and folding.

Sheet A carries a dark printed motif on its front. The backside of adjacent Sheet B shows a corresponding dark pattern in the area where the two sheets contacted.

The relevant evidence is the relationship between the printed front and receiving back, not simply the darkness of the mark.

Preserve the identified pair and its original orientation. Photograph the affected faces and their relationship before any additional handling where practicable. If the sheets have already been separated, retain their identities without trying to recreate the transfer.
