The printer needs to establish the actual print process and review when the mark was observed relative to printing, delivery, stacking, storage and converting.

The specific investigation concerns whether the ink or coating film transferred through contact before it was sufficiently set or dry, and what production evidence could distinguish that possibility from another explanation.

An anti-scuff coating specification does not, by itself, explain the apparent image transfer between these sheets.

Example B: A Formed Sleeve Shows a Pale Line After Tray Travel

A candle gift brand reviews a formed printed sleeve containing a sliding tray.

After the tray moves through the sleeve, a pale line is noticed along an internal printed area. The observation is not an image-shaped deposit on the backside of a neighbouring printed sheet.

The initial question is whether the line existed before the tray moved. If no earlier view exists, the time of its appearance remains uncertain.

The next question concerns the actual interface: which tray edge or surface approaches the marked sleeve area, in what direction, and under which assembly or handling conditions?

The converter can review the sleeve and tray geometry. The printer can assess whether the visible change concerns the ink film, surface finish or another material layer.

If a contact point is implicated, a construction change and a surface-treatment change remain different possible responses. Neither should be described as an effective remedy without relevant comparison evidence.

A pale line is not, on its own, proof of deficient abrasion resistance.

The Two Mechanisms Can Interact Without Becoming the Same Defect

Setoff and scuffing are not necessarily independent of the full printing and finishing process.

Sappi’s historical guidance discusses how measures associated with sheet separation can also affect later surface abrasion. That illustrates why an investigation should consider the complete print-to-converting sequence instead of treating every mark as a request for a stronger topcoat.

It does not justify a buyer specifying spray powder, press chemistry, temperature or machine settings.

The guides concern established commercial printing processes, particularly conventional sheetfed inks. Their drying explanations and production advice should not be applied automatically to UV-curable inks, toner-based digital printing or other systems with different mechanisms.

Where the printing method is not confirmed, identifying that method belongs at the beginning of the technical investigation.

A project may also have both observations: ink transfer in a printed stack and a separate surface mark after forming. Resolving one does not demonstrate that the other has been resolved.

Preserve the Evidence That Changes the Printer’s Next Investigation

For suspected setoff, the useful submission is the original sheet pair, its face orientation, the image-to-transfer relationship and the earliest known production stage of the observation. Ask the printer to investigate the actual setting, drying and stacking conditions and identify what evidence supports its assessment.

For suspected abrasion, provide the marked component, its preceding condition where documented, the opposing contact surface and the relevant movement or finishing stage. Ask the printer and converter to determine what material layer changed and whether contact or construction needs further investigation.

Do not wipe the suspected transfer, deliberately rub a sample to create a new mark, or replace the original evidence with an unrecorded rearrangement. Any formal testing method and acceptance criteria should be established by the responsible technical parties for the actual materials and intended handling conditions.

For the located surface and preceding action, use the surface-scuff observation guide. That record describes what was seen without establishing the cause. Keep a proposed finish change in the print-finish brief, and connect replacement evidence through the sample revision record.

Packrivo can help coordinate the packaging specification, supplier questions and subsequent sample-review requirements. It does not independently certify ink drying, scuff resistance or the success of a proposed treatment.

The useful outcome is not a universal anti-scuff finish. It is a more precise investigation: sheet-to-sheet ink transfer during printing and stacking, or surface change associated with an identified mechanical contact.

That distinction determines which evidence the printer needs before the packaging proposal changes.

Sources checked 10 October 2026. The two Sappi technical guides show Version 001 and © 2012; copyright is not a confirmed publication date. They address historical conventional sheetfed printing guidance, not universal press settings, current certification or a diagnosis of the illustrated marks. No actual sample, printing process or proposed treatment was tested.

Check the receiving face before comparing the mark

Name a new hypothetical contact pair PAIR30: printed A_FRONT faces B_BACK. A returned image, PHOTO_B_FRONT, instead identifies the front of sheet B. It may document a real face in a future project, but under these invented identities it does not show the receiving back named in the proposed contact. Comparing motif positions without resolving that mismatch can send the printer the wrong investigation.

Hypothetical configuration Named object Relationship Input or next scope
PAIR30 A_FRONT proposed faces B_BACK
PHOTO_B_FRONT PHOTO_B_FRONT documents B_FRONT
PAIR30 PHOTO_B_FRONT does not document B_BACK
PAIR30 B_BACK requires EXISTING_FACE_RECORD_IF_AVAILABLE_NO_RECREATE
PAIR30 CORRECT_FACE_IDENTITY does not prove INK_STATE_TIMING_TRANSFER_OR_ABRASION_CAUSE
PAIR30 MISSING_FACE_VIEW remains UNKNOWN_NOT_CLEAN
PAIR30 SHEET_PAIR_QUESTION not closed by ANTI_SCUFF_SLEEVE_PROPOSAL

The next useful request is the existing B_BACK record with its orientation and sheet identity, if one exists. Do not turn a missing record into a claim that no transfer was present, and do not recreate contact to obtain a more convincing pattern. A_FRONT and B_BACK still need their actual relationship established; naming them in the worksheet is not evidence that they touched.

This face check comes before choosing wet setoff or later abrasion as the explanation. A corresponding deposit on the correct receiving face can support a focused question, while a view through the original sheet or a photograph of its other side concerns another observation. Even a correctly located pair does not establish ink state, timing or unique cause. Keep the earliest documented stage beside each view.

For a formed sleeve with a pale line, retain the moving contact and preceding surface condition separately. A supplied anti-scuff finish proposal does not close the sheet-pair question, and a printer’s setting/drying response does not prove that a sleeve travel mark was resolved. The worksheet makes the missing face record answerable without prescribing a press change, rubbing action or drying interval.

Download the setoff contacting sheet face identity evidence record (.csv). It includes the original table fields and scenarios alongside the added relationships. HYPOTHETICAL rows are editorial examples or required review scopes, not actual records. Actual quantity, configuration, component and file identities, materials, process, specification, copy, method, condition, observation, owner, decision, evidence and dates are blank. ACTUAL_BLANK is a separate empty starting row; enter permitted project evidence before using an actual record. A blank means unknown.

Use the Describe Surface Scuffs Before Requesting a Finish Change for its separate question.

Source scope checked 17 October 2026: Sappi Sheetfed Ink Setoff and Ink Chalk and Scuff show Version 001 and copyright 2012; those are not verified publication dates. Conventional sheetfed process explanations distinguish investigations and may use overlapping terminology; no actual printing cause, universal press setting or accepted treatment is established. The added configurations and calculations are hypothetical, with actual evidence and decisions pending.

Discuss this packaging specification with Packrivo. We coordinate independent suppliers. MOQ: 500 pieces per product/design; illustrative quantities are not production offers. Confirm materials, samples, price and timing for your project.

title: Box Lid Clearance Across Component Tolerances
html:
A gift box can have positive nominal lid clearance and still allow an interference combination when its components reach different ends of their permitted dimension ranges. Checking each component against its own limits is not the same as checking the space left in the complete assembly.

In a purely hypothetical rigid-box example, the nominal clearance above a product is 2.0 mm. Adding a 1.0 mm information card reduces nominal clearance to 1.0 mm. But the more important change is in the calculated range: the minimum possible gap moves from +0.8 mm to −0.4 mm.

That negative endpoint means the specified component ranges permit a combination that cannot fit within the assumed rigid, closed-lid geometry without interference. It is not an observed packaging defect or an estimate of how often interference will occur.

Define the vertical dimensions before combining them

Consider a shallow gift box holding a rigid product on a seated support. The lid closes above the product, and a card may be placed directly over its highest point.

Use four dimensions:

  • H — usable closed-lid height: the vertical distance from the finished inside-base reference plane to the underside of the lid in its specified fully closed position.
  • T — seated support height: the distance from that same base reference plane to the surface supporting the product.
  • P — product height: the vertical distance from the support surface to the product’s highest packed point.
  • K — added card-layer thickness: the height occupied by the card directly above that point, when this placement is used.

These quantities must describe the same assembled configuration. H is not the box’s advertised external height, and T is not necessarily the loose thickness of an uninstalled insert.

The example assumes one vertical measurement direction, a common base datum, additive heights, rigid noncompressible components, and no changes in orientation or seating during closure. It also treats the stated dimension limits as combinations that are not otherwise restricted by the design.

Those assumptions are essential. They allow the remaining vertical gap to be expressed as:

C = H − T − P

When the card occupies the same vertical stack:

C = H − T − P − K

A positive C represents a modeled gap. Zero represents nominal geometric contact under this model. A negative C represents an overlap that the assumed rigid components cannot accommodate without changing the geometry.

The general idea is dimensional fit between components. KEYENCE’s What is Fit?, an undated measurement education page accessed on 10 October 2026, explains clearance and interference using mating shaft-and-bore features. That example supports the distinction between clearance and interference, but it does not prescribe dimensions or tolerances for gift boxes.

Calculate the gap across the original component ranges

All numbers below are invented solely for this hypothetical teaching example. They are not Packrivo measurements, supplier specifications, recommended packaging tolerances, or customer results.

Dimension Minimum Nominal Maximum
Usable lid height H, 30.0 ± 0.5 mm 29.5 30.0 30.5
Seated support T, 8.0 ± 0.3 mm 7.7 8.0 8.3
Product height P, 20.0 ± 0.4 mm 19.6 20.0 20.4
Optional card K, 1.0 ± 0.2 mm 0.8 1.0 1.2

All table values are in millimetres.

Without the card, calculate the nominal gap first:

C nominal = 30.0 − 8.0 − 20.0 = 2.0 mm

Next calculate the smallest remaining gap. This occurs when usable lid height is at its minimum while the occupied support and product heights are at their maxima:

C minimum = 29.5 − 8.3 − 20.4 = 0.8 mm

The largest modeled gap comes from the opposite combination:

C maximum = 30.5 − 7.7 − 19.6 = 3.2 mm

The resulting interval is:

Without card: 0.8–3.2 mm

Under the stated additive and rigid assumptions, every combination within these dimension ranges leaves a positive vertical gap at this particular interface.

That does not establish a suitable clearance for the product. It only establishes that the modeled vertical stack does not cross zero within the specified intervals.

The distinction between an assembly result and an individual dimension is central to NIST IR 6223, Design for Tolerance of Electro-Mechanical Assemblies: An Integrated Approach, published in September 1998. Its introduction and Section 4.1 distinguish worst-case analysis, which examines extreme component combinations, from statistical analysis using distribution information.

The NIST report concerns electro-mechanical assemblies, not packaging. This article applies the elementary high-low interval principle to an explicitly hypothetical packaging geometry; it does not adopt the report as a current packaging standard.

The added card makes the gap interval cross zero

Now place a card layer directly above the product’s highest point.

Its hypothetical nominal thickness is 1.0 mm, with a permitted range of 0.8–1.2 mm.

The nominal calculation becomes:

C nominal = 30.0 − 8.0 − 20.0 − 1.0 = 1.0 mm

A nominal-only review might conclude that the card still fits because the result is positive.

But the smallest gap must account for the thickest permitted card together with the other limiting dimensions:

C minimum = 29.5 − 8.3 − 20.4 − 1.2 = −0.4 mm

The largest remaining gap is:

C maximum = 30.5 − 7.7 − 19.6 − 0.8 = 2.4 mm

The new interval is:

With card: −0.4–2.4 mm

The minimum combination occupies 29.9 mm of the available 29.5 mm. The modeled shortfall is therefore 0.4 mm.

Calculated state Without card With card
Minimum gap +0.8 mm −0.4 mm
Nominal gap +2.0 mm +1.0 mm
Maximum gap +3.2 mm +2.4 mm

The card does more than subtract its nominal thickness. Its own dimensional range extends the spread of possible assembly clearances.

Every input in the minimum-gap calculation remains inside its individual hypothetical limits. Yet the combined dimensions exceed the usable height of the closed box.

This is the reason a component-by-component dimensional acceptance review cannot answer the complete fit question on its own.

A negative modeled gap does not mean a real package has negative air space. It means the idealized closed geometry contains incompatible occupied and available dimensions. An actual component might bend, compress, shift, prevent full closure, or contact another surface. Which behavior occurs cannot be determined from these intervals.

Nor does the interval indicate a failure percentage. It shows an extreme combination permitted by the assumed inputs, not how often those endpoints coincide. The calculation supplies no manufacturing distributions, correlations, sampling evidence or statistical yield estimate.

Identify which dimension or interface must change

Once the modeled minimum gap crosses zero, the design question becomes more specific than whether the nominal box height looks sufficient.

The relevant minimum-gap relationship is:

C minimum = H minimum − T maximum − P maximum − K maximum

This expression identifies four possible contributors, but it does not decide which component should be changed.

The responsible designer might consider increasing usable closed-lid height, revising the seated support, changing the product’s packed position, or moving the card outside the vertical path above the product.

Each choice changes a different physical interface.

Increasing the advertised exterior height does not necessarily increase H by the same amount. The lid, wrap, lining and closed position must still be considered.

Reducing the loose thickness of an insert does not necessarily reduce its installed support height T. The relevant dimension is its position when seated.

Changing product orientation may change its highest packed point, but it also changes the geometry being analyzed. An angled product cannot automatically retain the same additive model.

Moving the card into a separate pocket might remove K from the stack above the product. It creates another placement question rather than proving that the revised arrangement fits.

The calculated 0.4 mm shortfall is the amount by which this particular worst-case combination exceeds zero clearance. It is not a recommended design increase. Zero clearance itself may be unacceptable for the product or package.

The design needs an agreed functional clearance requirement. The responsible party can then compare that requirement with the minimum predicted gap for the actual construction.

For the underlying measurement definitions, Packrivo’s dimensions and acceptance-method guide explains how to specify reference points and measurement conditions. Its care-card pack-out guide addresses placement and loading order. This calculation answers a narrower question that those workflows leave open: what range of resulting clearance follows from the combined component ranges?

Keep the interval attached to the actual construction

A worst-case arithmetic model is useful only when its dimensions represent the same physical arrangement.

Consider a foam holder that compresses under the product. Its installed support height may depend on loading, and the original rigid T range may no longer describe the assembly.

A hinged box can also have local clearance controlled by lid rotation, rather than a single vertical distance. A tilted jar, raised jewellery setting, turned paper edge or incompletely seated insert may introduce contact outside the section used for the calculation.

Another limit arises when the component extremes cannot physically occur together because their dimensions are linked. In that case, independently combining every interval endpoint can overstate the feasible range. The actual relationships need to be established before replacing the simple model.

An installed section should therefore identify where each quantity begins and ends, which finished surfaces it includes, and whether the complete construction permits the assumed additive relationship.

For formed lid and base interfaces, the separate Packrivo article on folded wall builds addresses the construction details that a simple height equation does not capture.

The interval also says nothing about whether a product is adequately retained, easily removed, protected from rubbing, or suitable for transport. Even a strictly positive calculated gap cannot certify those outcomes. Representative physical review and any agreed performance evaluations remain separate decisions.

Keep the clearance calculation attached to named interfaces

Use the same base datum in the drawing and worksheet. H and T start at that plane; P starts at the installed support surface; K belongs only when the card lies above the product in the analyzed path. A separate card pocket cannot inherit the same K subtraction without locating its geometry.

For the existing hypothetical dimensions, the worksheet retains all four min/nominal/max inputs and both resulting clearance rows. Before using the arithmetic for a real design, the responsible designer should state whether compression, a tilted product, linked component limits or local lid rotation invalidate the rigid additive assumptions. Leave the required functional gap open until that requirement is agreed; neither zero nor 0.4 mmis a design recommendation.

Download this article’s project record (CSV). The record includes field definitions, labeled teaching examples and a blank project row. Add source evidence and the details of your actual project.

For a sourcing discussion, send the shared-datum section, four component ranges and the functional gap still to agree. Packrivo coordinates supplier questions; the responsible technical or commercial parties confirm the actual method, configuration and terms.

Use the calculation to request a specific design response

Return to the hypothetical card addition.

Before the card, the modeled clearance remains between 0.8 and 3.2 mm. After the card, the modeled interval becomes −0.4 to 2.4 mm. The negative minimum flags a design combination that the stated rigid stack cannot accommodate.

The next useful question is:

Does the card really occupy the same vertical stack as the product’s highest point? If it does, which finished dimension, seating position or card interface will the designer revisit so the minimum modeled clearance meets the project’s actual requirement?

The answer should identify the construction to be reviewed, not simply supply another nominal box size.

Packrivo can help coordinate that question with the relevant packaging proposal, drawings and supplier response. The arithmetic helps buyers locate a potential dimensional conflict; it does not substitute for the designer’s geometry assessment, a representative finished sample, or functional testing.

The decision is straightforward: evaluate the remaining clearance interval, not only the nominal gap, and revisit the interface when the permitted combination conflicts with the required space.

Sources checked 10 October 2026. NIST IR 6223 was published in September 1998 and concerns electro-mechanical assemblies; KEYENCE’s measurement-education page shows no confirmed publication date. The elementary interval calculation is applied here to the stated hypothetical rigid packaging stack, not as a packaging standard, a physical fit result or a statistical yield estimate.

title: Cushioning Curves: Bearing Area and Static Loading
html:
A larger cushioning area does not automatically give a jewellery, candle or gift product better protection during shipping. Spreading the same weight over more cushion area reduces static loading, but a dynamic cushion curve can show poorer shock performance at both low and high loading levels.

In this guide
  • Static Loading Locates a Point on a Dynamic Cushion Curve
  • Bearing Area Is Not the Entire Foam Footprint
  • Doubling Bearing Area Moves the Loading Point Left
  • Both Ends of a Cushion Curve Can Be Unfavorable
  • Read the Candidate Positions Against Matching Test Conditions
  • Shock Curves Do Not Replace Vibration or Complete-Package Evaluation
  • Ask for the curve that could answer the two loading coordinates
  • Bring the specific open question to the project brief

The useful decision is not simply whether the cushion is thick or generous. It is whether the product’s weight and effective bearing area place the proposed cushion within a suitable region of a relevant dynamic shock curve.

Without a curve representing the intended conditions and a defensible product-fragility criterion, that protection decision remains unresolved.

Static Loading Locates a Point on a Dynamic Cushion Curve

Static loading describes the weight supported by a cushion divided by the area carrying that weight.

Static loading = Supported weight ÷ Effective bearing area

When weight is expressed in pounds-force and area in square inches, the result is pounds per square inch (psi).

The word static describes the loading coordinate. It does not mean that the cushion curve is an ordinary static compression test.

A dynamic shock cushion curve relates that loading coordinate to peak deceleration recorded during controlled impact testing. The horizontal axis normally represents static loading, while the vertical axis represents peak deceleration, commonly expressed in G.

Westpak’s Packaging Dynamics #4 presentation, dated July 2015, explains this relationship on slides 31–37. Its separate cushion curve analysis description describes dynamic shock characterization of cushioning materials under specified test conditions.

A curve must therefore belong to an identified cushioning material and relevant test arrangement. Its shape and reported response depend on conditions including material thickness and impact input. It cannot be treated as a universal performance curve for every foam product.

Bearing Area Is Not the Entire Foam Footprint

A jewellery holder may occupy nearly the whole bottom of a box, but that does not mean its entire surface supports the product.

A ring resting against two cushion features does not automatically load the empty space between them. A candle supported by selected pads may leave other material untouched. An opening cut into a foam block is not bearing area simply because it lies inside the insert’s outside dimensions.

The effective area calculation must concern material genuinely sharing the supported load in the relevant orientation.

Multiple pads also require care. Adding their visible surface areas assumes that all those areas participate in carrying the stated weight. If one pad carries substantially more load than another, a single average static-loading figure can hide different local loading conditions.

Likewise, a decorative or retaining surface should not be counted as a weight-bearing surface without establishing its actual role.

These distinctions matter before reading the curve. An inaccurate area produces an inaccurate horizontal-axis position, even when the arithmetic itself is correct.

Doubling Bearing Area Moves the Loading Point Left

Consider a purely hypothetical small gift product with a supported weight of 4 pounds-force.

Two proposed cushioning layouts use genuinely load-sharing areas of different sizes.

Hypothetical layout A

Supported weight: 4 lbf
Effective bearing area: 8 in²

Static loading = 4 ÷ 8 = 0.50 psi

Hypothetical layout B

Supported weight: 4 lbf
Effective bearing area: 16 in²

Static loading = 4 ÷ 16 = 0.25 psi

The second layout doubles the effective bearing area while keeping the supported weight unchanged. Its nominal static loading is therefore half that of the first layout.

These values are invented teaching inputs and arithmetic results, not measurements from customer packaging, supplier samples or laboratory tests. In particular, the 16 in² calculation assumes that the additional area genuinely carries the load.

On a cushion curve, the change from 0.50 psi to 0.25 psi moves the design point left along the horizontal axis.

It does not establish that the peak shock deceleration decreases.

If a suitable measured curve happened to place 0.50 psi near a lower-response region and 0.25 psi on an underloaded section, the larger bearing area could produce a less favorable shock response under those test conditions.

Another material or test arrangement could produce a different comparison. Neither outcome can be assigned to these hypothetical layouts without applicable data.

The useful result of the calculation is therefore the location of two candidate loading coordinates—not a ranking of their protective performance.

Both Ends of a Cushion Curve Can Be Unfavorable

A dynamic cushion curve often has a lower-response region between two less favorable loading conditions.

At relatively low static loading, the supported object may not sufficiently deform the cushion during the impact. The resulting shock pulse can be short, with relatively high peak deceleration.

This is an underloaded cushion condition.

Increasing effective bearing area while maintaining the same supported weight reduces static loading. If that change moves the design farther into the underloaded region, adding cushion area can work against the intended shock response.

At relatively high static loading, the opposite problem can arise. The cushion may run out of useful deflection during the impact and bottom out, creating a high-deceleration response.

This is an overloaded cushion condition.

Westpak’s July 2015 presentation distinguishes underloaded, properly loaded and overloaded behavior on slides 34–37. Its examples show why the lower portion of a relevant curve matters more than simply maximizing or minimizing contact area.

The lower portion is not automatically a safe region, however. Even the lowest peak deceleration on an applicable material curve must be interpreted against the actual product’s fragility and the intended shock conditions.

There is no universal optimum psi value that can be assigned to every foam, thickness, product or shipping environment.

Read the Candidate Positions Against Matching Test Conditions

To evaluate the hypothetical 0.50 psi and 0.25 psi positions, the buyer would need a dynamic cushion curve for the proposed material under relevant conditions.

The curve should identify the cushioning material or grade, tested thickness, impact input or drop height, test method, specimen arrangement, reported response and measured static-loading range.

The two positions must fall within a range supported by the relevant test data. A smooth-looking curve is not permission to extrapolate outside the measured region.

The buyer should also avoid comparing curves obtained under materially different conditions as though their vertical-axis results were interchangeable.

The public scope of ASTM D1596-14(2023) describes dynamic shock cushioning characterization using acceleration-time data from impacts on material specimens. It explicitly distinguishes material-level data from performance of the exterior packaging assembly and cautions about predicting in-package results.

That publicly available scope does not provide the complete paid test procedure or establish an acceptance limit for a particular product.

A suitable curve can help a technical reviewer compare the two nominal loading positions. It cannot establish product survival without a relevant fragility criterion and consideration of the actual packed configuration.

If the product’s fragility is unknown, the result remains a material-response comparison rather than a protective pass/fail decision.

Shock Curves Do Not Replace Vibration or Complete-Package Evaluation

Cushioning also influences vibration response, but the shock curve does not tell the entire vibration story.

Westpak’s presentation treats impact cushioning and vibration amplification or attenuation separately. Vibration behavior depends on loading and frequency-dependent response, including possible amplification near resonance.

A loading position that appears promising for a particular impact condition does not automatically demonstrate favorable vibration performance.

The finished packaging system introduces further differences. A foam specimen tested under controlled impact conditions is not identical to a fitted jewellery holder, a candle insert or a complete gift set inside an outer shipping carton.

Actual product geometry, contact locations, restraints, box construction and loading orientation can all affect how the system responds.

Packrivo’s guide to mailer box protection addresses the separate task of reviewing the assembled shipping package. The packaging insert materials guide explains why fit and material form must be defined rather than inferred from a material name.

For a proposed mailer with fitted insert, the dynamic curve question is narrower: does the available cushioning evidence describe the intended loading and shock conditions?

Packrivo can coordinate the relevant component specifications and technical questions during sourcing discussions. Qualified technical parties must determine appropriate material evaluation, complete-package testing and acceptance requirements.

The practical conclusion is that more bearing area is not automatically better cushioning. Calculate the loading position from genuinely supported weight and bearing area, then interpret that position only against suitable dynamic evidence.

If the relevant curve or product-fragility information is missing, neither the smaller nor the larger area has demonstrated adequate shock protection.

Ask for the curve that could answer the two loading coordinates

Keep the static-loading calculation and the measured material response in different fields. Layout A’s four pounds-force over eight square inches gives0.50 psi; Layout B’s same supported weight over sixteen gives0.25 psi. Those arithmetic coordinates do not identify their G values.

Decision input Record for each actual candidate Open when missing
Supported weight and area Actual orientation and genuinely load-sharing area Do not use the insert outside footprint as automatic bearing area
Material curve Identified grade, thickness, impact input, test method and measured range No curve intersection or extrapolated response
Product criterion Responsible fragility requirement and scope No protection pass/fail
Complete package Product, restraints, box, loading and route Material specimen data does not approve the full assembly

The new curve sketch intentionally has no numeric ticks or plotted A/B points. Its U-shaped form explains that either low or high loading can be unfavourable in an applicable response curve. It is not evidence that these two hypothetical layouts occupy either region.

Ask the responsible technical reviewer whether a supplied curve represents the actual proposal and whether both loading coordinates fall inside its measured range. Record a missing material identity, thickness or impact condition as a specific request instead of choosing a smooth curve from an unrelated foam.

The insert form and material guide defines the fit proposal. The complete distribution evaluation scope establishes the separate packed-system question. Neither the lower psi nor a larger bearing area ranks protection without the relevant evidence and product criterion.

Download the cushioning curves record (.csv). This file contains field definitions, clearly fictional teaching entries and a blank actual-project row. Keep unknown evidence open rather than copying the example as an approval.

Bring the specific open question to the project brief

For cushion evidence, provide supported weight, true load-sharing area, material grade and thickness, impact conditions and product fragility basis; request the corresponding curve and complete-package assessment scope. Send the current configuration, actual records available, quantity by design, destination and the unresolved question through Packrivo’s packaging inquiry. Packrivo coordinates sourcing and project questions with independent suppliers; the responsible parties confirm materials, service, methods and commercial terms.

Sources checked 10 October 2026. Westpak’s presentation is dated July 2015; its companion service page shows no confirmed publication date. ASTM D1596-14(2023) public catalogue and scope information was reviewed, including the official indexed scope where direct access was unavailable; the paid procedure was not read. The weight and bearing areas are hypothetical, and no actual material or complete package was tested.

title: Paper Packaging Curl Can Come From Uneven Moisture Exchange
html:
A stack of wavy care cards or a curling paperboard insert does not automatically mean the dieline is wrong. Paper can change shape when moisture enters or leaves different parts of the material unevenly.

Before changing cut dimensions, distinguish three possibilities: moisture exchange at the exposed edges of a stack, different moisture responses across the two faces of a sheet, and deformation that may be associated with the material construction or physical damage.

These are different technical questions. A photograph of a curled sheet, or one dimension taken while it is distorted, cannot establish a permanent tooling fault.

Exposed edges can change before the centre of a stack

Paper is hygroscopic: it absorbs or releases moisture as it responds to its surrounding environment. This response varies with paper grade and exposure history.

Sappi’s Climate and Paper technical brochure distinguishes two important patterns in stacks of printing paper.

When exposed edges take up moisture and expand relative to the less-exposed centre, the edges can become wavy. When the edges lose moisture and contract relative to the centre, a tight-edge condition can develop.

The distinction is not simply between a humid room and a dry room. It concerns the difference between the paper’s existing moisture condition and its surroundings, and how that difference develops across the stack.

For a gift brand receiving flat care cards or paperboard components, the position of the deformation is therefore useful information.

Waves concentrated around exposed edges suggest a different question from deformation distributed evenly across an entire sheet. A stack that appeared flat while protected but changed after opening also has a different history from one that arrived visibly distorted in intact packaging.

Neither observation measures moisture content or proves the cause.

Sappi’s Paper Conditioning & Characteristics further explains that paper generally expands and contracts more across the grain than along it. The grain relationship can influence the visible distortion, but knowing the grain direction alone does not establish whether a sheet was cut incorrectly.

Curl across a sheet can involve its two faces

A sheet that curves upward or downward presents a different pattern from wavy edges around a stack.

In a simplified moisture-imbalance mechanism, one face of a sheet absorbs more moisture than the other. Differential expansion can make the sheet bend. Sappi’s Climate and Paper brochure describes one-sided moistening that can cause curling toward the drier side.

That explanation provides a useful physical model, not a reliable way to diagnose every finished packaging component from its curl direction.

A printed care card may have different coverage on each face. A sleeve may have a coating on one side. Paperboard used in a rigid gift box may be combined with a decorative wrap, adhesive or laminate.

Those constructions can change moisture movement, introduce other stresses or restrict how the material deforms.

Sappi’s separate Paper & Aqueous Coat Performance / Sheet Curl & Distortion discusses how substrate absorption, coating application and drying conditions interact in a specific printing process.

The buyer should therefore identify the actual two-face construction before treating curl direction as evidence of a particular cause.

Moisture imbalance may contribute to deformation, but so may uneven material structure, converting stresses or physical damage. A crushed corner, permanently creased panel or distorted bonded construction requires separate consideration.

Even if moisture conditions later become more balanced, a finished component is not guaranteed to return to its original shape.

A protected care-card sample can make the comparison more meaningful

Consider a hypothetical jewellery gift brand receiving a stack of printed care cards.

The stack appears flat when first observed through intact protective wrapping. The cards are then opened in a different room, and wavy exposed edges become noticeable.

This is an invented teaching example, not a measured customer incident. No temperature, relative humidity or paper-moisture readings are available.

The observation supports a moisture-history question: could the exposed edges have exchanged moisture with the new surroundings differently from the interior of the stack?

It does not confirm that humidity caused the waves, and it does not show that the cutting outline has changed.

Suppose the brand has a separately retained, still-protected sample of the same card revision.

That protected sample gives the reviewer a potentially useful comparison, provided its paper grade, print, finish and known history are sufficiently comparable.

The responsible reviewer should first agree the observation state. If the protected sample must be opened, the opening and comparison conditions should be documented because opening it changes its exposure.

Compare the location and character of the deformation. Are the exposed edges wavy while the central areas remain relatively flat? Does an individual card show a broader curve between its two faces? Was either sample already damaged or formed?

If the previously exposed stack is wavy while the protected comparison remains flat, the difference is consistent with an exposure-related mechanism. It is not proof that moisture was the sole cause.

If both show similar deformation, the buyer still needs to consider their common material, construction and earlier history.

Neither result establishes that the cards will flatten again. A useful comparison narrows the next technical question; it does not promise recovery.

Curl and cut geometry need separate reviews

A warped card may appear shorter, narrower or uneven when viewed from above. A raised edge can change the projected outline without necessarily changing the location of the original cut. Moisture exchange can also change the sheet’s actual dimensions within its plane, with the grain relationship affecting its response. Curl is therefore not only a projection question, and a changed dimension does not by itself establish a tooling error.

For that reason, measuring a distorted component without a defined method can mix two different questions:

Is the paper currently flat enough for the intended use? And were its cut features produced at the correct positions?

Changing the dieline to compensate for an unexplained curl risks altering artwork margins, fold positions or component fit without resolving the deformation mechanism.

A technical comparison should establish the actual material revision, relevant cut features, reference points and suitable preparation state before judging geometry. The converter should define an appropriate measurement approach that does not conceal or introduce damage.

If the intended cut features show a reproducible positional mismatch under an agreed comparable review, the tooling or dieline deserves examination.

If the only observation is waviness after exposure, that evidence is insufficient to justify a dieline change.

For packaging that is already folded, wrapped or glued, the reviewer must also separate sheet distortion from the effects of forming and bonding. A warped rigid-box lid is not necessarily governed by the same simple mechanism as an uncoated loose care card.

Material construction and moisture history should guide the next supplier question

The useful next question is not simply, "Can you make the card flatter?"

For the hypothetical care-card batch, a more specific request would describe the protected and exposed observations, identify the card revision, and ask the paper or converting supplier which material characteristics and comparison conditions are relevant.

The response should clarify whether edge moisture exchange, two-face construction, grain direction, coating or an existing physical set needs assessment.

There is no justified universal humidity percentage or fixed 24-hour conditioning rule for every gift box, sleeve, care card and insert. Sappi’s published pressroom recommendations concern specified printing-stock operations; they are not automatically finished-packaging warehouse specifications.

The broader Packrivo packaging sample review guide can help place this observation within an actual component review. The packaging supplier brief provides a route for communicating the relevant material, construction and unresolved questions.

Packrivo coordinates packaging sourcing and project questions; it does not establish moisture causes through its own laboratory testing.

The practical decision is to preserve the distinction between moisture-related shape changes, construction-related deformation and actual cut-position errors. Make the technical comparison first. Change the dieline only when the appropriate evidence points to a geometry problem.

Source review: 10 October 2026. The publication date of Sappi’s Climate and Paper brochure was not established. The two cited Printer Technical Service tips show copyright 2012 and Version 001; those labels are not a confirmed publication date. Their printing-paper, conditioning and coating explanations do not diagnose a finished packaging component or prescribe warehouse humidity or recovery time.

Do not attribute a changed coating and changed exposure to one cause

Build four invented history records before assigning a cause. BASE_WRAPPED29 and BASE_OPEN29 share a stated base card construction but differ in wrapped/open exposure state. COATED_WRAPPED29 and COATED_OPEN29 instead use a different one-face coating construction, again with wrapped/open states. These are proposed comparison identities, not actual samples or observed deformation.

Hypothetical configuration Named object Relationship Input or next scope
BASE_WRAPPED29 BASE_WRAPPED29 assumed construction BASE
BASE_WRAPPED29 BASE_WRAPPED29 assumed exposure state WRAPPED
BASE_OPEN29 BASE_OPEN29 assumed construction BASE
BASE_OPEN29 BASE_OPEN29 assumed exposure state OPEN
COATED_WRAPPED29 COATED_WRAPPED29 assumed construction CHANGED_ONE_FACE_COATING
COATED_WRAPPED29 COATED_WRAPPED29 assumed exposure state WRAPPED
COATED_OPEN29 COATED_OPEN29 assumed construction CHANGED_ONE_FACE_COATING
COATED_OPEN29 COATED_OPEN29 assumed exposure state OPEN
PAPER29 BASE_WRAPPED29_VS_BASE_OPEN29 proposed contrast EXPOSURE_IF_OTHER_HISTORIES_COMPARABLE
PAPER29 BASE_OPEN29_VS_COATED_OPEN29 proposed contrast CONSTRUCTION_WITH_OTHER_HISTORIES_REVIEW
PAPER29 BASE_WRAPPED29_VS_COATED_OPEN29 both changed NO_SINGLE_CAUSE_ATTRIBUTION
PAPER29 WRAPPED_STATE does not establish MOISTURE_CONTENT_OR_EQUAL_PRIOR_HISTORY
PAPER29 PROPOSED_COMPARISON does not predict CURL_DIRECTION_CAUSE_RECOVERY_OR_CUT_ERROR

Comparing base-wrapped with base-open can frame an exposure question if their other histories and review conditions are sufficiently comparable. Comparing base-open with coated-open changes construction, so it frames a different question. Base-wrapped versus coated-open changes both axes; a shape difference between those two alone cannot be attributed to exposure or coating separately. The worksheet makes that double change visible rather than producing a preferred explanation.

The wrapped label does not establish moisture content or equal prior history. Opening a retained sample changes its state, and a coating operation can have its own drying and stress history. Ask the responsible reviewer how to establish a meaningful comparison before opening or conditioning samples. Preserve earlier observations under the actual state in which they were made; no common humidity, duration, heat or flattening treatment is prescribed.

Sappi’s stack-edge moisture gain/loss explanations remain separate from single-sheet two-face imbalance and coating/drying effects. Grain can influence a response without proving a cut error. Even a useful contrast would narrow investigation, not diagnose a sole cause or guarantee recovery. The output is a request naming the construction and exposure variables that need separation before changing a dieline or committing to a corrective process.

Download the paper curl coating exposure comparison confounded cause record (.csv). It includes the original table fields and scenarios alongside the added relationships. HYPOTHETICAL rows are editorial examples or required review scopes, not actual records. Actual quantity, configuration, component and file identities, materials, process, specification, copy, method, condition, observation, owner, decision, evidence and dates are blank. ACTUAL_BLANK is a separate empty starting row; enter permitted project evidence before using an actual record. A blank means unknown.

Use the Packaging Sample Inspection Checklist Before Approval for its separate question.

Source scope checked 17 October 2026: The publication date of Sappi’s Climate and Paper was not established. Two Printer Tech Tips show copyright 2012 and Version 001, not verified publication dates. Printing-stock, conditioning and coating explanations do not diagnose finished packaging or prescribe humidity, drying, recovery or cut compensation. The added configurations and calculations are hypothetical, with actual evidence and decisions pending.

Discuss this packaging specification with Packrivo. We coordinate independent suppliers. MOQ: 500 pieces per product/design; illustrative quantities are not production offers. Confirm materials, samples, price and timing for your project.

title: Packaging Colour Matches Under Different Lights
html:
A cream gift box and its tissue may look like a coordinated set under a printer’s viewing light but noticeably different under a shop lamp. Neither component has to change for that to happen. Changing the light can change how each material appears—and can change the visible relationship between them.

A Printed Tissue Sheet: Plan the Fold and Product Contact is a relevant component when the same gift includes printed tissue and a box. Compare those actual substrates and finishes together under the selected viewing conditions; matching screen colours do not approve the physical set.

For a jewellery, candle or gift brand, the practical decision is where the packaging colours need to work together. A satisfactory match in one agreed viewing environment does not establish a match in every environment where the finished set will be seen.

Different Light Can Break an Apparent Colour Match

A box wrap and a tissue sheet can produce similar perceived colours under one light even though their underlying spectral properties differ. When the illumination changes, those differences may become visible.

This is the principle behind illuminant metamerism. The CIE International Lighting Vocabulary, 2020 edition, defines metamerism in terms of spectrally different colour stimuli producing the same tristimulus values in a specified colour system. In practical colour matching, a metameric pair can appear to agree under a reference illuminant and separate when that illuminant changes.

The important distinction is between the appearance of each component and the relationship between the two.

If both cream components look warmer under a different light but still coordinate, their overall appearance has changed without necessarily creating a new mismatch between them.

If the tissue looks distinctly pinker than the box under the second light, even though they looked alike under the first, the pair has developed a visible difference that matters to the packaging design.

That observation is consistent with possible illuminant metamerism. It is not, by itself, proof of the technical cause.

The physical samples remain unchanged during this comparison. What changes is the light reaching and reflecting from them. The CIE’s colour stimulus function definition describes the relationship between a source’s spectral distribution and the reflecting properties of an object.

This is why matching a named cream colour on two different materials is not automatically the same as matching their appearance across different lights.

The Viewing Environment Depends on Where the Set Is Seen

A controlled print-viewing condition gives a buyer and printer a shared place to compare physical colour. It is useful precisely because the conditions can be specified rather than left to chance.

The public scope of ISO 3664:2025 covers viewing conditions for reflective and transmissive images, including critical comparison of prints and appraisal at illumination levels resembling practical use. Its controlled-viewing framework does not establish that a packaging pair will also match under a particular retail lamp.

For a jewellery gift set displayed open in a boutique, the lighting over the displayed box and tissue may be important. For an online candle brand whose packaging is mainly opened in customers’ homes, the unboxing environment may be more relevant. A gift set photographed for a campaign introduces a separate image-production question, but its photograph should not replace a physical comparison.

Select the environments from the way customers actually encounter the packaging.

If both shop display and home unboxing matter, a print-viewing comparison alone cannot close the cross-light appearance question. The brand must decide whether it requires close coordination in both settings or can accept a different colour relationship in one.

A Standard Illuminant Is Not Every Real Lamp

CIE standard illuminants specify spectral distributions for colour calculations. The CIE’s public description of ISO/CIE 11664-2:2022 explains the intended uses of D50 and D65. These named reference distributions help specify a comparison; the actual viewing light remains a separate physical condition.

They should not be treated as universal substitutes for the lighting inside every shop, studio or home.

A lamp described as 3000 K or 4000 K is not fully specified for colour-matching purposes. Correlated colour temperature describes a characteristic of a light source’s chromaticity; it does not identify its complete spectral distribution. The CIE definition of correlated colour temperature makes that distinction clear.

Two different lighting systems can have similar nominal colour temperatures while producing different colour-rendering behaviour for particular materials.

When a specific store environment matters, identify the actual source or representative lighting arrangement rather than assuming that a Kelvin label completely describes it.

A Hypothetical Cream Box and Tissue Comparison

Consider a hypothetical small jewellery brand preparing a gift set with a cream paper-wrapped box and cream tissue.

Both proposed components are reviewed beside each other under an agreed print-viewing light. The buyer judges them visually coordinated. This is an illustrative observation, not a reported sample result or measured colour match.

The same box wrap and the same tissue are then viewed together under a specified lamp used in the intended store display. Nothing is reprinted, replaced or retouched.

Under that second light, suppose the tissue appears more peach-coloured than the box wrap. The brand wanted a restrained near-match, so the new contrast is distracting.

The question is not which component has suddenly become the wrong cream. It is whether the proposed pair meets the intended appearance requirement in the store environment.

To make that comparison meaningful, both pieces should be exposed to the same identified light during each viewing, with their relative position, backing and viewing geometry kept as consistent as practical. Tissue translucency and the way the sheet is layered can also affect its visible appearance, so the arrangement should represent its intended use.

The two conditions should be compared separately, without uncontrolled mixed lighting making the result difficult to interpret. A reviewer should allow for visual adaptation and should not use a phone photograph as the final comparison.

In this hypothetical example, the result is:

  • Under the agreed print-viewing light, the pair appears coordinated.
  • Under the identified store lamp, the pair appears insufficiently coordinated for the brand’s stated purpose.

No spectral reflectance data, numerical colour difference or universal pass/fail tolerance is implied. The observation creates a specific design and sourcing question, not a laboratory diagnosis.

The Response Depends on the Required Colour Relationship

The brand has several meaningful choices.

If the retail presentation depends on a close cream-to-cream match, the store-light difference needs further review. The buyer can ask the responsible printer or material supplier whether an alternative ink, substrate or material combination could better maintain the intended relationship across the selected lighting conditions. Any proposed alternative still requires relevant physical comparison; its success cannot be assumed.

If the tissue only needs to complement the box, deliberate contrast may be more practical than attempting a near-identical cream on two different surfaces. A visibly lighter or contrasting tissue can be an intentional design decision rather than an unsuccessful attempt at exact matching.

If one environment matters more than another, the brand can prioritize that environment, provided the limitation is understood. For example, the brand might prioritize its principal retail display and accept that the two components may look less alike in some home lighting.

None of these choices guarantees uniform appearance under every lamp. The useful output is a defined visual objective for the real environments that matter to the product.

This decision is different from choosing the physical reference itself. Packrivo’s physical colour approval guide addresses reference ownership and the agreed sample. A multi-light comparison asks whether that selected pair still achieves the desired visual relationship when illumination changes.

Not Every Lighting-Dependent Difference Is Metamerism

A visible change between two settings does not automatically establish illuminant metamerism.

A screen or camera can alter a colour comparison through display behaviour, exposure, white balance or image processing. Two photographs made under different lights do not isolate the spectral behaviour of the physical materials.

Gloss and surface texture introduce another complication. A laminated box wrap may produce directional reflections that an uncoated tissue does not. If the appearance changes mainly with viewing angle, specular reflection or surface geometry may be involved. Such a difference should not be described as proven illuminant metamerism merely because a lamp was moved.

Fluorescent materials, including some optical brighteners, add a further consideration. Their response can depend on ultraviolet content as well as visible illumination. The CIE’s public description of ISO/CIE 23603:2024 distinguishes visible-range and ultraviolet-range methods when assessing daylight simulators using defined specimen pairs.

That standard concerns the quality of daylight simulation. Its published description is not an acceptance certificate for a finished packaging pair.

If the cause matters technically, a qualified printing or colour-measurement source may need to evaluate the relevant material properties and viewing or measurement conditions. A visual comparison alone cannot identify reflectance spectra, fluorescence behaviour or a formal metamerism index.

Nor does one colour-difference number, without its illuminant and other measurement conditions, establish that two physical materials will coordinate in another light.

Define the Match Across the Conditions That Matter

Before choosing a coordinated box, tissue and label, describe their intended relationship in the settings where they will be viewed together.

A print-viewing condition can remain the common reference for a printing decision. A second viewing environment can answer whether the proposed components continue to achieve the brand’s desired appearance at display or unboxing.

If the same unchanged pair looks coordinated in one light but separates in another, the brand has learned something useful even before identifying the technical mechanism. It knows that a single-condition visual match is insufficient for its particular design objective.

Packrivo can help coordinate sourcing questions about proposed materials, print finishes, physical references and the viewing evidence that a supplier may be able to provide. A responsible printer or specialist must establish any required technical measurement method, material changes and acceptance criteria.

A colour match made under one light is a result for that viewing condition—not a promise that the entire packaging set will match under every light.

Source review: 10 October 2026. The cited CIE vocabulary entries belong to CIE S 017:2020. Public descriptions of ISO 3664:2025, ISO/CIE 11664-2:2022 and ISO/CIE 23603:2024 were consulted; their paid full texts were not read. These sources explain definitions and viewing frameworks, not a measured result for the hypothetical packaging pair.

Retain one physical pair across three light checkpoints

Use invented box face B1 and tissue T1 at C0 under L-A, C1 under L-B and C2 back under L-A. These IDs are a comparison plan, not actual lamps, samples or observations. No deliberate material change is proposed between checkpoints, but identity alone does not prove the pieces stayed unchanged.

Checkpoint Physical pair Viewing light Record independently
C0 B1 + T1 L-A reference to identify Initial actual relationship
C1 Same B1 + T1 L-B source to identify Relationship under second condition
C2 Same B1 + T1 Return to L-A Whether earlier relationship returns
Controls Same actual arrangement Separate identified sources Backing, layers, orientation, handling

Keep tissue layering, backing and relative geometry in the record. A newly folded sheet or changed finish would introduce another input, even if the familiar IDs remain on the forms. The neutral gray icons are uncalibrated identity symbols, not matching targets or a simulation of the two lights.

Record what the pair actually looks like at each checkpoint before naming a cause. A relationship that changes under L-B raises a cross-light design question; it does not establish metamerism without the relevant technical evidence. If a difference persists upon return, retain other material, handling or viewing explanations. The CSV supplies no color coordinates, spectral data, Delta E or tolerance, and this short comparison defines no exposure lifetime.

Download the packaging colour metamerism record (.csv). HYPOTHETICAL rows are invented examples. Use ACTUAL_BLANK for permitted project inputs; replace that row label only when recording actual facts. Empty evidence, observation and date fields mean unknown or not performed, never acceptance. Keep checkpoints and revisions separate.

Send the same physical pair, actual light identities, consistent arrangement and separate checkpoint observations before requesting a technical explanation. Packrivo coordinates independent suppliers. These records establish no supplier offer, service availability or MOQ exception; its published baseline is 500 pieces per product/design.

title: USPS Rectangular Parcel DIM Weight Needs the Complete Rounding Sequence
html:
For a rectangular parcel using applicable USPS commercial Priority Mail weight-based pricing, dimensional weight is not calculated by simply multiplying the measured dimensions and dividing by 139. USPS first requires each outside dimension to be rounded up to a whole inch. Those rounded dimensions determine whether the parcel crosses the one-cubic-foot threshold.

The sequence matters for small jewelry, candle and gift brands. A seemingly minor difference in finished shipping-carton dimensions can change the calculated weight basis. Another small reduction may change nothing at all.

The calculation uses the finished parcel’s outside dimensions

Start with the complete rectangular parcel as it will be shipped, including its closure, packing materials and any features affecting its outside measurements.

A supplier’s quoted internal box dimensions describe usable space for packing. They are not automatically the parcel dimensions used for shipping calculations. Board thickness, the finished construction, tape and bulging surfaces may affect the exterior.

For a brand choosing dispatch-carton sizes, the Packrivo guide to shipping box sizes explains why internal fit and finished external dimensions belong to different decisions.

Record the parcel’s outside length, width and height in inches, together with its complete packed weight in pounds. Keep the original measurements available instead of replacing them with rounded values.

USPS rounds the dimensions before testing the volume threshold

Under USPS Domestic Mail Manual 223, sections 1.4.1 and 1.4.2, the rectangular-parcel dimensional-weight calculation follows this order for the applicable Priority Mail pricing and delivery zones:

  1. Measure length, width and height in inches.
  2. Round each dimension upward to the next whole inch.
  3. Multiply those three rounded dimensions.
  4. If the result exceeds 1,728 cubic inches, divide it by 139.
  5. Round that division result upward to the next whole pound of dimensional weight.
  6. Compare dimensional weight with actual weight under the applicable postage increment. Use the greater weight for the specified pricing comparison.

The threshold is strictly greater than 1,728 cubic inches. A calculated volume of exactly 1,728 cubic inches does not trigger this dimensional-weight step.

The separate actual-weight rule in DMM 223, section 1.1(a) rounds a fractional pound up to the next whole-pound postage increment for the relevant weight-based Priority Mail pricing.

USPS also defines upward rounding in DMM 604, section 7.1.3. It is not nearest-whole-inch rounding, and it is not permission to round a measured dimension down.

An invented parcel crosses the threshold after rounding

Consider a completely hypothetical rectangular shipping carton with the following finished outside dimensions:

16.1 × 12.1 × 8.1 inches

Assume its actual packed weight is 4.2 pounds.

These are invented numerical inputs, not observations from a factory, carrier measurement, packing trial or customer shipment.

Calculation stage Hypothetical result
Original measured dimensions 16.1 × 12.1 × 8.1 in
Round each dimension upward 17 × 13 × 9 in
Multiply rounded dimensions 1,989 in³
Compare with the threshold 1,989 exceeds 1,728 in³
Divide by the rectangular DIM divisor 1,989 ÷ 139 ≈ 14.3093525 lb
Round dimensional weight upward 15 lb
Round hypothetical actual weight 4.2 lb → 5 lb
Compare the two weight increments 15 lb versus 5 lb

The dimensional-weight comparison produces 15 pounds.

There is an important distinction hidden in the numbers. Multiplying the original, unrounded measurements gives only 1,577.961 cubic inches. But that is not the volume to use for the threshold test under this rectangular dimensional-weight sequence.

The rounded dimensions produce 1,989 cubic inches instead. That result crosses the threshold and leads to the 15-pound dimensional weight.

This arithmetic establishes the weight basis for the stated hypothetical calculation. It is not a postage quotation, an observed carrier charge or evidence that a real parcel has been accepted.

A smaller hypothetical parcel falls below the threshold

Now consider a separately proposed rectangular parcel with finished outside dimensions of:

16 × 12 × 8 inches

Each dimension is already a whole number. The calculated volume is:

16 × 12 × 8 = 1,536 cubic inches

Because 1,536 does not exceed 1,728, the dimensional-weight calculation described above is not triggered.

If this different hypothetical parcel also weighed 4.2 pounds, its actual-weight postage increment would be 5 pounds under the cited weight-based rule.

The important result is the change in calculation status: the first hypothetical parcel triggers the dimensional-weight comparison, while the second does not.

That does not establish that the smaller carton can hold the same product, presentation packaging, protective inserts or cushioning. It also does not prove a postage saving. The second configuration needs its own fit and protection review before it can become a usable packaging alternative.

A dimension reduction can leave the DIM result unchanged

Not every fraction of an inch makes a difference.

Return to the first invented parcel. Suppose only its longest outside dimension changes from 16.1 inches to 16.05 inches. Keep the other two hypothetical dimensions at 12.1 and 8.1 inches.

Both 16.1 and 16.05 round upward to 17 inches.

The entire rounded calculation therefore remains:

17 × 13 × 9 = 1,989 in³

1,989 ÷ 139 ≈ 14.3093525

Rounded dimensional weight = 15 lb

The parcel is physically shorter in the invented comparison, but its calculated dimensional weight does not change.

This reveals two different boundaries worth checking before proposing a redesign:

  • Whether the change moves an outside dimension into a different whole-inch rounding interval.
  • Whether the resulting rounded volume and dimensional-weight calculation cross a threshold that changes the final weight increment.

Even crossing an individual dimension’s rounding boundary does not automatically change the final dimensional-weight increment. The complete calculation still has to be performed.

Never report a dimension as smaller than it actually is to change its billing result. A legitimate packaging comparison requires a genuinely different, properly measured finished parcel.

Dimensional weight is not the final shipping charge

This calculation is deliberately limited to the applicable commercial USPS Priority Mail rectangular-parcel weight-based rule for delivery Zones 1–9.

Other Priority Mail pricing arrangements require separate treatment. USPS-produced Flat Rate packaging has its own price basis. Eligible Cubic pricing uses different measurements and rounding rules. Priority Mail Open and Distribute tray boxes and specific customer agreements can also have different pricing arrangements.

Nonrectangular parcels have a separate calculation in DMM 223, section 1.4.3. Their measurement, adjustment factor and divisor must not be replaced with the rectangular calculation.

The rectangular rule also specifies a 70-pound price treatment when calculated dimensional weight exceeds 70 pounds; neither invented example reaches that condition.

No surcharge, other applicable fee, actual postage amount or carrier acceptance outcome has been calculated here.

For a real project, confirm the intended USPS product and pricing arrangement. Give the shipping owner the complete packed parcel’s external dimensions, actual packed weight, origin, destination and relevant packaging characteristics. Request an applicable service quotation rather than assigning a monetary saving from dimensional-weight arithmetic alone.

For preparing carton measurements and weights, see Packrivo’s carton-data guide. For decisions involving another service or carrier, use the separate carrier classification guide rather than carrying this USPS divisor into an unrelated calculation.

Packrivo can coordinate packaging sourcing questions and compare proposed external dimensions with internal fit requirements. It does not independently certify dimensional-weight calculations, conduct shipping tests or determine carrier charges.

The useful design decision is whether a genuine change to the completed parcel alters the rounded calculation without compromising the packaging’s intended function.

Official source and date limitation

Primary reference: USPS Domestic Mail Manual, 223 — Commercial Mail Priority Mail, Prices and Eligibility, especially sections 1.1, 1.3, 1.4.1, 1.4.2, 1.4.3 and 1.5.

Supporting rounding reference: USPS DMM 604, section 7.1.3.

Both public online references were accessed on 10 October 2026. The rectangular-parcel measurement and divisor steps in DMM 223 section 1.4.2 display USPS revision markers dated 12 July 2026. This article follows that accessible rule text rather than treating an earlier quick-service guide as the controlling current divisor.

This is a dated explanation of one USPS commercial Priority Mail calculation, not a universal parcel-shipping formula. Applicable USPS rules and prices should be checked again when arranging an actual shipment.

Crossing an inch boundary can still leave the DIM pound unchanged

Use three new invented rectangular parcels under the same applicable commercial Priority Mail weight-based, Zones 1–9 scope. A29 measures 19.1×10.1×9.1 inches; B29 changes the first dimension to 19 inches; C29 changes it to 18 inches. Assume 4.2 lb actual packed weight for each. No physical fit or protection has been established for any proposed size.

Hypothetical configuration Named object Relationship Input or next scope

A29 W assumed input 10.1 in
A29 H assumed input 9.1 in
A29 ROUNDED_VOLUME calculated from A29_L_UP*A29_W_UP*A29_H_UP; 2200 in3
A29 DIM_QUOTIENT calculated from A29_VOLUME/139; 15.827338129496402 lb
A29 DIM_INCREMENT calculated from ceil(A29_DIM_DIV); 16 lb
A29 POSTAGE_WEIGHT_INCREMENT calculated from ceil(A29_ACTUAL_ASSUMED); 5 lb
A29 COMPARISON_WEIGHT calculated from max(A29_DIM_UP,A29_ACTUAL_UP); 16 lb
B29 L assumed input 19 in
B29 ROUNDED_VOLUME calculated from B29_L_UP*B29_W_UP*B29_H_UP; 2090 in3
B29 DIM_INCREMENT calculated from ceil(B29_DIM_DIV); 16 lb
C29 L assumed input 18 in
C29 ROUNDED_VOLUME calculated from C29_L_UP*C29_W_UP*C29_H_UP; 1980 in3
C29 DIM_INCREMENT calculated from ceil(C29_DIM_DIV); 15 lb
RECT29 A29_TO_B29 crosses inch boundary but DIM_INCREMENT_UNCHANGED16
RECT29 B29_TO_C29 changes DIM_INCREMENT16_TO15
SOURCE29 DMM2231_4_3_VS_PB22705 unresolved NEAREST166_VS_UPWARD139_EFFECTIVE12JULY2026

After upward whole-inch rounding, A29 is 20×11×10=2,200 in³. Its 2,200÷139≈15.8273 becomes 16 DIM lb. B29 is 19×11×10=2,090 in³; 2,090÷139≈15.0360 also becomes 16 DIM lb. Thus A-to-B crosses an inch boundary and reduces rounded volume, but not the final DIM pound. C29 gives 18×11×10=1,980 in³; 1,980÷139≈14.2446 becomes 15 DIM lb. All three exceed 1,728 in³; actual 4.2 lb becomes a separate 5 lb postage increment, lower than each DIM result.

Work backward from a proposed comparison increment as well as forward from dimensions. For an active rectangular DIM result no greater than 15 lb under this 139 divisor, rounded volume must be no greater than 15 × 139 = 2,085 in³, while still being above the separate 1,728 in³ trigger for this branch. B29’s 2,090 in³ is 5 in³ beyond that mathematical boundary, which explains why its reduction from A29 still leaves 16 DIM lb. This is not a five-cubic-inch physical trimming instruction: rounded dimensions change discretely, and the finished package needs its own fit and protection review. The inverse check identifies which calculation boundary an authentic redesign would have to cross; it supplies neither a target carton specification nor postage savings.
