title: AQL 2.5 and Packaging Inspection Decision Rules
html:
AQL 2.5 does not mean a packaging buyer has agreed to accept 2.5% defective products in every shipment. It also does not mean an inspector must find exactly 2.5% defective items before rejecting a lot.

An AQL designation helps define a statistical acceptance-sampling approach. The actual accept-or-reject decision depends on the agreed sampling plan, what is counted, and how the sample is selected.

For a small jewelry, candle or gift brand, the practical question is whether an inspection instruction describes a real decision rule or simply displays the words “AQL 2.5.”

AQL Describes a Quality Reference, Not a Shipment Allowance

Acceptance sampling uses observations from selected items to decide the disposition of a defined lot. Its primary purpose is not to determine the precise proportion of defective items throughout that lot.

The NIST Engineering Statistics Handbook, Section 6.2.1, makes this distinction between deciding lot acceptability and estimating lot quality.

AQL is one reference used in designing or selecting sampling plans. It is associated with the probability of accepting lots at a designated quality level, not with permission to supply a fixed percentage of nonconforming products.

For example, a statement such as “AQL 2.5 allows 25 defective jewelry boxes in every 1,000” is not a valid interpretation of a sampling result.

A statistical plan may accept a lot containing nonconforming items. It may also reject a lot whose actual nonconforming proportion is below the designated AQL. These possibilities arise because the decision is based on a sample rather than complete knowledge of the lot.

The selected plan’s operating characteristics determine the relevant acceptance probabilities. AQL alone does not provide them.

A Single-Sample Plan Needs a Sample Size and Acceptance Number

A basic attributes single-sampling plan can be written as (n, c):

  • n is the number of items selected for inspection.
  • c is the maximum number of nonconforming items permitted in that sample for lot acceptance under this particular counting plan.

If the observed number of nonconforming items exceeds c, the lot is rejected under the plan.

Consider an entirely invented plan, (20, 0).

Twenty items are selected from a defined lot under the assumed valid sampling procedure. The plan accepts the lot if zero sampled items are classified as nonconforming. If one or more sampled items are nonconforming, the plan rejects the lot.

These numbers are for explanation only. They are not recommended for any real packaging order, do not come from an ISO 2859 table, and should not be substituted for an agreed inspection procedure.

The comparison is straightforward:

Hypothetical sample observation Meaning under (20, 0)
Zero nonconforming items among 20 Accept the lot under this illustrative plan
One nonconforming item among 20 Reject the lot under this illustrative plan

The first result does not mean all other items have been examined or proven conforming.

The second result does not mean every item in the lot is defective.

NIST’s Section 6.2.2 describes single-sampling plans, the acceptance number, operating-characteristic curves, and the risks associated with accepting or rejecting lots at different quality levels.

An instruction that says only “inspect to AQL 2.5” leaves the actual plan unresolved. It does not independently establish the sample size, acceptance number, counting basis, sampling procedure or agreed treatment of different nonconformities.

Counting Nonconforming Items Is Different From Counting Defects

The distinction becomes important when one packaging item has several problems.

Imagine a hypothetical gift box with two surface marks and one misaligned printed element. Assume, purely for this illustration, that all three observations fail the agreed requirements.

That is one nonconforming box with three individual nonconformities.

If the plan counts nonconforming items, the box contributes one to the sample’s nonconforming-item count. It does not contribute three.

A different plan may count individual nonconformities rather than the number of items containing them. Its counting rules and acceptance criteria must be separately defined.

The same distinction applies to candle cartons with multiple print issues or jewelry boxes showing more than one agreed appearance failure.

Whether an observation is actually a nonconformity, and how it is classified, depends on the applicable agreed requirements. AQL 2.5 by itself does not supply those definitions or establish the significance of each issue.

A buyer should therefore distinguish a report of “three defects” from a report of “three nonconforming boxes.” Those statements may describe very different sample outcomes.

Lot Identity Does Not Prove Valid Sample Selection

A sampling plan needs a defined population from which items are selected.

Identifying that population and choosing a valid sample are different tasks.

A lot reference might establish which production grouping or received quantity is under review. Item identifiers can show which physical pieces were examined. Neither fact alone proves that those pieces were selected according to the statistical procedure.

Suppose an inspector takes 20 attractive-looking jewelry boxes from an accessible, neatly arranged group while ignoring other parts of the defined lot.

Even if those 20 boxes have no observed nonconformities, the selection does not support the random-sampling assumptions of the illustrative plan.

The issue is not whether the inspector recorded the observations carefully. It is whether the selection procedure supports extending a sample-based decision to the intended lot.

If the lot contains different component versions or distinct production groupings, the inspection scope and applicable sampling approach must be resolved rather than silently treating everything as one interchangeable population.

A convenient, handpicked sample cannot become statistically representative merely because the resulting inspection report contains an AQL designation.

A Clean Sample Cannot Establish Zero Defects Throughout the Lot

The uncertainty can be demonstrated with a simple invented probability calculation.

Assume a hypothetical population in which the probability that an independently selected item is nonconforming is 5%. Assume a common probability across selections, and a lot sufficiently large relative to the sample for the binomial approximation to apply.

Under the illustrative (20, 0) plan, the probability of observing zero nonconforming items is:

P(zero observed) = 0.95^20 ≈ 0.3585 = 35.85%

Under those assumptions, a zero-nonconforming-item sample occurs approximately 35.85% of the time, even though the assumed underlying nonconforming-item probability is 5%.

This is arithmetic under a specified hypothetical model. It is not a measurement of an actual packaging lot, an estimate obtained from inspecting a real shipment, or a recommended acceptance plan.

It also does not establish the probability for a handpicked sample or a small finite lot where the model assumptions do not hold.

The calculation illustrates why passing a sample-based plan is different from proving that every item in the lot is conforming.

NIST’s Section 6.2.3.2 explains how the binomial operating-characteristic calculation relates a sampling plan to its probability of lot acceptance, including the assumption that the lot is large compared with the sample.

An accepted lot has met the defined sampling decision rule. It has not received a statistical guarantee of zero nonconforming items.

Reinspection Follows the Original Agreed Procedure

When a sample exceeds the acceptance number, repeatedly drawing new samples until one passes is not a valid substitute for following the agreed rejection procedure.

Repeated sampling changes the effective decision process and can increase the opportunity to obtain a passing result without resolving the original findings.

The appropriate next disposition depends on the actual agreement. It may involve holding the affected lot, investigating the findings, an authorized sorting or corrective process, replacement, or reinspection under explicitly defined conditions.

A fresh inspection result should not erase the original rejection or be treated as automatic acceptance. Any permitted reinspection must follow the original agreed procedure, including its applicable conditions for further examination and disposition.

This distinction matters particularly when a packaging order includes multiple components. A decision about sampled printed sleeves does not automatically determine the acceptability of inserts, lids or completed packs that were outside the inspection scope.

Existing Packaging Records Serve a Different Purpose

Packrivo’s packaging acceptance record explains how requirements, findings, corrective actions and decisions remain connected. The incoming lot reference guide explains how reviewed items retain their source identity, while the incoming damage hold guide addresses observed damage and unresolved affected quantities. Those records help maintain traceability and manage actual findings. They do not select a statistical sampling plan or determine its acceptance probabilities. The separate decision explained here is whether the statistical instruction itself is complete and whether its result is being interpreted within its proper limits.

Complete the AQL 2.5 inspection request before counting

Translate the label into a record that the responsible inspection provider can actually assess. For the invented (20,0) illustration, the counting unit is one box and the counted outcome is the number of nonconforming boxes. Three classified findings on one box still contribute one nonconforming item under that specific rule.

Instruction field What the request must identify Keep unresolved when missing
Lot and unit Named grouping and whether one unit is a component or complete set Do not combine unidentified versions by appearance
Plan reference Applicable procedure and selected rule supplied by its responsible owner The words AQL 2.5 do not supply n or c
Classification Agreed requirement and method for counting items or individual findings A visible mark is not automatically a classified nonconformity
Selection and disposition Agreed selection method, result and authorized next action A clean handpicked sample does not close the statistical decision

Keep the worked probabilities above attached to their stated independent binomial assumptions. This record adds the missing decision inputs; it does not select an inspection level, reproduce an ISO table or authorize a real lot to be accepted.

Download this article’s project record (CSV). The record includes field definitions, labeled teaching examples and a blank project row. Add source evidence and the details of your actual project.

For a sourcing discussion, send the lot boundary, proposed counting unit and unresolved inspection-rule reference. Packrivo coordinates supplier questions; the responsible technical or commercial parties confirm the actual method, configuration and terms.

An AQL Statement Needs an Agreed Decision Rule

When an inspection proposal states “AQL 2.5,” a packaging buyer should not translate that phrase into a permitted percentage of defective items.

The instruction must identify the applicable inspection procedure and its actual decision rule, including the lot under review, the inspection unit, the basis for classifying and counting nonconformities, and the sampling and acceptance conditions.

Without that information, “AQL 2.5 passed” is an incomplete explanation of what was examined and what decision was reached.

Packrivo can help coordinate packaging specifications and inspection questions with the relevant project parties. Statistical plan selection, technical evaluation and any contractual acceptance decision must remain with the appropriately responsible parties under the actual agreement.

The essential distinction is simple: acceptance sampling produces a conditional decision about a defined lot, not permission for a fixed percentage of defective products or proof that every unexamined item is conforming.

Source scope: The statistical explanations draw on Sections 6.2.1, 6.2.2 and 6.2.3.2 of the NIST Engineering Statistics Handbook, undated public online pages accessed 10 October 2026. This article does not reproduce paid ISO 2859 tables, establish a current ISO edition or claim compliance with any particular inspection standard.

title: Colour-Difference Numbers Need the Named Formula
html:
Two reports can use the label “Delta E” and show different values even when both calculations start from exactly the same CIELAB coordinates. Before a gift brand treats a lower number as a closer colour match, it needs to know which formula produced each result. A CIE 1976 ΔE*ab number and a CIEDE2000 ΔE00 number are not two interchangeable readings on one scale.

One CIELAB Pair, Two Different Results

Consider the first public software-validation pair published by Gaurav Sharma, Wencheng Wu and Edul N. Dalal. These are numerical test inputs, not measurements of a gift box, ink, printed proof or finished material.

Coordinate Reference Sample
L* 50.0000 50.0000
a* 2.6772 0.0000
b* −79.7751 −82.7485

For the 1976 formula, subtract reference coordinates from sample coordinates:

  • ΔL* = 0
  • Δa* = −2.6772
  • Δb* = −2.9734

The Euclidean CIELAB difference is:

ΔEab = √[(ΔL)² + (Δa*)² + (Δb*)²]

= √[0² + (−2.6772)² + (−2.9734)²] = 4.001063… ≈ 4.0011

For the identical coordinate pair, the authors’ published CIEDE2000 validation value is ΔE00 = 2.0425, using unit parametric factors (kL = kC = kH = 1).

Named computation Result Provenance
CIE 1976 ΔE*ab 4.0011 Arithmetic shown above
CIEDE2000 ΔE00 2.0425 Published software-validation value

Nothing about the coordinates changed between the calculations. The second number is smaller because the mathematical rule is different. It does not mean a physical print improved, and neither number is an approval grade.

Why CIEDE2000 Cannot Be Obtained by a Fixed Multiplier

CIE 1976 ΔE*ab measures straight-line distance between coordinates in CIELAB space. CIEDE2000 instead computes adjusted lightness, chroma and hue differences, with weighting that depends on the colour pair. It also includes a coupling term associated with chroma and hue. These changes aim to relate numerical differences more closely to relative perceived differences in the formula’s intended domain; they do not make it a universal packaging-appearance test.

The International Commission on Illumination’s ISO/CIE 11664-6:2022 description identifies CIEDE2000 as an extension of the 1976 formula. The 2022 edition replaced 2014 with a minor revision: the year is a standard-edition identifier, not evidence that two calculations made under different formulas are equivalent.

CIEDE2000 also uses parametric factors kL, kC and kH, associated with lightness, chroma and hue. As Konica Minolta explains, the unit setting applies under standard conditions, while factors may vary with measurement conditions. Thus even the word “CIEDE2000” may be insufficient for a reproducible numerical comparison if the factors are omitted.

There is no sound single conversion ratio between ΔE*ab and ΔE00. The influence of the weighting changes with the input pair, so a ratio inferred from this one test cannot be applied to the next colour pair. Nor should anyone assume two formulas always order all candidate pairs identically.

The Buying Decision When Reports Disagree

Imagine a buyer receives two calculation summaries, each headed simply “Delta E.” Both use the validation coordinates above. Summary A shows 4.0011; summary B shows 2.0425. If A is ΔE*ab and B is ΔE00, those totals describe the same two coordinate sets. Ranking summary B as the better colour result would compare formulas, not samples.

The useful decision is do not rank these numbers or transfer an acceptance limit from one formula to the other. First establish the named formula and edition or implementation basis, and for ΔE00 obtain the declared kL, kC, kH settings. If two actual candidate reports are to be judged against one numerical criterion, have the responsible measurement or printing source supply valid calculations on the same agreed formula, factors and relevant CIELAB input basis. Do not multiply a previous result by a fixed “correction” or infer equivalence from similar rounded totals.

A focused response could say:

“Before comparing these Delta E figures, please identify whether each is CIE 1976 ΔE*ab or CIEDE2000 ΔE00, give the ΔE00 parametric factors, and confirm whether both can be calculated consistently from the relevant original CIELAB data.”

An unresolved formula identification is a reason not to make a numeric comparison—not a reason to reject a physical sample as defective.

What These Numbers Still Cannot Establish

Real colour coordinates require a meaningful measurement context. The underlying colour stimulus, chosen observer, illuminant, white/reference normalization, and material/finish state must make the reports relevant to the intended comparison. Using the same formula cannot repair measurements taken under incompatible conditions. Nor does a computed difference establish how a formed package will look under the brand’s agreed viewing conditions.

The public ISO scope for CIEDE2000 covers qualifying CIELAB stimuli perceived as reflecting or transmitting objects; it excludes stimuli that appear to emit primary light or specularly reflect such light. A metallic or strongly specular finish, or an RGB preview viewed as a light-emitting display, cannot automatically inherit the conclusion from this flat mathematical example. The standard does permit suitably normalized display simulations of reflecting/transmitting objects, but a screen preview is not physical print proof.

For physical target selection and viewing conditions, use Packrivo’s colour approval guide. For changes between flat and formed solid areas, use the solid-panel review. And when checking a report against an ordered configuration, see the report applicability guide. Those are separate decisions; none makes two different Delta E formulas interchangeable.

The Rochester original test dataset and implementation paper support the mathematical example, not a tolerance for actual packaging. Packrivo can coordinate sourcing questions with a proposed printing partner; it does not claim to operate an accredited colour laboratory or to certify any print from these figures.

The defensible next step is a like-for-like calculation, followed by a separately agreed physical approval decision.

Two distances from a reference do not give the distance between candidates

Keep the original published CIEDE2000 validation pair separate and use a new, entirely invented CIE 1976 calculation. Let R=(50,0,0), A=(52,0,0) and B=(48,0,0) in CIELAB. The values are mathematical vectors, not measured reference or supplier samples. All three comparisons use the same Euclidean Delta E76 formula.

Hypothetical configuration Named object Relationship Input or next scope
VECTORS29 REF_R29_L assumed input 50 CIELAB_coordinate
VECTORS29 REF_R29_a assumed input 0 CIELAB_coordinate
VECTORS29 REF_R29_b assumed input 0 CIELAB_coordinate
VECTORS29 CAND_A29_L assumed input 52 CIELAB_coordinate
VECTORS29 CAND_A29_a assumed input 0 CIELAB_coordinate
VECTORS29 CAND_A29_b assumed input 0 CIELAB_coordinate
VECTORS29 CAND_B29_L assumed input 48 CIELAB_coordinate
VECTORS29 CAND_B29_a assumed input 0 CIELAB_coordinate
VECTORS29 CAND_B29_b assumed input 0 CIELAB_coordinate
VECTORS29 REF_R29_VS_CAND_A29 calculated from sqrt(sum((x_axis-y_axis)^2)); 2 DeltaE76
VECTORS29 REF_R29_VS_CAND_B29 calculated from sqrt(sum((x_axis-y_axis)^2)); 2 DeltaE76
VECTORS29 CAND_A29_VS_CAND_B29 calculated from sqrt(sum((x_axis-y_axis)^2)); 4 DeltaE76
VECTORS29 CALCULATIONS use only CIE1976_EUCLIDEAN_NOT_CIEDE2000
VECTORS29 TWO_REFERENCE_DISTANCES_EQUAL2 does not establish CANDIDATES_EQUAL_OR_DISTANCE2

The difference from R to A is 2, and from R to B is also 2. But A and B lie on opposite sides of R along L*, giving a direct A-to-B difference of 4. Therefore two reports each stating 2 from the reference do not establish that their candidates are 2 apart, identical, or mutually acceptable. The pair being compared belongs in the record alongside the formula.

This is a different missing fact from comparing Delta E76 with Delta E00. Even when formula names match, a reference-to-candidate result cannot simply stand in for candidate-to-candidate agreement. Request the appropriate pairwise calculation from compatible original inputs if that is the buying question. Do not use this one-dimensional illustration as a universal doubling rule: other coordinate directions give other relationships.

For real printing, coordinate provenance, observer, illuminant, normalization, specimen and finish still have to be suitable. CIEDE2000 would additionally need its named implementation basis and kL/kC/kH; its result is not calculated or inferred by a fixed ratio here. ISO/CIE 11664-6:2022 public scope and the Rochester software-validation resources do not supply a commercial tolerance. No display swatch, metallic appearance, physical improvement or print approval follows from the three invented numbers.

Download the Delta E pairwise candidate reference distances record (.csv). It includes the original table fields and scenarios alongside the added relationships. HYPOTHETICAL rows are editorial examples or required review scopes, not actual records. Actual quantity, configuration, component and file identities, materials, process, specification, copy, method, condition, observation, owner, decision, evidence and dates are blank. ACTUAL_BLANK is a separate empty starting row; enter permitted project evidence before using an actual record. A blank means unknown.

Use the Packaging Color Approval With a Physical Reference for its separate question.

Source scope checked 17 October 2026: ISO/CIE 11664-6:2022 public scope/description and the Rochester 2005 paper/data were acquired; the paid full standard was not. The original 2.0425 software-validation value is not a print tolerance. The added CIE 1976 vector arithmetic establishes no physical colour match, metallic appearance or display proof. The added configurations and calculations are hypothetical, with actual evidence and decisions pending.

title: Plastic Bag Warnings Depend on the Bag Definition and Size
html:
A protective bag around a household gift item may look like an ordinary packaging component, but a Rhode Island warning decision cannot be made from appearance or the words “plastic bag” on a quotation.

Rhode Island General Laws § 11-9-16 first defines the bags covered by its provision. A separate table then sets warning type sizes. The opened-end diameter used to determine whether a bag falls within the definition is not the same measurement as the length-plus-width total used for the warning type.

A gift brand considering polyethylene protective packaging should resolve those two questions in order, rather than starting with a warning artwork template.

The Statutory Bag Definition Has Cumulative Conditions

Under subsection (a), the relevant definition requires a polyethylene bag intended for household use or for packaging articles intended for household use. It must also have:

  • An opened-end diameter greater than 5 inches.
  • Film thickness less than 1 mil (0.001 inch).

The definition excludes bags used for food products weighing not more than five pounds. That is a specific exclusion, not an exemption for every bag associated with food.

The provision also refers to standards established under the U.S. Department of Commerce’s commodity standards division for film thickness. The published section does not itself supply a complete measurement procedure.

These conditions should be treated individually.

For example, a supplier describing a protective sleeve as “plastic” has not established its polymer identity. An “OPP” description should not be treated as evidence that the proposed material is polyethylene. Confirm the actual film material rather than assigning a statutory category from a general packaging nickname.

The inequalities also matter. An opened-end diameter of exactly five inches is not greater than five inches. A film thickness of exactly one mil is not less than one mil.

An unresolved material or dimension should remain an unresolved definition question, not become an assumed compliance result.

Opened-End Diameter and Warning Type Size Answer Different Questions

The bag definition uses the diameter at the opened end.

Subsection (c) uses the combined length and width of the bag to determine the warning type-size band.

The statutory table is:

Combined length + width Warning type size
60 inches or more 24 points
40 inches to less than 60 inches 18 points
30 inches to less than 40 inches 14 points
Less than 30 inches 10 points

These are different dimensional tests.

A laid-flat bag width on a quotation does not, by itself, establish the statutory opened-end diameter. The published section does not prescribe a conversion formula between those measurements.

Nor should a buyer infer an opened-end diameter by treating length and width as interchangeable.

For a gusseted or otherwise unusual bag construction, the actual dimensional references need to be clarified before relying on a classification. A dieline may provide useful dimensions without establishing every measurement required by the legal definition.

A Hypothetical 31-Inch Total Selects the 14-Point Band

Imagine a small gift brand preparing a nonfood household article for sale in Rhode Island.

The brand proposes a separate polyethylene protective bag around that article.

For this hypothetical example, assume the following facts are already established:

  • The bag material is polyethylene.
  • Its intended use is packaging the household article.
  • Its opened-end diameter is greater than five inches.
  • Its film thickness is less than one mil.
  • The stated food-product exclusion does not apply.

These are illustrative assumptions, not physical measurements, supplier declarations or evidence of an actual product.

Now consider the bag’s proposed dimensions:

Length: 16 inches

Width: 15 inches

The warning-size calculation is:

16 + 15 = 31 inches

Thirty-one inches falls within the statutory range beginning at 30 inches and ending below 40 inches.

The relevant warning type-size row is therefore 14 points, subject to the provision’s complete conditions.

The result is a type-size classification for this hypothetical bag. It is not an approval of warning wording, placement, legibility, printing quality or legal applicability to a real transaction.

In particular, the 31-inch combined dimension cannot substitute for the separately assumed opened-end diameter.

The Warning Must Have an Appropriate Path to Each Bag

Section 11-9-16(b) addresses packaging, delivering or selling household-use articles in covered bags, and selling or distributing covered bags for household use.

Subsection (c) permits the required warning to be printed on, attached to, or accompany each bag. It also requires conspicuous presentation in boldface type according to its size table.

A warning therefore does not necessarily have to be printed directly on the polyethylene film. But the selected presentation method must still satisfy the applicable statutory conditions.

The official section supplies warning language and allows substantially equivalent wording. The complete wording and presentation requirements should be reviewed in the original Rhode Island statute, rather than reconstructed from a shortened design example.

There is an important limitation concerning outer wrappers.

The section provides a specific allowance for placing the warning on the outside wrapper of packages of bags intended only for home-processing use, with freezer bags and garbage-disposal bags given as examples.

That narrow provision should not automatically be extended to an ordinary shipping master carton containing protective bags intended to accompany individual gift products.

A master carton used to transport packaging components is not automatically the qualifying home-processing bag wrapper described by the provision.

A Changed Thickness Does Not Establish General Safety

Return to the hypothetical protective bag.

Keep its intended use, polymer identity and other assumed characteristics unchanged, but change one fact: the film thickness is now exactly one mil.

Because subsection (a) specifies thickness less than one mil, that revised bag does not meet this particular definition on the stated assumptions.

Its length and width could still total 31 inches. That arithmetic does not repair the failed definition condition.

This is a narrow legal-scope distinction, not a safety conclusion.

Not meeting this section’s definition does not demonstrate that the bag is safe for household use, exempt from every other applicable requirement, or acceptable under a particular retailer’s or distribution platform’s rules.

Similarly, uncertainty about polymer identity, opened-end diameter or the food-product exclusion should not be converted into a claim of exemption.

Record the Definition Result Before Preparing Warning Artwork

A buyer can turn this analysis into a conditional decision for each proposed bag version.

First, establish the material, intended use, food-exclusion question, opened-end diameter and film thickness using information appropriate to the actual configuration.

If the definition conditions are met, separately establish the length and width, calculate their combined total, and identify the statutory type-size row.

Then determine how the warning is proposed to reach each bag, without assuming that an ordinary master carton qualifies for the narrow home-processing wrapper allowance.

If the physical facts or applicable legal interpretation remain unresolved, keep the warning design decision open rather than treating a draft layout as approval.

After the statutory scope and type-size questions have been resolved, the brand can assign responsibility for the actual warning wording and review the small type against the selected printer’s specifications. Neither artwork workflow replaces the earlier legal definition check.

Packrivo supports packaging sourcing and project coordination. It does not manufacture the bag film or approve legal warning compliance.

Primary legal reference: Rhode Island General Laws § 11-9-16, Plastic bags — Labeling. Official public text accessed October 10, 2026. Its displayed legislative history lists 1959 and 1960 enactments, without a separately displayed current revision date. Application to an actual bag and transaction remains subject to verification.

Carry the bag revision into its warning-carrier layout

Keep the original 31-inch example intact and examine another invented revision near the 40-inch boundary. For BAG_A29 and BAG_B29, assume polyethylene, household-article use, opened-end diameter greater than 5 inches, thickness less than 1 mil and no applicable food exclusion. These premises establish only the exercise’s definition and use scope; the film and dimensions have not been measured.

If a further version uses exactly 1 mil film, it fails the definition’s less-than-1-mil thickness condition on the assumed facts. Keeping a 40-inch sum does not repair that condition. Conversely, a large length-plus-width total cannot substitute for the separate opened-end diameter test. Flat width is not converted into diameter, and an unknown polymer or food-exclusion fact stays open.

Carry the changed band into the warning carrier, not straight into approved artwork. This example invents no card dimensions, missing words or fit result, and it does not solve a space problem by shrinking the required type. A printer’s file specification cannot override the applicable legal requirement. The warning must still reach each bag through a permitted path; the narrow home-processing wrapper allowance is not assumed for a normal master carton. title: An Opened Hot-Melt Carton Joint Can Break at Different Layers
html:
When an outer carton arrives with a hot-melt-bonded joint already open, the visible break does not explain why it happened. It may have run along the boundary between adhesive and carton surface, through the adhesive itself, or through the carton material. More than one pattern may be present.

Knowing where the joint separated helps frame the next technical investigation. It does not establish fault, acceptable bond strength, or a validated repair.

Both faces of the opened joint tell part of the story

Consider the opposing surfaces that were bonded together.

On one face, adhesive may remain as a relatively continuous strip, while the corresponding receiving area looks largely uncovered. This is consistent with separation near an adhesive–substrate interface.

If adhesive appears split and remains on both corresponding areas, the break may have passed within the adhesive, called cohesive fracture.

If a paper liner or board fibres have been pulled from the carton and remain attached across the joint, part of the fracture may be within the substrate.

These are possible patterns, not visual certificates. An apparently bare face may have a thin residue or surface layer that cannot be resolved by ordinary viewing. Exposed patches can coexist with adhesive remnants and torn fibres.

The undated BÜHNEN technical explanations distinguish interfacial failure, cohesive failure and substrate failure.

Three similar pop-opens raise different technical questions

Imagine three hypothetical outer cartons for a gift brand. Their specified joints use hot-melt adhesive; each carton arrives with a joint already open.

All three look similarly unsealed from the outside, yet their apparent fracture locations differ. These invented observations are not actual inspections or test results.

Joint A: One receiving face looks mostly uncovered.

A band of adhesive appears on one face, while the matching region on the other looks largely bare.

This suggests interfacial separation in those regions, not proof of contamination or unsuitable glue.

The technical reviewer needs to establish which carton liner, print, coating or film actually met the adhesive and whether the intended contact was formed.

Was the hot melt still able to engage that receiving face when the bond was made? Could it have set before the surfaces were brought together, or was contact otherwise incomplete?

These are competing questions, not findings. The intended face-and-layer information belongs with the glue-zone guide.

Joint B: Apparent adhesive remnants occur on both faces.

Matching areas show torn-looking hot-melt material on each side.

A split within the adhesive becomes a relevant possibility, but glue on both sides does not prove cohesive fracture across the whole joint.

The reviewer needs to assess how the actual adhesive was expected to behave under the joint’s opening loads and known temperature history, including whether the remnants correspond across the fracture area.

Henkel’s undated hot-melt pop-open guidance lists adhesive on both faces among observations associated with more than one failure scenario, including cold- and heat-related problems.

That appearance cannot establish either cause by itself.

Joint C: Carton material stays attached at the joint.

A section of paper liner appears torn away from one carton face and remains with adhesive on the other.

The next question shifts toward where the liner or board divided and what loads acted on that region.

Was the break within a carton ply, a laminated layer, or only in portions adjacent to another fracture type? Could the visible tear have developed during later handling rather than the initial opening?

A fibre tear alone does not prove defective board, excessive transit forces, or a sufficiently strong carton joint.

Mixed fracture areas and opening loads complicate the pattern

An opened seam need not fit one label.

One end may expose the receiving surface, the middle may show adhesive on both faces, and an edge may carry torn board fibres.

This is a mixed fracture pattern. Recognising the distinct regions is more accurate than assigning a single fracture type to the whole joint.

BÜHNEN’s undated fracture-pattern explanation explains that the manner of loading matters. Direct separation and peeling can produce different fracture appearances.

An unexpected opening during distribution does not have a known, uniform test load merely because its fractured surfaces remain visible. The applied forces, their direction and the sequence of opening may be uncertain.

This is why an image cannot establish a single correction. Contact conditions, environmental exposure, substrate layers and mechanical loading can interact. A mixed appearance does not automatically mean multiple independent defects.

An unwanted pop-open is not a passed bond evaluation

In a deliberately destructive bond evaluation, cohesive fracture or substrate tear can sometimes be favourable compared with separation at an adhesive interface.

BÜHNEN describes substrate fracture as potentially positive within a fracture-mechanics test, where the evaluation purpose and conditions are defined.

That interpretation does not transfer automatically to a carton that was intended to remain closed but opened unexpectedly.

Visible fibre tear cannot convert the incident into an acceptance pass. Nor can adhesive on both faces establish a numerical bond strength or compliance result.

The reviewer still needs the intended closure performance, actual construction, relevant loading conditions and appropriate evaluation basis.

A report covering a different construction should not be treated as proof for this joint. The test-report configuration guide addresses that separate applicability question.

The useful outcome is a narrower technical investigation

Preserve the two already-opened bond faces and their received relationship. Do not clean, re-glue, rearrange or peel them further to create a clearer-looking pattern. Do not create destructive test samples.

If part of the original fracture has been disturbed or is missing, acknowledge that limitation.

The existing transit-damage guide addresses received condition, incident location and packaging version. The additional task here is deciding which physical fracture mechanisms require investigation.

For interfacial-looking areas, the responsible carton and adhesive specialists should assess the actual bonding surfaces and how contact was formed.

For apparent cohesive separation, they should examine the adhesive’s behaviour under relevant loading and environmental conditions.

For substrate fracture, they should consider board or liner construction and the local loading of the joint.

For mixed areas, more than one path may remain open. The responsible technical parties must decide what additional evaluation is appropriate and whether any proposed correction is adequately supported.

This reasoning applies to a confirmed hot-melt-bonded carton joint. If the joining material is unknown, identify it before assuming a hot-melt failure mechanism. Evidence for hot melt cannot automatically be transferred to tape, pressure-sensitive adhesives, epoxies or foil-bonded constructions.

A fracture plane narrows the investigation. It does not, by itself, explain the opening or validate a remedy.

Pair corresponding regions before calling a fracture cohesive

Use a new invented map of two already-open faces, A and B, without opening another joint. Pair A 1 with B 1, A 2 with B 2 and A 3 with B 3 using an established orientation reference. Assume visible adhesive at A 1 with B 1 largely uncovered; at A 2 largely uncovered with adhesive at B 2; and A 3/B 3 unavailable. These are fictional observations for teaching, not inspected cartons.

Hypothetical configuration Named object Relationship Input or next scope
REGION29 A1 corresponds to B1
REGION29 A1 assumed appearance ADHESIVE_VISIBLE
REGION29 B1 assumed appearance LARGELY_UNCOVERED
REGION29 A2 corresponds to B2
REGION29 A2 assumed appearance LARGELY_UNCOVERED
REGION29 B2 assumed appearance ADHESIVE_VISIBLE
REGION29 A3 corresponds to B3
REGION29 A3 assumed appearance UNAVAILABLE
REGION29 B3 assumed appearance UNAVAILABLE
REGION29 A1_AND_B2_ADHESIVE not evidence of CORRESPONDING_COHESIVE_SPLIT
REGION29 A3_B3 leave UNKNOWN
REGION29 ALREADY_OPEN_FACES do not CLEAN_REGLUE_ROTATE_TO_FAKE_MATCH_OR_EXTRA_PEEL

It would be true in a loose description that adhesive appears somewhere on both faces. It would be false to conclude from that alone that corresponding adhesive was split throughout the joint. A 1 and B 2 belong to different pairs. Each known pair instead raises an interface-related question under the assumed appearance, while missing pair 3 stays unresolved. Thin residue, surface layers and mixed fracture can still complicate either apparently uncovered region.

The useful output is the region-to-region correspondence, not a verdict of cold glue, hot glue, contamination or adequate bond. Keep received orientation, photo scope and any missing or disturbed area visible. Do not clean, re-glue, rotate pieces to suggest a match or peel additional material to produce a clearer pattern. The responsible technical reviewer must decide what examination is appropriate for the actual joint and loading history.

BÜHNEN’s interface, cohesive, substrate and fracture-pattern explanations and Henkel’s pop-open discussion support these distinctions without establishing unique causes from one appearance. A fibre-bearing region would add a substrate question, not an acceptance certificate. The region map complements the glue-zone construction record: one locates intended material contact, the other identifies which already-opened areas can actually be compared. Actual material, process, loading and corrective decision remain blank.

Actual quantity, configuration, component and file identities, materials, process, specification, copy, method, condition, observation, owner, decision, evidence and dates are blank. ACTUAL_BLANK is a separate empty starting row; enter permitted project evidence before using an actual record. A blank means unknown.

Use the Glue Zones Need the Current Drawing and Surface Layers in One View for its separate question.

Reliable individual publication dates were not confirmed. They prescribe no actual adhesive temperature, repair, unique cause, accepted strength or seal result. The added configurations and calculations are hypothetical, with actual evidence and decisions pending.

title: A Closure Seal Needs a Defined Opening-Indication Event
html:
A closure seal answers a recipient-facing question only when its physical change is tied to a specified event, at a named joint, during a defined period. A mark can suggest that a seal was disturbed; it cannot, on its own, identify who acted, why they acted, or whether the entire gift box stayed unopened.

A Visible Indication Depends on Its Material and Trigger

An ordinary closure sticker may hold or decorate a lid without having a designed opening indication. An indication-oriented construction instead relies on a particular change when a specified action occurs. The location of that change matters as much as the marketing term.

Indication concept Event described in manufacturer literature Where the change is intended to appear
Facestock indication An attempt to detach the label In the label’s face material
Surface-transfer indication Detachment from the receiving surface On the box surface previously under the label
Destructible material An attempted removal that damages the film In the seal material itself

These are mechanism categories, not verified options for any particular gift box. Avery Dennison’s 2019 historical portfolio distinguishes facestock-retained indications, transferred surface indications and destructible films. That document describes historical constructions, not their present availability or suitability.

One identified example is 3M’s 7381/7866 technical data sheet, revised June 2024. It describes a VOID indication in the facestock during an attempted removal, with a corresponding transfer to the receiving surface. It also explains that suitable adhesion is necessary, that opaque graphics can conceal the indication and that dispensing can trigger the feature prematurely.

Its typical technical information and industrial-use cautions are not proof of performance on a wrapped gift box. This named product is an illustration from manufacturer literature, not a Packrivo-offered or verified grade.

The trigger must be described accurately. A label reacting to an attempted peel is reporting an event involving that label; it is not directly observing every possible movement of the lid. Equally, an indication visible only after a label has been lifted might not answer a recipient who expects an exterior, before-opening inspection.

Authorized Packing Can Consume the Indication

Consider a hypothetical brand that receives assembled, empty lift-off gift boxes already closed. A proposed one-use seal spans the front lid-to-base joint, J1. Before any recipient receives a gift, the brand’s packing team must lift each lid, insert the item and complete the presentation.

If that necessary opening disturbs the sealed joint in the way that triggers the proposed mechanism, the indication may already be consumed during legitimate preparation.

A recipient seeing the changed material later cannot distinguish that event from an unauthorized act merely by reading the mark. The same ambiguity can arise if a giver legitimately opens a completed gift to add a note. The material responds to a physical event, not to permission or motive.

Two clocks are therefore possible.

Since the supplier first closed the empty box includes the packing team’s expected opening.

Since final gift pack-out refers instead to the completed, filled package intended for handover.

For this hypothetical brand, choose the second clock for the recipient-facing design requirement. Do not promise that a one-use indication intended to cover the first clock can meaningfully certify the second.

This choice does not rewrite the box’s earlier history. No later seal or clean-looking closure proves what happened before the chosen reference event. If the brand genuinely needs evidence about empty-box handling as well, that is a separate question requiring separately established evidence, not a conclusion to extract from one mark.

The Recipient-Period Requirement Belongs to One Joint

For J1, the brand can make a specific provisional choice:

After final pack-out, an attempted disturbance of the label bridge at the front lid-to-base joint should produce a distinguishable change in the outward-facing facestock that a recipient can inspect without first peeling the seal.

The defined interval, named joint and expected viewing location are part of the requirement, not outcomes already demonstrated.

A proposal that only exposes a transferred mark on the surface underneath the detached label may answer a different inspection question. A proposed destructible film may create a material break instead of a printed pattern. Neither is automatically wrong; neither can be treated as equivalent to the chosen facestock-visible requirement without an actual proposal and relevant evidence.

There are two linked feasibility questions.

First, does the specified disturbance produce the proposed change on the actual finished J1 surface, with its wrap or coating?

Second, does the recipient see the change with the actual artwork and intended viewing condition?

Packrivo’s label adhesion article covers surface and application records; its removal-observation article covers what can be observed after peeling. The separate decision here is whether an observed physical event communicates the intended recipient-period meaning.

One Indicated Joint Is Not a Complete Opening History

Even if a proposed indicator performs at J1 under agreed conditions, it says nothing by itself about other package joints or other possible opening paths.

No visible change at J1 is not proof that the entire gift box was never opened. A visible change is also not proof of dishonest tampering: packing, a giver’s ordinary handling or another disturbance could have caused the relevant physical event.

The usable outcome is a bounded design statement:

“J1 is the front lid-to-base seal on the final filled gift box. The intended reference begins at final pack-out. Review whether an attempted disturbance at J1 leaves an unambiguous, recipient-visible change in the outer facestock under the intended viewing condition. The mechanism, substrate response and visibility remain unverified. Do not interpret the indication as proof of intent or whole-package integrity.”

That statement gives a sourcing and project-coordination discussion a concrete purpose without pretending to approve a security process.

Unlike the return-mailer second-seal decision, which concerns closing a used package again, this decision is about the meaning and limits of one potential indication after a declared start event.

It remains a proposed requirement until an identified construction and relevant physical evidence support it.

Artwork coverage can hide the required indication location

Hold the original J 1 final-pack-out reference period constant, then vary where the proposed recipient would see an indication. FACE_OPEN29 reserves face area I 1 without opaque artwork. FACE_COVER29 adds an opaque graphic over I 1. SURFACE_ONLY29 instead describes a proposed indication on receiving area R 1 underneath a removed label. These are layout and mechanism premises, not actual VOID responses or tested constructions.

Hypothetical configuration Named object Relationship Input or next scope
FACE_OPEN29 FACE_OPEN29 proposed location I1_FACE
FACE_OPEN29 FACE_OPEN29 proposed artwork NO_OPAQUE_ARTWORK
FACE_OPEN29 FACE_OPEN29 proposed view EXTERIOR_BEFORE_PEEL
FACE_COVER29 FACE_COVER29 proposed location I1_FACE
FACE_COVER29 FACE_COVER29 proposed artwork OPAQUE_GRAPHIC_AT_I1
FACE_COVER29 FACE_COVER29 proposed view EXTERIOR_BEFORE_PEEL
SURFACE_ONLY29 SURFACE_ONLY29 proposed location R1_RECEIVING_SURFACE
SURFACE_ONLY29 SURFACE_ONLY29 proposed view ONLY_AFTER_LIFT
SEAL29 J1 retains FINAL_PACKOUT_REFERENCE_PERIOD
FACE_OPEN29 CLEAR_AREA_I1 does not prove INDICATION_RESPONSE
FACE_COVER29 OPAQUE_GRAPHIC reopens INDICATION_VISIBILITY
SURFACE_ONLY29 R1_AFTER_LIFT not equivalent to FACE_VISIBLE_BEFORE_PEEL

An uncovered I 1 is a place to investigate visibility, not proof that the label develops an indication there. Covering it introduces a separate masking question: even if a proposed mechanism responds, the final graphic can obscure what the recipient is expected to inspect. Do not carry a plain-material demonstration into printed-layout acceptance without reviewing the actual construction and artwork together.

SURFACE_ONLY29 answers another viewing sequence. If R 1 is accessible only after lifting the seal, it cannot simply replace a requirement to inspect the exterior before peeling. A particular material may combine face and transferred indications, as the identified 3M example describes; that does not make all constructions interchangeable. The download preserves mechanism location, artwork coverage and intended inspection state as different relationships.

None of the three proves tamper prevention, motive, whole-package integrity or the package’s earlier history. Retain the selected interval and joint while asking the converter which actual construction, surface and printed face can address the requirement. Avery’s 2019 portfolio remains historical;3M 7381/7866’sJune 2024 TDS is a specific example with adhesion, graphics and premature-dispensing limits. No current offer, trigger, ageing result or dispensing process is accepted here.

Actual quantity, configuration, component and file identities, materials, process, specification, copy, method, condition, observation, owner, decision, evidence and dates are blank. ACTUAL_BLANK is a separate empty starting row; enter permitted project evidence before using an actual record. A blank means unknown.

Use the Record Removal Conditions Before Asking for a Removable Label for its separate question.

Source scope checked 17 October 2026: Avery Dennison’s 2019 portfolio is historical. The named 3M 7381/7866 TDS revised June 2024 describes a particular material with adhesion, graphic-masking and premature-dispensing limitations; neither source proves current availability, security or an actual gift-box response. The added configurations and calculations are hypothetical, with actual evidence and decisions pending.

title: Overseas Personalisation Printing Needs a Data-Transfer Decision
html:
Before sending recipient information to a separate overseas printing company, a brand whose processing is covered by UK GDPR needs to decide whether the arrangement is a restricted transfer and who is responsible for it.

Keeping the file on a UK server does not remove that decision. Allowing the overseas printer to access the file may trigger the same transfer rules as sending a copy.

The practical rule is to identify the receiving legal entity, apply the Information Commissioner’s Office (ICO) three-step test, and establish the appropriate transfer mechanism before sending information or enabling access. A small order, a processor agreement or an agreed print specification does not automatically satisfy those requirements.

The three-step test applies to the proposed information flow

The ICO asks organisations to determine whether all three conditions are met:

  1. UK GDPR applies to the processing. Establish whether the relevant personal information and processing activity fall within UK GDPR. The fact that printing takes place abroad does not, by itself, answer this question.
  2. The organisation initiates a transfer to an overseas organisation. Identify who chose the receiving organisation and designed the arrangement that causes the information to be sent or made accessible. The person physically uploading the file is not necessarily the initiator.
  3. The receiver is a separate legal entity. Establish whether the recipient is another company or other separate organisation, rather than part of the same legal entity.

When all three conditions are met, the proposed flow is a restricted-transfer arrangement requiring a lawful covering mechanism.

The receiving organisation’s legal establishment matters. A storage location, overseas workstation or familiar brand name cannot substitute for checking the actual entity involved.

See the ICO’s detailed three-step guidance.

Sending a file and permitting remote access require the same classification

Consider an entirely hypothetical gift brand, BrandEntity, established in the UK. It controls recipient-personalisation data and wishes to use SeparatePrinter, an independent company established outside the UK.

The only illustrative field identifier is RecipientFieldR1. It stands for information that would identify a recipient in a real printing workflow. No actual recipient information is used in this example.

BrandEntity chooses SeparatePrinter directly and determines how that printer will receive the information.

Proposed arrangement Three-step result Decision before proceeding
A — File delivery. BrandEntity sends a personalisation file containing RecipientFieldR1 to SeparatePrinter. UK GDPR applies; BrandEntity initiates the overseas transfer; SeparatePrinter is a separate legal entity. All three: Yes. Restricted transfer. Do not send until a covering mechanism is established and relevant checks are complete.
B — Remote viewing. The same SeparatePrinter receives permission to view RecipientFieldR1 in a file stored on BrandEntity’s UK server. Same processing scope, initiator and separate receiving entity. All three: Yes. Restricted transfer occurs when the overseas organisation accesses the information. Do not enable access without ensuring the covering mechanism is in place when access is made possible.
C — Same-entity employee. An employee of BrandEntity, working abroad as part of that same legal entity, accesses the UK-held file. UK GDPR applies and the overseas access is initiated, but there is no separate receiving legal entity. Step three: No. Not a restricted transfer under this test. Other UK GDPR obligations, including appropriate security, still require review.

These outcomes do not depend on whether the printer can download the file. Viewing personal information remotely can be sufficient.

There is an important timing distinction in arrangement B: the restricted transfer occurs upon the overseas organisation’s access, but the required covering mechanism must already have been ensured when BrandEntity makes access possible. The review cannot be postponed until after the first viewing session.

Nor does the same-entity result extend automatically to another company within BrandEntity’s corporate group. A group subsidiary may be a separate legal entity even if it shares ownership, branding or management.

The initiator is determined by who chooses the processing route

In arrangements A and B, BrandEntity deliberately selects SeparatePrinter and establishes the overseas printing arrangement. BrandEntity therefore initiates the transfer.

Now suppose BrandEntity separately employs a hypothetical UK print studio to prepare the artwork.

If BrandEntity has chosen and contracted with SeparatePrinter, then instructs its UK studio to upload the file, BrandEntity remains the initiator. The studio operating the upload button does not change that responsibility.

A different arrangement produces a different answer.

Suppose the UK studio acts as BrandEntity’s processor, designs its own printing service, selects an overseas sub-processor and contracts with that overseas company to deliver part of the service. Under the ICO’s approach, the UK studio would normally initiate the restricted transfer to its chosen sub-processor.

The UK studio must have BrandEntity’s prior specific or general written authorisation before engaging that sub-processor. Existing general written authorisation may cover the engagement without fresh authorisation for each change, subject to the required notice of intended additions or replacements and BrandEntity’s opportunity to object. Authorisation is not the same as initiating the transfer.

The party responsible for the transfer rules depends on the actual contractual and processing structure, not simply whether it is called the brand, supplier, controller or processor.

Whoever initiates the transfer must address the transfer rules. Other parties retain their applicable UK GDPR and contractual responsibilities.

A covering mechanism must be established before access

Once the three-step test identifies a restricted transfer, the initiating organisation needs to establish which lawful route covers it.

The current UK GDPR framework includes Article 44A, introduced in February 2026, with three principal routes:

  • UK adequacy regulations: Check whether applicable UK regulations under Article 45A cover the relevant destination, territory, sector or organisation and the proposed transfer.
  • Appropriate safeguards: Assess an applicable Article 46 safeguard, potentially including a properly executed UK International Data Transfer Agreement (IDTA) or International Data Transfer Addendum. The ICO also requires a transfer risk assessment (TRA), any necessary additional protections and legally effective safeguards.
  • Specific derogations: Assess whether an Article 49 exception actually applies where the other routes do not cover the transfer. An ordinary, recurring personalisation service should not assume an exceptional route is available merely because the print quantity is small.

Article 44A also refers to possible restrictions under Article 49A that must be considered where relevant.

The Data (Use and Access) Act changed the terminology of the Article 46 assessment. UK legislation now refers to a data protection test, while the ICO continues to call the practical assessment a TRA. The test requires a reasonable and proportionate determination about whether protection following transfer would be materially lower than in the UK.

Merely proposing an IDTA, naming a contract template or obtaining approval for a printing purchase does not establish appropriate safeguards.

If no applicable covering mechanism can be established, the decision is not to enable the restricted transfer.

For the hypothetical SeparatePrinter arrangements, the destination-specific legal position, contractual documents and assessment results remain unknown. Neither arrangement A nor B is approved by this article.

See the ICO’s guidance on transfer mechanisms.

The output is an access decision, not another artwork approval

Before releasing personal information, the brand can create one concise decision record for each proposed printing route.

That record should identify the UK GDPR processing scope, the receiving legal entity and its establishment, whether information will be sent or remotely accessed, the party initiating the transfer, the three-step answers, and the applicable mechanism review status.

For the hypothetical arrangements A and B, the provisional decision record would read:

RecipientFieldR1 → SeparatePrinter → Restricted transfer identified → Mechanism unverified → DO NOT SEND / DO NOT ENABLE ACCESS.

This is not a security certificate or a legal approval. It is a specific instruction that prevents the printing workflow from proceeding on an unverified assumption.

A brand may also investigate whether truly generic, non-personal packaging artwork can be printed separately and recipient-specific personalisation added locally. Whether that production arrangement is practical requires separate confirmation.

Replacing a name with an internal code is not automatically anonymisation. If the information remains personal data in BrandEntity’s hands as controller, it remains personal data for its printer acting as processor, whether or not the key or mapping table is shared. For a recipient that is neither a processor nor a joint controller, whether the information is genuinely anonymous in that recipient’s hands requires a separate assessment.

This access decision complements, rather than repeats, existing packaging planning:

  • How to Personalize Gift Packaging addresses where changing content belongs.
  • Gift-Ready Ecommerce Packaging addresses how order and recipient instructions reach fulfilment.
  • A Print File Manifest addresses artwork files, fonts, linked assets and output versions.

Those decisions do not establish permission to transfer personal information internationally.

Packrivo coordinates packaging sourcing and project questions; it does not determine whether a particular organisation’s international data-transfer mechanism satisfies UK GDPR.

The next action is to settle the legal-entity, initiator and mechanism questions before granting a printer access to recipient information—not after the artwork has already been released.

Sources and legal scope

This article uses the ICO’s brief international transfers guide and detailed international transfers guidance, updated 15 January 2026.

The legislative reference is UK GDPR Chapter V, checked against the official 30 September 2026 revision, particularly Articles 44A, 45A, 46, 49 and 49A. The ICO’s separate controller–processor contract guidance is marked as under review following the Data (Use and Access) Act.

All printing arrangements, entities and field identifiers in this article are illustrative. No destination, safeguard, provider arrangement or transfer has been assessed or approved for a real business. This is general buyer education, not legal advice.

CODE29 adds OrderTokenR1, assumed linkable to a person in the controller’s records, for a separately established overseas printer acting as processor. title: Read Foam Compression Data Against the Intended Deflection
html:
A foam compression value is useful for a jewelry holder proposal only when it describes the compression state the design is expected to create. If a supplier’s technical sheet reports compression at 25% deflection, but the proposed pad would be compressed by 20%, those are different states. The 25% value cannot simply be relabeled or proportionally adjusted to answer the 20% question.

For a small jewelry or gift brand, the immediate decision is not which foam is best. It is whether the available compression data can support a comparison at the intended deflection.

Calculate deflection from the original foam height

Compression deflection describes how much a material’s height decreases relative to its original, uncompressed height.

Consider a purely hypothetical flat foam pad:

  • Uncompressed foam height: 10 mm
  • Available gap when the package is closed: 8 mm
  • Reduction in height: 2 mm

Assuming the pad is compressed uniformly between two flat surfaces, its relative deflection is:

Deflection (%) = (Original height − Compressed height) ÷ Original height × 100

(10 − 8) ÷ 10 × 100 = 20%

The denominator is the original 10 mm foam height, not the remaining 8 mm gap. Dividing 2 mm by 8 mm would incorrectly describe this example as 25% compression.

This distinction matters because compression data is commonly associated with a particular percentage of the original specimen thickness.

Now imagine the same uncompressed pad in a different enclosure. If the available gap becomes 7.5 mm, the nominal deflection becomes 25%. If it becomes 9 mm, the nominal deflection becomes 10%.

These calculations identify geometric states. They provide no compression force, stress, safe contact pressure, or material recommendation.

The example also assumes that 10 mm describes the foam itself. If a proposal includes a separate backing, adhesive or other relatively noncompressible layer, the buyer must establish the actual foam thickness and the clearance available to that foam. Total assembly thickness should not automatically become the denominator.

Match the supplier data to the calculated percentage

A supplier might provide a technical data sheet containing one compression value measured at 25% deflection.

For the hypothetical 10 mm pad installed in an 8 mm gap, that is not the target state. The design calculation identifies 20% nominal deflection, while the supplied value describes 25%.

The distinction follows the measurement explanation in Rogers Corporation’s guide to compression force deflection, published November 12, 2024. Its discussion of percentage deflection and compression response concerns elastomeric materials, particularly sealing and gasketing applications.

The useful principle for a gift-packaging buyer is narrower: identify which percentage of compression the reported value actually represents.

If the manufacturer provides a relevant curve covering 20% deflection, the buyer can identify the corresponding position on that curve for technical review. If the sheet supplies only a 25% point, the response at 20% remains unsupported by that point alone.

Even when a datasheet’s percentage matches the calculated percentage, the material identity and test basis must still be checked before the value is considered applicable.

Read the reported quantity and its unit

The words compression force deflection can be misleading when the actual technical result is expressed as stress rather than total force.

A compression result might be reported as:

  • Stress or pressure: for example, kPa or psi.
  • Force: for example, N or lbf.
  • Relative deflection: a percentage of the original specimen height.

These quantities answer different questions.

A stress value describes force relative to an area under the stated test conditions. A force value describes the total applied force for the specified test arrangement. Neither should be read without its unit and specimen information.

For example, a result whose vertical axis is labeled kPa cannot be treated as a total force in newtons. Converting stress into a force estimate would require an appropriate loaded area and a valid relationship between the test and the intended loading arrangement.

Rogers’ January 17, 2025 article, Foam Firmness vs Density and Why Its Important, explains foam compression behavior using stress and strain. It also identifies ASTM D1056 for its BISCO silicone materials and ASTM D3574 for its PORON polyurethane materials.

Those are manufacturer-specific material and testing references, not interchangeable test procedures or universal requirements for jewelry packaging.

The buyer should therefore preserve the exact reported quantity, unit, method and material identity. The CFD abbreviation alone does not establish what the numerical value means.

A nonlinear curve prevents simple proportional estimates

Suppose the supplier reports compression behavior at 25%, but the intended geometry implies 20%.

It may be tempting to multiply the reported value by 20/25 and use the result as an estimate.

That is not a justified general calculation.

Foam compression response can be nonlinear. The relationship between deflection and resistance may change as the cellular structure compresses, and a curve can become steeper over part of its range.

Rogers explicitly discusses this nonlinear behavior in its 2024 compression guide. Its illustrated comparisons also emphasize using the same specimen thickness when comparing material curves.

A single 25% data point does not establish the response at 20%. Nor does a nominally similar product name establish that a curve from another grade applies.

A defensible comparison needs suitable grade-specific information at or covering the intended deflection, interpreted within its declared measurement basis. Numerical interpolation or extrapolation should not be introduced without technical support appropriate to that material and curve.

When reviewing a curve, the relevant questions are whether it represents the proposed grade and thickness, how its axes and units are defined, and what measurement method and conditions apply. If loading history or another test condition matters to the comparison, its basis should also be established.

The manufacturer data helps define a material response under its stated conditions. It does not automatically predict the behavior of a finished jewelry holder.

A shaped jewelry cavity changes the loading geometry

A flat compression specimen and a finished foam jewelry holder are not the same mechanical arrangement.

Consider a holder with a cut opening for a ring. The surrounding foam may have different remaining widths, depths and supporting surfaces. A product may touch only selected locations rather than compressing a uniform, continuous pad.

A backing layer may carry part of the load. A cut edge may bend rather than undergo uniform through-thickness compression. The closed box may also create different clearances at different locations.

As a result, the nominal 20% calculation for a flat pad does not establish a uniform 20% compression throughout a shaped holder.

It also cannot determine the local pressure applied to a ring, gemstone setting, plated surface or delicate finish.

The separate Packrivo guide to foam fabrication and layer proposals addresses the physical construction needed to define such a holder. The insert-material guide addresses form, fit and product contact.

Neither question should be replaced with an unsupported force calculation from a flat-specimen datasheet.

Conditions may also affect how measurements are compared. Packrivo’s sample-conditioning guide explains why preparation and environmental histories should remain identifiable rather than being assumed equivalent.

Actual product-contact suitability, recovery after compression and transport cushioning performance remain separate evaluations. A compression curve alone does not establish any of them.

Record the compression-state evidence decision

Return to the hypothetical flat pad with a 10 mm uncompressed height and an 8 mm available gap.

The useful buyer decision is:

Intended nominal deflection: 20%. Available supplier data: 25% compression point. Evidence status: the supplied point does not directly describe the intended state.

The next request should identify the proposed foam grade, the compressible thickness in the actual component, and data for that grade at or covering the intended 20% deflection. The response should state whether the result represents stress or force, its unit, and the applicable specimen, method and conditions.

If a complete relevant curve is available, its 20% region can be reviewed without inventing a new value. If no suitable data is available, record the compression response at 20% as unknown rather than treating the 25% point as an answer.

If the assembly changes to a nominal 7.5 mm gap, the geometric calculation changes to 25%. The existing 25% point then aligns in percentage, but still requires checks of material identity, thickness, test basis and actual holder loading geometry.

This is the boundary of the decision. The buyer can establish whether the proposed design state and supplied compression evidence correspond. That comparison does not itself establish a suitable foam grade or an acceptable force on the jewelry.

For a Packrivo sourcing and project-coordination discussion, the practical output is a precise missing-data question tied to the proposed component, rather than an unsupported material approval.

Subtract a separate backing before calculating foam deflection

Add an explicitly noncompressible backing to a new flat-pad exercise. FOAM_F1 has an assumed free thickness of 10 mm; BACK_B1 is assumed 2 mm and unchanged under this geometry. The free assembly is 12 mm. CLOSED_A29 offers a 10 mm total gap for both layers, leaving 10 − 2 = 8 mm for the foam. Its nominal foam reduction is 2 mm, and its deflection is 2 ÷ 10 = 20%.

Hypothetical configuration Named object Relationship Input or next scope
LAYERS29 FOAM_F1 assumed input 10 mm
LAYERS29 BACK_B1 assumed input 2 mm
LAYERS29 ASSEMBLY calculated from FOAM_FREE+BACKING; 12 mm
CLOSED_A29 ASSEMBLY_GAP assumed input 10 mm
CLOSED_A29 FOAM_F1 calculated from CLOSED_A29_TOTAL_GAP-BACKING; 8 mm
CLOSED_A29 FOAM_F1 calculated from FOAM_FREE-CLOSED_A29_FOAM_GAP; 2 mm
CLOSED_A29 FOAM_F1 calculated from CLOSED_A29_REDUCTION/FOAM_FREE*100; 20 percent
CLOSED_B29 ASSEMBLY_GAP assumed input 11 mm
CLOSED_B29 FOAM_F1 calculated from CLOSED_B29_TOTAL_GAP-BACKING; 9 mm
CLOSED_B29 FOAM_F1 calculated from CLOSED_B29_REDUCTION/FOAM_FREE*100; 10 percent
LAYERS29 BACK_B1 assumed NONCOMPRESSIBLE_UNCHANGED_AND_UNIFORM_FLAT_LOADING
LAYERS29 GEOMETRY does not supply CFD_FORCE_PRESSURE_OR_SUITABILITY

Dividing the same 2 mm reduction by the 12 mm free assembly would give about 16.67%, but that answers the wrong denominator for the stated foam-only compression. The backing has not become compressible foam. CLOSED_B29 instead offers an 11 mm total gap, leaving 9 mm for F 1 and giving 10% nominal deflection. Both calculations depend on the declared unchanged backing and uniform flat loading, not on an actual measured stack.

The worksheet links total gap, backing thickness, remaining foam gap and foam free thickness, so a changed layer can be traced to the affected calculation. If adhesive, flock, an additional film or a compressible backing is introduced, the two-layer premise is incomplete. Leave the applicable clearances open until the offered construction explains them. A rounded assembly thickness on a quotation cannot fill the missing foam thickness.

Neither geometry supplies a CFD response. A manufacturer’s 25% point does not directly answer either 20% or 10%; no proportional scaling of that point is used. Obtain appropriate grade/thickness data with a named force or pressure quantity, unit, method and conditions. The original Rogers sources concern their material explanations and sealing/gasket examples, not a packaging-protection or jewellery-contact approval. A cavity or partial contact can also invalidate the flat, uniform geometry assumed here.
