title: Mark Liner Corner Overlaps Before Checking Usable Space
html:
Mark proposed liner corner overlaps before checking usable space in a loaded box. Show the local layers and the product position at each relevant corner. An outside box dimension or a flat liner drawing leaves the formed corner interface unresolved.

The useful output is a local section and a measurement-state note. It helps separate a corner question from a request to change every inside dimension.

Identify the proposed overlap

The box-liner reference identifies lining along box walls. Ask the supplier to show how its actual liner meets or overlaps at the corners. The catalogue does not establish one universal corner construction.

Name the corner positions and the layers present. Keep the liner, outer box and any wrap distinct in the section. Record whether the sample represents the final material and formed state.

Mark a common datum for any measurement. Use the dimension acceptance method when the reading will become an acceptance criterion, including instrument and agreed state.

Map local space against the product

Place the complete product or holder in the proposed orientation. Show the corner or edge nearest the overlap. A local raised area can create an interface different from the main wall’s clear span.

Record the actual point measured or observed rather than a general interior-size label. If a folded layer is present only at one corner, preserve that local difference in the map.

Corner record Input Evidence
Position ID Named box corner and reference face Top/side location view
Layer build Proposed overlapping parts Supplier section or sample detail
Measurement state Formed, lined and loaded condition Method and datum
Product relationship Nearest complete envelope point Located contact view
Other corners Same or different construction Separate observations
Revision Changed layer or geometry Affected corner recheck

Do not average a local corner observation into a universal cavity value without an agreed method. Name what was actually measured.

Follow a hypothetical lined gift tray

Suppose a gift holder fits along the middle of a lined box but meets a proposed overlap at one rear corner. The buyer names that corner C3 and the holder point HP3, retaining the complete installed view.

The supplier is asked to show C3’s layer build and assess its relationship to HP3. A general outside-size reply leaves the local issue open. The buyer does not enlarge the whole box immediately.

If the proposal changes the liner joint, record that as a component change. If it changes the holder, keep that separate. The next sample should identify which interface is being compared.

Keep local evidence traceable

A useful question is: ‘Please confirm the finished layer build at C3 and the agreed way to review HP3 clearance.’ It names the location and required response without inventing a tolerance.

If another corner has the same proposed build, document its actual view before carrying the observation across. A drawing can show intended symmetry while assembly still needs its own evidence.

This original sketch locates dimensional and contact questions. It does not establish retention, protection or a universal liner thickness. Any such requirement needs a defined responsible review.

Send the corner section

Bring the local layer view, product point and measurement-state record through Packrivo’s enquiry. The next response should confirm the actual corner construction and identify the relevant revised evidence.

Compare local corner deductions without averaging the cavity

Use a deliberately simplified, rigid one-dimensional section with a common transverse datum D0. Assume an unlined span of 100 mm and a holder width of 96 mm at the same section. At location C1, hypothetical left and right liner deductions are 1 mm each. The modeled free span is 98 mm and the signed difference from the holder is +2 mm. These are invented inputs, not measured layers, recommended allowances or supplier tolerances.

C1_MODEL24 RIGHT assumed local input C1; 1 mm

The arithmetic assumes those deductions describe the relevant opposing surfaces at one height and direction, with no compression or deformation. It cannot be applied to a curved or differently oriented holder by reading an outside box width. A positive modeled margin does not establish insertion, grip, retention or protection; a negative signed value only identifies overlap within this assumed section model. The actual complete envelope, local section and agreed measurement method remain necessary.

Keep a liner-joint revision separate from a holder revision. If a changed section also moves the holder or changes the reference faces, replace the corresponding inputs before comparing it. title: Keep Left and Right End Caps Identified Through Packing
html:
Keep end-cap positions and part identities separate through packing. Record which support goes at each end, whether the parts are identical and which product features they meet. A left/right label can describe installed positions without proving that two different parts exist.

This record is useful when a paired-support proposal changes. It keeps the actual parts, product ends and instruction linked rather than relying on a generic photo of two caps.

Identify both product ends and supports

The corrugated end-cap reference describes supports tailored to product shape and dimensions. That supports asking for the actual end geometry. It doesn’t establish that every pair is handed or carries a verified protective result.

Name the product’s two ends using stable features or reference faces. Add the supplier’s actual part IDs at those positions. If one common cap is confirmed for both, record that explicitly.

Show the installed orientation and any inner wrap. A cap reversed on a product may meet another feature even when its loose silhouette looks similar.

Use the sample revision record for the wider product and packaging trail. This log focuses on the paired end relationship.

Carry the pair through assembly and change

Record how supports are delivered, identified and installed. Keep the point where another outer-pack component hides them in the instruction. Staff need the part reference before that stage.

If the product changes at one end, identify the support and instruction affected. Do not mark the whole pair current merely because the other end still matches the earlier proposal.

Pair record First end Second end Evidence
Product end Stable feature/orientation Stable feature/orientation Matched product drawing
Support part Actual ID or confirmed shared part Actual ID or confirmed shared part Supplier part map
Installed face Reference orientation Reference orientation Loaded side views
Delivered identity Part grouping or marking proposal Part grouping or marking proposal Supplied-state record
Change Affected product/support field Affected product/support field Revision response
Instruction Action and position Action and position Current packing sequence

Keep part equality as a confirmed fact or an open question. An attractive mirrored drawing should not decide it.

Follow a hypothetical long gift product

Suppose a long dry-gift item has a projecting attachment at one end and a plain surface at the other. The proposed paired supports meet those different features. The buyer names the product ends A and B and asks the source to identify the actual cap parts.

If the source proposes different parts, their identities remain in the supply and packing records. If it proposes one shared part, the installed orientations are still recorded. Both arrangements can be discussed without inventing handedness.

Later the attachment changes only at end A. The log links that change to its support interface and preserves end B’s earlier record, while keeping any full-system review dependency open.

Use a position-specific question

Ask: ‘Please confirm the support part and installed face at product end A after the attachment change.’ It gives the source a specific configuration. A reply with the same product length alone may not answer the end feature.

Review the actual revised pair inside the proposed outer pack. Keep wrap and product versions named. Correct cap identification is not a transport-test result or a universal retention claim.

Any required handling or distribution evaluation should use the complete paired system under an agreed method. The log supplies identity and change context without declaring that evaluation passed.

Send the pair and affected end

Bring both end drawings, actual support IDs and the change log through Packrivo’s enquiry. The next supplier response should name which paired relationship remains current and which needs new evidence.

An unchanged second end does not approve the revised pair

Use an invented paired system to isolate the attachment change. PAIR_OLD24 names product end PA1 with support CA1, and end PB1 with support CB1, under instruction I1. PAIR_CANDIDATE24 proposes PA2 and support CA2 at end A, while PB1 and CB1 remain the named end-B references. Wrap W1 and outer pack O1 are held constant in the example, and the proposed packing instruction becomes I2.

title: Foam Packaging Inserts: Fabrication and Layer Scope
html:
Turn a foam-holder idea into a candidate component drawing and layer recipe before sampling. Identify depth-cut versus through-cut geometry, backing, adhesive, flocked faces and exposed cut faces, then record how the component arrives. This proposal record prepares fabrication questions; product-surface contact observations belong to a separate review.

Draw the component section before choosing the recipe

Ask the supplier which cutting, bonding or surface-coating operations they propose for each component in the offered section. Use that fabrication description to request the actual layer recipe. A proposed process category does not establish that a supplier can make every geometry in a chosen grade.

Label the foam component, cavity outline and section plane. For a depth-cut pocket, request the proposed cavity depth and remaining bottom layer. For a through-cut top piece, identify the separate backing or other offered support beneath the opening.

The flexible PU grade reference identifies material grades and technical fields. Attach the actual offered grade to the component drawing rather than using a generic foam name as its fabrication specification.

Assign a layer and face identity

Give the base foam, backing and any bonding layer separate BOM rows. Identify proposed thicknesses and attachment method as supplier fields, with unknowns left open. A total finished thickness does not explain which pieces or interfaces create it.

If flock is proposed, label the covered face F1 and the exposed cut face C1 separately. Mark where the surface layer stops relative to the cut. Ask whether fabrication occurs before or after another offered layer operation when that affects the actual component proposal.

Record the supplied state: one prepared component, a loose top/backing kit or another offered arrangement. State who completes any local bonding or fitting operation. The output should explain the component construction and remaining preparation before a sample instruction is issued.

Use a component-drawing and layer-recipe table

The hypothetical alternatives below are original planning examples, not measured samples or universally compatible processes.

Proposal field Depth-cut candidate A Through-cut/layered candidate B
Component/section I1, pocket section AA I2, top-piece section BB
Cut geometry Pocket with remaining bottom to be proposed Opening passes through top layer T1
Backing Integral remaining bed in offered section Separate backing B1 identified
Bonding Only if another layer is offered Adhesive/attachment row AD1 to confirm
Faces Base face and cut wall IDs Optional flock face F1 and exposed cut face C1
Supplied state Prepared pocket component or stated kit Attached assembly versus loose T1/B1 kit
Required output Candidate drawing, grade and fabrication response Candidate section, layer BOM and preparation owner

Compare an illustrative component recipe

Imagine the buyer requests one holder outline but receives a pocketed block proposal and a cut-through top/backing proposal. Request the two sections and layer recipes first. They can be different physical components even when their plan view is similar.

The converter should identify which grade, cutting method and layer order are being offered for each candidate. Keep an unsupported method or missing adhesive row open. The buyer can select which construction to sample once the component drawing and supplied state are defined.

Handoff fabrication scope before the contact review

Compare the depth-cut PU bed, through-cut EVA holder and flocked foam holder through their component sections. Use the insert-material method to retain offered grade identity.

The separate finish-contact observation method concerns the product touching packaging during handling; this record outputs a fabrication/layer proposal. The converter supplies drawing and recipe facts, the packing owner confirms local preparation and the buyer selects the candidate sample scope. Send the component sections and remaining recipe questions through your packaging brief. MOQ is 500 pieces per design; material, sample and commercial details are confirmed for the project.

Keep the integral bed separate from a bonded backing

For an invented bare-foam pocket A, assume a 20 mm block and 14 mm cut depth, leaving 6 mm integral bed. Alternative B uses 14 mm through-cut top T1 and 6 mm backing B1. Their known layer subtotal is 20 mm before the unknown AD1 attachment and optional F1 surface layer. B's finished thickness remains unconfirmed.

Candidate Assumed geometry Known arithmetic Still missing
A: bare pocket 20 mm block;14 mm depth 20-14=6 mm integral bed Actual grade, section and fabrication
B: layered T1 14 mm;B1 6 mm 14+6=20 mm before other layers AD1, F1 and finished thickness
Faces F1 optional surface;C1 exposed cut face No contact-pressure calculation Covered face limits and product compatibility

An equal subtotal does not make the constructions interchangeable. A's bottom is part of one block; B introduces a separate backing and attachment interface. Do not enter 20 mm as B's finished value while those additional layers are unknown.

The cutaway and exploded sections identify construction questions, not production templates. Colored F1 indicates a possible surface treatment only; it does not establish flock chemistry or coverage on C1. Obtain the offered grade, actual layer recipe and supplied state. Keep the person who completes local bonding or fitting identifiable. Product-contact compatibility and any foam response under compression need their separate evidence.

title: Name the Tray Edge That the Product or Hand Touches
html:
Name the formed tray edge that the product or hand touches, and record the action at that contact. Keep the actual material and sample state with the observation. A general request for a smoother tray can lose the location needed for the supplier to assess the proposed construction.

This map documents an interface and user action. It does not declare an edge safe, compliant or defective from a concept image.

Identify the edge on the actual tray

The thermoformed-tray reference establishes the formed tray and cavity context. Ask the supplier to show the actual perimeter, cut or formed edge in its proposal. The maker’s general capabilities do not verify the finish of your sample.

Give the relevant edges stable IDs on a top and side view. Distinguish the outer perimeter, cavity rim and any removal opening. Record whether the sample represents the final material and edge construction.

Include the product and any inner wrap or holder. A product resting on a broad cavity surface creates a different question from a hand reaching across its rim.

Record the touching action

Describe the stage when contact occurs: loading, closing, first grip or product removal. Keep the starting pack state visible. A hand touching a loose tray on a desk doesn’t necessarily represent access inside the complete box.

If the reviewer changes the grip or moves another item, preserve the action as a deviation or another proposed sequence. It can help explain the issue while leaving the original action unresolved.

Edge-map field Entry Evidence
Edge ID Perimeter, cavity rim or opening Marked wider view
Construction Actual material and edge proposal Supplier response/sample identity
Contacting part Product, wrap or hand Located close view
Action stage Loading or named access action Starting and contact states
Changed action Extra support or movement Deviation recorded
Next response Specific edge question Revision and review scope

Use the sample checklist for acceptance scope. Any requirement about edge condition needs a responsible agreement and appropriate evidence, beyond this location record.

Follow a hypothetical carded-gift tray

Suppose a formed tray holds a carded accessory in an outer box. During removal, the card edge meets one part of the cavity rim. The buyer names that tray edge E3 and card corner CC1, retaining the installed starting view.

The source is asked to review E3/CC1 and the intended removal route. A generic tray material description leaves that particular interface unanswered. The buyer avoids assigning a cutting or forming cause from a photograph.

A revised proposal may change the cavity opening, edge construction or card route. Each change remains identified so the next sample can be compared against the same task.

Keep material facts separate from judgement

Ask: ‘Please confirm the proposed edge construction at E3 and the evidence needed for the stated contact requirement.’ That names the location and leaves technical assessment with the responsible source.

Record observations in plain terms, including contact location or a changed grip. Do not label a concept edge with an unsupported safety result. If a specialist review is required for the use, keep it as a separate open item.

After a material or geometry revision, update the sample identity and repeat the relevant action. An unchanged outside tray outline does not necessarily describe the same contacted edge.

Send the located interface

Bring the edge map, actual component information and action views through Packrivo’s enquiry. The next response should address the named edge and use condition, followed by review under the agreed scope.

A material change and an edge change need different comparisons

Identify the original E3/CC1 removal interface, then separate two candidate responses. BASE24 names material M1 and edge revision ER1. MATERIAL24 proposes M2 with ER1 retained. GEOMETRY24 retains M1 but proposes ER2. CARD1, box B1 and the requested removal task remain identified. These are invented reference combinations; no actual material grade, edge radius or forming setting is specified.

BASE24 BASE24 uses edge revision ER1
BASE24 BASE24 uses interface E3_CC1
MATERIAL24 MATERIAL24 uses material M2
MATERIAL24 MATERIAL24 uses edge revision ER1

GEOMETRY24 GEOMETRY24 uses edge revision ER2
GEOMETRY24 GEOMETRY24 uses interface E3_CC1

Each combination has its own source-section, location-correspondence, same-route, actual-contact and requirement-review scopes in the CSV. Ask whether the E3 location still corresponds when ER2 changes the opening or rim. Reusing an edge ID is useful for following an issue, but it is not evidence that the local geometry stayed unchanged. If the feature moves or disappears, the source needs to identify its replacement location.

A material-only reply does not answer whether the revised sample presents the same contacted edge, and an unchanged outside outline does not establish the local construction. Keep a product/card contact observation separate from a hand-contact requirement. title: Review the Release Direction of a Pulp Cavity
html:
Review the release direction of a proposed pulp cavity with the product and holder installed as intended. Mark the contact points, starting grip and path out of the cavity. A product fitting into a concept recess does not show whether the customer can remove it through the same route.

This original sketch is a communication tool for a supplier proposal. It doesn’t prescribe tooling angles or claim a moulded-pulp component is verified for the product.

Identify the actual formed-part proposal

The moulded-pulp maker reference describes formed parts such as trays and end supports. That establishes a material/form context, not the fit or release geometry of a small gift cavity. Ask for the actual drawing and sample.

Name the product, holder and installed outer-pack state. Identify which surfaces are intended to touch and which remain open questions. Include any inner wrap that sits between the product and cavity.

Use the insert material guide for broader form selection. The release sketch begins after a specific cavity proposal is under discussion.

Draw touchpoints and a starting grip

Mark each proposed touchpoint on a side or sectional view. Show where fingers can reach before the product is moved. A gap visible in an isolated holder may be covered by the outer box wall or another item.

Draw the intended exit path and any change of direction. Keep supporting hands or a removal feature visible if they belong to the use. Avoid diagnosing the cause of difficult removal from a photograph alone.

Release field Input Observation
Installed state Holder, product and outer-pack identities Complete starting view
Touchpoints Named product/cavity surfaces Section and located photos
Starting grip Finger route before movement Hand access view
Exit path Direction and stages Actual removal sequence
Changed action Extra tilt, support or moved part Deviation retained
Next proposal Located supplier response Revision and recheck state

Keep contact with a cavity wall separate from an inaccessible grip. They can produce different questions even when the product ultimately comes out.

Follow a hypothetical ornament cavity

Suppose a gift ornament sits in a proposed pulp holder inside a box. The opening view looks acceptable, but the customer grip is near the surrounding wall. The buyer sketches that installed state rather than demonstrating removal from the loose holder.

A reviewer lifts the ornament along the intended route and records the point where another movement is needed. The sketch names touchpoint CP1 and starting grip GP1. No cause or production setting is assigned from that observation.

The supplier is asked to assess CP1/GP1 on the actual cavity proposal. A revised sample may change access, contact or another feature; those changes remain separately identified.

Preserve the useful comparison conditions

Ask: ‘Please review GP1 and the intended exit path with holder H1 installed in box B1.’ It names the configuration. A loose material swatch cannot answer the installed release question.

Keep product orientation, inner wrap and outer-wall state fixed when comparing revisions. If one changes, record the new condition before describing the result as a cavity-only change.

A clear removal observation does not establish retention, cushioning or repeated-use performance. Those requirements need their own agreed evaluation. The sketch locates the human action and the next source question.

Send the installed release job

Bring touchpoint views, starting grip and the complete removal sequence through Packrivo’s enquiry. Keep the next response tied to the actual proposed component, followed by review of the relevant revised sample.

Removing the loaded holder first creates another release job

Keep an invented starting configuration P1 inside pulp holder H1, with inner wrap W1, installed in box B1. PRODUCT_FIRST24 asks whether P1 can leave H1 while H1 stays inside B1. HOLDER_FIRST24 proposes taking the loaded H1/P1 arrangement out of B1 before releasing P1 from H1 outside the box. Both aim to make the product available, but the second proposal introduces another object movement and a different product-release condition.

Hypothetical configuration Named object Relationship Input or next scope
PRODUCT_FIRST24 P1 proposed movement OUT_OF_H1_WHILE_H1_IN_B1
HOLDER_FIRST24 H1_WITH_P1 proposed movement OUT_OF_B1
HOLDER_FIRST24 P1 proposed movement OUT_OF_H1_OUTSIDE_B1
HOLDER_FIRST24 H1_WITH_P1 requires LOADED_HOLDER_GRIP_EXIT_AND_SUPPORT

The CSV gives each movement its own source container, target state and job reference. PRODUCT_FIRST24 has one proposed product-release job. HOLDER_FIRST24 has a loaded-holder removal job followed by a product-release job. Its first job requires a way to grip, move and support H1 with P1 still present; no tab, grip location or ability to perform that work is assumed. A loose-holder demonstration begins after that extra job and therefore cannot close the original installed GP1 question.

Keep CP1 contact and GP1 starting access separate in both requests. A change that exposes a grip does not, by itself, describe the cavity contact during travel. Conversely, a changed cavity interface can leave the outer wall in the same place. Name the holder’s final position as well: a product outside H1 while H1 remains in B1 differs from a product outside an already removed holder. Leave W1’s after-state open until the actual sequence identifies it; do not assume the wrap stays with H1.

Rollguard’s source identifies formed pulp applications, including trays and end supports; it does not supply this small gift’s release geometry. Request the actual formed component, complete contents and intended sequence. A selected route still needs its own evidence, and neither proposed sequence establishes retention, cushioning, repeated use or a tooling angle.

title: Identify Handed Divider Parts in the Loading Plan
html:
Identify differently handed divider parts on the actual drawings before writing the assembly and loading plan. Keep left, right and shared parts distinct, with their installed orientations shown. A mirrored-looking illustration does not establish that two pieces are interchangeable.

This sheet applies when the proposed divider has differing parts. If the source confirms one common part, record that fact instead of inventing left and right versions.

Use the drawing to define part identity

The divider reference establishes the component direction. Ask the supplier which pieces differ in outline, slots, folds or another construction detail. Identify those differences on the proposal rather than assigning a part by colour alone.

Give each differing part a stable ID and name the orientation when installed. A loose part turned over can look like its counterpart while creating another slot relationship. Show the print side or reference face if relevant.

The grid-divider direction connects parts to cells. This sheet adds the identification work needed before those parts are interlocked or loaded.

Map identity through assembly

Show where each part is picked, oriented and installed. Include the point at which another piece hides its identifying feature. The instruction should make the correct relationship available before that point.

Keep shared parts explicitly shared if the source confirms them. A separate part number for every position can create unnecessary ambiguity when one piece is genuinely repeated.

Part field Left or differing part Right or counterpart Assembly check
Identity Actual drawing/part ID Actual drawing/part ID Source confirms difference
Reference face Installed orientation Installed orientation Before interlocking
Distinct feature Slot/fold/outline location Corresponding feature Visible pick reference
Installed position Named cell or side Named cell or side Formed layout view
Supply Counts and grouping Counts and grouping Delivered set matches plan
Change Affected revision Affected revision Instruction rechecked

Use the supplied-state guide to define whether parts arrive loose, bundled or preassembled. The identification method should match the actual handoff.

Follow a hypothetical unequal-cell divider

Suppose a gift set uses different-width cells around two products. The proposed divider includes two strips with different slot positions. The buyer names them D-L and D-R using the supplier drawing and marks the installed reference faces.

A reviewer follows the assembly plan. If the strips are swapped, the record shows the mismatch at the named slot rather than calling the whole divider too tight. The supplier can clarify the pick or orientation instruction.

If the source later proposes a common strip for both sides, the sheet records that construction change. It doesn’t retain an unnecessary handed distinction merely because the first drawing used one.

Make the instruction usable after bundling

Ask the supplier how the differing pieces can be identified in their delivered state. A temporary marker on an engineering model may not belong on a production part. Record the proposed identification method and its scope.

A specific question is: ‘Please confirm the delivered identity and installed reference face for D-L and D-R.’ A final formed photo alone leaves the pick step open.

Review the revised assembly with actual parts and complete contents. This tool records identity and sequence; any protective or retention requirement needs separate evidence. Correct part selection doesn’t establish those results.

Send the differing parts together

Bring the part drawings, installed map, supplied-state request and open pick questions through Packrivo’s enquiry. The next response should confirm which pieces differ and how their identities survive through packing.

One common part identity can still require two physical strips

Use one invented assembly with installed positions PL and PR referenced to FACE_A. HANDED23 requires one D-L at PL and one D-R at PR: two strips in total. COMMON23 is a proposal for one D-C at PL and another D-C at PR, also two strips. One shared part identity reduces the number of distinct IDs in this example; it does not reduce the physical strip requirement to one.

COMMON23 D-C assigned to PR; 1 strips

The CSV preserves a separate one-strip assignment row for each position, with source group and installed-face references, plus a derived two-strip total linked to those rows. The original unequal-cell, two-product example remains a separate source question about slot positions and handed geometry. No common drawing has been returned, and the proposed D-C identity establishes no interchangeability or successful fit.

Ask the source to confirm geometry before replacing handed labels. Then review picking identity, installed orientation, the located slot match, complete cell fit and supplied-state labels for the chosen configuration. Loose, bundled and preassembled delivery can expose or hide identity at different moments. Use a documented engineering reference where needed without assuming a production printing or marking method.

Do not turn a loose strip over and infer that it belongs in the other installed position. The actual slot, fold and outline relationship must match the fixed reference face. A divider quantity map also does not establish vertical load support, buckling resistance or transport protection. Keep actual counts, source reply, assembly observation and decision evidence blank until the responsible parties identify and review the actual parts.

title: Place the Removal Tab Where the Customer Can Reach It
html:
Place a proposed holder removal tab against the customer’s actual hand route in the complete pack. Show the product, holder, box opening and tab together. A tab on an isolated insert can be visible yet unreachable after the product and surrounding walls are in place.

This method creates an access layout for a proposed feature. Ask the supplier to confirm the tab and attachment construction; a general insert catalogue doesn’t prove that feature is included.

Name the part the tab is meant to move

The liner-insert reference establishes the component context. State whether the proposed tab lifts an entire holder, reveals an item or starts another agreed removal action. These are different requirements.

Mark the tab’s connection to the component it moves. If it is a loose decorative pull, keep that distinction visible. The source should identify the actual attachment or fold before a functional review.

Add the full product envelope and outer opening. The insert-fit guide handles the item’s location; this layout adds the hand and movement space needed after opening.

Draw the starting finger route

Choose the intended pack position and identify where fingers enter before anything is moved. Show any lid, rim, card or neighbouring item still present at that stage. Avoid drawing the hand through a wall or behind an inaccessible product.

Record the direction the tab should move and where the holder or item goes next. If another hand supports the pack, show that support. A staged three-handed demonstration may leave the customer action unanswered.

Access field Input to mark Sample question
Target part Holder or item moved by tab Is the intended part identified?
Connection Supplier-proposed attachment or fold Does sample represent it?
Starting reach Finger entry with full contents Is tab available before movement?
Travel Direction and surrounding parts What meets during action?
Support User grip and pack position What other support is required?
After state Moved holder/item position Can next removal step occur?

A visible tab and an accessible tab belong to different observation fields. Keep both rather than choosing only a close-up of the pull.

Work through a hypothetical holder lift

Suppose a jewelry gift uses a holder with a proposed paper tab near one corner. With the product loaded, the corner lies close to the outer wall. The buyer sketches finger entry and records whether the tab can be reached before the holder is lifted.

If a reviewer first shifts the product to expose the tab, that action is a deviation or a new proposed sequence. The source can discuss another tab position or access route against that actual layout.

A revised tab needs the same target part and full contents in its review. A loose sample tab being pulled on a desk doesn’t close the installed access question.

Ask the next question by interface

Call the removal tab RT1, holder H1 and adjacent wall W1 in the hypothetical map. Ask: ‘Please review RT1 access beside W1 with the complete H1 configuration.’ It gives the source a located task.

If the attachment or holder construction changes, keep that revision separate from the tab’s visual placement. Appearance, access and functional acceptance can be different statuses on one sample.

Any force, retention or repeated-use requirement needs a separately agreed method. The original layout records a proposed human action without claiming a universal easy-release result.

Send the starting and after states

Bring the target-part identity, connection proposal, finger route and action views to the packaging enquiry. The next supplier response should address the actual installed feature, followed by review with all contents present.

A product-first workaround does not establish initial tab access

Name the complete starting arrangement before judging the tab. BASE23 uses RT1 proposed to connect to holder H1 beside wall W1 with product P1 present. RELOCATE23 proposes RT2 for the same holder, wall and product. PRODUCT_FIRST23 retains RT1 but introduces a separate movement of P1 before gripping it. The worksheet does not prescribe how P1 moves or establish that moving it is possible or permitted.

PRODUCT_FIRST23 PRODUCT_FIRST23 uses pre action MOVE_P1_BEFORE_GRIP
PRODUCT_FIRST23 RT1 access question at AFTER_P1_MOVE_ONLY

For PRODUCT_FIRST23, access is questioned after the P1 movement only. That later view cannot establish reach before anything moved. If actual customer instructions require the tab first, the workaround has not answered that requirement.

Confirm which object the tab is intended to move. A tab connected to H1 is not evidence that it lifts P1, releases jewelry from the holder or reveals every accessory. Keep the card, lid/rim and neighbouring contents in the actual starting view. Show the ordinary support action with the selected route; a cropped close-up should not conceal another grip or a removed obstruction.

The generated diagram is an evidence map, so it does not invent an accessible finger gap or an attachment mechanism. PackMojo’s liner catalogue identifies an interior packaging component, not an included removal feature or a force rating for RT1. title: Write Mounting Instructions With Front and Back Views
html:
Write jewelry-card mounting instructions with matched front and back views for each important step. Identify the card, jewelry and attachment method, then show the customer’s release route separately. A front presentation photo can conceal the work behind the card and leave packing staff to improvise it.

The output is a work card for one confirmed configuration. It should describe the actual joining proposal rather than prescribe generic hole sizes or use the jewelry itself as a forming tool.

Identify the mounted configuration

Avery’s jewelry display-card examples show front positions and rear backing or chain management. Use that relationship to request both views of your proposal. The article’s DIY measurements are not universal instructions for your item.

Name the card drawing and the jewelry variant. Include projecting clasps, pins or chain ends in the rear view. Record the separate backing, tie, tape or other attachment proposed by the responsible source.

Keep mounting instructions distinct from the holder-fit review. One describes how the item is attached; the other describes its resulting envelope and fit in the pack.

Write one action per view pair

For each step, show the front state and the rear relationship it creates. Keep the card orientation fixed so left and right remain clear. If a tool or fixture is required, identify it as part of the agreed process.

State what staff do before the card enters the outer box or bag. A final assembly image should not hide a rear attachment that requires access later unavailable after packing.

Work-card field Front view Back view or instruction
Starting state Card and item orientation Loose attachment components
Mounting step Position created on face Confirmed connecting action
Rear management Front remains in intended position Backing, chain or other parts
Packed state Resulting displayed item Complete rear envelope
Customer release Starting grip Confirmed removal action
Reference Jewelry/card revision Attachment and instruction version

Do not substitute a similar jewelry item for the intended variant without a new configuration note. Its rear connections may differ despite a similar front silhouette.

Follow a hypothetical necklace-card instruction

Suppose a gift brand mounts a necklace on a card and manages excess chain behind it. The front image shows the desired necklace position. The work card also identifies the proposed rear management method and the sequence before the card is packed.

A reviewer follows those instructions without verbal coaching. If the chain is routed another way to complete the step, that deviation is recorded. The supplier or responsible packing source can then clarify the intended process.

The customer’s release action gets its own view pair. It should not be assumed to reverse all factory or packing steps, particularly where another attachment is proposed for removal.

Use a located sequence question

Call the front position FP1 and rear attachment RA1 in the hypothetical record. Ask: ‘Please confirm the mounting action that creates FP1/RA1 before the card is packed.’ This is more specific than asking for a finished front photo.

If a revised item changes its clasp or chain, update the rear envelope and instruction. A front artwork revision alone does not explain that physical change.

Keep any contact, retention or handling requirement separate from the instruction’s clarity. A successfully followed work card is process evidence, not a certified protection or durability result.

Send matched views and the release job

Bring the card and item identities, front/back steps and open release questions through Packrivo’s enquiry. The next response should confirm the actual attachment and order for that configuration, followed by a review of the resulting complete mounted pack.

An unchanged front view can conceal a changed mounting instruction

Extend the hypothetical necklace record with two versioned combinations. V1_23 uses card C1, jewelry JW1, clasp K1, rear reference RA1 and instruction I1. Proposed V2_23 retains C1 and the same described front appearance FP1 but uses jewelry JW2, clasp K2, rear reference RA2 and instruction I2. The front similarity is an assumption for this example, not evidence that the new clasp fits.

title: Choose the Tissue Fold Before Placing the Printed Mark
html:
Choose the final tissue fold before placing a positioned printed mark. Map the flat sheet, fold order and visible face with matching references. A motif centred on a flat sheet can end up hidden, divided or facing away after the actual packing action.

This tool starts with the intended gift presentation. It records where the artwork should be seen, while the printer separately confirms the material and printing proposal.

Use one sheet reference through the fold

The tissue printing reference distinguishes position and non-position layouts. Ask which process is proposed for the desired visual job. The map does not establish placement accuracy or a supplier’s production tolerance.

Give the sheet four stable edge references and identify its print side. Mark the proposed fold lines on a working copy. Keep the product or box orientation visible so a rotated sheet cannot appear unchanged in the next photo.

Name the intended motif and the stage where the customer should see it. A repeating pattern may need another review from a single positioned mark. Record that choice rather than forcing both into the same artwork instruction.

Use the tissue component brief for paper, ink and contact questions. This map stays on artwork after folding, instead of repeating all material specifications.

Show overlaps and the final face

Photograph or sketch the sheet before folding, after each important fold and in the final pack. Mark which regions become hidden. Keep the outside visible face distinct from the product-contact face.

Write the packing order alongside the map. A motif placement that depends on one specific sequence needs that sequence available to staff. Do not assume a different fold order creates the same presentation.

Artwork-map field Reference Evidence
Sheet orientation Named edges and print side Flat starting view
Fold order Stable fold IDs Intermediate views
Motif Artwork ID and desired stage Final visible location
Overlap Covered regions Hidden/visible boundary
Pack relationship Product face and orientation Complete final presentation
Revision Artwork and fold instruction Changed relationship to recheck

The set checklist can hold the wider bag or box components. Keep the same final set in the motif review if those parts affect visibility.

Follow a hypothetical gift-box wrap

Suppose a brand wants a green abstract mark visible at the top of tissue around a gift box. The first flat layout centres it on the sheet. After the proposed folds, an overlap covers part of the mark.

The buyer names motif M1 and overlap O1, then compares moving M1 with changing the fold order. Those are separate options. The next proposal identifies which one changes and preserves the box orientation.

If the printer supplies a sample on another paper, retain that material limitation. The fold map can still explain position while leaving the final printing and contact evidence open.

Write a useful handoff note

A specific instruction is: ‘M1 should be visible on final face VF1 after folds F1 and F2 in the stated order.’ It links artwork to a named action. A request to centre the logo gives the printer no final-fold reference.

For a repeating design, record which degree of partial pattern visibility is intended without inventing a universal rule. The buyer’s presentation preference and the printer’s proposed process need separate replies.

Review the formed sample with the same fold instruction. If staff use another order, note the deviation before treating the view as evidence for VF1. The tool checks the intended presentation, not printing capability or sales effect.

Send the final-fold target

Bring the sheet map, motif IDs, folding sequence and complete presentation through Packrivo’s enquiry. The next response should tie the proposed artwork and printing scope to the same final view.

Keep mark movement separate from fold-order movement

Name three invented tissue candidates while holding the edge reference, print side and product orientation constant. BASE23 uses mark M1 with F1 then F2. MOVE_MARK23 uses proposed mark M2 with F1 then F2. REORDER23 retains M1 but uses F2 then F1. M2 identifies a changed location, not another approved logo. No actual fold geometry or print coordinates have been supplied.

MOVE_MARK23 MOVE_MARK23 uses second fold F2

Every candidate has its own after-first-fold, final-visible-face and product-contact-face scopes. A view rotation of the same folded object is not a change of fold order. Keep E_TOP, E_RIGHT, E_BOTTOM and E_LEFT tied to the same flat-sheet orientation when the actual drawings are returned.

The original O1 example says overlap hides part of M1 after the stated fold. It does not prove that moving the mark or reversing folds will resolve it. Request a marked flat sheet and the matching intermediate/final views for each candidate. A positional-print proposal and a repeating non-position print also need different expectations for partial marks; the responsible artwork owner must state the actual requirement.

title: Identify Handle Joints in the Paper-Bag Brief
html:
Identify the handle and its hidden joining work separately in a paper-bag brief, then review both with the complete gift loaded. Ask for inside and outside views of the proposed attachment. A colour-matched handle swatch leaves the joint, reinforcement and delivered assembly unresolved.

The useful record names the visible part, the hidden interface and the use configuration. It gives the supplier a precise question without assigning a carrying rating from a photograph.

Ask for the actual joining proposal

The paper-carrier reference includes handle options. That supports specifying the handle as a component, while the attachment and reinforcement need their own source response.

Name the handle material, visible grip and proposed attachment method. Identify any covering layer or reinforcement. If the joining detail is hidden, request a section or inside view instead of inferring it from the outside.

Record whether handles arrive fitted or as separate components. Include who completes any remaining work. The same outside appearance can hide different assembly responsibilities.

For a euro tote proposal, keep top reinforcement and base construction in separate fields. Neither should be assumed merely because the carrier looks stiff.

Connect joint identity to loaded use

Provide the whole gift envelope and actual weight, including tissue and cards. Show how the hand grips the handle around those contents. Ask the source what evaluation scope is appropriate if a carrying requirement is specified.

Keep a local action observation distinct from a capacity claim. Record user support, starting orientation and any rearrangement. A short handoff does not establish how an untested joint performs over unspecified use.

Handle record Input or source reply Loaded evidence
Visible handle Material and grip shape Starting hand access
Hidden joint Attachment and location Inside/outside matched views
Reinforcement Proposed layer and extent Relationship to mouth and gift
Base Actual construction proposal Gift seated position
Delivered state Fitted or separate parts Assembly owner and instruction

Use the gift-set checklist to keep added tissue and cards in the loaded envelope. An omitted component can leave a different handle-access condition from the final pack.

Work through a hypothetical carrier sample

Suppose a boxed ornament sits in a paper carrier with tissue above it. The buyer sees the chosen handle outside but does not know the inside attachment. The sheet marks joint J1 as awaiting a construction view while handle material H1 is documented.

The source supplies the proposed J1 detail. The buyer then reviews H1/J1 with the complete gift configuration G1, retaining the tissue in its intended position. If tissue is moved to make the grip easier, that action is recorded.

A revision can change the handle length or the hidden reinforcement. The next review identifies which field changed instead of describing the whole bag as version two without a construction record.

Keep the next question component-specific

A useful request is: ‘Please confirm J1 for H1 and show its inside relationship to the proposed top reinforcement.’ It asks for the hidden interface. A handle colour reply alone leaves J1 open.

If a source gives a performance statement, keep its scope and evidence separate from the local sheet. The construction record should not turn a vendor’s general claim into confirmation for G1.

Once the proposed joint and supplied work are clear, retain their identities with the sample. Any final functional acceptance should name the actual configuration and method; appearance approval remains another decision.

Send the hidden interface

Bring handle and joint identities, inside views and the full loaded configuration to the packaging enquiry. This original sheet helps organize the next supplier response without claiming a tested carrying capacity.

A new handle and a new joint create a new evidence combination

Use two invented visible-handle references H1 and H2 and two hidden-joint references J1 and J2. The four proposed combinations are H1_J1, H1_J2, H2_J1 and H2_J2. Keep the same complete gift G1 and tissue TS1 in each combination. The labels identify construction questions; they do not specify a knot, adhesive, stitch or reinforcing patch that the source has not confirmed.

H1_J1 H1_J1 uses joint J1

H1_J2 H1_J2 uses joint J2

H2_J1 H2_J1 uses joint J1

An inside photograph needs to show the actual offered joining work and any covering layers, while a loaded view must identify the complete contents and grip. A tissue move to expose the joint is a separate inspection action, not the untouched customer starting state.

Evidence for H2_J1 and H1_J2 does not automatically establish H2_J2. The visible-handle revision and hidden-joint revision can meet in a configuration that has never been reviewed together. Ask the supplier to identify which sample represents that combination and what the loaded review covers. Keep decorative appearance, construction identification and any functional acceptance as separate decisions.

Confirm whether handles arrive fitted or as separate parts and who completes the joining work. Top reinforcement and base construction remain distinct fields. title: Gift Bag Loading Needs Clearance Around the Box Corners
html:
Review the path a gift-box corner takes through the bag opening, not only its final fit at the base. Record the usable mouth, handle route, box projections and loading orientation together. A transient snag during insertion should become a located opening question rather than another generic bag-size request.

Separate the loading envelope from the seated gift

The original boxed-base tote construction pattern illustrates a formed base and separate handle attachment. The fabric converter leaflet identifies fastening and handle options. These support construction vocabulary, not a universal clearance formula for loading a box.

Provide the finished gift box with ribbon, primary wrap and card projections included. Record its corners and widest local features, then identify the bag’s usable mouth and any handle, channel or seam that occupies that space.

Draw the intended entry orientation. The box may be inserted straight, rotated through a named action or loaded before another component is positioned. Keep that action separate from its final resting position so the converter can answer the actual mouth question.

Locate contact during the entry movement

Use the actual bag and complete boxed gift for the review. Pause at the point where a corner approaches the mouth, seam or handle. Photograph the contact location and record whether staff change the angle, move the handle or adjust a decoration.

Treat that adjustment as a proposal or observed packing action with an owner. The buyer may accept it as the intended sequence, or ask for another opening/handle arrangement. Keep it visible instead of hiding the change behind a photograph of the gift already seated at the base.

Review the removal route as well. A box that enters through one angle may need a different grip after the bag is fully packed. Record any inaccessible corner or handle obstruction at that stage without assuming the insertion observation settles customer access.

Use a corner-path loading record

This original Packrivo worksheet uses a hypothetical candle gift with a projecting bow.

Loading field Illustrative entry Next question
Gift envelope Finished box BX1 including bow R1 Which local projection enters first?
Usable mouth Actual opening and handle positions Where is the narrow or obstructed area?
Entry orientation Packing owner’s intended direction/rotation Is this the agreed loading sequence?
Corner contact Rear corner C1 beside seam S1 Request a located opening or seam proposal
Seated result Box and tissue at the formed base Keep final base fit separate
Removal Customer grip with handles in final position Review actual access before acceptance

Compare an illustrative base-fit and entry issue

Imagine a tote whose formed base accepts the box, while the bow catches at a handle during entry. Increasing the base dimensions alone would not describe the located issue. Send the mouth/handle view and the complete gift envelope to the converter.

The response might change the opening, handle location or agreed loading action. Retain the earlier sequence and compare the revised sample with the same box and bow. The buyer can then decide the next arrangement from visible evidence rather than inferring bag fit from a flat width.

Send the mouth question with the contents state

The existing gift bag and tissue method handles the broader static contents and carrier plan. Compare the box-bottom fabric tote through its formed base and handle fields when that structure is proposed.

The buyer supplies the finished gift. The converter identifies the opening and construction proposal. The packing owner records the actual entry action, and the buyer accepts that route or requests a specific change. Keep the final sample and decision tied to the same contents state.

Bring the corner-path record and unresolved mouth/handle question to the packaging brief. MOQ is 500 pieces per design; materials, sample scope and commercial details are confirmed for the project.

A new loading sequence needs its own complete-gift exit review

Keep final gift BX1 plus bow R1 fixed, then distinguish two invented sequence candidates. COMPLETE_FIRST23 proposes attaching the bow before the complete gift enters. DECORATE_INSIDE23 proposes entering BX1 alone and attaching R1 inside afterward. No attachment method, inside access or feasibility has been confirmed. The alternative is a question for the actual packing owner, not an instruction to reach into an unsuitable carrier.

COMPLETE_FIRST23 R1 attachment stage BEFORE_ENTRY
COMPLETE_FIRST23 BX1_R1 requires COMPLETE_GIFT_EXIT

DECORATE_INSIDE23 R1 attachment stage INSIDE_BAG_AFTER_ENTRY
DECORATE_INSIDE23 BX1_R1 requires COMPLETE_GIFT_EXIT

The CSV records one box and one bow in the final gift for both candidates, but different entry envelopes and bow-attachment stages. DECORATE_INSIDE23 also creates an inside-decoration access and method requirement. Its entry view cannot be used as evidence that the complete BX1/R1 envelope fits through the mouth. The proposed sequence has changed work rather than demonstrated an improved bag opening.

For both candidates, retain independent corner-path, handle-position, seated-state, final-bow-condition and complete-gift-exit scopes. The customer encounters the completed gift, even if staff inserted an undecorated box. A final bow can therefore reintroduce the original mouth or handle question during removal. Review the actual customer grip and final handle position rather than assuming loading and exit are interchangeable.

Use C1 and S1 to locate a corner/seam concern and record any rotation or temporary handle movement. If the converter instead proposes a new mouth or handle location, name the revised construction and compare it with the same contents and declared sequence. title: Gift Carrier Handoffs Need Acceptance Across Bag, Gable and Tote Formats
html:
Compare a gift carrier through the same complete boxed gift and the handoff action, then record each structure’s different acceptance questions. A paper bag, integral-handle carton and box-bottom fabric tote need different opening, base and handle evidence. Keep those observations together instead of repeating a generic load-and-lift sequence.

Keep the contents fixed across carrier proposals

Name the actual gift box, tissue, card and decoration being handed to the customer. Record the finished envelope and complete packed mass as inputs. Use that same arrangement when comparing carrier forms so a changed ribbon or smaller box does not disappear into the result.

The original carton carrier reference identifies an integral-handle construction. It supports the structural category, while the offered gable or other integral-handle drawing defines its actual head folds and grip. The fabric-maker tote pattern illustrates boxed-corner base formation and handle attachment as a different construction.

The carrier label alone should not decide acceptance. Mark the actual bag anchor, integral handle panel or fabric seam that receives the relevant action. Keep any carrying suitability or loading limit as an offered project question requiring its own evidence.

Use structure-specific checks during handoff

For a paper bag, locate its usable mouth, base and attached handle anchors. For a gable or integral-handle carton, identify the formed head/handle panels and base setup. For a box-bottom tote, locate the boxed seams, lining and handle attachment relative to the gift.

Review how the complete box enters and rests in each form before the handoff. Then record the actual grip, lifting/set-down action and customer access under the agreed conditions. Keep an observed mouth snag or inaccessible handle linked to the structure and state where it occurs.

If the gift arrangement must change for a carrier, record that as a different packout rather than declaring the two proposals equivalent. The buyer should be able to see whether it is the carrier, contents or handoff sequence that changed.

Use a cross-carrier acceptance matrix

This original Packrivo comparison uses one hypothetical boxed gift. It does not assign carrying ratings.

Make the comparison lead to a specific next sample

Imagine the same candle gift fits the base of all three carriers, but its ribbon catches at one loading mouth. Keep the base-fit observation and the mouth issue separate. Ask the relevant converter for a located opening proposal instead of changing every carrier dimension at once.

The next sample should retain the boxed gift and its decoration, or explicitly name the changed contents. The buyer can then choose which access route to develop and which interface needs more evidence. A broad impression that one carrier looks premium does not resolve a snag at a named corner.

Link the structures to the actual handoff record

Use the existing gift bag and tissue checklist for the shared contents and handoff brief. Compare the gable-top handle box and the box-bottom fabric tote through their own construction fields.

The buyer supplies the fixed contents and intended use. Each converter supplies its drawing and supplied state. The packing owner returns the actual loading/handoff evidence, and the buyer records the chosen route and remaining sample question.

A separate G2 proposal contains the same box, tissue and card but zero bows. These are illustrative component quantities, not a bundle offer or a recommendation to omit decoration. title: Check Nearby Packs in the Retail Fixture Layout
html:
Check a retail fixture with multiple sale-ready packs in their intended positions, then record contact during removal of a selected unit. Keep neighbouring packs present in the action view. A hanging hole that fits an isolated hook doesn’t settle side-by-side or front-to-back interference on the full display.

The useful tool is a multi-pack drawing with a few named collision points. It helps the supplier review fixture spacing and pack geometry without turning a staged photo into a universal clearance rule.

Draw the complete neighbouring layout

The hook display reference identifies hanging-pack use. Request the actual hook geometry and attachment proposal. Include the retaining ends, rows and complete pack envelopes.

Assign each relevant pack a position ID. Show side spacing, front-to-back stock order and any row above or below. Keep the hole and raised hanger panel connected to the full pack body.

Mark the selected unit and its intended removal route. A customer can move the unit through more space than the hole occupies, particularly when lifting it past a retaining end.

Use the counter-hook direction or floor-hook direction for their actual fixture proposal. The collision map stays tied to its own placement and stock pattern.

Record contact by stage and pair

Begin with the full starting layout photographed. Review removal without clearing adjacent stock as an unrecorded aid. Pause at the point where parts meet and name both of them.

A collision pair can be pack-to-pack, pack-to-hook or pack-to-body. Keep those categories as factual location descriptions, not causes or performance judgements. The supplier needs the actual part relationship.

Collision field Entry Evidence
Selected pack Position ID and full envelope Starting layout
Neighbour Adjacent pack or fixture part Front and side map
Action stage Lift, travel or exit Located contact image
Changed action Extra turn or cleared stock Deviation recorded
Proposed response Spacing, pack or route change Supplier reply
Recheck state Same or revised stock layout Matched comparison view

Do not use a single successful hole-fit observation as approval of all rows. A top row and lower row can meet different neighbours during the same customer action.

Follow a hypothetical paired-hook display

Suppose two hooks carry carded ornaments side by side. Each hole fits its hook when reviewed alone. With both stocked, the selected pack meets its neighbour while being lifted over the retaining end.

The buyer marks selected pack P2 and neighbour N2 at the contact stage. The source is asked to assess that pair on the full layout. Enlarging the hole alone may leave the body-to-body contact unanswered.

If the supplier proposes more space or another pack orientation, record the actual change. Review the same selected-unit action with the confirmed new layout rather than removing the neighbour for the next photograph.

Keep useful deviations in the record

A reviewer may tilt the pack or move neighbouring stock to finish removal. Preserve the action and ask whether it should be part of the intended use. A workaround can explain the issue while still leaving the original route unresolved.

Keep a full-stock and reduced-stock map separately if both are relevant. Their neighbours and travel envelopes differ. A favourable reduced state should not erase a collision found in the full state.

The original map documents contact and access. Any stability, load or accessibility evaluation needs a responsible method and actual conditions; no such result follows from a drawing.

Send the collision pair

Bring the front/side layout, selected unit, neighbouring pair and action photos to Packrivo’s enquiry. Ask the next question by location and stage so the response can be reviewed against the same configuration.

Removing a neighbour changes the collision question

Use three invented layout references for the P2/N2 question. FULL23 uses L1 with N2 present. SPACING23 uses proposed layout L2, also with N2 present. CLEARED23 uses L1_REDUCED after N2 has been removed before the customer action. The first two retain the neighbouring-pack question; the third introduces a separate operation. No spacing, angle or successful removal is assigned to any proposal.

Hypothetical configuration Named object Relationship Input or next scope

FULL23 N2 has presence PRESENT; 1 packs
FULL23 N2 staff action RETAIN_DURING_ACTION
SPACING23 FIXTURE uses layout L2
SPACING23 N2 has presence PRESENT; 1 packs
SPACING23 N2 staff action RETAIN_DURING_ACTION
CLEARED23 FIXTURE uses layout L1_REDUCED
CLEARED23 N2 has presence ABSENT; 0 packs
CLEARED23 N2 staff action REMOVE_BEFORE_CUSTOMER

The CSV creates separate lift, travel and exit rows for P2 against N2, hook H1 and fixture body BODY1 in each layout. N2 has numeric presence one in the stocked layouts and zero in CLEARED23. A pair marked absent cannot become a no-contact result for the full layout. Likewise, clearing N2 says nothing about whether P2 still catches the retaining end or the fixture body.

A source response proposing more spacing needs an identified L2 layout and its own stocked action views. A response proposing clearance of a neighbour needs an operating owner and permission for that extra action. An isolated hang-hole observation answers neither response completely. Keep the full package body and other front-to-back or above/below neighbours in the actual drawing even if the teaching map concentrates on one located pair.

Record a turn or tilt as a changed action, not invisible help. Keep actual contact, route, fixture, stock pattern and decision evidence blank until reviewed. title: Plan Refilling Before Approving the Display Layout
html:
Plan refilling with the display partly stocked, then record the order used to add units and the final facing pattern. Keep customer removal and staff replenishment as separate actions. A successful loading demonstration on an empty tray can leave the actual retail refill job unresolved.

The useful output is a remaining-stock sketch and a short sequence. It shows the supplier which space and access route staff need while other units stay in place.

Choose the refill trigger and starting pattern

The retail display reference establishes the use context. Your project must define its own replenishment action. State whether staff refill after a row empties, after a chosen stock state or by replacing a whole component.

Photograph or sketch the starting pattern. Name which units remain and whether staff first move them forwards. A count alone does not describe their positions.

Record the complete unit envelope and facing direction. If new stock arrives in another wrap or orientation, include that preparation work rather than assuming it enters exactly like the original display fill.

For a tray floor display, one tray’s refill can differ from another’s. Keep the tray ID and neighbouring stocked trays in the starting record.

Write the replenishment sequence

Use one action per step, starting from the partly stocked view. State who performs it and from which side. Include any movement of remaining units as an action with its own resulting state.

Keep customer grip separate from staff entry. Both can use the same opening, yet the refill bundle may need more room or a different order than one-unit removal.

Sequence field Input Evidence
Trigger Chosen stock state Starting layout image
Remaining units IDs and positions What stays during refill
Preparation New stock envelope and orientation Any unpacking or turning step
Entry action Staff side and route Partly loaded action view
Reset Facing and row order Final replenished layout
Changed component Profile or divider revision Impact linked to current instruction

Use the change-control record if refill requires a revised profile, divider or fixture. The operation should stay linked to the structural change that enables it.

Work through a hypothetical card-pack refill

Suppose a counter display holds two rows of gift-card packs. The front row is empty while the rear row remains. The brand wants staff to refill the front without removing the rear stock.

The buyer records that starting pattern and asks a reviewer to add the new front units using the proposed route. If the reviewer first moves rear packs, that action goes into the sequence instead of being omitted.

A supplier can then discuss an opening profile, row spacing or another refill method against the same arrangement. The buyer doesn’t call every successful final full photo evidence of the original method.

Keep a useful exception record

Call the starting pattern R0 and the first entry action A1. If a bundle catches at one side, name the unit and display part. A located question such as ‘Can A1 add front units while R0 remains unchanged?’ gives the source a concrete task.

After a revision, begin again from R0 or explicitly record a revised starting pattern. Do not compare an empty revised tray with a partly full earlier tray as if only the profile changed.

The method records assembly and access observations. It does not predict sales, establish a refill-speed improvement or certify the fixture’s load. Those outcomes need separate evidence if required.

Send the starting and reset states

Bring the remaining-stock sketch, action sequence and final reset view to the packaging enquiry. The next supplier response should identify which structure or operation is being confirmed, then connect it to the actual refill instruction.

A full reset photo can conceal two different refill jobs

Extend R0 with explicit invented identities: old units O1, O2 and O3 occupy RP1, RP2 and RP3, while FP1–FP3 are empty. New units N1, N2 and N3 wait outside the display. STAY23 leaves each old unit at its rear position and adds its corresponding new unit to the front. ADVANCE23 first moves each old unit to the front, then adds new stock to the vacated rear positions. These are two proposed jobs starting from the same R0.

Both arithmetic end states contain three old plus three new units, or six packs. The count does not make their assignments equivalent. The worksheet therefore carries six source-to-target rows for each method, including source position, final position, operation reference and one-pack quantity. An operator needs to know which stock moves and when, not merely that the final tray looks full. No stock-rotation rule is inferred from the labels old and new.

ADVANCE23 adds work and an intermediate state; the example does not claim that the rear entry route is physically available. title: Set Display Front-Wall Height Around the Customer Grip
html:
Set a retail display’s front-wall height around the sale-ready unit and the customer’s grip route. Review full, half-full and last-row states before fixing the profile. A front wall that shows the product well in a full display can leave a different reach question after units are removed.

The front profile also carries artwork, but the customer action needs a defined space first. Treat grip and information area as linked decisions rather than choosing a large panel and hoping the contents remain easy to reach.

Choose the unit and grip route

PackMojo’s display box reference identifies retail shelf and counter presentation. That supports the use context. It doesn’t prescribe your front-wall height or establish that one display profile improves sales.

Provide the actual sale-ready unit, including any card, bag or individual carton. Mark where a customer should grip it. The gripped envelope may differ from the product alone if an outer card extends above it.

State whether units are lifted vertically, tipped slightly or removed through another proposed route. Keep that action with the row layout. An unrecorded tilt can make a difficult profile appear to work.

Compare the foldable packaging directions when selecting the tray construction. Keep this article’s front-wall and grip review tied to a display that remains on the counter.

Review three stock states

Start with the intended full arrangement and record the unit facing direction. Ask a reviewer to remove a front unit using the chosen grip. Observe contact with the front wall and neighbouring units.

Repeat with the proposed half-full arrangement. State whether staff have moved remaining units forwards; that is part of the display operation, not a hidden correction. Keep a starting photo before the removal action.

Finally review the last row or final unit in its intended position. The visible face and reach can differ from the full state. A profile decision should include that later condition if it belongs to the planned use.

Keep restocking separate. If staff refill from above or replace the whole tray, record that action as another requirement rather than assuming the customer grip review covers it.

Use a front-wall access sketch

Draw a side view for each stock state using the same front-wall profile. Add the row layout and grip route to the record.

State Unit position Grip observation Next question
Full Front and adjacent units Finger entry and wall contact Profile or arrangement change if needed
Half full Remaining layout as planned Reach and neighbouring movement Staff repositioning requirement
Last row Final intended positions Visible face and removal route Profile, holder or refill response
Artwork Available front face after profile choice Copy visible in relevant states Artwork area to confirm
Reference Unit, tray and profile revisions Matched starting views Changed state needing recheck

The table records actions and observations. It doesn’t assign an ergonomic score or turn a sample view into a conversion result.

Follow a hypothetical gift-card display

Suppose a counter tray holds upright gift-card packs. The brand wants a large front motif, but customers are intended to grip the lower portion of each pack. The first sketch shows where that grip meets the proposed front wall.

The buyer reviews the full, half-full and last-row arrangements. In the last-row condition, the reviewer needs a different reach. That observation is recorded before the front profile and artwork are finalized.

The supplier may propose a shaped cutout, another unit position or another tray configuration. Compare each response against the same grip route and stock states. A lower wall is one possible proposal, not a universal answer.

Separate profile choices from staff repositioning

For the hypothetical gift-card display, call the initial front-row grip G1 and the last-row grip G2. Keep their starting unit positions in the sketch. If staff are expected to move units forwards, add that operation to the half-full and last-row states.

Ask the supplier: ‘Please review access to G2 with the stated front profile and remaining arrangement.’ That names the actual later-state question. A photo of a full display does not answer it, even when the same tray and units are shown.

If the response proposes a cutout, identify its changed profile on the side sketch and update the available artwork area. If it instead proposes moving units, update the staff action. These are different changes and should not disappear under the same phrase ‘better access’.

Compare the revised proposal using the same sale-ready unit and chosen grip. Record neighbouring-unit movement and any changed hand action without inventing an ergonomic score. The final brief should say which stock states and operator actions it covers. It can settle a practical display profile while leaving load, handling and sales performance outside that observation scope.

Confirm access before closing the artwork area

The four corner display tray direction adds prepared-corner setup to the same retail-use brief. Use its structural questions alongside this front-wall tool rather than repeating them here.

Send the three-state sketches, unit envelope, proposed grip and open profile question through Packrivo’s enquiry form. Review the supplier’s formed sample in the intended display position before treating the front-wall profile and its artwork area as settled.

Distinguish a changed profile from a staff advancing operation

Use an invented two-row layout with three positions per row. FP1–FP3 are the front positions; RP1–RP3 are the rear positions. FULL23 holds six sale-ready U1 packs, HALF23 retains the three rear packs, and LAST23 retains only RP2. These counts define this example, not an actual tray capacity. The CSV assigns every position a numeric occupancy and leaves actual layout, observations and decisions blank.

Hypothetical configuration Named object Relationship Input or next scope
FULL23_LEAVE DISPLAY uses profile WF1
FULL23_CUTOUT DISPLAY uses profile WF2
HALF23_LEAVE DISPLAY uses profile WF1
HALF23_ADVANCE DISPLAY uses profile WF1
HALF23_CUTOUT DISPLAY uses profile WF2
LAST23_LEAVE DISPLAY uses profile WF1
LAST23_ADVANCE DISPLAY uses profile WF1
LAST23_CUTOUT DISPLAY uses profile WF2

Compare two kinds of response. LEAVE keeps remaining units in their starting positions under profile WF1. ADVANCE moves each remaining rear unit to the corresponding front position, also under WF1; this proposal applies only to HALF23 and LAST23, where the front is empty. It requires an explicit staff operation before the customer action. A full layout has no advancing proposal into occupied front positions. CUTOUT retains the stock positions but proposes profile WF2. None is selected or shown to improve access.

For each proposed configuration, request evidence of the chosen grip, neighbouring-unit movement and available artwork. A front-wall change can alter the information area; an advancing operation changes the starting layout and operating responsibility. Comparing a full WF1 photograph against an advanced last unit would combine stock state and staff work. Keep those changes identifiable before asking whether the profile itself answered the original G2 reach question.

A position map supports a precise sample request without inventing a hand clearance or ergonomic score. Use the same complete U1 envelope and intended grip on the formed sample, then record any changed hand action. This access record does not determine display balance, carrying load or sales response. The stability and customer-access guides address those separate questions.
