title: Name the Loading End and the Customer Opening Separately
html:
Name the loading end and customer opening separately on a carton panel map before artwork is fixed. Record who uses each end, what direction the product travels and which printed face is visible. Even when both actions use the same end, they need separate instructions and review evidence.

A label such as top can change meaning when the carton is turned for packing. Stable panel and end names make the handoff more useful than relying on an unlabelled photograph.

Use a fixed front reference

Choose the intended sales front and its reading direction on the working drawing. Name the two ends against that reference. Keep the names unchanged when a screenshot or paper model is rotated.

The reverse tuck reference provides one example where end-flap orientation differs. Use the actual supplier drawing to confirm your proposal. The action map doesn’t prescribe straight or reverse tuck as a universal answer.

Show the product in its complete packed orientation. Include a backing card or attachment whose leading edge changes the entry. The loose item’s appearance doesn’t settle which end the packer should use.

Keep the end map linked to the current artwork handoff. A front-panel or structure revision can change the reading and opening relationships.

Record two users and two actions

For loading, identify the operator’s starting position, leading product edge and closing order. For customer access, identify the starting grip, release feature and removal route. Do not assume the second is the reverse of the first.

If both use one end, record that shared location explicitly. The packing action can still involve a fixture or support that the customer will not have.

Action record End/panel identity Input and evidence
Packing entry Named loading end Leading edge and full envelope
Packing closure End used after insertion Confirmed flap order
Customer start Named preferred opening Grip and visible instruction
Product removal Exit end and orientation Loaded action sequence
Artwork relationship Front/back reading faces Sales and opening views
Alternative route Permitted or unreviewed end Separate status and evidence

A preferred end and an alternative end should not share one approval cell unless both actions were actually reviewed under the agreed scope.

Follow a hypothetical jewelry-card carton

Suppose a jewelry card has a hanging hole at one end and a projecting ornament at the other. Staff insert the card from the lower end in the proposed packing sequence, while customers are directed to the upper end.

The buyer labels those routes separately and photographs the leading edge during loading. The customer review begins with the carton in its sales orientation, without turning it to use the easier end.

If the upper removal catches at the card hole, the record names that contact and the customer route. A successful lower loading action does not close it. The reverse tuck product direction can carry the structural proposal alongside this user/action diagram.

Make the instruction survive a rotated view

In the hypothetical diagram, call the ends E-A and E-B and keep an upright front arrow. Write ‘packer uses E-B’ and ‘customer uses E-A’ as two entries. Those names remain meaningful when the pack is laid horizontally.

Ask the supplier: ‘Please confirm the E-A removal route for card C1 with the proposed end construction.’ It locates the question more clearly than requesting an easier opening without identifying the user or end.

If the artwork team moves the instruction, review its visible face at the start of the customer action. A message printed on a hidden flap may be unavailable until after the action it is meant to explain.

Send the two-action map

Bring the fixed-front drawing, complete product envelope and separate loading/opening records to Packrivo’s enquiry. This original tool clarifies responsibilities and panel relationships; it does not establish closure durability or protection.

Check when the opening instruction becomes available

Compare OPPOSITE22, where the packer uses E-B and the customer uses E-A, with SAME22, where both use E-B. Shared location does not merge the actions: the packer may have a different support or starting orientation from the customer. Keep loading, packing closure, customer start and product exit as distinct records under either proposal.

OPPOSITE22 CUSTOMER uses end E-A
SAME22 PACKER uses end E-B
SAME22 CUSTOMER uses end E-B

Do not infer availability from a flat artwork layout showing every flap simultaneously.

title: Check Prepared Bottom Joints Before Loading
html:
Check prepared bottom joints before loading the carton, with the supplier’s actual forming instruction beside the sample. Record what arrives completed, which actions staff perform and the final position they inspect. Once the contents cover the base, a missed setup question becomes harder to locate.

This method produces a before-load checklist for one carton revision. It should be written from the confirmed proposal rather than a generic instruction associated with the words auto bottom.

Observe the delivered preparation

The prepared-bottom reference identifies pre-glued flaps in one display configuration. That supports distinguishing supplied joints from forming work. It doesn’t define the base sequence of every other carton.

Photograph the sample as delivered and identify the proposed joints. Ask the supplier which joint surfaces are completed and which remain operator actions. Mark any hidden detail that needs clarification.

Use the delivery-state guide for the wider handoff. This checklist narrows that scope to the empty base immediately before loading.

Keep the sample material and drawing revision named. A plain model can help explain the route, but a substituted construction should not become the final joint reference silently.

Write observable checklist entries

Use entries a packer can see against the drawing, such as the named flap in its confirmed final position. Avoid a vague instruction to make the base secure. The responsible source should confirm the intended relationship.

Include any pressing, seating or alignment step that belongs in the forming instruction. If an extra action appears during review, record it as a question before making it the new default.

Checklist entry Reference Evidence or status
Delivered joints identified Supplier-marked prepared areas Confirmed or awaiting view
Forming sequence available Current instruction revision Each action named
Final joint position visible Formed drawing/detail Before-load inspection image
Extra action recorded Located part and stage Supplier response needed
Loading permitted Agreed final empty-base state Responsible operator checkpoint
Version current Material, drawing and sample IDs Superseded references removed

Copy the checklist into the packing record with the actual part names. A checkbox should refer to a confirmed visible condition, not an unsupported capacity claim.

Follow a hypothetical prepared-base sample

Suppose a gift brand receives a carton sample with prepared base joints. During expansion, one fold remains partly inward. The buyer records that location while the carton is still empty and asks whether another seating action belongs in the instruction.

The record keeps ‘delivered joint present’ separate from ‘final formed position confirmed’. Both can be true or unresolved at different times. A loaded closed photo would conceal that distinction.

After a supplier response, the buyer updates the specific checklist entry and reviews another setup on the same named construction. The contents are added only after the before-load state is documented.

For an auto bottom outer carton, this empty-base check should remain separate from the later top-sealing operation. The body name doesn’t combine the two approvals.

Keep an exception visible at the bench

Call the hypothetical unresolved joint J2 and the forming stage F2. A useful question is: ‘Please confirm J2’s final position after F2 and the inspection view before loading.’ It gives the supplier a part and action to answer.

If the response revises the material or joint construction, create a new checklist version. Keep the earlier exception in its original record rather than deleting evidence of why the instruction changed.

This is a process communication aid. Load, handling and distribution requirements need their own agreed evaluation with the full configuration; a checked empty base does not establish them.

Send the before-load gap

Bring supplied and formed views, the current instruction and open joint IDs to the packaging enquiry. The next action should confirm the actual setup condition, then connect that confirmation to the packing record.

A new instruction and a new prepared bottom reopen different records

Keep the fictional J2 question at stage F2 attached to BASE22, using BX1/MAT1/I1. Compare CLARIFY_ACTION22, which retains BX1 and MAT1 but proposes I2, with CHANGE_CONSTRUCTION22, which proposes BX2/MAT2 and its own instruction reference. A new instruction file is not automatically a changed joint, and a new material or joint should not inherit every old checklist entry.

CLARIFY_ACTION22 CLARIFY_ACTION22 uses material MAT1

CHANGE_CONSTRUCTION22 CHANGE_CONSTRUCTION22 uses material MAT2

Conversely, a view of an empty formed base needs the current construction identity so it is not mistaken for the intended prepared joint.

Ask whether the source response clarifies an existing required seating action or changes the construction itself. Record the actual answer and replace the affected instruction and inspection reference together. If an extra pressing, alignment or seating step has not been confirmed, retain it as the original exception rather than making it a default from observation alone. Loading should not conceal the evidence gap before the owner resolves the actual before-load condition.

title: Write the Bottom-Tab Sequence for the Packing Bench
html:
Write a manual bottom-tab instruction from the actual supplier-approved carton sequence, with one action and photo per step. Show the final engagement and the check required before loading. A ‘1-2-3 bottom’ label doesn’t give staff a complete work instruction or establish that every similarly named carton uses the same tabs.

The useful output is a short instruction another packer can follow on the same carton revision. Start with the delivered form, not a completed box that hides the tabs.

Get the confirmed tab sequence

Packhelp’s snap-lock bottom description identifies four interlocking closure tabs. This supports the interlocking-base direction. Ask your supplier to confirm the actual tabs and sequence for the proposed carton; the catalogue does not provide your work instruction.

Assign tab names from the supplier drawing or a clearly marked working copy. Keep those names on the instruction photos. If the drawing changes, review the sequence again before carrying over old photographs.

Record the supplied state and any prepared seam. Staff should know which parts arrive completed and which they must form. An extra adhesive or tape step needs to be stated if it belongs in the proposed process.

The delivery-state guide covers that handoff. This method turns one manual base sequence into a repeatable bench instruction.

Photograph one action per frame

Begin with an empty carton in the starting orientation. Use a consistent viewpoint that shows the relevant tab and receiving feature. Keep fingers clear enough that the action is visible.

Capture the state before an action and the state after it. Write a short verb-led instruction, such as fold the named tab into the confirmed position. The actual direction and order must come from the proposal, not a generic sequence copied from another carton.

Show the final engagement from the view staff will use to inspect it. Add an inside or underside view if needed, and label its purpose. A photo of the closed top gives no evidence about the base.

Include the point where loading becomes permitted. This prevents staff from covering an incomplete base before performing the check.

Use a photographed work-instruction record

Build the instruction around the actual number of actions. The example fields below are placeholders for your confirmed sequence.

Instruction field Entry Image requirement
Starting state Carton revision and orientation Empty delivered form
Action step Named tab, direction and next position Before and after views
Final engagement Confirmed receiving feature Close view showing completed relationship
Before-load check Observable condition and responsible operator Inspection view without contents
Exception Unresolved tab or changed action Separate issue photo, no workaround hidden
Version Drawing, instruction and sample IDs Current approved reference

Keep the instruction distinct from a load or transport evaluation. A correctly formed base can be a process requirement without proving the finished pack’s capacity.

Follow a hypothetical packing-bench handoff

Suppose a small gift brand receives flat snap-bottom cartons with a prepared side seam. One packer knows the forming sequence, while another has only seen the closed carton. The buyer requests the supplier-confirmed tab instruction and photographs the actual sample.

The instruction shows the starting orientation, each named movement and the completed base before the gift set is inserted. An independent reviewer follows it using the same sample version and records any unclear step.

If the reviewer needs an extra movement, the buyer asks whether it belongs in the sequence or indicates an issue. The team does not silently add a workaround and describe the original instruction as complete.

Review the instruction with someone using it

For the hypothetical bench handoff, give the confirmed carton revision a clear instruction ID. Ask a reviewer to follow the photographs without verbal coaching. Record which action is unclear and which tab or final position they cannot identify.

If the reviewer folds a different tab first, document that action and compare it with the supplier-confirmed sequence. Do not infer that both sequences are permitted merely because the empty base eventually looks closed. Ask the responsible source which sequence and final engagement should control the instruction.

A useful reply request is: ‘Please confirm the action shown in frame F3 and the inspection condition before loading.’ It gives the supplier one location to correct. A new closed-box photograph would leave the instructional gap unchanged.

Keep any approved correction in the photos and written verbs together. If the drawing changes, mark the earlier instruction superseded instead of leaving two apparently current versions at the bench. The review checks whether the instruction communicates the confirmed process; it does not establish assembly speed, capacity or a transport result.

Send the sequence and open steps

Use the snap bottom outer-carton direction when the instruction also belongs to a slotted outer pack with a separate top seal. Keep those two closing operations distinct.

Submit the tab drawing, instruction frames and unresolved steps through Packrivo’s enquiry. The next response should confirm the exact sequence and before-load check for the current carton revision.

Resolve an extra movement before issuing the next instruction

Use I1 for the original hypothetical BX1 instruction and F3 for the located frame question. F3 is a reference to evidence, not a command to fold a third tab. Likewise, the catalogue's four interlocking tabs do not establish that the actual instruction has four actions, four photographs or a universal order.

REQUIRED_ACTION22 REQUIRED_ACTION22 next required scope I2_MATCHED_PHOTO_AND_VERB
NOT_IN_SEQUENCE22 F3 conditional source response SOURCE_DOES_NOT_CONFIRM_AS_REQUIRED
NOT_IN_SEQUENCE22 NOT_IN_SEQUENCE22 next required scope LOCATED_EXCEPTION_REVIEW_NO_SILENT_WORKAROUND

Keep two possible source responses separate. REQUIRED_ACTION22 assumes the responsible source confirms that a missing movement belongs in the actual sequence. The next requirement is a proposed I2 with the corrected photograph and written verb together, followed by the agreed empty-base check. NOT_IN_SEQUENCE22 leaves a located exception requiring review; staff should not add the movement silently and describe I1 as complete.

Ask the reviewer to identify which tab, direction or final position could not be understood, without verbal coaching. The source must confirm the actual action before a new instruction is issued. If the response changes the drawing or supplied preparation rather than just clarifying the communication, give that construction its own reference and revisit the relevant frames. Keep superseded I1 available as history while preventing two apparently current instructions at the bench.

title: Compare Folded Wall Builds Before Pairing Lid and Base
html:
Compare folded wall builds on the formed lid and base before treating their dimensions as a matching pair. Record each blank, its final layer positions and the surfaces that meet during closure. A flat dieline comparison can miss a different finished interface after both parts are assembled.

The useful output is a two-blank record plus a paired section. It lets the buyer distinguish a wall-formation question from a lid-over-base question without inventing a universal allowance.

Identify the two formed parts

The foldable lid and base reference establishes the separate-component direction. Ask the supplier to show the actual wall folds for its proposal. The catalogue does not confirm every wall layer or retaining feature on your drawing.

Name the lid blank LB1 and base blank BB1, or use the supplier’s own stable IDs. Add the formed views beside their flat drawings. Record the material and revision used for each.

Mark the inside and outside wall faces after folding. If a fold creates another layer, show its final position instead of measuring the flat blank as if it were the finished wall.

Use the dimension acceptance method when a recorded measurement will become an acceptance requirement. State whether it refers to the flat part, formed empty component or loaded paired set.

Build a two-blank wall record

Copy the fields below into your project sheet. The rows describe what to collect rather than assigning a particular wall construction.

Wall-build field Lid blank Base blank Paired question
Identity Lid drawing and sample revision Base drawing and sample revision Are the intended parts paired?
Fold order Confirmed actions Confirmed actions Is each part fully formed?
Layer position Inside/outside finished faces Inside/outside finished faces Which surfaces meet?
Retention Confirmed wall-retaining detail Confirmed wall-retaining detail Does either move during pairing?
Formed envelope Named dimension state Named dimension state What fit evidence is needed?
Open item Missing layer or action Missing layer or action Owner and next response

Keep a wall that remains partly formed marked as unresolved. A lid may fit over that temporary shape while leaving the final wall interface unanswered.

Work through a hypothetical two-piece set

Suppose a brand reviews a folding gift tray and lid. The base walls are formed from one blank, while the lid uses a different fold proposal. The buyer records LB1 and BB1 separately and asks the supplier to identify their final inside and outside surfaces.

On the first sample, one base wall needs an additional seating action. The buyer records that step before loading or pairing. A fit photograph taken before the action cannot close the finished pair.

The next review pairs the fully formed parts. Contact along one lid side is recorded as a paired issue with LB1/BB1. The buyer does not add a general clearance to all four walls without a source response.

A frame tray and lid has another paired interface that can use the same recording principle, while keeping its actual frame and wall details distinct.

Use different statuses for wall and pair decisions

In the hypothetical record, the lid fold can be ‘instruction confirmed’, the base fold ‘additional step awaiting response’, and paired fit ‘not yet reviewed’. These statuses prevent one attractive closed view from becoming blanket approval.

Ask the supplier: ‘Please confirm the final BB1 wall position and then review its paired interface with LB1.’ It names the part, action and next relationship. A new lid dimension alone may leave the base question open.

After a revision, retain the original wall records and add the changed field. A new material or fold can reopen the formed envelope even if the outside size label stays the same.

Send formed-wall evidence

Bring both blank records, formed views and the paired section to Packrivo’s enquiry. This original comparison tool helps locate the next construction question. It does not prescribe converting settings, tolerances or protective performance.

Distinguish completing BB1 from replacing it with BB2

A partly formed base and its completed state can share the same blank drawing. Name BB1_PART and BB1_FINAL separately from a proposed replacement drawing BB2. This avoids calling an unfinished wall a different design, or calling a changed design merely another photograph of the old part. The intended lid still has its own LB1 identity and formed-state evidence.

Hypothetical configuration Named object Relationship Input or next scope
BB1_PART BB1_PART uses drawing BB1
BB1_PART LB1_FINAL pair review with BB1_PART
BB1_FINAL BB1_FINAL uses drawing BB1
BB1_FINAL LB1_FINAL pair review with BB1_FINAL
BB2_FINAL BB2_FINAL uses drawing BB2
BB2_FINAL LB1_FINAL pair review with BB2_FINAL

BB1_PART can document the original additional-seating question but cannot close final paired fit. Once the responsible source confirms the actual action and final relationship, BB1_FINAL needs its inside/outside faces, retaining detail and formed envelope recorded. Those are evidence requests here, not instructions that a seating movement has been approved or performed.

A BB2_FINAL proposal is another configuration with its own material and fold references. Pairing it with LB1_FINAL needs a fresh review of the actual meeting faces even if an outside size label is unchanged. Keep a lid-fold instruction decision, a base-forming decision and a paired-fit decision distinct. A familiar lid file cannot establish its relationship to every base state or revision.

The CSV retains the original fictional instruction-confirmed lid, extra-step-pending base and not-yet-reviewed pair as separate statuses, then adds the drawing/state distinction. No wall layer count, retention mechanism, folding order or dimensional allowance is invented. Ask for both final formed parts and the actual paired section before interpreting a closed photograph as evidence of the intended complete interface.

title: Set Product Display Height Before Confirming the Neck
html:
Set the product’s displayed position before confirming the neck in a rigid box. Record the base, holder, product and neck as a height stack, then review the lid in the closed state. A taller visible neck doesn’t by itself define where the product sits or how much of it the customer sees.

The opening view is the useful starting point. Choose what should be visible when the lid comes off, then ask for a construction that places the complete product and holder accordingly.

Separate neck height from product display height

PakFactory’s shoulder-neck structure explanation describes an added neck portion and its relationship to the closed box. Use that component distinction without adopting its protection claims or assuming a specific overlap.

Ask the supplier to identify the base, neck, lid and holder in a side section. Establish a common datum, such as the finished inside base surface. Each height should be labelled against that datum rather than against a different outside edge.

Record which part of the product should appear above the holder or neck. A decorative face, clasp or top cap may be the view that matters. The maximum product height still belongs in the closed-lid review even if it is not the display focus.

The dimension acceptance guide helps define measurement state. This height stack narrows that agreement to one layered opening and closure relationship.

Build the stack from the actual contents

Start with the complete sale-ready product, including attached cards or ties. Show its position in the proposed holder. Record the holder’s installed height, not only its loose-part thickness.

Add the proposed neck position and the lid’s inside envelope to the section. Ask whether dimensions describe finished wrapped parts. A bare structural model and a wrapped assembly should have different sample-state notes.

Keep the open display goal separate from the closed fit goal. A product can look well placed when open while still leaving a lid contact question. Conversely, a closed pack can fit while the product sits lower than the intended opening view.

Use a height-stack record

Give the section a fixed orientation and datum. Fill measured or proposed values with their source; the table provides fields rather than invented dimensions.

Layer or state Record Evidence
Datum Finished inside base reference Marked side section
Holder Installed support and visible opening Loaded sample before lid placement
Product Display feature and highest packed point Same oriented product in holder
Neck Proposed upper edge relative to datum Supplier drawing and formed view
Open state Desired visible product area Customer-view photograph
Closed state Lid inside envelope and contact questions Loaded closure review

Keep the source beside each value. If a datum or holder changes, identify every dependent height that needs another review.

Follow a hypothetical ornament presentation

Suppose a brand wants the face of a round ornament visible when the lid is removed. The holder initially places it below the neck’s top edge. The buyer records the display feature and the proposed layer heights in a section.

The team can discuss raising the holder, revising the neck or changing the desired view. Those options should be compared with the complete product height and lid proposal. Raising the product may reopen the closed-lid question.

After a supplier proposes a revision, review the loaded opening view and then the closed state on the same sample. Do not use a photo with one holder for display and a different holder for closure while calling them one approved set.

The height stack is a buyer communication tool. It doesn’t prescribe universal clearances or establish that a neck protects the product. Any support or handling requirement needs separate evidence.

Record changes against the common datum

For the hypothetical ornament stack, call the inside-base datum D0, the installed holder H1 and the product’s desired visible face PV1. Keep the proposed neck edge and highest packed product point referenced to D0. This prevents values copied from different views being mistaken for directly comparable heights.

Ask the supplier: ‘Please show PV1 in the proposed open state and the highest packed point inside the matching closed lid.’ It requests two views of one linked configuration. A raised display rendering with no lid section leaves the closure relationship open.

If the holder is raised, record its revision and review every height that depends on it. The neck can stay unchanged while the closed lid question changes. If the neck is revised instead, keep the holder identity fixed so the next comparison remains understandable.

Use proposed and observed fields separately. A dimension on a drawing is a proposal until its agreed sample and measurement evidence are linked. The height stack can carry both without turning a concept illustration into a measured result. Close the open view and closed fit under their own scopes, then preserve that paired revision for reorder discussion.

Send one linked open-and-closed brief

Submit the datum section, holder and product details, desired display feature and lid questions through the packaging enquiry. Ask the supplier to confirm the linked geometry. Keep the accepted stack with its sample and drawing revision so a later holder change doesn’t bypass the lid review.

Compare a raised holder with a lower neck under one stated model

Use an idealized rigid, vertical one-axis example to see why two display changes can reopen different closed-state questions. All numbers below are invented millimetres, not recommended sizes, tolerances or supplier measurements. D0 is the finished inside-base datum. H is installed support height; F is the visible-feature offset above that support; P is the product's maximum height above it. N is neck-top height and L the closed lid-underside height from D0. For this model P includes the complete packed height, including any attached card or tie in the vertical path; changing that envelope creates another input.

Hypothetical configuration Named object Relationship Input or next scope
BASE22 FEATURE calculated from H+F; 22 mm
BASE22 RELATIVE_NECK calculated from H+F-N; -3 mm
BASE22 HIGHEST calculated from H+P; 30 mm
BASE22 LID_GAP calculated from L-H-P; 5 mm
HOLDER_RAISE22 FEATURE calculated from H+F; 26 mm
HOLDER_RAISE22 RELATIVE_NECK calculated from H+F-N; 1 mm
HOLDER_RAISE22 HIGHEST calculated from H+P; 34 mm
HOLDER_RAISE22 LID_GAP calculated from L-H-P; 1 mm
NECK_LOWER22 FEATURE calculated from H+F; 22 mm
NECK_LOWER22 RELATIVE_NECK calculated from H+F-N; 1 mm
NECK_LOWER22 HIGHEST calculated from H+P; 30 mm
NECK_LOWER22 LID_GAP calculated from L-H-P; 5 mm

Assume H=10, F=12, P=20, N=25 and L=35. The feature height is H+F=22, or 3 below the neck. The highest product point is H+P=30, leaving modeled space L-H-P=5 beneath the assumed closed lid. Raising the holder by 4 makes H=14: the feature reaches 26, or 1 above the unchanged neck, while the highest point reaches 34 and the modeled space becomes 1. Lowering only the neck by 4 instead gives N=21: the feature remains22, now1above the neck; the highest point remains30 and modeled lid space stays5.

These are alternative model configurations, not two consecutive changes or evidence that a whole decorative face is visible. They hold the product orientation, feature offsets and closed-lid reference fixed. The model excludes compression, tilt, local contacts and construction changes. If changing the neck changes the lid's seated position, L must be replaced and the comparison recalculated; the old result cannot silently carry over.

The CSV stores each assumed input and calculated output numerically with millimetres, formula and exact input-scope references. Positive modeled space does not establish a suitable functional gap, side fit, closing action, product support or transport protection. The buyer still needs the same actual sample configuration reviewed open and closed, with its own display and fit decisions. Changing the desired visible feature is a third original option and should update the feature definition rather than reuse F unnoticed.

Actual quantity, configuration, component and file identities, materials, process, specification, copy, method, condition, observation, owner, decision, evidence and dates are blank. ACTUAL_BLANK is a separate empty starting row; enter permitted project evidence before using an actual record. A blank means unknown.

title: Lift Off Lid Gift Boxes: Leave a Clear Finger Grip
html:
Leave a defined grip route for a lift-off lid and review it with the complete product and holder in place. Mark where fingers start and which edges they meet as the lid rises. An attractive close-fitting lid can still leave the intended opening action unresolved.

The Lid-and-Base Jewelry Box shows the two-piece opening arrangement relevant to this grip review. Mark the actual finger-entry position on the proposed sample rather than inferring access from the closed-box image.

The buyer’s task is to describe the intended action clearly enough to review. Do that before asking for a tighter lid, a deeper overlap or a new notch. Those are possible construction responses, not substitutes for an opening requirement.

Choose the opening position

State whether the box rests on a table, is held in one hand or uses another defined setup. Identify which faces the user can grip. A lid that is easy to lift in a carefully staged photograph may be handled differently in use.

PakFactory’s shoulder-neck reference identifies a lid-and-base-related structure with an additional neck. That supports distinguishing the parts. It doesn’t establish a universal grip area, lid fit or lifting force.

Show the proposed lid overlap and accessible base surfaces on a side view. Add the product and holder envelope. Keep the drawing reference clear about finished wrapped parts rather than bare board alone.

The jewelry insert fit guide concerns product location. This sketch adds the user’s finger route around the lid and rim.

Map finger entry and contact

Mark the starting grip areas on two sides or another proposed position. Show the direction the lid should rise. If a notch, tab or other opening aid is proposed, identify it and ask the supplier to confirm its construction.

On the sample, begin with the lid closed and complete contents inside. Record where fingers first touch and whether another part must be moved to obtain a grip. Keep that change visible in the action record.

View the opening through its first movement and later lift. Contact may happen at the start or after the lid edge passes a neck or rim. Name the stage rather than assigning a single overall ease score.

Record any product or holder contact separately. Finger space for the lid and access to the product are two linked tasks, but a successful lid lift doesn’t prove the item can then be removed.

Use a grip and access sketch

Keep a side sketch and a top sketch with matching face names. Add one row for each observed action stage.

Stage Location to mark Observation
Start Accessible lid and base grip areas Actual finger entry and support
Initial lift Lid rim against base or neck Contact and any changed grip
Continued lift Passing edge and product envelope Movement clear of contents
Lid removed Product and holder grip area Next removal action
Reference Finished-part and sample revisions Final or substitute materials

A contact observation should include the named face and stage. This gives the supplier a useful location to compare with its proposed fit.

Work through a hypothetical necklace box

Suppose a brand proposes a lift-off jewelry box with a lid extending close to the table. The customer is intended to hold the base steady and lift the lid from the sides. The buyer records that starting setup on the grip sketch.

The first sample leaves little exposed base at the chosen grip points. The reviewer records the actual change needed to lift it, rather than calling it approved after moving the box into a different position.

The supplier may propose a different overlap, an opening aid or another form. The buyer compares the revised action against the same loaded configuration. The choice remains specific to that use rather than a claim that shallower lids are always better.

Keep the intended starting position fixed

For the hypothetical necklace box, call the side grip points G1 and G2 and mark the table position in the sketch. Record the user support expected at the base. If the reviewer lifts the entire pack to find a grip, preserve that action as a deviation from the starting requirement.

Ask the supplier: ‘Please review access to G1 and G2 in the closed loaded state and propose a response for the intended table opening.’ This locates the task without prescribing a universal lid overlap. A supplier can then discuss the actual geometry or an opening aid.

For the revised sample, begin again from the table position and document the first lid movement. If another grip is part of the proposed use, update the sketch and review it deliberately rather than carrying over the original requirement unchanged.

Keep the lid action and product removal in separate rows. The lid may be accessible while the holder still blocks a card edge, or the product may be easy to remove after an awkward opening. The record should expose both tasks and keep any acceptance criteria tied to the actual finished sample state.

Send the grip requirement with the loaded envelope

Use Packrivo’s enquiry form to send the opening setup, grip sketches, loaded dimensions and located observations. Ask the responsible supplier to propose and confirm the interface. Any measured opening-force or repeated-use requirement needs a separately agreed method.

Record a changed starting grip before calling the lid action complete

For invented loaded box B1, the requirement is to begin on the table, keep the base supported there and start the lid lift at G1/G2. The diagram marks intended faces only; it does not establish finger access or a completed opening trial.

Stage Proposed requirement Record separately
Start B1 stays on table; G1/G2 identified First unassisted grip
Initial lift Lid moves; base remains supported Any whole-box lift or changed grip
Continued lift Contents remain identified Lid/product contact
Lid removed Separate product-removal route Holder and product access

If a reviewer lifts the whole pack first to find a grip, retain that action as a change from the stated starting requirement. The team can deliberately revise the intended use, or ask for another construction proposal; it should not keep the old requirement while hiding the different action.

The CSV separates starting setup, first action, assistance, deviation and product removal. All actual observation cells remain blank here. G1/G2 are planning locations, not guaranteed hand spaces or universal dimensions. A lid removed successfully would still leave product access to review. Any opening-force or repeated-use claim needs its own agreed method and evidence.

Download the lift off lid gift box opening record (.csv). HYPOTHETICAL rows are invented examples. Use ACTUAL_BLANK for permitted project inputs; replace that row label only when recording actual facts. Empty evidence, observation and date fields mean unknown or not performed, never acceptance. Keep checkpoints and revisions separate.

Send the starting setup, matched grip views, actual deviations and separate product-removal question with the loaded dimensions. Packrivo coordinates independent suppliers. These records establish no supplier offer, service availability or MOQ exception; its published baseline is 500 pieces per product/design.

title: Drawer Box Pull Tabs: Review the Loaded Tray
html:
Review a drawer pull with the complete loaded tray and the proposed attachment present. Show where the hand grips, how the pull moves and which parts it contacts. A loose ribbon swatch or empty drawer can communicate appearance while leaving the attachment and loaded opening action unresolved.

Use the Drawer Jewelry Box to locate the proposed pull on the complete tray. Request the attachment detail and review access with the loaded contents; the concept does not establish pull strength or opening force.

The pull may be the first part a customer touches. Its position belongs in the opening brief, while its attachment needs a separate construction response. Keep both visible before approving a colour or decorative style.

Identify the pull and attachment separately

PackMojo’s rigid drawer catalogue distinguishes ribbon and thumb-notch variants. This supports treating the opening aid as a specified feature. It doesn’t establish your pull’s attachment method or a force rating.

Ask the supplier to show the pull outside and its proposed attachment inside the tray. Record the material, visible length or shape, attachment location and any lining that covers it. Do not infer a hidden joint from the external concept image.

State whether the pull remains available when the drawer is fully closed. If it folds into a recess or lies against another panel, show that starting position. The customer should not need a different unrecorded grip to begin opening.

The sample checklist covers the wider approval. This form focuses on one pull, one attachment and one opening action.

Review the action with complete contents

Load the actual product, holder and cards. Position the closed pack as intended for use. Record the hand location and pull direction before the drawer begins moving.

Observe whether the pull meets the sleeve edge, tray lining or product during the action. Keep a wider view showing the loaded configuration. A close view of the pull alone can hide what moved elsewhere.

Use the agreed opening behavior. If the tray is intended to stop while attached, review that end state; if it should slide free, include the final exit. A pull should not be treated as a travel stop unless the supplier confirms that separate function.

If the sample needs extra support or another grip, record the change. Don’t omit it from the review because the drawer eventually opened.

Use a pull and attachment review form

Keep the inside and outside images linked to the same sample. The fields below separate appearance, construction and action.

Field Input Observation
Pull identity Material and visible shape Starting grip availability
Attachment Supplier-confirmed location and method Inside and outside views
Loaded state Product, holder and card revisions Contents position before action
Hand action Grip, support and pull direction Actual movement or changed grip
Contact Pull-to-sleeve or other named interface Location and stage
After view Attachment and pull after action Visible change or no change observed

These are observation fields. They don’t create a pull-force test or a repeated-use rating; agree such requirements separately if the project needs them.

Follow a hypothetical ribbon-pull sample

Suppose a gift box contains a card-mounted pendant in a drawer. A green ribbon pull is proposed at the tray front. The buyer asks for the attachment view and records whether the lining covers the joint.

During the loaded opening action, the ribbon contacts the lower sleeve edge. The reviewer records that contact stage and the actual grip. The supplier can then discuss pull position, attachment or the sleeve interface against the same proposal.

If a revision changes ribbon length and attachment position, keep both changes in the record. Compare the same loaded action on the revised sample. A nicer outside photograph doesn’t close the hidden attachment question.

Keep hidden attachment and visible grip in one record

For the hypothetical pendant tray, call the outside ribbon P1 and the proposed inside joint J1. Save the closed starting view, loaded opening view and inside attachment view under the same sample ID. This makes an apparently simple colour or length revision traceable to the construction it uses.

Ask the supplier which layers cover J1 and whether the review sample represents the proposed attachment. A demonstration model may use a temporary joint. Record that limitation rather than presenting its opening action as evidence for the production proposal.

A useful request is: ‘Please confirm J1 for pull P1 on loaded tray T1 and review the contact at the sleeve edge.’ It joins the hidden detail to the visible action. A reply showing only a ribbon swatch leaves the joint and loaded interface unresolved.

If a later proposal changes the pull material, visible length or joint, record each changed field. Review the same starting grip and loaded travel. Keep visual appearance approval separate from any agreed functional acceptance. The form should let the buyer see what has been reviewed, what is still a concept and which part needs the next supplier response.

Bring the action and attachment evidence together

Send the loaded configuration, inside attachment view, starting grip and contact observations through Packrivo’s enquiry. Ask for the next proposal by named interface. Keep decorative approval separate from any functional acceptance or evaluation requirement.

Keep the three evidence views under one loaded-tray revision

For invented necklace drawer T1, outside pull P1 and hidden attachment J1 must remain one configuration question. The concept packet shows a closed view and a loaded opening direction, while the actual inside-attachment view is requested. The empty tray intentionally shows no joint method or confirmed joint location.

View Can frame the question Missing actual evidence
Closed T1/P1 Starting grip Actual closed loaded photo
Loaded opening Sleeve-edge interface Actual action and support observation
Inside attachment J1 construction request Actual attachment view/method
Revised P2/J2 Separate changed fields Matching revised loaded review

Do not close J1 from a ribbon colour swatch or a successful concept animation. Ask which layers conceal the proposed joint and whether the supplied sample represents it. No adhesive, stitch or fastener is prescribed by the illustration.

Use one sample revision across all three views. If P2 changes both visible length and J2 attachment, record both changes before comparing the loaded action. Keep end-of-travel behaviour separate: the pull is not evidence of a drawer stop. The CSV's actual photos, observations and dates remain blank; these generated concepts are not substitutes for sample evidence or a pull-force rating.

Download the drawer box pull tab record (.csv). HYPOTHETICAL rows are invented examples. Use ACTUAL_BLANK for permitted project inputs; replace that row label only when recording actual facts. Empty evidence, observation and date fields mean unknown or not performed, never acceptance. Keep checkpoints and revisions separate.

Send same-revision closed, loaded-action and inside-attachment evidence, with appearance and functional decisions kept separate. Packrivo coordinates independent suppliers. These records establish no supplier offer, service availability or MOQ exception; its published baseline is 500 pieces per product/design.

title: Decide Whether the Drawer Should Stop or Slide Out
html:
Decide whether the packaging drawer should remain captured at an agreed opening position or slide fully free before reviewing its travel. Show the desired end state, product removal route and support for the tray. Ask the supplier to confirm any stop mechanism; a sleeve’s closed rear end isn’t an outward travel stop.

A drawer concept can look convincing while leaving its final opening action undefined. The buyer should choose the user task first, then ask for a construction that can be reviewed against it.

Choose the end state as a use requirement

For a captured tray, describe the opening position needed to reach the product and how the tray is supported there. For a removable tray, describe where it will be placed once free and how the product is taken out.

PackMojo’s rigid drawer reference identifies a sleeve and sliding drawer. This supports the two-component relationship, not a built-in outward stop for your proposal. A stop must be identified on the supplier’s actual drawing.

Keep the desired behavior distinct from the mechanism. ‘Tray remains captured while the product is removed’ is a requirement. A ribbon, tab or other proposed restraint is a construction response that needs confirmation.

The jewelry structure guide compares broad opening formats. This record resolves one specific end-state decision within the drawer direction.

Show product access at the chosen position

Place the complete product and holder in the tray. Mark the opening position in a side view, then show the finger route to the item. If a product extends above the tray, include that height in the access view.

For a captured tray, ask whether the remaining sleeve overlap leaves the required holder area exposed. For a removable tray, review the transition as it becomes free rather than looking only at the tray sitting separately on a table.

Record where the user supports the sleeve and tray. A sample action performed with two convenient extra hands may not represent the intended customer use. Describe the actual grip instead of claiming universal ease of opening.

Use a travel and end-state record

Keep one chosen end state per proposal row. Use the decision record to compare options without assuming a mechanism.

Decision Captured proposal Removable proposal
Desired end state Tray remains joined at named position Tray exits fully
Product access Visible holder and grip area at stop Access once tray is supported outside
Support User grip and remaining overlap User grip during final exit
Mechanism Supplier-confirmed restraint if proposed Unobstructed exit route to confirm
Evidence Loaded opening and removal sequence Loaded exit and placement sequence

A drawn arrow that ends at a convenient point doesn’t prove a stop exists. Ask the supplier to show the parts responsible for the proposed behavior.

Follow a hypothetical necklace-card pack

Suppose a brand wants a necklace card removed while the drawer stays attached to its sleeve. The initial concept shows a partly open tray but no restraint. The buyer records the captured end-state requirement as unresolved.

The supplier is asked to propose and identify the construction that provides that state. The next loaded sample is reviewed for access at the proposed position and for the user support required during removal.

Alternatively, the brand may choose a fully removable tray that rests on a table. That is a different use choice, not a failed version of the captured proposal. The record changes the expected exit action and the sample evidence accordingly.

Do not invent a stop by adding a decorative pull or making the drawer tighter. The proposal must name its functional detail, and any required retention evaluation needs an agreed method.

Write a clear end-state instruction

For the hypothetical necklace drawer, a captured-state instruction can read: ‘Open to the supplier-confirmed retained position, support the sleeve as shown and remove the card through the exposed area.’ Keep this as a proposed use instruction until the actual retention construction is confirmed.

A removable-state instruction instead needs the final tray exit and a place to support it. The two instructions should have separate sketches. Combining a captured opening photo with a fully removed access photo can hide the difference in what the customer is expected to do.

Ask the supplier: ‘Please identify the proposed feature that keeps the loaded tray captured at the required access state.’ If no such feature is proposed, the captured requirement remains open. Increasing sliding resistance or adding a decorative ribbon is not evidence of a defined stop.

When the actual sample is reviewed, record product access and support at the proposed end state. Any required retention or repeated-use evaluation must have a separate agreed scope. The decision record helps select the intended behavior without inventing a mechanism or a performance result from a concept image.

Send the end-state choice before the mechanism

Bring the product access sketch, desired captured or removable behavior and support record to the packaging enquiry. Review the supplier’s actual mechanism separately from the concept. Keep travel, product access and any performance requirement in distinct approval fields.

Check full card withdrawal separately from reaching the card

A card being visible or reachable at a partly open position does not establish that it can be withdrawn through the available route. For the fictional necklace-card pack, name captured position PC and free-tray state PF. Both proposals retain sleeve S1, tray T1, holder H1 and card C1, but require different action evidence.

Hypothetical configuration Named object Relationship Input or next scope
CAPTURED22 CAPTURED22 uses sleeve S1
CAPTURED22 CAPTURED22 uses tray T1
CAPTURED22 CAPTURED22 uses end position PC
REMOVABLE22 REMOVABLE22 uses sleeve S1
REMOVABLE22 REMOVABLE22 uses tray T1
REMOVABLE22 REMOVABLE22 uses end position PF

CAPTURED22 asks for card reach, complete withdrawal, support at PC and the confirmed outward-stop feature separately. The stop remains unconfirmed here. REMOVABLE22 asks for the final tray exit, supported placement and card withdrawal. A photograph of C1 after the tray has been removed cannot answer how the card is taken out while T1 remains captured at PC.

Ask the supplier to show the actual feature responsible for the captured requirement, then review access with that feature and the complete contents. If the required card route needs more exposed space than the proposal provides, return the located access question rather than inventing a larger stop position or extra customer grip. The reviewer must document the support actually used; convenient extra hands should not disappear from the record.

The diagram names tasks and missing evidence without drawing a fictitious restraint. A closed rear, decorative ribbon or higher sliding resistance does not establish an outward stop. The buyer can choose a removable route instead, with a revised use instruction and its own evidence, while any retention, repeated-use or protection requirement remains a separate agreed evaluation. The CSV does not default either use choice or any actual result.

Download the drawer captured removable end state record (.csv). It includes the original table fields and scenarios alongside the added relationships. HYPOTHETICAL rows are editorial examples or required review scopes, not actual records. Actual quantity, configuration, component and file identities, materials, process, specification, copy, method, condition, observation, owner, decision, evidence and dates are blank. ACTUAL_BLANK is a separate empty starting row; enter permitted project evidence before using an actual record. A blank means unknown.

Use the Review a Drawer Pull With the Loaded Tray for its separate question. Use the Custom Packaging Sample: Approval Checks That Matter for its separate question.

References apply to the materials, processes or guidance named in each source. Worked configurations and dimensions are teaching examples, not tested specifications or production limits. Use the project’s material specification, drawing and formed sample for approval.

Discuss this packaging specification with Packrivo. We coordinate independent suppliers. MOQ: 500 pieces per product/design; illustrative quantities are not production offers. Confirm materials, samples, price and timing for your project.

title: Map Sleeve Seam Contact During Tray Travel
html:
Map the sleeve seam against the loaded tray’s travel and record contact at entry, midway and removal. Keep seam-side contact separate from general clearance elsewhere in the sleeve. A closed fit photo can miss a local obstruction that appears only while the tray moves past the prepared seam.

This is a narrow diagnosis record for the moving interface. It helps a supplier locate the question before the buyer requests a larger sleeve, another board or a different finish.

Locate the seam on the actual sleeve

PackMojo’s tray and sleeve reference describes a two-piece construction with a sliding tray. That supports reviewing movement between components. Your supplier must confirm the actual seam and fold construction for the proposed sleeve.

Ask for a view of the sleeve interior and identify the prepared seam. Mark it on a simple cross-section or open working sketch. If the joining detail is hidden, request clarification instead of assigning it from the outside photograph.

Label the tray’s leading end and customer pull end. State which direction it enters and whether removal uses the same end. A contact map loses meaning if the tray is reversed between trials without a note.

The sample revision guide keeps the broader version trail. This map adds specific locations along one tray’s travel.

Observe movement in named stages

Load the actual tray with its product, holder and cards. Place the sleeve in the intended orientation. Follow the proposed entry route without squeezing or twisting the sleeve as an unrecorded workaround.

Pause near the mouth, midway and the final position. On removal, record where a contact begins or ends. Use a wider view to locate it and a closer view to show the seam relationship.

Mark contact away from the seam separately. A high product point against the roof is a different issue from a tray edge against an internal overlap. Both may occur in one sample, but they deserve different questions.

Use a seam and travel issue map

Draw the sleeve as a simple tunnel with the seam side labelled. Add the action record below without assigning unverified friction values.

Stage Location Parts meeting Evidence
Entry Sleeve mouth and seam side Leading tray edge and prepared overlap First-contact image
Midway Named point along travel Tray perimeter and sleeve interior Position and movement note
Closed Final seated position Tray and remaining envelope Closed configuration view
Removal Customer pull route Same parts during exit Contact onset and release
Other contact Roof, opposite side or contents Named separate interface Separate issue ID

Include drawing, seam and loaded-tray revisions. A new sleeve paired with an old tray should be treated as a new comparison configuration.

Follow a hypothetical seam-side obstruction

Suppose a folded tray carrying a gift card enters a sleeve smoothly at the mouth but catches midway near the seam side. The buyer records the exact travel stage and keeps the loaded tray orientation fixed.

The supplier is asked to compare that point with the seam proposal. The buyer doesn’t enlarge all sleeve dimensions immediately. If another contact appears at the roof, it receives a separate issue row rather than being labelled as the same seam problem.

A revised proposal may alter the seam, tray edge or another part. The map identifies what changed and which stage needs another check. The later sample is reviewed along the same route with the same complete contents.

Log a changed grip as part of the travel evidence

For the hypothetical sleeve, name the midway seam contact T2-S and the roof contact T2-R if both exist. Keep separate image references. That naming gives the supplier two located interfaces instead of one general complaint that the drawer is tight.

If a reviewer twists the tray to pass T2-S, record the changed action and the original obstruction. A workaround can be useful evidence, but it should not replace the intended route in the comparison. Ask whether the proposed construction should accommodate that action or be revised for the original one.

A precise question is: ‘Please review T2-S on the current sleeve and loaded tray, and identify the seam-related response.’ If the supplier proposes another board as well as another seam, record both changes. The next sample needs the same product configuration to support a useful comparison.

Keep a revised tray paired with its actual sleeve, even if the components carry familiar names. A contact disappearing under a different pairing doesn’t close the original configuration automatically. The map should say which pair and route were reviewed and which evidence remains open.

Send the located movement question

For a frame-tray configuration, the frame tray and sleeve direction adds the frame perimeter to the moving envelope. Use its component brief alongside this localized issue map.

Send the seam sketch, loaded configuration and stage images through Packrivo’s enquiry form. Ask for a response tied to the actual contact point. The map is an observational method, not a friction test or a repeated-use rating.

Keep each sleeve and tray pairing in its own travel record

A proposal changing sleeve S1 to S2 does not establish what happened with every tray. Build a four-pair planning matrix: S1/T1, S1/T2, S2/T1 and S2/T2. Keep complete contents P1 and orientation D1 named in every row. These are proposed comparison configurations, not four fabricated fit tests or a claim that all pairings are useful production options.

Hypothetical configuration Named object Relationship Input or next scope
S1_T1 S1_T1 uses sleeve S1
S1_T1 S1_T1 uses tray T1
S1_T2 S1_T2 uses sleeve S1
S1_T2 S1_T2 uses tray T2
S2_T1 S2_T1 uses sleeve S2
S2_T1 S2_T1 uses tray T1
S2_T2 S2_T2 uses sleeve S2
S2_T2 S2_T2 uses tray T2

For each selected pair, separate entry, midway, closed and removal observations. At every stage keep the seam-side question distinct from the roof question. A record for the original T2-S seam-side location should not absorb a T2-R roof contact simply because both occur while the tray moves. The CSV therefore gives each pair, stage and interface its own evidence request.

Ask which exact pair a supplier's returned photograph or action record represents. A new sleeve with a new tray can be reviewed as that complete candidate, but cannot retrospectively close the old S1/T1 issue. If the purpose is to understand the effect of only one component change, retain the other component, contents and route and document any difference. A changed material or prepared seam belongs in that identity too.

Keep a twist, squeeze or altered grip under its own action record instead of hiding it when the tray eventually passes. The matrix supports a specific next reply about a named pair and stage; it supplies no friction value, universal clearance or causal diagnosis. title: Packaging Print File Checklist: Fonts, Links and Output
html:
Prepare a print-file manifest that lists the native artwork, accepted output, font state, linked assets and printer requirements. Record missing or changed assets before handoff and assign who creates the final output. A packaged folder helps organize the files, but the receiving printer still needs a named accepted version.

Keep the native file and output roles explicit

The official Adobe Illustrator Package guidance describes collecting linked graphics and necessary fonts with the document and a package report. It also explains missing-asset information and the need to check font-copying permission. That function is useful context, not proof of printer acceptance.

Name the native artwork file, the reference PDF and the intended print output separately. Record their revisions and the drawing used for placement. The receiving printer should know which file can be edited, which shows the accepted appearance and which output is intended for production use.

Give font state its own field: live text, outlined text or another confirmed handoff. Keep the supplied copy and the designer’s responsibility visible when changing that state. Where font files are shared, the font owner should confirm the actual permission to do so.

Review links, assets and the report

List each linked image or supporting asset, its identity and whether the link resolves in the delivered package. Record assets embedded in the artwork separately from linked originals where relevant. A file name alone does not establish that the printer received the intended version.

The Glenroy artwork specification is a printer-specific example requesting supporting files and defined font/output states. Ask the actual selected printer for its own accepted software/output requirements rather than assuming a package report satisfies every process.

Use the package report or another actual preflight record to locate missing links or fonts. Assign the designer to return corrected assets and the output creator to confirm the resulting version. Keep any substitution attached to the file manifest so it is not hidden inside a regenerated PDF.

Use a print-package preflight manifest

The following hypothetical gift-box records are an original handoff aid.

File or requirement Example record Owner and evidence
Native artwork BX1_ART_r02.ai linked to drawing BX1_DWG_r02 Designer supplies editable state
Output PDF BX1_OUT_r02.pdf, accepted appearance reference Named output creator and buyer approval
Fonts Live/outlined state and missing-font report Designer confirms state and handoff permission
Linked image Asset IMG1, expected version and resolved link Designer supplies the actual supporting asset
Printer requirements Selected process/output specification Printer confirms accepted format/version
Receipt Manifest and files acknowledged by receiving owner Keep unresolved assets explicitly open

Resolve an illustrative missing-link handoff

Imagine the reference PDF looks complete but the native artwork report shows a missing linked image. Retain the PDF’s appearance role and the missing native asset as separate facts. The next action is to supply or deliberately replace that asset under a recorded revision.

After the designer returns the package, the output owner should identify the PDF generated from it. The buyer reviews the affected appearance, while the printer confirms the required file state. This keeps an output regenerated from a changed asset from being confused with the earlier accepted reference.

Send the manifest with an output owner

The existing artwork handoff method supplies the broader approval route. Use the drawing-change record when the file package needs a revised structure or layout reference.

The designer supplies the files and actual asset states. The printer defines the accepted technical handoff. The output owner identifies the final generated version, and the buyer records its appearance approval. A filename convention helps find the file but does not replace those roles.

Bring the manifest, selected printer requirements and unresolved asset/output questions to your packaging brief. MOQ is 500 pieces per design; artwork, sample scope and commercial conditions are confirmed for the project.

Retain the old appearance while correcting the native source

Imagine native ART2 has a missing IMG1 link while reference PDF2 still shows the earlier appearance. ART3 and PDF3 are proposed revised identities, not delivered files. A complete-looking PDF does not show that the editable package contains its required source asset.

Record Invented state Next owner/action
ART2 native IMG1 link missing Designer resolves or records deliberate replacement
PDF2 reference Earlier appearance retained Keep its original review scope
ART3 native proposal Corrected asset state to document Designer supplies exact package
PDF3 output proposal Not accepted Output owner identifies exact generated file
Fonts Copying permission unknown Owner confirms permitted handoff

Do not silently replace PDF2 with a regenerated file under the same name. Link ART3's changed asset and the output created from it, then review the affected appearance. A printer's technical acceptance is still a separate response.

The CSV separates file role, source link state, output origin, appearance decision and receiving acknowledgement. Actual file hashes and dates remain blank because no files were exchanged. Adobe's Package function can gather links, fonts and reports, subject to font permissions; it does not guarantee that a specific printer accepts the package. Keep missing assets, proposed corrections and accepted output identities distinct.

Download the packaging print file checklist record (.csv). HYPOTHETICAL rows are invented examples. Use ACTUAL_BLANK for permitted project inputs; replace that row label only when recording actual facts. Empty evidence, observation and date fields mean unknown or not performed, never acceptance. Keep checkpoints and revisions separate.

Send the manifest, real package report, permitted assets and selected printer requirements with one named output owner. Packrivo coordinates independent suppliers. These records establish no supplier offer, service availability or MOQ exception; its published baseline is 500 pieces per product/design.

title: Actual-Size Proofs Make Trim and Die-Cut Relationships Reviewable
html:
Use an actual-size proof to locate artwork against the current trim, die-cut and crease drawing. Verify the output scale, identify the relevant objects and retain the selected converter’s safe-area requirements. The result should be a located overlay decision, not a general statement that the digital proof looks correct.

Keep page trim and package cutting identities separate

The official Adobe marks and bleeds guidance explains trim marks and artwork extending beyond the trim/crop area. It supplies those file concepts, not universal die-cut tolerances or safe distances for your package.

Identify the current structural drawing and its units. Name the cut, crease and any other relevant construction lines separately from the PDF page boundary. The designer and converter should agree which lines are used for the package review.

Record how the actual-size output was verified. Keep the file, print/export settings and scale reference with the review. If a screenshot or enlarged view is used to locate an issue, retain it alongside the actual-size evidence rather than treating its screen dimensions as the product dimensions.

Inspect the relationship at the named object

The printer’s artwork specification is an example of tying usable artwork to an accurate dieline and print layout. The selected converter still supplies the requirements that control this project’s objects, edges and folds.

Mark the supplied logo, text block, window or other object beside the relevant cut/crease line. Ask whether a distance, alignment or repeated panel relationship needs review under the actual selected specification. Leave missing safe-area values to the converter instead of borrowing a default from another box.

Review the complete artwork orientation after folding as well as its flat relationship. If the object moves to another panel when the drawing changes, keep that as a layout revision. A clean crop at the page boundary can still leave a different package-cutting question.

Use an actual-size overlay checklist

This original Packrivo aid records a hypothetical logo beside a gift-carton cut line.

Relationship Illustrative record Next confirmation
Output scale File PDF1, actual-size verification retained Designer records output method/reference
Structure Drawing BX1 and units Converter identifies package cut/crease lines
Trim/bleed PDF trim boundary versus structural cut Printer confirms the intended file relationship
Object A1 Logo beside cut C1 on panel F1 Actual selected safe-area requirement
Formed orientation F1 shown on formed sample S1 Buyer reviews visible placement
Exception Located alignment or clearance issue Revised file/drawing and accepted owner

Resolve a hypothetical scale and cut question

Imagine a proof preview shows a logo centered on the visible page, but the structural cut line is offset within that page. The next action is to verify the file scale and package drawing, then locate the logo against the actual cut. Centering it in the page is not the same decision.

The converter can return the applicable requirement and the designer can prepare the revised overlay. Review the changed object at actual size and retain the old and new drawing/output references. The buyer can then accept a specific relationship instead of approving every technical aspect of the proof at once.

Handoff the overlay with the selected rule

Use the artwork handoff checklist for the supplied files. The dieline-change record identifies linked layout checks, and the sample approval guide records which evidence still requires a formed or physical sample.

The designer owns scale and object placement in the output. The converter owns the structural lines and project-specific rule. The buyer accepts the visible arrangement using the named evidence. Keep any unresolved feature with a next owner rather than calling the full proof technically approved.

Share the actual-size overlay, drawing revision and located question through the packaging brief. MOQ is 500 pieces per design; artwork, samples and commercial terms are confirmed for the project.

Separate an export-scale correction from moving the artwork object

Name three fictional configurations for the same BX1 drawing and logo A1. BASE22 uses PDF1/ART1. EXPORT_ONLY22 proposes PDF2 from the same ART1. ARTWORK_MOVE22 proposes PDF3 from revised ART2. The first changes the output reference; the second changes the artwork reference. Neither is declared correctly scaled or positioned merely by being the newer file.

BASE22 BASE22 uses artwork ART1
BASE22 BASE22 uses drawing BX1

EXPORT_ONLY22 EXPORT_ONLY22 uses artwork ART1
EXPORT_ONLY22 EXPORT_ONLY22 uses drawing BX1
ARTWORK_MOVE22 ARTWORK_MOVE22 uses output PDF3
ARTWORK_MOVE22 ARTWORK_MOVE22 uses artwork ART2
ARTWORK_MOVE22 ARTWORK_MOVE22 uses drawing BX1

For every configuration, retain three separate questions: what evidence establishes the output scale, where A1 sits against package cut C1, and how panel F1 reads after forming. A corrected export can address a scale problem without moving A1's intended position in the artwork. Moving A1 within ART2 can address layout while leaving export settings unverified. The designer and converter should identify which question the returned evidence actually answers.

Keep TRIM1 as the PDF page boundary and C1 as the structural cut; CR1 is a crease reference. The teaching sketch is unscaled and supplies no distance between them. A logo centered on the visible page is not necessarily centered on the package face defined by the structural drawing. Use the converter's actual line identities, units and relevant rule rather than replacing that question with a tidy crop.

title: Product Identity Needs a Place After the Belly Band Is Removed
html:
Map which product identity, care and reference information remains when a belly band is removed. Assign each required supplied field to a retained product, card or box surface and review that removal state. A removable band can introduce the gift, while the customer still needs an identifiable item after the band is discarded.

List the information that needs to survive removal

This is an original Packrivo handoff tool. The product owner supplies the actual identity and approved information; the worksheet does not create a barcode standard or decide regulatory copy.

Identify the band fields and the point at which the band is removed. List which supplied name, variant, care instruction or project reference the customer needs afterward. Keep required and optional information separate instead of duplicating everything by default.

Give each retained field a physical carrier: the actual product/primary pack, a kept card or a permanent box area. Record its position and the supplied wording or reference. A filename or information visible only on the discarded band does not identify the retained item.

Review the band-off state with the complete pack

The paper belly band defines the removable construction. This tool adds the information handoff after that removal. Load the complete gift, remove the band through its intended route and retain the customer-facing state for review.

Check whether the remaining product/card/box identity still corresponds to the actual contents. If a gift has multiple variants, use the real supplied matching reference and keep its owner visible. Do not create a fake identifier merely to make an illustration resemble a retail label.

Record information that becomes inaccessible after another component is removed. The buyer should decide whether the card stays with the gift, the box remains useful or the primary product needs a different approved information position.

Use a retained-identity map

These hypothetical gift references illustrate the decision; they are not real product SKUs or an actual order.

Supplied information On removable band Retained carrier after removal
Product name Band field N1 Approved name on actual primary pack
Variant reference Supplied project field V1 Matching approved field on retained card/pack
Care information Short pointer if supplied Approved text on a card intended to be kept
Project/reference field Only if supplied for this purpose Named retained box/card location
Removal point Customer slides band off gift box Band-off photo with retained fields visible
Missing identity Field exists only on discarded band Product owner/design owner resolves location

Resolve an illustrative band-only identity

Imagine two gift variants share a similar outer box and their supplied variant names appear only on different belly bands. When the customer removes a band, the remaining pack may no longer show the intended reference. Record that specific field rather than asking for generally more branding.

The product owner can decide which approved field should remain on a card or primary pack. The designer then returns the actual placement and file, and the buyer reviews the band-off arrangement with the correct contents. This gives the handoff a retained identity without turning the article into barcode-placement guidance.

Handoff retained fields to the artwork owner

Use the artwork handoff checklist to keep the approved wording and file revisions with the placement. The next route is band construction, retained information map, artwork handoff and the packaging brief.

The product owner supplies the real identity and approved copy. The designer places it on the agreed retained carrier. The packing observer returns the removal state, and the buyer decides which fields remain open. Keep those responsibilities explicit before accepting the complete presentation.

MOQ is 500 pieces per design. Packrivo helps prepare the brief and coordinate the remaining information/packaging questions; the actual artwork, sample scope and commercial details are confirmed for the project.

Check whether the retained carrier survives the next removal state

A field can survive band removal yet disappear when the customer later separates a card. Compare two hypothetical placements for the supplied V1 variant field: CARD_ONLY22 assigns it to C1, while PRIMARY22 assigns it to primary pack P1. The fields are location references, not actual variant names, retail identifiers or proposed care wording.

Review two explicit states: BAND_OFF_CARD_KEPT and the optional BAND_OFF_CARD_REMOVED. Under the first assumption, the C1 field still has its carrier. Under the second, a field located only on C1 has lost that carrier. The P1 placement remains available in these particular assumed states because P1 is retained. Those are planning relationships, not evidence of customer behavior or a claim that all information must be duplicated.

Ask the product owner which removal states actually need the identity. If the card is intended to stay with the gift and that meets the requirement, a primary-pack duplication may be unnecessary. If the customer needs the variant after separating the card, request an approved retained position. Keep the name, care and project-reference fields independent; the product owner determines their required or optional scope and supplies the actual copy.

Keep those decisions separate before handing the selected placement and artwork revision onward.
