title: Embossing Needs a Back-Surface Contact and Clearance Map
html:
Map the back surface of an embossed panel before fixing the relief location. Identify what touches that surface after converting, including an insert, product, card or another stacked panel. Review the actual relief and those contacts together so the appearance decision does not leave an unresolved internal clearance.

Record relief on both faces of the panel

The original Holmen embossing explanation describes shaping paperboard using a stamp and counter-die, with restrictions linked to board construction. It also discusses preserving relief during stacking. Use that context to request the offered board, tool and relief proposal rather than assuming a universal depth.

Give the embossed object and panel a stable identity. Show the front appearance and the corresponding back area on the drawing. Mark a fold, edge or internal component that approaches that back area after the box is formed.

Keep the proposed relief sample and board grade attached to this map. If the early appearance sample uses a different material, record the substitution and retain the final-board question. An attractive front image alone does not identify the formed panel’s internal contact.

Identify what occupies the space behind the relief

The FSEA designer guide explains embossing die/counter identities and artwork considerations. It supports naming the tool proposal, not a universal gap behind every embossed gift panel.

Place the insert, card and actual product in their final arrangement. Locate any contact with the back of the relief when the box is loaded and closed. If another panel lies against it during flat delivery or stacking, record that state separately from the customer’s opened pack.

Ask the converter or finisher which relief/tool or layout field should be reviewed at the located contact. The buyer may keep the position, request an internal clearance proposal or choose another appearance location. Each option should stay tied to the same board and formed state.

Use a front and back contact map

This original Packrivo aid uses hypothetical panel and component IDs.

Feature or state Example record Question to resolve
Emboss E1 Brand mark on lid panel L1 Offered relief/tool and board identity
Back area Corresponding region beneath E1 What touches it after forming?
Insert I1 Finished holder below the lid Actual loaded clearance/contact
Card C1 Care card position near rear panel Does the card occupy the relief space?
Supplied stack Prepared panels in their delivered state What relief-contact state needs reviewing?
Next decision Retain or change the named interface Finisher response and buyer approval reference

Review an illustrative lid and holder

Imagine an embossed lid on a jewelry gift box. The front relief is the intended visual detail, but the holder or care card may approach its back area when the lid is seated. Draw that relationship before asking for a deeper or differently positioned effect.

The finisher can explain the actual tool/board proposal, while the holder converter can return the relevant height or layout. Review the complete resulting sample and record which contact is accepted. Keep appearance approval and holder clearance linked, without treating either one as proof of a tested packaging outcome.

Handoff the two-sided decision

The drawing-change method records the affected panel and linked insert. The sample revision record keeps replacement relief evidence connected to the configuration.

The designer identifies the relief object. The finisher confirms the tool and board-related proposal. The packing or holder owner returns actual contact evidence, and the buyer decides the accepted arrangement. Those named responsibilities make the next review more specific than a general request to improve embossing.

A card move and a relief move reopen different relationships

An answer about the card in the loaded pack cannot establish what happens between delivered panels. title: Packaging Foil Placement Around Folds and Glue Areas
html:
Map each proposed foil element against the current fold lines and glue areas before artwork approval. Identify the foil process, material and nearby interface, then ask the printer to confirm the proposal. Keep any required separation as a supplier-specific decision rather than adding a universal distance to the file.

This map is useful after a reflective treatment has been chosen. Its job is to expose the few places where that artwork meets the construction. It doesn’t replace the printer’s production specification.

Name the foil process before mapping it

The Foil & Specialty Effects Association’s foil process guide distinguishes hot, cold and digital techniques. That distinction supports asking which process is proposed. It doesn’t establish the same restrictions for all processes or substrates.

Record the selected printer’s process name, substrate and surface treatment. If those are undecided, mark the placement map as provisional. A metallic-looking mock-up cannot identify the manufacturing process.

Use the finish choice guide if the desired effect is still open. This method begins when the specific foil artwork needs a construction review.

Map elements and interfaces on the current dieline

Give each foil element a stable ID, such as F1 for a front motif and F2 for a lid border. Place those IDs on the artwork layer without changing the structural lines. Keep a named dieline revision beside the map.

For each element, identify the nearest fold, cut or glue interface that needs discussion. A crossing element and a nearby element are different cases. Mark the relationship rather than assuming the same margin covers both.

Ask the printer or converter to confirm glue areas on the proposed construction. A designer should not infer every glue area from the flat outline. Show any supplier-confirmed region clearly and preserve the original structural file.

Write the desired appearance in the formed state. A border may need to read across two panels, while a small motif may stay entirely on one face. Those requests give the printer context for its response.

Use a foil conflict map

Keep the map as a short drawing attachment and a response table. Each row needs one located relationship and one next action.

The entries below are hypothetical, not observed production results. Record the drawing and artwork revisions, proposed process, substrate, response owner and evidence references above the table.

Foil / interface Proposed relationship Question for printer or converter Decision status
F1–C1 Sleeve border F1 crosses crease C1 Can this artwork be used at C1 with the named process and material? What sample review is needed? Open: process review and formed appearance
F1–G1 The same border approaches provisional joining region G1 Please confirm G1 on this construction. Does the seam-side segment require a change? Open: joining region confirmation and artwork decision

Record a supplier-requested margin with its source and scope. If the process changes later, ask whether that instruction still applies rather than carrying it across automatically.

Follow a hypothetical sleeve border

Suppose a brand proposes a foil border across the front and side of a folding sleeve. The border crosses a crease, and another part approaches the prepared seam. The buyer creates two rows because the relationships are different.

The printer is asked to review the crease crossing for the proposed material and process. The seam row asks whether the foil artwork conflicts with the confirmed joining area. No universal number is inserted before those replies arrive.

If the converter confirms G1 and requests moving only the seam-side segment, the designer prepares a revised artwork file. Mark F1–G1 as revised, awaiting confirmation against that file. F1–C1 stays open until its separate review is completed; if the revision changes the crossing at C1, review that relationship against the new file too. That makes approval specific rather than calling the entire foil layer approved after one correction.

Record each printer response as a scoped instruction

In the hypothetical sleeve map, the same border F1 crosses crease C1 and approaches joining region G1. Record F1–C1 and F1–G1 as separate relationships, each with its own response and decision status. A printer instruction about G1 should not automatically be copied onto C1 because both are close to the same foil border.

When a source gives a separation requirement, record the exact proposed process, substrate and drawing revision it covers. Keep the original reply attached. A margin may become irrelevant after the foil process or seam construction changes, so the scope needs to travel with the instruction.

Ask a located question: ‘Please review border F1 against confirmed region G1 for this foil and sleeve proposal.’ A reply asking the designer to move the seam-side segment of F1 should be reflected in the artwork revision and the F1–G1 row. If G1 is still only a provisional region, retain that uncertainty.

For the formed sample, keep position and surface appearance decisions separate. The motif can occupy the agreed location while its physical effect still needs review. Record which decision the sample closes and which remains open. This makes the map useful at handoff without turning a supplier’s local instruction into an unsupported general rule.

Close placement with formed evidence

Review the foil on the formed component in the intended light and orientation. A digital layer proof can show position, while the physical sample shows the proposed surface result. Keep those approvals distinct.

The artwork handoff checklist helps attach the final map to the current file. Send unresolved element IDs and supplier replies through the packaging enquiry. The next action should name the element and interface that still needs confirmation.

Reopen both relationships when the foil process changes

A new hypothetical alternative changes a proposed hot-foil process HOT_r1 to a digital process DIGITAL_r2. Keep F1–C1, the crease crossing, and F1–G1, the joining-area relationship, as separate records under each proposal. No process has been selected or qualified.

Scenario scope Exact object or route Hypothetical input or output Calculation or record boundary
Process scoped relation HOT_r1_F1_C1 Unobserved; actual fields blank Fictional process proposal; independent margin/source/formed sample and decision remain unknown
Process scoped relation HOT_r1_F1_G1 Unobserved; actual fields blank Fictional process proposal; independent margin/source/formed sample and decision remain unknown
Process scoped relation DIGITAL_r2_F1_C1 Unobserved; actual fields blank Fictional process proposal; independent margin/source/formed sample and decision remain unknown
Process scoped relation DIGITAL_r2_F1_G1 Unobserved; actual fields blank Fictional process proposal; independent margin/source/formed sample and decision remain unknown

The earlier seam-side instruction belongs to its stated process, material and drawing. A process change cannot silently carry that instruction onto the new route, and one F1–G1 response does not approve F1–C1. Keep any requested separation, source and sample reference empty until the responsible printer supplies them.

Retain the original conditional artwork revision as history. If the revised border also changes the crossing, reopen that specific relationship. A formed position decision and the physical reflective appearance remain different questions even after the flat layer is located correctly.

Download the packaging foil placement folds glue record (.csv). It covers the original scenarios and this added comparison. HYPOTHETICAL rows are invented planning examples. Actual quantity, value, configuration, method, owner, observation, condition, decision, evidence and dates are blank because no actual project record has been obtained. Copy a relevant row and replace its type with ACTUAL only when entering permitted project evidence; keep the example and actual record separate. ACTUAL_BLANK is an empty starting row. A blank is unknown, never approval.

The related Foil, Embossing or Spot UV: Choose by the Effect Needed guide concerns a separate requirement. Use this record for the specific comparison above rather than treating that guide as evidence of a completed result.

Follow affected structural and layout decisions with the drawing change impact record. Keep the actual appearance reference separate with the physical color comparison.

References retain their stated general-guidance or manufacturer-example scope. Worked figures and records are teaching examples, not observed orders, stock, prices or measured performance.

title: Reversed Type Needs Its Background, Print Process and Finish Reviewed Together
html:
Review reversed packaging type with its background color construction and finishing layer attached. Identify each negative text object and the selected printer’s reverse-type rule, then inspect the actual-size proof or sample specified for that question. Positive-type acceptance should remain a separate record.

Name the negative text and its surrounding field

The original Glenroy flexographic guidelines distinguish reverse type from positive type and discuss background/color registration concerns. That process-specific example supports asking the actual printer for its own reverse-type requirements. It does not establish one minimum size for every carton or label.

Mark the negative text object, panel and background on the artwork. Record whether the background is a single named color, several separations or another offered construction. Keep the font and intended printed scale with that object rather than evaluating the text alone.

Identify any gloss, varnish, film or other proposed finish crossing the background and letters. The finishing relationship should be named on the same panel map so the proof or sample is reviewed in its intended state.

Separate the technical rule from the appearance decision

The coating technical sheet provides a named coating/substrate/application example. Its grade properties are relevant only to that proposal, not to every reversed-text finish. Ask the printer or finisher to confirm the actual finish over the object and the evidence supplied for reviewing it.

Inspect the negative letter shapes at the intended printed size and retain an enlarged view only to locate a specific observation. Record filled-in areas, unclear boundaries or another visible reading issue in ordinary terms, with the proof/sample identity and conditions. Let the printer assess the process-specific cause.

If the response proposes changing the background, type or finish, list exactly which field changes. The designer should return a revised output showing the whole object, not a cropped corrected word separated from its actual background.

Use a reverse-type background and finish map

The hypothetical gift-sleeve entries below are an original decision aid, not an industry file standard.

Object relationship Example input Owner and next evidence
Negative text T2 Small brand line reversed from front panel F1 Designer supplies object and font state
Background A1 Printer’s offered color/separation proposal Printer names actual reverse-type rule
Finish V1 Offered coating over the named area Finisher confirms grade and boundary
Output scale Actual-size artwork reference Designer confirms scale and panel
Observation Located reading/stroke question Printer returns assessment and revised evidence
Accepted state Text/background/finish revision together Buyer records the complete appearance decision

Keep a changed background in the comparison

Imagine a reversed brand line on a dark gift sleeve. One proposal changes the background construction while retaining the same text outline. That is a changed technical scope even if the screen preview appears similar.

Request a response that identifies both the background and text rule. Review the finish relationship on the resulting proof or sample and retain the accepted artwork version. The decision should name the complete state; it should not approve the text while the finish remains an unspecified later addition.

Handoff the complete negative-text object

The artwork handoff method keeps the output connected to its printer requirements. Use the color-reference record for the agreed background appearance.

The designer identifies the object and file. The printer confirms the process rule; the finisher confirms the relevant layer. The buyer accepts a named appearance reference or keeps the object open. This makes the next action answerable without broad claims that small reversed type always works.

Share the negative text, background/finish map and selected printer question through the packaging brief. MOQ is 500 pieces per design; print, sample and commercial details are confirmed for the project.

Treat a combined background and finish as a separate candidate

Keep T2 fixed and name the proposed baseline background BG1 and finish FIN1. A fictional comparison can then contain BG2/FIN1 as a background-only change, BG1/FIN2 as a finish-only change, and BG2/FIN2 as a combined candidate. All four states retain panel F1. The labels do not specify a color recipe, coating grade or technical performance.

Hypothetical configuration Named object Relationship Input or next scope
BG1-FIN1 BG1-FIN1 uses background BG1
BG1-FIN1 BG1-FIN1 uses finish FIN1
BG1-FIN2 BG1-FIN2 uses background BG1
BG1-FIN2 BG1-FIN2 uses finish FIN2
BG2-FIN1 BG2-FIN1 uses background BG2
BG2-FIN1 BG2-FIN1 uses finish FIN1
BG2-FIN2 BG2-FIN2 uses background BG2
BG2-FIN2 BG2-FIN2 uses finish FIN2

The combined candidate cannot inherit a whole-state decision by adding two separate approvals. A response for BG2/FIN1 was made with FIN1; a response for BG1/FIN2 was made with BG1. Neither is evidence of the complete BG2/FIN2 state. Request its actual-size output and the relevant proof or sample with the offered finish represented. Keep missing evidence visible even when the screen composite looks unchanged.

For each state, the printer confirms the applicable reverse-type rule and background construction, the finisher confirms the layer and boundary, and the buyer reviews the complete appearance. If the type outline changes too, give it a replacement text identity instead of continuing to call it unchanged T2. An enlarged letter detail can locate an issue but cannot replace intended-size reading with its real background and finish.

The download retains the original A1/V1 relationship and the original background-change questions, then maps every new configuration to T2, F1, its background and finish. Each has separate technical, actual-size and complete-appearance review requests. Screen swatches in the teaching image are uncalibrated symbols; they do not show how any selected print will fill, reflect or read. Real observations, decisions and source evidence remain blank.

Actual quantity, configuration, component and file identities, materials, process, specification, copy, method, condition, observation, owner, decision, evidence and dates are blank. ACTUAL_BLANK is a separate empty starting row; enter permitted project evidence before using an actual record. A blank means unknown.

title: Small Packaging Type Needs the Selected Printer’s File Specification
html:
Review small positive packaging type against the selected printer’s actual file specification, with the font, color and background identified. Keep the text object at its intended output size and record any exception by object and panel. A generic minimum font size cannot replace that process-specific review.

Define the positive text object being reviewed

The Glenroy flexographic specification gives different positive and reverse-type guidance and discusses vector type and color construction. It demonstrates that type requirements belong to a particular printing process. Its stated values are not Packrivo’s universal limits for every package.

List the small text objects on the current artwork: product descriptor, care statement, website or another supplied line. Record the panel, font, intended printed size and whether the text is live or outlined. Keep the actual copy with the object so a technical adjustment does not silently change its meaning.

Identify the print color and background beneath the text. Ask the selected printer to name the specification or accepted file rule used for this object. A specification reference is more useful than an informal statement that the font seems fine on a monitor.

Review at the intended printed size

Prepare the relevant artwork at its actual output scale and record how that scale was checked. Compare the small positive text under the printer’s stated rule and the intended physical reading conditions. An enlarged inspection view can locate a stroke problem, but should accompany the actual-size view rather than replacing it.

If the printer proposes a font, color or size change, record it against the named object. Ask whether the change affects panel space, adjacent copy or the accepted artwork version. Keep the response as a proposed exception until the designer and buyer have reviewed the resulting file.

Positive text and reverse text should use separate object records. If another paragraph is reversed from a solid background, route it to that task instead of assuming the same acceptance applies. The difference matters when the printer’s own file rules distinguish the two.

Use a positive-type exception map

This is an original Packrivo aid for matching a specific text object to the selected printer’s rule.

Print construction Positive dark type on the offered board face Printer confirms process/color rule
Rule reference Selected printer’s specification/version Use its actual relevant field
Actual-size review Output file F1, scale checked Record the observed reading/stroke question
Exception Printer proposes adjustment to T1 Buyer accepts/rejects revised output explicitly

Resolve one illustrative text exception

Imagine a care paragraph that fits neatly on the back of a small gift carton. The printer asks for a change to its positive text treatment. Keep the request attached to that paragraph rather than redesigning all packaging typography without a reason.

The designer can return the altered object with its new artwork revision. The buyer reviews the copy and intended printed appearance, while the printer confirms the file conforms to its selected process. If the new text no longer fits the same panel, record that layout change as another decision.

Handoff the rule, exception and accepted output

Use the artwork handoff checklist to retain fonts and output identities. The drawing-change record helps when the adjustment affects the panel layout.

The designer owns the revised file. The printer owns the technical rule and process confirmation. The buyer owns acceptance of the supplied words and final appearance. Keep the named object and reference visible across those responses.

Bring the small-type object map, actual-size file and selected printer question to your packaging brief. MOQ is 500 pieces per design; the printing proposal, sample scope and commercial conditions are confirmed for the project.

Keep the same care copy visible across two technical alternatives

Give the original care paragraph a shared requirement COPY-C1. The baseline output F1/ART1 places text T1 on B1. Two hypothetical alternatives are F2/ART2 with a changed font treatment, and F3/ART3 with a changed paragraph layout. The copy requirement remains COPY-C1 in both. No care wording, font size or actual technical exception is invented for this example.

F1 F1 uses artwork ART1
F1 F1 uses copy COPY-C1
F2 F2 uses artwork ART2
F2 F2 uses copy COPY-C1
F3 F3 uses artwork ART3
F3 F3 uses copy COPY-C1

Check each returned output in four separate ways: conformity to the selected printer's actual rule, reading at intended output size, correspondence to the supplied copy, and fit within the named panel. A technically conforming revised font can still omit a sentence or change a line break into another artwork area. A paragraph that fits can still leave the printing question unanswered. Neither outcome follows from the filename or a monitor enlargement.

Ask the designer to identify what changed in F2 or F3 and retain the full B1 context with nearby artwork. Ask the printer to identify the exact specification/version and which object its response covers. The buyer then reviews the supplied words and intended appearance on that output. If a response changes B1 or the structure, create a new panel relationship instead of leaving the old fit question looking closed.

The CSV links each output independently to COPY-C1, T1, B1 and its artwork version. Actual words and real file/evidence references are blank until permitted project inputs are entered. An enlarged detail remains a locator alongside actual-size evidence. This positive-type record does not transfer acceptance to reversed text or supply a generic minimum size, stroke rule or readable-result guarantee.

title: Large Solid Print Areas Need Review on the Named Formed Panel
html:
Review a large solid print area as a named panel with a recorded substrate, process and evidence stage. Keep the flat proof and converted sample linked, then describe the visible difference under agreed conditions. The next printer question should locate the appearance issue instead of asking for generally better color.

Give the solid area a boundary and a process

Fogra’s sheet-fed offset research examines substrate properties and solid-tone behavior under controlled printing conditions. It supports recording the paper and process with the printed result. It does not supply a universal ink setting or an acceptance value for your gift box.

Name the large face and its solid-color object on the current drawing. Mark its boundary, adjacent artwork and any finishing layer. Record whether the proposed printer uses a spot color, a process-color build or another confirmed arrangement. Keep the chosen physical reference separate from those production fields.

Specify which face is being reviewed after converting. A viewing angle can change when a panel is formed into a box, so retain the panel ID and orientation. Keep fold cracking and exposed-cut-edge questions in their own records; this tool focuses on the appearance of the named solid area.

Identify what each proof can show

The Glenroy print guidelines distinguish proof purposes and describe process-specific print considerations such as plate breaks. Use that as an example of why the actual printer should define the evidence supplied. Its flexographic details cannot be transferred automatically to an offset or digital proposal.

Ask whether a file preview, flat printed proof or formed sample is being sent. Record the substrate and finish state for that evidence. A sample printed on another stock remains useful for the questions it actually answers, but its substitution should stay visible in the comparison.

Write observations in plain, located terms: uneven appearance across panel F1, a line visible at a named boundary or a difference between two areas under the same lighting. Attach the photograph and viewing conditions. Avoid diagnosing an ink or press cause before the printer has assessed the evidence.

Use a large-solid panel observation record

This original Packrivo worksheet links an appearance observation to the actual panel and next response.

Field Hypothetical entry What remains to confirm
Panel/object Front face F1, solid object A1 Current artwork and drawing IDs
Print proposal Selected printer’s process and color build Named grade and print setup scope
Flat evidence Proof FP1 on the stated stock Whether appearance or only position is reviewed
Converted evidence Formed sample S1, same face orientation Final finish and contents state
Observation Visible uneven area near the right side of F1 Printer’s assessment of located evidence
Decision Request another appearance proof for F1 Response owner and accepted reference

Compare an illustrative flat and formed review

Imagine a candle gift box whose front face is printed as one dark solid. The buyer likes the flat preview but later notices a visible difference when the face is upright on the formed sample. Retain both evidence IDs and the same face reference before changing the color or board.

The printer may need to clarify a process, substrate or finishing difference. Record the proposed explanation as a response requiring review, with any replacement evidence linked to the same panel. Your decision can then say which appearance is accepted and under what reference conditions.

Keep the printer response attached to the color decision

The color approval method names the physical reference and conditions. Use the sample revision record when a new solid-area sample replaces an earlier one.

The designer identifies the artwork area. The printer assesses the process-specific question and sends the agreed evidence. The buyer approves the named appearance reference or keeps a particular panel open. This assignment helps keep a general comment about color from spreading into unrelated structure changes.

Share the panel ID, substrate/process proposal and located observation through the packaging brief. MOQ is 500 pieces per design; printing, material, samples and commercial terms are confirmed for the project.

Check whether a proof represents the intended stock and finish together

An unchanged artwork file does not make evidence interchangeable. Assume a fictional ART1 contains solid object A1 on front F1. Compare four explicitly named states: B1-U, B1-F, B2-U and B2-F, where B1/B2 are alternative stocks, U means unfinished and F means the proposed final finish. Those labels are scope identities, not actual material grades or observed print results.

B1-U B1-U uses finish U
B1-U B1-U uses artwork ART1

B1-F B1-F uses artwork ART1

B2-U changes both fields. Keep each flat and formed evidence request under its own configuration. This prevents someone from choosing a favorable flat view on one stock and a favorable formed view on another as though they represented one candidate.

State the purpose of each incoming item before comparison: position, color direction or final-panel appearance. Ask the printer to confirm the grade, process, color build and finish represented by that exact item. Then compare F1 in the agreed orientation beside the physical reference. A photographic difference can be documented without claiming an ink, substrate or finishing cause; those explanations need the printer's process-specific assessment.

It adds the four complete stock/finish configurations and separate flat/formed evidence rows, with no sample defaulted as accepted. The buyer's output is an evidence gap list for the selected state, not a ranking of screen greens. There is no invented uniformity tolerance, ink setting or promise that changing stock or finish improves the solid.

title: Printing White on Kraft Paper: Artwork and Proof Guide
html:
Printing white on kraft paper requires a clear instruction for each artwork area: visible white ink, a white underprint beneath color, or unprinted kraft showing through. Name the proposed substrate and selected printer before approving the file. A white screen background does not tell a printer which of those results you want.

Use this guide to produce an artwork map and a short proof request for a kraft box or sleeve. It does not prescribe ink settings or promise that a particular printer can reproduce the illustrated appearance.

Separate three white-area decisions on kraft packaging

A visible white logo is part of the final design. A white underprint is a supporting ink area behind another color. An unprinted opening leaves the kraft surface visible. The same white-looking object on a computer screen could be interpreted in more than one way unless its intended role is stated.

The PRINTING United Alliance white-ink explanation describes how the white layer and nonwhite substrate influence the colors seen above them. It also distinguishes surface and reverse printing. That distinction is useful context, not a technical setup specification for your kraft carton.

Keep the design intention separate from the printer’s proposed method. Ask whether white ink is available for the selected job and how it is represented in the required file. If an alternative substrate or process is proposed, record that changed scope before comparing it with the original kraft option.

Make a white ink and underprint artwork map

Give each relevant object a short ID and connect it to the current artwork revision. Identify the intended kraft face and grade. A note saying “white logo” is incomplete if it does not identify which logo, which panel and whether the white should remain visible.

Object Intended role Question for the printer
W1 front logo White visible in the finished design Which white process and proof can demonstrate its appearance on the stated kraft?
W2 colored leaf White underprint beneath the colored object How should the separate white mask relate to the color boundary?
W3 outer margin Natural kraft remains visible; no white ink, colored ink or added finish in this specified area Does the supplied file exclude all white and colored ink and all unwanted surface treatments from W3? Confirm that a panel-wide coating or finish will not cover this area.
Small lettering Visible white, subject to feasibility What detail limitations apply to the actual size, grade and process?

The W1/W2/W3 entries are hypothetical. Replace them with your actual objects. For W3, the example requests no added finish as well as no ink. If your design intentionally uses a clear coating or another treatment, identify it explicitly and revise the W3 instruction; “no white ink” alone does not define an unprinted, untreated area. Keep the printer’s mask, separation and registration requirements with its response. Do not invent a universal offset or small-text limit from an attractive illustration.

Review the proof against the question it can answer

A positional preview can show where the logo sits. It does not necessarily demonstrate the final white appearance on the chosen board. Ask the printer to identify the proof type, material and process represented, and state which decisions it supports.

Glenroy’s flexographic artwork guidelines discuss that printer’s white-ink and reverse-text considerations. Use them as an example of process-specific instructions. Their requirements must not be copied to an unrelated kraft-box printer as a universal rule.

For an appearance review, connect the actual reference to the chosen substrate and viewing conditions. Record the result and unresolved differences. If the supplier substitutes the kraft grade, coating or process, check whether the earlier proof still answers the intended appearance question.

Use a complete hypothetical handoff example

Imagine a small gift brand preparing artwork revision S-02 for a kraft sleeve. Its round logo should be white, its teal leaf should use a printer-confirmed white underprint, and the surrounding W3 margin should retain natural kraft with no white ink, colored ink or added finish. No physical sleeve has been produced for this example.

Handoff field Illustrative entry Decision status
Artwork reference S-02 with W1/W2/W3 object labels Design intention recorded
Substrate Kraft grade and printed face not yet confirmed Supplier response needed
White method Request the selected printer’s proposal No ink or opacity approval
Proof Ask which proof covers position and which covers appearance Review scope open
Approval owner Brand’s named reviewer to be entered Not approved

This produces a specific reply request: identify the substrate and print route, explain the required white file layer, and propose a proof for the intended result. It is more useful than asking the supplier to “make the white match the screen.”

Prepare the print discussion before requesting a quote

Send the current artwork, object map, packaging structure, intended kraft grade if known, quantity per design and destination. Include the unfinished questions rather than filling them with guesses. The printer confirms the technical setup; the buyer records the appearance decision supported by the proof.

Use the artwork handoff checklist to connect files to their revision, and the print finish brief if other treatments share the panel. You can send the kraft artwork map for a packaging discussion. Packrivo coordinates requirements with independent suppliers; a file discussion is not a confirmed process offer.

Download the white-area map CSV. It includes field definitions, the labeled hypothetical example and blank fields for your project.

White ink on kraft questions

Does a white object in a PDF request white ink?

It may be a design intention or simply the page background. State the intended white role and follow the selected printer’s file requirements.

Does every kraft printer offer the same white result?

No result is established by this guide. Ask the selected printer about its process and the proof that demonstrates the proposed appearance.

Must every colored object have white underneath?

Define the desired appearance first. Visible kraft influence may be intentional. Ask the printer to confirm the layer arrangement for each object.

Can a mockup approve opacity?

A mockup can explain position and hierarchy. It does not establish the white-ink appearance of the actual material and print route.

Key takeaways

  • Name visible white, white underprint and unprinted kraft separately.
  • Connect each instruction to an object, revision, substrate and printer.
  • Approve only the questions supported by the actual proof.

Source scope: public industry and printer documents checked 16 October 2026. This article is a buyer handoff method; it supplies no process settings, universal tolerance or measured print result.

title: Printing on Uncoated Paper: Review the Proposed Stock
html:
Review artwork on the proposed uncoated paper, with the sample’s material identity and proof scope recorded. Compare specific elements such as fine copy, pale colour and solid areas under consistent viewing conditions. A screen proof or a print on another paper can communicate layout but leaves the intended surface unresolved.

A buyer’s comment that a proof ‘looks different’ gives the printer little to locate. Naming the element, material and view makes the next question usable. You can do that without claiming an instrument-based colour result.

Identify the material and proof scope

Holmen’s technical information records surface roughness and ink absorption as distinct paperboard properties. Use that distinction to avoid treating the paper surface as an unnamed background. It doesn’t predict the appearance of your artwork on every uncoated paper.

Ask for the proposed grade, maker where known, print process and any added treatment. Record whether the proof uses that material or a substitute. If the source can only provide a substitute at this stage, keep its limitation attached to the proof.

State which decision the proof is meant to settle. Layout, colour direction, small-copy legibility and final surface appearance are different questions. One sample may cover several, but its role should be stated.

The colour approval guide covers the broader reference agreement. This worksheet narrows the review to named artwork elements on one proposed uncoated substrate.

Choose the artwork elements that matter

Select a small set of locations on the actual file. Give each an ID and describe it, such as A1 for small black care copy or A2 for a pale ivory panel. Keep the IDs unchanged if the artwork is revised.

Include elements that the reader must use, not only the largest decorative area. A care instruction that looks weak in one view deserves its own observation. Avoid converting that impression into a universal minimum type size without a printer’s specification.

Use consistent viewing conditions for the comparison. Record the light, viewing distance and whether the material is flat or formed. If a later photo uses a different light, say so rather than treating its appearance as a direct comparison.

Build an element-by-element proof page

Keep a wider sample photograph with the close views. The table ties an observation to a location and to the decision still open.

Element ID Artwork feature Proof evidence Next decision
A1 Required fine copy Actual paper, viewing distance and observed readability Printer review or revised proof
A2 Pale colour area Named physical reference and sample view Accept appearance or request comparison
A3 Large solid area Location and visible surface observation Clarify print or paper proposal
Material Grade and treatment Confirmed or substitute substrate Resolve any final-material gap
Proof scope What this sample represents Printer’s stated role and date List decisions it cannot close

Do not fill the evidence column with ‘good’ or ‘bad’ alone. A located description gives the printer something to assess against the same sample.

Work through a hypothetical care-card proof

Suppose a gift brand proposes an uncoated care card with a pale background and small black instructions. A digital proof confirms the panel order. The physical paper proof is then reviewed for A1, the instructions, and A2, the pale area.

The buyer records that the instructions are readable at the intended distance in the stated light. The pale area remains an appearance question because the physical reference has not yet been agreed. Those are two separate decisions, even on one card.

If a second proof changes paper grade as well as artwork, keep both changes in the record. Ask for a comparison that clarifies which proposal is intended for production. Avoid comparing unrelated proofs while describing them as only a colour revision.

For a formed component, repeat the relevant viewing position after folding or assembly. A panel partly hidden by the pack cannot be judged only from the flat card. Keep this step tied to actual use rather than expanding it into a generic print checklist.

Give each proof element its own decision

For the hypothetical care card, A1 can have the status ‘layout confirmed, readability observation recorded’ while A2 remains ‘physical colour reference required’. Keep the proof’s material identity beside both rows. These statuses describe the evidence available, not a blanket production approval.

Ask the artwork owner which information must remain readable in the actual pack. If the card is partly covered by a holder, identify that installed view separately from the flat proof. A fine-copy observation at the desk and an access observation inside the pack answer different questions.

The next printer request should name the unresolved element: ‘Please provide A2 on the proposed uncoated grade against the agreed physical reference.’ A new screen image can update layout but won’t close the named substrate comparison.

If another paper is proposed, create a new material row rather than overwriting the original identity. Keep the same element IDs so the team can compare the relevant observations. A proof review becomes useful when each accepted decision has a scope and each open one has a source, element and next response, without forcing the whole card into a single good-or-bad label.

Send the proof gap to the printer

Provide the element IDs, proof scope, material reference and located observations through Packrivo’s enquiry. The useful next action is to resolve the unconfirmed substrate or element with the responsible printer, then review that specific revised evidence.

Keep the proof comparison separate for every element and view

Use two new hypothetical proof references: P1 represents the proposed uncoated substrate and P2 represents a substitute. A1 fine copy, A2 pale area and A3 solid area keep the same IDs. The actual grade, printing and observations remain unknown.

Scenario scope Exact object or route Hypothetical input or output Calculation or record boundary
Separate element view P1_PROPOSED_A1 Unobserved; actual fields blank P1_PROPOSED A1 flat view; observation and decision unrecorded, material identity and viewing conditions required
Separate element view P1_PROPOSED_A1 Unobserved; actual fields blank P1_PROPOSED A1 installed view; observation and decision unrecorded, material identity and viewing conditions required
Separate element view P1_PROPOSED_A2 Unobserved; actual fields blank P1_PROPOSED A2 flat view; observation and decision unrecorded, material identity and viewing conditions required
Separate element view P1_PROPOSED_A2 Unobserved; actual fields blank P1_PROPOSED A2 installed view; observation and decision unrecorded, material identity and viewing conditions required
Separate element view P1_PROPOSED_A3 Unobserved; actual fields blank P1_PROPOSED A3 flat view; observation and decision unrecorded, material identity and viewing conditions required
Separate element view P1_PROPOSED_A3 Unobserved; actual fields blank P1_PROPOSED A3 installed view; observation and decision unrecorded, material identity and viewing conditions required
Separate element view P2_SUBSTITUTE_A1 Unobserved; actual fields blank P2_SUBSTITUTE A1 flat view; observation and decision unrecorded, material identity and viewing conditions required
Separate element view P2_SUBSTITUTE_A1 Unobserved; actual fields blank P2_SUBSTITUTE A1 installed view; observation and decision unrecorded, material identity and viewing conditions required
Separate element view P2_SUBSTITUTE_A2 Unobserved; actual fields blank P2_SUBSTITUTE A2 flat view; observation and decision unrecorded, material identity and viewing conditions required
Separate element view P2_SUBSTITUTE_A2 Unobserved; actual fields blank P2_SUBSTITUTE A2 installed view; observation and decision unrecorded, material identity and viewing conditions required
Separate element view P2_SUBSTITUTE_A3 Unobserved; actual fields blank P2_SUBSTITUTE A3 flat view; observation and decision unrecorded, material identity and viewing conditions required
Separate element view P2_SUBSTITUTE_A3 Unobserved; actual fields blank P2_SUBSTITUTE A3 installed view; observation and decision unrecorded, material identity and viewing conditions required
Proposed substrate P1 Unobserved; actual fields blank Actual proposed grade, maker, process and treatment unknown
Substitute substrate P2 Unobserved; actual fields blank Substitute grade is a separate material identity, not just a color correction
Physical reference A2 Unobserved; actual fields blank Agreed physical appearance reference not supplied

Record flat and installed views separately for each element on each proof. A printer response about P1/A1 readability does not close P1/A2 appearance, P2’s substrate gap or access when the card sits behind a holder. The table leaves those observations and decisions empty.

Retain the original digital layout evidence under its stated role. If both artwork and paper change between P1 and P2, describe both changes before comparing them. The next request can then name one element, one substrate and one view without pretending that a screen image or a substituted grade proves the final surface.

Download the printing on uncoated packaging paper record (.csv). It covers the original scenarios and this added comparison. HYPOTHETICAL rows are invented planning examples. Actual quantity, value, configuration, method, owner, observation, condition, decision, evidence and dates are blank because no actual project record has been obtained. Copy a relevant row and replace its type with ACTUAL only when entering permitted project evidence; keep the example and actual record separate. ACTUAL_BLANK is an empty starting row. A blank is unknown, never approval.

The related Packaging Color Approval Starts With a Physical Reference guide concerns a separate requirement. Use this record for the specific comparison above rather than treating that guide as evidence of a completed result.

Preserve changed evidence in the sample-version comparison. Carry the scoped result into the artwork handoff record.

References retain their stated general-guidance or manufacturer-example scope. Worked figures and records are teaching examples, not observed orders, stock, prices or measured performance.

Discuss this packaging specification with Packrivo. We coordinate independent suppliers. MOQ: 500 pieces per product/design; illustrative quantities are not production offers. Confirm materials, samples, price and timing for your project.

title: Include Turned Paper Edges in Lid-Fit Reviews
html:
Review rigid-box lid fit with the proposed wrap edges turned into their final positions. Identify which wrapped surfaces meet as the lid closes and opens. Keep a record of local contact, sample state and material revision so the supplier can separate a wrap-edge issue from a wider box-dimension question.

An unwrapped structural model can help explore the box form. It leaves a different interface from a finished wrapped proposal. State which sample you are reviewing before using its fit as an approval reference.

Identify the turned edges in the finished interface

PackMojo’s rigid-box process explanation describes wrap material extending slightly into the box interior. This supports reviewing the turned edge as part of the finished construction. It doesn’t define the turn-in depth or clearance for every rigid box.

Ask the supplier to mark where the lid and base wrap turns finish. Add the proposed lining or neck if present. Keep each layer named on a side section so a reviewer can identify the part that touches.

Record the material and sample state. If the sample is unprinted, unfinished or built with a substitute wrap, say so. Its fit observation shouldn’t silently become approval of the final surface stack.

Review contact during closure and opening

Place the base in the agreed position and lower the lid using the intended grip. Observe where contact starts. Keep the action consistent rather than pressing at another corner to make a difficult fit look complete.

Lift the lid again and inspect the contacting edge. Describe the visible location, such as the inner lid rim against the base’s rear turned edge. A plain ‘tight lid’ comment loses the interface information.

Use the dimension acceptance method when a measurement is needed. Name whether the dimension belongs to underlying board, finished wrapped part or the loaded set.

Keep contact and visual edge appearance in separate notes. One records the movement; the other records what a customer sees. A change that improves one may require another look at the other.

Use a wrap-edge interface checklist

Attach a close-up and a wider location view for each contact. Mark unknown layer details as supplier questions.

Interface field Entry Evidence
Meeting surfaces Named lid and base edges Marked side section
Turned layers Wrap, lining and other proposed parts Supplier construction reply
Starting contact Location and closure stage Photo before further pressure
Opening contact Location during lift Short action record
Sample identity Part, wrap and drawing revision Matched sample set
Requested response Interface clarification or revised proposal Supplier reply linked to same location

Keep an unwrapped and wrapped observation in separate rows if both exist. Their difference is useful evidence of sample scope, but it doesn’t prove a single cause without the construction details.

Follow a hypothetical lid-fit question

Suppose a brand reviews a small gift box first as a structural model and then with the proposed ivory wrap. The wrapped lid contacts a rear edge earlier in the closing action. The buyer photographs that location and records the two different sample states.

The supplier is asked to identify the finished layer arrangement at the rear interface and propose the next review. The buyer doesn’t add an arbitrary allowance to every side of the box. The record gives the supplier a precise location to assess.

If a revision changes the turn-in or lining, record that construction change and repeat the same lid action. If dimensions change instead, link the new drawing. A label such as ‘version two’ is insufficient when two different interfaces may have changed.

This is a fit communication method. It doesn’t prescribe wrapping machinery, universal tolerances or a lid-force test. Any acceptance method must be agreed for the actual construction and intended use.

State which finished interface the record covers

In the hypothetical lid record, call the rear interface R1 and the opposite front interface F1. Record contact at R1 during initial lowering, while F1 has no visible contact under the same action. This distinguishes a local question from an assumption that every side needs the same dimensional change.

Keep the wrapped and structural-model samples named separately. If the supplier confirms different wrap or lining proposals between them, add those layers to the section. If it cannot yet confirm them, retain that construction gap rather than treating the comparison as proof of a cause.

A useful question is: ‘Please confirm the finished layer arrangement at R1 on sample S2 and the proposed revision to that interface.’ It gives the source a location, sample and requested response. An outside-size reply alone may not answer it.

Review the next sample in the same starting position and record when the lid first meets R1. Keep any new contact elsewhere as a separate row. The interface can be accepted under an agreed fit method after that review, while an unknown wrap construction or another contact remains open. One improved closing photograph shouldn’t erase those distinctions.

Send the interface evidence with the sample revision

Use Packrivo’s enquiry to send the marked section, sample state, contact photos and specific open question. Review the supplier’s revised wrapped sample before treating that interface as settled. Keep the approved parts and wrap revision together for any later reorder.

Separate a layer-stack revision from a dimension revision

The original S1 structural model and S2 wrapped example answer different questions. Extend the record by naming S2's drawing D1 and layer stack L1. Consider S3 as a proposal retaining D1 but changing the stack to L2; consider S4 as a separate proposal changing the drawing to D2 while retaining L1. These are hypothetical alternatives, not approved corrections or a diagnosis of why the lid met R1.

Hypothetical configuration Named object Relationship Input or next scope
S2 S2 uses drawing D1
S2 S2 uses layer stack L1
S3 S3 uses drawing D1
S3 S3 uses layer stack L2
S4 S4 uses drawing D2
S4 S4 uses layer stack L1

Keep both R1 and opposite F1 in every candidate's review. At each interface, distinguish initial lowering from opening contact. A supplier response that changes the rear turn-in may still need an observation at the front after the lid moves. Conversely, changing an overall dimension can affect several locations and should not be described as a purely local layer correction.

Ask which actual finished surfaces are included in L1 and L2: lid wrap turn, base wrap turn, lining or neck where present. If the proposed stack is not confirmed, preserve the missing construction field. Do not infer a total layer thickness from a photograph or assign a universal allowance. The unwrapped S1 record stays outside the finished-state acceptance chain; it cannot substitute for either proposed wrapped candidate.

The CSV retains the original fictional rear early-contact and front no-visible-contact statements under S2 only. It adds configuration-to-drawing and configuration-to-stack relationships, then separate R1/F1 lowering/opening requests. Actual contact stage, method, observation, measurement and disposition remain blank. A useful next reply identifies S3 or S4 and the interface evidence it will provide, so a favorable photograph at one edge cannot close another edge or the complete finished fit.

Actual quantity, configuration, component and file identities, materials, process, specification, copy, method, condition, observation, owner, decision, evidence and dates are blank. ACTUAL_BLANK is a separate empty starting row; enter permitted project evidence before using an actual record. A blank means unknown.

title: Place Rigid-Box Wrap Seams Away From the Main View
html:
Map rigid-box wrap seams against the views customers actually see: closed front, opened pack and handled edges. Ask for the proposed seam layout and mark where important artwork crosses it. Decide the preferred placement on a formed sample rather than treating the underside as the only possible hidden face.

A rigid box can be turned over while being opened, or held at an angle that exposes a side seam. A front rendering is therefore only one view in the placement decision. Record the others before the wrapping layout becomes fixed.

Get the proposed wrap layout

PackMojo’s rigid-box manufacturing explanation describes a printed substrate wrapped around a formed board structure. That establishes the separate wrap layer. Your supplier must confirm the actual seam, corner and turned-edge layout for the proposed box.

Ask for a marked formed view and, where useful, the wrap layout. Identify joins, corner edges and the main artwork face separately. A wrap sheet is not the same drawing as the underlying board structure.

The jewelry box structure guide helps choose an opening format. This method addresses surface placement once that format has been chosen.

Define the views before ranking seam positions

Choose the closed front view, the first opened view and the likely handling view. Describe the orientation in plain words, such as lid raised while the base rests on a table. If photographs will show an additional underside view, include it.

For each view, identify the faces and edges that matter. Give the main display face a higher priority only if your brief calls for it. A lower-priority face can still carry required information that needs a readable surface.

Mark the proposed seam position on those views. Check whether a logo-free design motif, border or continuous line crosses the join. If alignment matters, state that as a sample question rather than assuming the wrap will meet invisibly.

Keep the placement decision distinct from workmanship acceptance. Choosing a quieter location doesn’t establish an acceptable gap, edge or surface condition. Those criteria need a separate agreement and evidence.

Use a face and seam map

Draw one simple box outline per view, then use the record to connect each marked face to a decision. The table can sit beside your sketches.

View Face or edge Seam relationship Decision
Closed front Main front, lid edge and visible side Seam visible or outside this view Preferred location and artwork crossing
First opening Inside lid and top rim Join or turned edge revealed Priority of visible surface
Handling Grip side and underside Edge seen while lifting Acceptable location to discuss
Photography Planned image angle Seam under actual lighting Photo reference for sample review
Revision Changed face or artwork New seam relationship Views needing another check

A seam may be invisible in one view and visible in another. Keep both observations; selecting only the favourable photo would make the brief less useful.

Walk through a hypothetical gift box

Suppose an ivory-wrapped lift-off jewelry box has a green border running around the sides. The main product photo shows the front, but the customer grips two opposite sides to lift the lid. The buyer includes both views in the seam map.

The proposed join lies on a side that becomes visible during handling. Rather than asking for an impossible ‘no seam’ box, the buyer asks the supplier to compare another placement and provide formed sample views of the border at the join.

If the supplier explains that the alternate location changes the wrap process, keep that reply in the map. The decision can then weigh the specific presentation request against the proposed construction, without claiming that either version is universally better.

Rank actual views instead of calling a face hidden

For the hypothetical bordered lid, the map can give the closed front view priority P1, the normal opening view P2 and the underside handling view P3. These are project choices, not industry grades. A seam location can then be discussed against a named view without claiming it is invisible in all use.

Attach a sketch to each priority. Mark the proposed seam in a consistent colour and the border crossing in another. If the seam is outside P1 but visible in P2, retain both observations. The supplier can assess a different placement against the full brief rather than one selected photograph.

A specific request is: ‘Please show the proposed join and border relationship in the normal lid-lift view.’ It asks for evidence of the actual interface. A reply with only a closed front rendering leaves that view unresolved.

Keep placement preference and workmanship criteria in different fields. The first says where the join should lie; the second concerns the agreed appearance of that join on the sample. A changed seam placement can reopen the border alignment check even if the box dimensions remain unchanged. That is the revision trigger the artwork team needs.

Give the artwork team a located decision

Send the view sketches, proposed seam layout and any crossing artwork through the packaging enquiry. Mark preferred and unresolved locations separately. Once the supplier responds, review the formed wrap before treating the seam placement as settled for the print file.

Compare two seam proposals against the same three views

Use the original ivory lift-off jewelry-box example to request two located alternatives: SIDE_OPTION with seam J1 on a side, and REAR_OPTION with seam J2 on a rear face. They are candidate layouts for the same box, not a request to add both joins. Keep the continuous green border and the supplier's actual construction in each request. No seam visibility or alignment result is assumed.

Hypothetical configuration Named object Relationship Input or next scope
SIDE_OPTION J1 located on SIDE
SIDE_OPTION J1 visibility CLOSED_FRONT; Unknown pending candidate-specific formed view; outside one view does not mean hidden in every view
SIDE_OPTION J1 visibility NORMAL_OPENING; Unknown pending candidate-specific formed view; outside one view does not mean hidden in every view
SIDE_OPTION J1 visibility HANDLING; Unknown pending candidate-specific formed view; outside one view does not mean hidden in every view
REAR_OPTION J2 located on REAR
REAR_OPTION J2 visibility CLOSED_FRONT; Unknown pending candidate-specific formed view; outside one view does not mean hidden in every view
REAR_OPTION J2 visibility NORMAL_OPENING; Unknown pending candidate-specific formed view; outside one view does not mean hidden in every view
REAR_OPTION J2 visibility HANDLING; Unknown pending candidate-specific formed view; outside one view does not mean hidden in every view

Cross each option with the same closed-front P1, normal-opening P2 and handling P3 views. For every option/view pair, record visibility and the border relationship separately. This produces six view comparisons and twelve distinct questions. A response showing only the preferred front photograph leaves the remaining views open, including the lid-lift and grip views that can expose another face.

The priority order P1/P2/P3 belongs to this fictional brief. It does not remove the lower-priority views from the record or mean that any seam on the underside is automatically acceptable. A buyer might prefer the rear proposal for one view but still need the converter's response about border continuity or a different wrapping operation. Keep that trade-off explicit rather than averaging the views into a made-up quality score.

After receiving formed views, decide placement preference separately from workmanship. The first selects a location under the named presentation priorities. The second needs the actual agreed appearance criteria and sample evidence for the join. A moved seam may keep the outer dimensions unchanged while reopening the border relationship. The worksheet's unknown cells and blank actual fields let those two decisions close at different times without pretending that either option has already been built.

title: Review Print Cracking on the Formed Fold
html:
Review print near a fold on the formed sample as well as the flat proof. Name the crease, photograph the same area before and after folding, and record the material and artwork revision. A visible line needs a location and comparison record before a supplier can discuss its cause or a change.

A flat artwork proof can look acceptable while the reader’s view changes after the carton takes shape. Keep the print observation distinct from a technical diagnosis. The buyer can document what appeared; the converter needs the proposed material and process to assess why.

Choose the exact printed crease to review

Identify the fold on the drawing and name the artwork crossing it. State whether it contains a solid background, fine line, small copy or another defined element. Keep the description specific enough to find the same area on a later revision.

Holmen’s creasing guidance describes creasing, surface cracking and the need to match the operation/tool geometry to the paperboard. This supports a converter review with identified conditions. It doesn’t make a buyer photograph a reliable diagnosis of moisture, tooling or coating.

Start from the actual material and artwork proposal. A plain structural mock-up can answer a fold-location question, but it won’t show how the proposed printed surface appears at that fold.

The print finishes checklist handles broader process choices. This method focuses on a paired observation of one printed crease after forming.

Make the photo pair comparable

Photograph the area flat before the agreed forming action. Keep the whole crease visible in one view and capture a closer view if needed. Use a consistent light and angle that lets a reviewer locate the printed element.

Form the sample according to the proposed instruction, then photograph the same location. Record whether the fold is partially or fully formed. Avoid repeatedly bending it for the photo unless repeated opening is part of the named review scope.

Keep the original images. An edited close-up may help point to a location, but retain the wider view and name the edit. Do not enhance contrast until a faint mark looks like a different physical condition.

Describe the visible result in plain terms: a light line through the green background, broken detail near one edge, or a mark visible only from a stated angle. Record ‘no visible change in this view’ when that is all the photo shows.

Use a flat-to-formed observation record

One row should identify one area on one sample. This keeps different folds or different material versions from becoming a single complaint.

Field Entry to keep Reason
Location Crease ID and adjoining panels Find the same fold on the drawing
Print Artwork revision and element crossing crease Identify the affected visual area
Material Board, caliper and surface proposal Connect observation to the sample
Action Forming instruction and stage Describe what occurred before the mark
Image pair Flat and formed photo IDs Compare like locations
Observation Visible line, break or no visible change Separate appearance from diagnosis
Next response Supplier explanation and proposed revision Keep the decision traceable

Ask the supplier whether another sample is needed to assess the issue. Record the response and any changed material, artwork position or converting proposal.

Follow a hypothetical dark lid fold

Suppose a brand places a dark green printed band across a hinged lid fold. On the flat sample the band appears continuous. After the intended forming action, the reviewer observes a light line near one end.

The buyer records the lid crease ID, material and artwork versions, then sends the flat and formed pair. The enquiry asks the converter to assess the proposed construction and recommend the next evidence. It doesn’t instruct the converter to change a machine setting based on the photograph.

If a revised sample moves the printed band away from the fold, record that artwork change. If the band stays but the material or process changes, record those changes instead. Compare the relevant revision; don’t mix the best photo from each sample into one apparent approval.

Keep appearance decisions separate from causes

For the hypothetical green lid band, an observation can read: ‘Light line visible near the rear end of C1 after the stated forming action.’ The cause field stays ‘awaiting converter review’. Keeping those two statements separate lets the buyer document a concern without claiming expertise the photograph doesn’t provide.

Record the intended customer view as another field. A mark visible in a close macro view may be reviewed differently from one visible in the normal opening position. Agree which view controls the appearance decision rather than changing the photo distance until the mark disappears.

The outgoing request should include the wider location view, flat close view and formed close view. Ask the supplier which material or converting information is needed to assess the named crease. If the response proposes a revised sample, identify what is expected to change before comparing it.

Keep the old and revised observations in separate records. A new sample with a different printed band can answer an artwork-location question, while leaving the earlier crease construction unexplained. Mark the scope actually accepted and preserve any unresolved technical question instead of giving the entire print process an undifferentiated pass.

Send a located observation, not a vague finish request

Bring the image pair and record to your packaging enquiry. Mark any unconfirmed cause as open. The next useful step is a supplier response tied to the same crease and proposal, followed by a review of the revised formed sample.

Compare an artwork correction with a construction revision separately

Build two alternative requests from the original fictional green-band issue. Give the baseline the explicit identity S1/ART1/B1/C1. S2 proposes ART2 on the same B1 with the band moved away from the fold. S3 retains ART1's crossing band but proposes B2. Neither candidate has been made or observed in this example. Their separate flat, formed and customer-view evidence fields remain blank.

Hypothetical configuration Named object Relationship Input or next scope
S2 S2 uses artwork ART2
S2 S2 uses board B1
S3 S3 uses artwork ART1
S3 S3 uses board B2

The artwork alternative can answer whether the newly placed band achieves the intended presentation. Even a satisfactory S2 appearance would not explain why the original band developed a light line at C1. The material alternative asks a different question: how does the same located artwork appear on the offered revised construction? A comparison that quietly moves the band and changes the board at once cannot isolate either difference from those records.

Send each proposal with the fields it changes and the fields it retains. For S2, ask the artwork owner to identify the new band location, then ask the converter which formed evidence remains necessary. For S3, obtain the actual material and converting proposal before comparing the same crease. If tooling, finish or forming action also changes, add those identities rather than calling it a board-only comparison.

Review the original wide location, flat close and formed close views together with the intended customer view. The CSV preserves the original hypothetical continuous-band and light-line descriptions as fictional observations, not actual findings. New candidate observations, technical explanation, decision and evidence stay empty. Select the presentation or further investigation actually supported; do not combine a flat view from one candidate with a formed view from another into an apparent approval.
