Give the earring style and mounting card separate identifiers. Show the pair from the front, side and rear with the intended backs attached. Record which parts of the jewelry contact the card and which need clearance from the insert, lining or surrounding package.

Describe how the posts pass through the card and where the backs sit afterward. If the design uses another attachment, explain that arrangement instead. Ask the jewelry owner to confirm the intended fastening and removal method so the packaging sample uses the real product as designed.

Record the card's finished size, material description, thickness if known and physical orientation. Keep artwork and cutout revisions identifiable. Two cards with the same printed logo can have different openings or stiffness; a photograph of the front alone cannot identify that difference.

Measure the mounted envelope rather than adding a guessed allowance to the earring's face dimensions. The envelope includes the card, jewelry, backs and any raised detail in the intended position. Define where each dimension starts and the condition of the assembly during measurement.

The measurement agreement guide helps you label those references. Its purpose here is to make the rear projection and complete height understandable to everyone reviewing the card.

Separate alignment from clearance

Alignment concerns where the pair sits on the display face. Clearance concerns how its mounted form occupies the surrounding space. Check those as separate questions so a symmetrical presentation doesn't hide contact between a post and the box.

Mark the proposed hole or attachment locations on the supplier's card drawing. Ask the supplier to confirm how those features will be made on the selected card construction. Keep dimensions and acceptance limits project-specific; there is no single useful hole spacing for every pair of earrings.

Seat the loaded card in the proposed box or support. Record how it is retained and whether it can move toward a wall or lid during the agreed handling review. If it tilts intentionally, include that position in the drawing and measurement record.

The Canadian Conservation Institute's guidance for metal objects provides context on avoiding physical contact damage during storage and handling. The jewelry owner and suppliers still need to establish suitable contact materials and the particular arrangement for this product.

Use this original worksheet to keep the observed geometry and handling questions together. It is a planning record, not an industry test method.

Original earring card backing clearance planning record
View or stage Record Decision it supports
Front face Pair alignment, drop length and displayed width Attachment locations and presentation
Rear face Back positions and post projections Space behind the mounted card
Card in support Retaining points and intended angle How the loaded card seats
Complete closure Box and lid contact observations Whether the arrangement needs revision
Removal Access to backs and the release sequence Whether the customer can remove the pair as intended

Trial the actual fastening and release

Have the intended packer load the card using the agreed method. Note whether the operator can reach the rear fastening points and whether attaching the second earring disturbs the first. Record the extra handling needed without changing the jewelry fastening to suit an unreviewed card.

Close the complete pack with all accompanying components. A care card behind the mounting card may compete for rear space; tissue above it may change the packed arrangement. Use the versions you intend to supply and name them in the review record.

Open the package and inspect the pair before removal. Note visible movement, card distortion or contact marks, if any, with their locations and the conditions observed. Avoid calling a mark a material failure until the responsible parties have investigated its cause.

Follow the removal sequence with the jewelry owner or another authorized reviewer. The customer may need to reach the backs before lifting the pair. If the card cannot be removed from its support, explain how that access is intended to work while the card stays in place.

For a hypothetical stud pair, the buyer might compare a freestanding card with a card retained in an insert slot. The first proposal makes the rear easier to reach; the second changes how the card sits. Those are questions to trial, not findings from a completed Packrivo project.

Keep each product style's review separate. A longer post or different back can change the envelope even if the printed card is unchanged. The multi-SKU fit matrix helps record which arrangements a shared card has actually been reviewed with.

Give the supplier an attachment brief

Send the mounted front, side and rear views with the card drawing and measured references. Add the intended box position, fastening sequence and customer removal order. Highlight unresolved rear clearance or access questions rather than asking for a card that merely "fits earrings."

Request a candidate that includes the attachment details you need to evaluate. A printed flat proof can settle copy and layout while leaving mounting and closure open. Keep those decisions distinct when reviewing the supplier response.

A paperboard insert direction may help describe a proposed support around the card. State how the loaded card is retained and where the rear fastening must remain accessible.

Bring that attachment brief to Packrivo's packaging inquiry with the actual earring style and backs identified. A useful discussion starts with the complete mounted pair and ends with a clear plan for reviewing its front, rear and release.

Compare rear space and projection from the same face

Assume each member of invented stud pair E1 has a rear projection of 10 mm measured normal to the rear card face, while the available space from that same face is 8 mm. The nominal shortfall is 10 – 8 = 2 mm. These are hypothetical inputs, not a sample measurement or permitted interference.

Member Available rear space Rear projection Nominal shortfall Decision
Left stud 8 mm 10 mm 2 mm Geometry needs revision/review
Right stud 8 mm 10 mm 2 mm Separate actual observation required
Front pair Alignment only Not a depth measurement Not applicable Rear scope remains open

Use one datum and direction for both inputs. A measurement from the front jewelry face cannot be substituted for rear clearance. The side sketch shows one representative mounted stud; it does not measure either actual member of E1 or prescribe hole spacing.

Keep the two member records even if the invented values match. Different backs or posts can change an actual envelope. Do not compress a back, force the card into place or modify the jewelry to erase the arithmetic conflict. Ask for a revised arrangement, then review fastening, closure and customer access separately. No universal clearance or acceptance limit follows.

Download the earring card packaging dimensions record (.csv). HYPOTHETICAL rows are invented examples. Use ACTUAL_BLANK for permitted project inputs; replace that row label only when recording actual facts. Empty evidence, observation and date fields mean unknown or not performed, never acceptance. Keep checkpoints and revisions separate.

Send both mounted members with matching rear-datum dimensions, backs and intended fastening/removal sequence. Packrivo coordinates independent suppliers. These records establish no supplier offer, service availability or MOQ exception; its published baseline is 500 pieces per product/design.

title: Necklace Packaging: Route Chains and Keep Clasps Accessible
html:
Plan a pendant chain route by separating the displayed length, the chain stored behind the support and the clasp the customer needs to reach. Check loading and removal with the actual jewelry and complete box. The route should preserve the intended presentation while leaving each fastening and release point identifiable for the packer and customer.

Use the Jewelry Mounting Cards: Check Attachment and Rear Clearance to compare the front-and-back support arrangement when describing the chain route. Confirm the actual card, clasp position and removal action in a sample; the concept does not establish the route for your necklace.

A necklace can look tidy from the front while its chain bunches behind the card. That hidden arrangement matters when the insert seats, the lid closes and the customer lifts the pendant. Review both sides before deciding that a presentation direction is ready for sampling.

Draw the route before choosing the retaining detail

Photograph the necklace in its proposed display position. Mark the pendant, chain attachment points, clasp and any adjustment section. Record the full necklace length and the part you want visible. Keep those measurements tied to the actual jewelry version.

Describe the remaining chain's intended destination. It might rest behind a mounting card, sit within a proposed paper pocket or follow another supplier-designed support. Ask the supplier to explain how that arrangement loads and releases. A pocket drawn in a concept image is still a proposed component.

Identify surfaces you want kept apart. The pendant may need separation from the clasp or loose links during the intended handling. The Canadian Conservation Institute's metal care guidance discusses limiting contact and physical damage during storage and handling. It provides context, not a retail jewelry material specification.

For the practical brief, describe the chain finish and any contact concerns to the jewelry and packaging suppliers. Ask for compatible contact materials to be proposed and reviewed. Avoid selecting a fabric or foam only because it looks soft in a photograph.

The insert measurement guide covers projections and chain storage alongside the box interior. Add a route drawing that shows which of those spaces the chain actually uses.

Make the rear arrangement visible

Show the back of the support with the chain loaded. Label the stored section and where the clasp remains accessible. Include the card's resting position in the box so the drawing doesn't imply space that the assembled insert has already occupied.

Check whether the chain crosses a fold, presses on an insert edge or shares space with another accessory. Keep the rear view and the assembled view together. A route can be clear on a loose card yet become difficult to reach after that card is fixed in place.

Treat each retaining detail as a question to answer. A slit, fold, tie or pocket may change how the packer handles the chain. Ask which parts are formed by the supplier and which are completed during packing, then trial that sequence with the intended operator.

This original route record can be copied into a supplier brief. Complete the open fields using the proposed construction and actual necklace.

Original pendant chain packaging route planning record
Route segment What to show Observation to record
Front display Pendant position and visible chain length Alignment and contact with the support
Front-to-rear transition Exact opening, fold or retaining detail Catching, bending or loading difficulty
Rear storage Position of the remaining chain Bunching and contact when the support seats
Clasp access Location and intended hand access Whether removal requires pulling hidden links
Customer release Order of releasing chain and lifting pendant Snagging, unintended force or unclear steps

A concept drawing can explain these segments. It cannot establish that the chain releases cleanly, that a material is compatible with its finish or that the complete pack protects it during delivery. Those questions need the appropriate physical evidence.

Trial loading and removal in a defined order

Begin with the necklace and the empty support. Load it using the proposed instructions without improvising another loop or hiding the clasp in a different position. Record any step that needs an extra tool, repeated adjustment or a second person.

Seat the loaded support in the box and close it as intended. Observe whether the rear chain changes the support's height or moves toward a closure. If a card or care leaflet is included, add it in the same order the packer will use.

Open the complete pack and follow the customer release sequence. Reach the identified clasp or release point first, then lift the pendant as instructed. Note where the chain catches, where the support moves and whether the user can see what to release next.

Keep the observations descriptive. "Links caught at the rear card fold during removal" gives the supplier a location and an action. "Chain tangles" may describe several different problems, including the storage layout, jewelry handling or an unclear release sequence.

Repeat the route review for the necklace versions it is supposed to cover. A different clasp, extension section or pendant setting can change the packed arrangement. The multi-SKU fit matrix helps keep those product-specific decisions separate while you explore a shared outer box.

Turn the selected route into a packing instruction

Retain one labelled front view, one rear view and a photograph of the complete loaded pack. Name the jewelry, support and box versions. State the loading order and which part the customer releases first; those details should agree with the sample reviewed.

If the supplier revises the pocket or retaining opening, reopen the observations affected by that change. The sample revision record lets you connect the original catching issue to the requested correction and replacement evidence.

Avoid writing a complex customer instruction to compensate for an unresolved route. A short release note can help explain an intentional construction, but a sample that requires hidden pulling still needs review. Ask whether the retaining arrangement can make the intended sequence clearer.

If you are exploring a jewelry box with insert, attach the front and rear route views to that structural inquiry. Its final retaining details still need a project proposal.

Bring the front and rear route views to Packrivo's packaging inquiry with the actual necklace details and any open contact questions. The useful outcome is a route someone can load and explain, with its release checked on the complete configuration.

Bind the rear route to the same front support

Use invented necklace N1 and support C1 to mark transition points T1/T2 and clasp K1. Front and rear views must identify the same physical points; a rear view reverses their apparent left/right positions. The diagram proposes a route on a loose card, with complete-box access unresolved.

Reference Proposed role Evidence still needed
T1/T2 Front-to-rear transitions Actual openings, loading and contact
Rear path Stored chain position Seating without bunching
K1 clasp Identified release question Access after C1 is installed
Complete box Support and product together Actual closing and removal sequence

Keep both images under C1 rather than combining the front of one revision with the back of another. The dotted rear path is a planning line, not a hidden pocket specification or proof that the chain stays there.

Record when K1 becomes reachable in the complete pack. If the card must move first, name its lifting route instead of telling the recipient to pull hidden links. All CSV observations remain blank here. Supplier instructions and an actual loaded trial must settle loading, contact and release; a visible clasp on a loose card cannot establish access inside the box.

Download the necklace packaging chain routing record (.csv). HYPOTHETICAL rows are invented examples. Use ACTUAL_BLANK for permitted project inputs; replace that row label only when recording actual facts. Empty evidence, observation and date fields mean unknown or not performed, never acceptance. Keep checkpoints and revisions separate.

Send matched front, rear and complete-box references with the actual necklace and unresolved release question. Packrivo coordinates independent suppliers. These records establish no supplier offer, service availability or MOQ exception; its published baseline is 500 pieces per product/design.

title: Care Cards in Gift Boxes: Recheck the Complete Fit
html:
Recheck a gift box as a complete pack whenever you add or change a care card. Record the card's finished folded size, position and loading order, then review lid clearance, product contact and removal. Keep the product and packaging versions fixed while comparing placements so the result explains the card's effect on the arrangement.

A card can occupy space above the product, behind an insert or inside a separate pocket. Those positions answer different packing needs. Choosing the smallest-looking card doesn't establish which placement lets the box close and gives the customer access to the instructions.

Describe the card in its packed state

Measure the card after cutting and folding, rather than taking its page size from the artwork file. Record thickness as supplied if known, the number of folds and any envelope or attachment. A flat sheet and a folded booklet with the same outside dimensions occupy different arrangements.

Use a plain identifier for the physical version, such as CARD-C2. Keep its copy revision alongside it. A spelling correction might leave the physical shape unchanged; adding a translated panel or another fold may require a new fit review. State which change you are evaluating.

Mark the intended card position on a photograph of the empty pack. Show which face the customer sees first and whether the card should come out before the product. A direction such as "include inside" leaves those decisions to the person assembling the sample.

Use the jewelry insert measurement guide to establish the underlying product arrangement. Your card review starts with that identified configuration and asks what the added paper component changes.

For artwork preparation, Adobe's trim and bleed guidance distinguishes the finished cut boundary from artwork beyond it. Keep the physical card dimensions separate from the artwork's bleed area when sending the fit brief.

Compare placements one change at a time

Begin with the pack without the proposed card and document the loading sequence. Add the card in one candidate position, then repeat that sequence with the same product, insert and box. Observe where the card moves or meets another component during closing and opening.

Compare a second position only after recording the first. If you change the box height and card position together, the next sample may work, but you won't know which change addressed the problem. Keep the first trial focused enough to support a specific supplier question.

A card placed above a pendant can affect the space below the lid. A card tucked behind an insert can change how that insert seats or how the customer retrieves it. Neither position is automatically preferable. Describe the proposed function and ask for a representative complete sample.

This worksheet is an original planning tool for a hypothetical pendant pack. It lists observations to make rather than test outcomes.

Original care card gift box fit planning record
Candidate Card position Loading question Closing question Removal question
A Above the displayed pendant Does the card rest where intended? Does it contact the lid or raised setting? Can it be lifted without pulling the chain?
B Behind the insert Can the insert seat with the card there? Is the packed height altered? Can the customer find and retrieve it?
C Separate pocket Is the pocket included in the supplied design? Does the pocket affect a fold or closure? Is the opening reachable?

Choose a candidate based on the recorded interaction and the presentation you want. Keep unresolved material or structural changes in a separate column. The supplier can then explain whether the chosen placement needs a revised insert, pocket or drawing.

Check the loading sequence as well as the final appearance

Ask the intended packer to assemble the candidate from the state in which the components will arrive. Record the order of product, card and insert placement. An attractive final arrangement may still require the packer to lift a fragile piece twice or reopen a secured insert.

Watch the card while closing the box. Note any bowing, trapping at a seam, movement toward a hinge or pressure on the product. Record the location and the action that produced it. Avoid converting an observed catch into a diagnosis before the supplier reviews the construction.

Open the complete pack and follow the intended customer sequence. Check whether the card hides the lifting point, catches on a clasp or blocks access to a product. Keep the removal observation separate from the closing observation; one can be acceptable while the other remains open.

Review the same arrangement with every product variant that will use it. The multi-SKU fit matrix gives those separate records a home. A card placement checked with a low pendant should not silently cover a taller setting or different chain arrangement.

If transport evidence already exists, ask whether the added component changes its scope. ISTA's retesting guidance identifies product, package and process changes as relevant to the retest decision. A card fit trial records handling observations; any transport evaluation needs its own agreed method.

Release a card placement someone can repeat

Write the selected card ID, position and loading order into the packing instruction. Add a clear photograph of the arrangement and name the sample reviewed. A sentence such as "CARD-C2 above the insert, removed before the pendant" is easier to repeat than an unlabelled photograph.

Keep physical placement approval separate from copy approval. The fit reviewer may accept the folded card while the text owner still needs to approve wording. Name both decisions so a physically suitable sample doesn't release unfinished instructions.

The informational card direction is a starting point for describing the paper component. Keep its finished shape and proposed placement in the same request.

Bring the chosen arrangement and remaining questions to Packrivo's packaging inquiry. Include the actual card, product and packaging dimensions where available. The next discussion should be about an identified addition to the pack and the evidence needed to accept it.

Separate local gap arithmetic from a complete fit decision

For an invented pendant pack, assume a local closed-lid gap of 3.0 mm above one high point and folded card C2 thickness of 0.6 mm. Placing C2 there leaves a nominal 3.0 – 0.6 = 2.4 mm at that one point. No physical pack has been measured or accepted.

Candidate Assumed input Arithmetic or gap Separate physical review
A: above product Local gap 3.0 mm; card 0.6 mm Nominal 2.4 mm Bowing movement contact removal unreviewed
B: behind insert Same card; seating effect unknown No new gap calculated Seating and retrieval unreviewed
Both Same identified box insert pendant No clearance target Closing/opening not performed

The subtraction assumes the card occupies that location without changing the other surfaces. It is not the minimum gap across the pack and does not account for bowing or movement. This example sets no tolerance or acceptable clearance.

Candidate B changes the input question. If the card alters insert seating, the earlier local gap cannot simply be reused. Record actual seating and product height first; leave B's gap and remainder blank until those inputs exist. The non-scale sections show layer order only. Keep lid closing, card retrieval and product removal as separate dated observations. Both trial rows remain unperformed, regardless of A's positive nominal number. Physical placement and copy approval retain separate owners.

Download the care card gift box fit record (.csv). HYPOTHETICAL rows are invented examples. Use ACTUAL_BLANK for permitted project inputs; replace that row label only when recording actual facts. Empty evidence, observation and date fields mean unknown or not performed, never acceptance. Keep checkpoints and revisions separate.

Send the folded card, placement candidates, actual local measurements and separate closure, contact and removal questions. Prepare the identified scope for a Packrivo inquiry. Packrivo coordinates independent suppliers. These records establish no supplier offer, service availability or MOQ exception; its published baseline is 500 pieces per product/design.

title: Packaging Material Claims: Match the Evidence Scope
html:
Review a packaging material claim against the exact component, supplied configuration and destination market before adding it to artwork. Record who issued the evidence, what it covers and who approves the wording. A useful claim record connects each proposed statement to the relevant documents and leaves unresolved questions visible.

Small brands often receive several documents for one packaging project: a board specification, an insert proposal, a label sheet and a statement about tissue. Start by identifying which component each document describes. Then decide whether the proposed wording accurately describes that component or the assembled package.

Start with the component and the exact wording

Write down the statement you want customers to read. “Recycled paperboard in the box base” has a defined subject. A general statement about the entire pack asks a broader question, particularly when the pack also contains an insert, adhesive, coating or label.

Separate the components in the bill of materials. Give each one a working reference and record the proposed material, finish and assembly state. Include the destination market because the wording and evidence requirements may differ between markets and uses.

The FTC Green Guides summary explains how environmental marketing claims should be substantiated and qualified in the United States. It distinguishes attributes such as recycled content and recyclability. Use the relevant guidance to frame the review, then have the responsible reviewer approve the actual market wording.

Ask for evidence that matches the supplied configuration

A document title is a starting point. Check its issuer, covered entity or site, date, product reference and scope against the quotation and sample configuration. Record validity or expiry where it applies, and ask the issuer to clarify an uncertain status. If the supplier changes the board, finish or source after review, return the claim to the person responsible for deciding whether the evidence still applies.

For a certification-related statement, ask which entity holds the certificate, which product or product group it covers and how the proposed artwork will be authorized. FSC describes chain-of-custody certification as the system connecting forest-based materials through the supply chain to finished products. Follow that scope through the actual supplied packaging rather than approving a logo from a screenshot of a certificate.

Keep the supporting records together: the component reference, document, quotation version, sample reference and proposed wording. Where a record is missing, assign a specific next question, such as “Please identify the product group and material reference covered by this certificate.”

Keep different material questions separate

The same component may require several reviews. A sourcing statement, an end-of-life claim and a food-contact use each ask a different question. Keep their evidence and approvals in separate rows so one answer cannot silently stand in for another.

Swipe sideways to read every column on a small screen.

Material review questions and evidence scope
Review question Record the scope Ask the responsible party
What is the stated recycled content? Component, material reference, calculation basis and supporting evidence Which supplied material and configuration does the statement describe?
Is proposed certification wording authorized? Certificate holder, covered product group, supplied reference and artwork permission Who can confirm the claim and label use for this packaging?
Is a recyclability or compostability statement suitable? Component or assembled pack, destination, conditions and evidence What wording and qualifications have been approved for the intended market?
Is a food-contact use intended? Actual contact component, contact configuration and destination Which documents and review apply to this intended use?

For an intended food-contact component, use the buyer document checklist to prepare the configuration and questions. Food-contact evidence addresses a different use question from a sourcing or environmental statement.

For EU projects, use Regulation (EU) 2025/40 as the primary legal text for packaging and packaging waste. The Commission guidance published on 10 June 2026 interprets selected provisions. Use those sources and the Packrivo PPWR buyer checklist to identify the questions for the actual component, role and market. The responsible market reviewer should approve the wording and its scope before print approval.

Use one record to move the review forward

Download the blank material-claim evidence worksheet. Add one row per component and proposed statement. The record should identify the missing answer and the person who will close it, alongside any documents already received.

Here is an illustrative planning example. It describes a document gap, not a verified material claim or completed client project.

Swipe sideways to read every column on a small screen.

Illustrative pending claim record
Component Proposed wording Current record Next action
Box base, reference BX1 Recycled-content statement for the board Supplier material reference received; supporting basis still pending Ask the supplier for evidence covering that exact board reference
Insert, reference IN1 Wording still undecided Material and finish are being compared Choose the configuration, then identify the statement and evidence to review
Printed pack artwork, revision A1 Claim panel held for review Component evidence is not yet complete Ask the named market reviewer to approve the final wording and its scope

Keep completed supplier documents in private project records. The public worksheet is a blank tool; the facts and questions you share in a brief should be the ones you can disclose.

Close the wording review before approving artwork

Before print approval, match the proposed claim to the current component specification and artwork revision. Record the wording, qualifications, reviewer and decision date. Reopen the review when a relevant material, supplier, configuration or market changes.

If the project still needs a component specification, start with the packaging brief guide. Packrivo can help organize the brief and coordinate supplier questions so the appropriate people have a clearer record to review.

Sources reviewed on 2 October 2026. The linked FTC guidance concerns US environmental marketing claims, FSC explains its certification system, and the EU regulation and Commission guidance provide legal context and selected interpretations. None of these sources certifies a Packrivo product or approves the example above.

Reopen one claim when the supplied reference changes

An invented record connects box base BX1, board B1 and document D1, then compares proposed BX2 using B2 with a changed finish. Assume only that fictional D1 names B1. There is no real certificate, content percentage or approved claim.

Field Invented entry Status and next question
Wording Box-base recycled-content statement proposed Exact words and qualifications pending
Document D1 names B1 Does issuer confirm B2 coverage?
Configuration BX2 / B2; changed finish Match exact supplied scope
Market/artwork US proposal / A2 Reviewer and presentation pending
Print release Claim panel held in example Material sheet is not wording approval

A finish change raises a scope question; it does not automatically invalidate every document. Ask the issuer whether D1 covers B2 and retain the actual answer under its reference. A response about base board remains distinct from one covering the complete decorated component.

Even a confirmed material scope leaves the market reviewer to decide whether the exact printed wording and nearby symbols communicate it accurately. The CSV therefore separates document-match status from wording approval, both open here. FTC guidance concerns substantiation and qualification of US environmental marketing claims; it approves neither this example nor EU compliance. This record follows a changed reference through evidence and artwork, rather than treating recycled content and recycling after use as the same question.

Download the packaging material claim evidence record (.csv). HYPOTHETICAL rows are invented examples. Use ACTUAL_BLANK for permitted project inputs; replace that row label only when recording actual facts. Empty evidence, observation and date fields mean unknown or not performed, never acceptance. Keep checkpoints and revisions separate.

Send the changed material and finish, exact intended statement and document gap to the issuer and responsible market reviewer. Prepare the identified scope for a Packrivo inquiry. Packrivo coordinates independent suppliers. These records establish no supplier offer, service availability or MOQ exception; its published baseline is 500 pieces per product/design.

title: Multi SKU Jewelry Packaging: Build a Fit Matrix
html:
Multi-SKU jewelry packaging needs a separate fit record for every product and packing configuration. Compare the packed envelope, contact points, loading and removal, lid closure and accompanying cards before deciding which parts of the packaging can be shared.

In this guide
  • Record the packed envelope for each jewelry SKU
  • Compare configurations before sharing components
  • Keep MOQ and design quantities separate from fit
  • Work through a hypothetical jewelry family
  • Use shared component IDs to make the fit matrix concrete
  • Send the current configuration for review

A shared outer box can be a useful direction to explore. Keep its proposed dimensions separate from the insert and artwork configurations, so a common appearance doesn’t hide different packing requirements or order quantities.

Record the packed envelope for each jewelry SKU

Give every SKU its own identifier and product version. Measure the item as it will be packed, including backing cards, wraps, posts, clasps and any other components that occupy space. Record dimensions with their units and the proposed orientation.

The largest jewelry piece won’t always describe the most demanding configuration. A smaller item may have a protruding post, an access requirement or a card positioned above it. Keep those details in the row rather than reducing the family to one maximum length and width.

Use the existing jewelry insert measurement checklist for the individual measurements. The matrix adds a different step: comparing those records across SKUs without losing the contact and handling requirements.

Identify surfaces the insert may touch and areas you want kept clear. Describe how the packer loads the item and how the customer removes it. If the intended contact material is still open, ask the supplier to propose it for review.

Include the card configuration in each row. Its folded size, position and orientation can affect the complete pack even when the jewelry dimensions stay the same. Keep final copy and artwork versions separate from the physical space the card occupies.

Compare configurations before sharing components

Assign a configuration reference to each proposed combination of outer box, insert, jewelry orientation and card. One SKU may need several configurations during planning. The reference tells the supplier and reviewer which complete arrangement a question concerns.

For the outer box, distinguish exterior dimensions from the usable interior. Ask how the supplier defines those dimensions and what the proposed insert occupies. Keep the box drawing version with the matrix; a name such as “small jewelry box” isn’t a dimensional reference.

Review four questions for every row:

  • Can the intended item and all accompanying components be loaded in the proposed order?
  • Which surfaces are in contact, and which need clearance?
  • Can the customer reach and remove the item as intended?
  • Does the complete configuration allow the proposed lid and closure to work as reviewed?

Ask the supplier which components it proposes to share and which would change. That could mean one outer drawing with separate inserts, or different outer sizes where a shared interior would leave unresolved questions. Treat either as a proposal to examine.

Explore the existing jewelry box directions after the packing requirements are visible. Compare the opening and configuration against the matrix, rather than choosing a structure solely from its product name.

Keep approvals row-specific. A decision for a necklace configuration covers the identified necklace, box, insert and card versions. Other rows remain open until their own review scope is addressed, even if the outer drawing is shared.

If transport evaluation is part of the project, agree its scope separately from the fit review. ISTA’s guidance on retesting a packaged product identifies product, package and process changes as relevant considerations. A completed fit matrix doesn’t claim an ISTA result or establish transport protection.

Keep MOQ and design quantities separate from fit

Packrivo’s starting MOQ is 500 pieces per product / design. Record the requested quantity beside each proposed packaging design. The combined number of jewelry pieces doesn’t by itself establish how the packaging order will be grouped.

A shared outer size can still involve different inserts, print files, finishes or supplied components. Ask the supplier to identify the proposed product and design breakdown, quantities and scope in writing. Don’t assume every jewelry SKU becomes one packaging design, or that every configuration can be combined automatically.

For example, requesting quantities for several jewelry SKUs gives the supplier useful demand information. It still needs to say which packaging components share a specification and which have separate design requirements. Keep that response alongside the fit matrix.

The 500-piece MOQ planning worksheet addresses that quantity discussion. Any exception to Packrivo’s starting policy needs an agreed written scope; a proposed common box is not an exception by itself.

Ask for a revised breakdown when an insert or artwork configuration changes. This lets the buyer compare the current proposal without carrying forward quantities based on a different design.

Work through a hypothetical jewelry family

Consider an illustrative family containing a necklace, a pair of stud earrings and a ring. The buyer wants a similar outside presentation. These are fictional planning entries, not client SKUs, reviewed samples or measured Packrivo results.

The matrix keeps each product’s open questions visible. This compact example shows the type of information to record; its product envelopes would still need actual measurements.

On a small screen, scroll the table horizontally to see every column.

Hypothetical jewelry SKU planning entries
Illustrative SKU Packed envelope includes Configuration to discuss Open review question
Necklace N Chain, clasp and backing card Box, support and card position Loading and removal of chain
Earrings E Pair, posts and backing card Cutouts and space above posts Contact and complete closure
Ring R Ring and proposed wrap Support and finger access Positioning and removal

The buyer would send real product records and ask the supplier to propose configurations. A common outer drawing may remain a candidate while the insert layouts differ. Each row identifies what needs a physical review before a shared-component decision.

Suppose the buyer later changes the necklace backing card. The record would update that input and mark the affected configuration for another review. It wouldn’t alter an unrelated ring decision without identifying a connection between the changes.

The matrix also makes unanswered supplier replies easier to handle. “All fit” needs a configuration reference, review method and decision scope. Ask which rows were reviewed and what evidence supports the response before closing their actions.

Download the multi-SKU jewelry fit matrix (.csv). It has blank rows for SKU and product versions, packed dimensions, contact and access needs, box and insert references, card configuration and the next review action. No row contains a default measurement or passed result.

Complete the product-input fields first, then keep supplier proposals and sample decisions against the same rows. Take that versioned matrix to a Packrivo packaging brief so the next discussion can address the open configurations rather than restarting from the outside box appearance.

Use shared component IDs to make the fit matrix concrete

Do not give each row a completely new box ID when the proposal is actually a common outer drawing. Reusing the same reference makes the shared candidate visible. Give distinct inserts their own identifiers and keep their review outcomes separate.

Hypothetical SKU Outer candidate Insert candidate Open question
Necklace N1 BOX-A / drawing D2 INS-N / drawing N3 Chain route and backing-card removal
Stud earrings E1 BOX-A / drawing D2 INS-E / drawing E2 Post space beneath the display face
Ring R1 BOX-A / drawing D2 INS-R / drawing R4 Setting height and grip for removal

This table proposes three arrangements; it does not show that BOX-A fits any of them. Measured envelopes, usable interior and loaded samples still decide whether the common outer remains suitable. An earring post below the face and a ring setting above it create different depth questions even when their visible widths are small.

When one row changes, identify the dependency. A different necklace card may affect INS-N only, or it may force a BOX-A depth change affecting all three rows. Ask the source to identify which drawings change before retaining the other review decisions.

Once configurations are physically accepted, use the packing component matching map to keep the approved inserts with the right products. The fit matrix chooses arrangements; the packing map controls their later selection. Neither record proves transport protection or authorizes combining MOQ quantities.

Download the multi SKU jewelry packaging project record (.csv). The file has named planning fields and blank project rows. It contains no preset acceptance limits or approved results.

Send the current configuration for review

Bring the completed record, actual product or component references, requested quantity by design and destination to Packrivo’s packaging inquiry. Name the specific open decision above so the next sourcing discussion can address it. Packrivo coordinates sourcing questions; material, sample, price and delivery terms need project confirmation.

title: Label Adhesion for Packaging: Surface and Use Checklist
html:
To plan label adhesion for packaging, describe the actual surface, how the label is applied and what happens afterward. Ask the supplier to propose an identified label construction and a sample review for those conditions.

In this guide
  • Describe the surface the adhesive will meet
  • Separate application conditions from later use
  • Agree the candidate and review before applying samples
  • Use the worksheet to resolve an illustrative gift-pack decision
  • Complete a label use record without inventing acceptance limits
  • Send the current configuration for review

A label that looks right on a flat proof still needs an application decision. A small gift brand may use similar artwork on a coated box, a glass jar and a folded tissue seal. Keep a separate record for each use, even when the graphics match.

Describe the surface the adhesive will meet

Start with the component that receives the label. Record its material, surface finish, shape and label position. “Paper box” leaves open whether the label meets an uncoated sheet, a printed surface, a coating or a wrapped outer layer.

Photograph the proposed position and send a sample of the actual finished component when that can be agreed. If its construction is unknown, mark it as an input for the packaging supplier. Avoid assigning a material from a concept image.

Avery Dennison’s pressure-sensitive material guidance explains why the receiving surface matters to adhesive contact. Its examples concern technical applications, so they aren’t a recommendation for your gift box or jar.

Record whether the label sits on a flat panel, curves around a container or bridges two surfaces. Include its finished size and position relative to edges, seams and folds. A supplier needs that geometry alongside the material description.

Surface preparation also needs an owner. Ask the component and label suppliers to agree a suitable preparation method for the actual finish. Describe dust, handling residue or other conditions they should consider; don’t select a solvent or cleaning process without checking compatibility.

The Packrivo label directions can help you describe the format. Keep the receiving component’s finish in the same brief so a shape choice doesn’t replace the adhesion question.

Separate application conditions from later use

Write down what happens at the packing bench before describing delivery or storage. Who applies the label, by hand or with equipment? What are the proposed surface and surrounding conditions, and how is the label positioned?

Then describe its later use. A label applied in one environment may be handled, stored or displayed in another. Record the expected conditions and the role of the label: identification, decoration, a removable instruction or bridging a closure.

Avery Dennison’s adhesive glossary distinguishes application temperature from service temperature. It also describes initial tack and ultimate adhesion separately. Those terms help frame a supplier question, but they don’t supply universal limits or a review time for every construction.

Ask the supplier which product-specific instructions apply, including application method, conditions and the interval before each observation. Keep the proposed timing with the identified face material, adhesive and liner. Don’t turn a supplier’s instruction for one candidate into a rule for all labels.

Unused-label storage belongs in the record too. Avery Dennison’s February 2026 storage bulletin discusses protection from dust and environmental changes. Request storage instructions for the finished labels you will receive instead of copying a generic temperature or shelf-life figure.

If the choice is mainly about the packing operator or delivery format, use the existing roll and sheet application checklist. The adhesion record answers the separate question of how that proposed label meets the actual surface.

Agree the candidate and review before applying samples

Give each supplier proposal a construction reference and version. Ask it to identify the face material, any finish, adhesive, liner and label dimensions. A phrase such as “permanent label” still needs the proposed material details and intended use.

Agree who applies the candidates, which finished components they use and what gets recorded. The supplier should explain the proposed application and evaluation method. Decide in advance how observations will lead to acceptance, another review or a revised proposal.

Use these four groups to organize the discussion. They are planning fields, not a test standard or acceptance limits.

On a small screen, scroll the table horizontally to see every column.

Label adhesion planning fields
Record group Buyer supplies Supplier confirms Keep with the review
Receiving surface Actual component and position Surface information needed Component version
Application Operator and packing conditions Method and applicable instructions Application record
Candidate Size and artwork reference Identified label construction Candidate reference
Later use Expected handling and exposure Proposed evaluation and timing Observations and decision

Describe observations plainly. “One edge lifted after the recorded handling step” is more useful than “adhesive failed” without a method or condition. Photograph the position and keep the candidate identity with the observation.

When comparing candidates, record the variables you intend to hold constant and any changes the supplier proposes. If the receiving finish, preparation or application method changes, identify that difference before comparing results.

A practical sample review covers its agreed conditions and configuration. Wider resistance, sealing or other performance claims need suitable supporting evidence and a defined evaluation. A short observation on one package doesn’t establish every later use.

Use the worksheet to resolve an illustrative gift-pack decision

Consider a hypothetical brand with the same logo on a coated gift box and a glass candle jar. The buyer has selected artwork, but the two receiving finishes and application positions are different. This is a planning example, not a completed Packrivo project.

The buyer would create two records and provide the actual components. For the box, the record identifies its finished outer surface and whether the label bridges a fold. For the jar, it identifies the container surface, curve and label position.

Each supplier response should identify the proposed construction and explain the review method for its intended use. The same logo doesn’t justify copying an adhesion decision from the box onto the jar. An unresolved finish or application condition stays an open input.

Download the label adhesion review worksheet (.csv). The file contains field names and blank spaces for your project, supplier answers, references and next actions. It doesn’t include invented readings, preset limits or sample approvals.

Fill the receiving-surface and intended-use fields first. Send them with the artwork size and component references, then ask the supplier to complete the construction and review fields. After an agreed review, add the observations and a decision tied to that candidate.

Bring those records to a Packrivo packaging brief. A clear surface description and review question give a person enough context to help organize the next supplier discussion.

Complete a label use record without inventing acceptance limits

The following pair of hypothetical entries shows why one logo can require two reviews. It contains no adhesive recommendation or preset test result. Replace every component and condition with the actual intended project.

Field Gift box record B1 Candle jar record J1
Receiving surface Printed coated lid; finish reference needed Actual glass jar; coating identity needed
Geometry Flat panel; label stays within face Curved side; outline and seam position needed
Application Hand application at packing bench Proposed hand or equipment route to identify
Later use Retail handling and storage to describe Handling, storage and exposure to describe
Supplier reply Identify face, adhesive, liner and instructions Identify separate candidate and instructions
Observation Pending agreed review Pending agreed review

Keep application temperature and later service conditions in different fields. Obtain the applicable limits and instructions for the identified offered construction. Do not copy a number from a different adhesive grade merely because both are called permanent.

Agree the observation points with the supplier before comparison. Name who applies the labels, the actual finished component, the preparation method permitted for that finish and the interval before each check. Record edge lift, wrinkles, movement or residue by location. Avoid diagnosing a material defect from a photograph alone.

The liner release record handles dispensing before bonding. The removable label review adds time-in-place and the intended removal result. The candle label placement map supplies the geometry for a jar candidate. Keep those evidence scopes linked to the same construction revision.

Download the label adhesion for packaging project record (.csv). The file has named planning fields and blank project rows. It contains no preset acceptance limits or approved results.

Send the current configuration for review

Bring the completed record, actual product or component references, requested quantity by design and destination to Packrivo’s packaging inquiry. Name the specific open decision above so the next sourcing discussion can address it. Packrivo coordinates sourcing questions; material, sample, price and delivery terms need project confirmation.

title: Packaging Approval Timeline: Dependencies Before Dates
html:
Plan packaging approval milestones by naming the input, owner and accepted output for each step before assigning dates. Identify which decisions depend on earlier approvals and which reviews can proceed separately. Then ask the responsible parties to confirm their sequence and timing against the actual files, samples and open questions in your project.

A requested arrival date gives the project a goal. The milestone plan explains what must be ready for that goal to be evaluated. It also shows where a missing input or revised sample changes the next decision.

Define what allows a step to begin

Start with the package and its intended use. The structural contact needs the product arrangement and relevant measurements before checking fit. The artwork owner needs the current structural layout before finalizing panel placement. The sample reviewer needs a named candidate and the checks they are expected to perform.

Give each step a specific input. "Artwork ready" might mean a working design to discuss, a file ready for proofing or artwork approved against the selected dieline. Use the description that matches the next action. Otherwise, two people may plan dates around different meanings of readiness.

The supplier brief checklist helps collect early inputs. Your milestone plan adds the dependencies between those inputs and the people who will review them. Keep the brief version next to the plan so later changes are easy to locate.

Define the output that closes the step. A structural review may produce a candidate drawing and a list of open fit questions. A sample review may produce a decision with a specific scope. A release should name the approved configuration and what the next party can do with it.

Adobe’s packaging PDF workflow document discusses production file processing in packaging workflows. It provides useful context for treating file readiness as a real handoff. Your project contacts must confirm the particular file and approval requirements for their work.

Separate dependencies from work that can overlap

Draw a simple sequence for decisions that must happen in order. A revised fit decision may need a physical sample. Final artwork placement may need the structural drawing to stop moving. Final shipment data needs the intended delivery format and packing arrangement.

Other work can proceed while those decisions are open. The buyer can confirm the destination postcode, name the approval owner or prepare copy for review. Record this as independent work with its own output. It gives the team useful progress without treating an unfinished dependent step as complete.

Ask each owner what they need from the preceding step. A production contact may need more than the buyer’s email saying "looks good." They may require specific files, a retained sample reference and confirmation of unresolved items. Include those requirements in the output field.

Use one person as the decision owner for each gate. Several reviewers can contribute observations, but someone must combine them into a clear response. If that owner is unavailable, assign an authorized substitute or mark the decision pending rather than scattering approval across messages.

Keep the planned date separate from the confirmed commitment. Add the basis for a date when the responsible party supplies it. A requested date, an estimate and a confirmed step should remain distinguishable as the plan develops.

Copy an approval dependency worksheet

Use this original worksheet to build the sequence with your project contacts. Fill the first four columns before asking for dates. Add further rows for separate components or reviews when they have different owners.

Swipe the table to view all fields.

Gate Input needed Decision owner Accepted output Dependency Timing status
Structure review Product brief and measured arrangement Named structural reviewer Drawing ID and open checks Product data ready Request, estimate or confirmed
Artwork review Current drawing and complete copy Named artwork approver Proof ID and approval scope Panel layout stable Owner to confirm
Sample review Candidate ID and agreed check list Named sample approver Decision, actions and evidence Candidate available Owner to confirm
Configuration release Required approvals and closed actions Named release owner Linked drawing, artwork and sample IDs Required gates accepted Owner to confirm
Shipment planning Delivery state and carton proposal Named packing contact Versioned shipment data Packing arrangement confirmed Owner to confirm

Use this worksheet for your project

Fill the input, owner, accepted output and dependency before assigning dates. Keep target, estimate and confirmed timing separate, with open actions visible.

Download the worksheet (.csv)

Open in Excel, Google Sheets or another spreadsheet app. Fill in your actual project details and keep the agreed file and sample versions with the record.

Give an open action the same treatment as a planned gate. Name its input, owner and closure evidence. "Awaiting sample" becomes more actionable when the record says which sample, who provides it and which review follows its arrival.

Use the sample approval checks to make that review’s output specific. Include any changes needed and the scope of the acceptance. That makes it easier to determine whether the configuration release can proceed.

Replan an illustrative candle gift project

In this hypothetical example, a small brand wants a box, insert and care card for a candle gift. The buyer has measured the jar but hasn’t finalized the card’s folded size. The structural review therefore includes an open input owned by the buyer.

While the buyer confirms that size, the artwork owner checks spelling and prepares copy. Final placement stays dependent on the current box drawing. The sample review is planned around a complete pack containing the jar, insert and card, so the output can address their interaction.

The first candidate shows that the card interferes with closure. The owner records a revision action, and the structural contact confirms which drawing and sample need updating. The release gate remains open while unrelated destination and delivery-format questions continue.

After the revised complete pack is reviewed, the buyer returns a scoped decision. The release owner links it to the correct drawing and artwork IDs. Each responsible party can then reassess timing from the current state rather than carrying forward dates based on the first candidate.

Ask for timing against the current plan

Send the dependency table with the requested delivery goal and the configuration version. Ask the contacts to identify unresolved inputs, their proposed sequence and the basis for timing. Keep the answer with the plan and update affected gates when the project changes.

Bring your target date, approval owners and unresolved inputs into a Packrivo milestone brief. A clear sequence gives the human review a practical basis for discussing the next step.

Reopen card-dependent gates and preserve unrelated work

Continue the fictional candle project with C2 replacing care card C1. Its folded dimensions remain missing. D2 drawing, A2 artwork and S2 sample are candidate references, not produced or accepted outputs. Identify which gates need the input while preserving separate destination work.

Gate Input Candidate output Planning state
Card definition C2 dimensions Defined C2 Open
Drawing C2, jar and insert D2 review Dependent on C2
Artwork D2 and confirmed copy A2 placement review Not accepted
Complete fit D2, C2 and contents S2 decision Not performed
Release Required A2 and S2 decisions Linked release Pending
Destination Address and delivered format Destination record May proceed separately

The D2 branch means both A2 and S2 need the current structural basis. It does not promise simultaneous work or imply an unprinted sample settles artwork. Ask each actual owner what further inputs its branch needs.

Retain C1/D1/A1/S1 history under its earlier scope. Do not change an old acceptance date to make it current. Earlier evidence can be linked if its applicability is reviewed; changed interfaces remain separate decisions. Requested, estimated and confirmed dates are distinct CSV fields, all blank here. A completed destination task does not clear the open card-dependent release. No lead time or delivery commitment follows from this dependency map.

Download the packaging approval timeline record (.csv). HYPOTHETICAL rows are invented examples. Use ACTUAL_BLANK for permitted project inputs; replace that row label only when recording actual facts. Empty evidence, observation and date fields mean unknown or not performed, never acceptance. Keep checkpoints and revisions separate.

Send the current version chain, missing C2 input and gate owners before asking parties for revised timing. Prepare the identified scope for a Packrivo inquiry. Packrivo coordinates independent suppliers. These records establish no supplier offer, service availability or MOQ exception; its published baseline is 500 pieces per product/design.

title: Packaging Freight Quotes: Carton Data to Prepare
html:
Prepare a packaging freight inquiry with the shipping carton count, outer dimensions, gross and net weights, units per carton and delivery format. Label every unit and say whether each value is measured or estimated. Add the pickup and destination details, then ask the freight provider to confirm the service and charging basis for that shipment.

The finished size of a gift box isn’t the shipping size of an order. Flat boxes, assembled boxes, separate inserts and bundled accessories can create different carton arrangements. A useful freight record describes the goods in the form they will actually travel.

Identify every shipping unit before totaling the order

Assign an ID to each carton type. Identical cartons can share a row with a count; a partly filled carton needs its own row if its contents, weight or dimensions differ. Include separately packed tissue, labels or inserts instead of assuming they travel inside the boxes.

Record units per carton and define the unit. “100 units” could mean 100 flat boxes, 100 assembled boxes or 100 complete sets with accessories. State the contents in the same row. Then reconcile the carton totals against the requested quantity for each component.

Packrivo’s starting order requirement is 500 pieces per design. That order quantity is separate from the carton count and the number of complete sets. A request for 500 boxes and 500 inserts needs a packing description that shows how both components travel.

State whether goods are loose cartons, palletized or in another proposed shipping arrangement. If palletization is planned, ask for the final pallet dimensions, weights and carton arrangement as a separate shipping record. The freight contact needs to know which outer unit they’re evaluating.

The folding gift box specifications explain why delivery state belongs in a packaging brief. Carry the agreed state into the freight record, and ask the packing contact to confirm the actual arrangement before comparing services.

Keep dimensions, weights and measurement status together

Measure the outer dimensions of the closed shipping carton in the intended packed state. Label length, width and height, and use one stated unit throughout the table. Record whether tape, bulging sides or another packing feature affects the final outer measurement.

State what net weight includes in your record. Ask the packing contact to identify the goods included and what they exclude as shipping packaging. Gross weight should describe the complete shipping unit as presented, with its carton and packing materials. Keep the definitions with the figures so another party can interpret them.

An estimate is useful for early planning when it’s labeled. Record the basis, such as a proposed carton arrangement, and the person who will replace it with a measured result. A change to assembly state or protective packing should trigger a check of the affected row.

FedEx’s US dimensional-weight explanation distinguishes dimensional weight from actual weight when describing its charging basis. Check the current service-specific rule with the provider. This worksheet deliberately computes geometric volume only, without applying a universal divisor or charge.

If you calculate carton volume, retain the original dimensions and unit. A carton measuring 50 cm by 40 cm by 30 cm has a geometric volume of 0.06 cubic metres. That arithmetic describes space; ask the provider to state how dimensions and weight affect its actual charge for the proposed service.

Copy a freight inquiry data worksheet

Use one row per distinct shipping unit. This original worksheet organizes an inquiry; the packing party and freight provider should confirm the shipment data and service basis.

Swipe the table to view all fields.

Shipping unit Count Contents and units each Outer L x W x H Net weight each Gross weight each Status and method
Carton type A Complete Define pieces or sets Value and unit Value, unit and scope Value and unit Measured or estimate, date, owner
Carton type B Complete if different Identify separate component Value and unit Value, unit and scope Value and unit Measurement or estimate basis
Other shipping unit Describe State carton arrangement Final outer dimensions Define included goods Complete unit weight Confirmation owner

Reconcile an illustrative flat box shipment

In this hypothetical example, a brand requests 500 flat gift boxes for one design. The proposed packing arrangement has five identical cartons, each holding 100 boxes. Each carton is estimated at 50 x 40 x 30 cm, with 12 kg net weight for the boxes and 13 kg gross weight including the shipping pack.

The buyer records 500 boxes, 60 kg total net weight and 65 kg total gross weight. The five cartons occupy 0.30 cubic metres based on the stated outer dimensions. All figures remain marked as planning estimates until the packing contact measures the final cartons.

The inserts are packed separately, so the buyer adds their row before sending the inquiry. The freight contact can now evaluate the whole shipment rather than only the boxes. If the brand later requests assembled delivery, the packing contact revises the carton arrangement and measurement status.

This example demonstrates reconciliation, not a standard packing density or freight offer. The useful check is that component quantities, carton counts and totals agree before the provider works from them.

Close the missing-component gap before requesting a total

The diagram intentionally stops at the box-only estimate. Continue the same hypothetical exercise by assuming, solely for calculation, that 500 inserts will travel in two further cartons of 250 inserts each. Each invented insert carton measures 40 × 30 × 25 cm and has 7 kg net and 8 kg gross weight. These are not a proposed packing density or measured shipment.

Estimated carton line Cartons × contents External size each Net / gross each Line totals
A: flat boxes 5 × 100 boxes = 500 boxes 50 × 40 × 30 cm 12 / 13 kg 60 kg net; 65 kg gross; 0.30 m³
B: separate inserts 2 × 250 inserts = 500 inserts 40 × 30 × 25 cm 7 / 8 kg 14 kg net; 16 kg gross; 0.06 m³
Combined shipment model 7 cartons; 500 boxes plus 500 inserts Two carton types, not one averaged size Defined component scope above 74 kg net; 81 kg gross; 0.36 m³

For line B, 0.40 × 0.30 × 0.25 = 0.03 m³ per carton; two occupy 0.06 m³ geometrically. Sum net and gross weights separately. The combined 1,000 component pieces could support 500 one-box/one-insert sets only if the components actually match; they are not 1,000 complete sets. Keep both carton rows and mark every value estimated until final packed measurements replace them. Ask the provider for charges against that version, service, destination and named delivery scope; 0.36 m³ is not a shipping price or dimensional weight.

Send a versioned shipment description

Keep the carton record with the corresponding packaging configuration and quantity. Replace estimates with confirmed measurements when available, and resend the data when the shipment changes. That gives each freight response an identifiable basis.

Bring the packaging quantity, delivery state and available carton data into a Packrivo delivery brief. Clear units and open questions help the human review identify what the packing and freight contacts need next.

Keep the current record with the project brief

Download the carton freight reconciliation CSV. It contains field definitions, clearly hypothetical examples and a blank actual-project row. Replace invented values with your own supported records; keep unknown fields open.

Packrivo coordinates packaging sourcing and project questions with independent suppliers. The worksheet is a discussion aid, not a confirmed quotation, manufacturing promise or sample approval. The published starting MOQ is 500 pieces per product/design; actual component, design and commercial scope require confirmation.

Source scope: FedEx explains US dimensional-versus-actual-weight charging context; numeric carton model is invented geometric arithmetic, not a carrier tariff or a freight quote. Public references checked 16 October 2026. All new illustrations are AI-assisted concepts. No real customer, test, shipment, stock, savings or production outcome is represented.

title: Incoming Packaging Inspection and Acceptance Record
html:
Inspect incoming packaging against the configuration selected for the order, then record which received units the observations cover and who decides their use. Keep the delivery identity, inspection basis, exceptions and disposition together. A signed receipt, an earlier approved sample or a photograph of one good item cannot substitute for that batch decision.

In this guide
  • Establish what arrived and what it should match
  • State the inspection basis before extending a finding
  • Separate identity, requirement and disposition
  • Compare three receiving decisions against the same requirement
  • Return a usable decision to the packing team
  • Attach one located view without extending it to the delivery
  • Bring the specific open question to the project brief

This guide begins after packaging has been delivered. Its output is an acceptance, rejection or continued-hold record for identified received goods. For changes between pre-production samples, use the sample-version comparison guide.

Establish what arrived and what it should match

Record the order and delivery references, component, quantity and available lot or carton identities before mixing the goods with earlier stock. Mark missing identity or quantity information as unresolved rather than inferring it from familiar artwork.

Bring the current order specification, drawing, artwork and relevant approved references to the receiving check. State which features each reference controls. A sample accepted for outside artwork may not establish the selected insert or the loaded closing arrangement.

Keep outer-carton condition and the condition of the packaging inside as separate observations. A crushed delivery carton can justify a closer check, but it does not identify the cause of damage to a gift box. Likewise, an intact carton does not prove that every unit inside matches the order.

State the inspection basis before extending a finding

Name the inspection method agreed for the actual order, who performs it and which requirements are checked. Define the lot or grouping the decision will cover and the inspection unit: a lid, a component or an identified complete set. Keep different revisions or unidentified groupings separate unless the agreed plan provides a basis for combining them.

If an acceptance sampling plan applies, retain its selection method and decision rules with the receiving record. State the agreed rules before evaluating the findings, rather than choosing a more convenient rule after seeing them. This article supplies neither a universal sample size nor an AQL threshold.

NIST’s explanation of acceptance sampling describes using information from a selected sample to decide a lot’s disposition. Its overview of sampling plans shows that the selection and decision rules belong to a specified plan. Checking whichever box is easiest to reach is not enough to claim a statistically representative result.

For each observation, name the carton or grouping, the reviewed item and its state during the check. Keep the number inspected and the number of nonconforming units separate. Also record whether the agreed rule counts units or individual nonconformities: one lid with two marks is not automatically two nonconforming lids.

Observation counts do not by themselves establish the delivery’s defect rate or acceptance. NIST distinguishes a lot disposition decision from an estimate of lot quality. Use the actual agreed plan to determine what the observations permit you to conclude.

If a project has no agreed basis for a needed acceptance decision, record the missing requirement and assign the next review. Do not invent a pass limit on the receiving bench.

Separate identity, requirement and disposition

Use the main acceptance record to combine the receipt evidence with the agreed requirements. Detailed item-to-carton tracing belongs in the supporting incoming lot reference record.

Part of the record Entry needed before a batch decision
Received grouping Order/delivery reference, component, available lot/carton IDs and quantity
Required configuration Checked feature, agreed requirement and controlling reference
Inspection basis Lot boundary, inspection unit, actual method, reviewed quantity and responsible person
Decision rules Pre-agreed acceptance/rejection rules and their reference, where applicable
Observations Located condition, nonconforming unit count, separate nonconformity count if relevant, and evidence
Unresolved extent Unchecked units, missing identity or an open requirement
Proposed response Further inspection, sorting, replacement or another project-specific action
Disposition Accepted, rejected or continued hold, with scope, decision owner and date
Packing handoff Which identified goods may be used, under the recorded decision

The table distinguishes what was observed from what is authorized for use. Receipt staff can document a condition while the named acceptance owner decides whether it meets the requirement.

Compare three receiving decisions against the same requirement

In this hypothetical example, the selected order calls for artwork revision A-03. The table shows how different evidence leads to different next decisions. It gives no numerical inspection limits and describes no actual Packrivo delivery.

Receipt evidence Requirement and rule to apply Decision scope
Reviewed artwork matches A-03, and the recorded checks satisfy the agreed rule Use the current requirement and documented acceptance basis The authorized owner may accept the identified grouping for the reviewed scope; unreviewed requirements remain visible
Reviewed artwork shows superseded A-02 Record the version mismatch and apply the agreed nonconformance/disposition rule Record rejection or another authorized action only for the scope established by the evidence and rule
Artwork appears to match, but selection, lot identity or the decision-rule reference is missing The evidence needed to support the required decision is incomplete Continue the identified hold while the named owner resolves the missing basis; do not invent acceptance or rejection

The distinguishing output is the reason for disposition: the required configuration, evidence obtained, applicable rule and authorized scope. A supplier response can add information, but it cannot erase the earlier observation or replace the responsible decision.

For goods with recorded visible damage that remain on hold, the separate incoming damage hold record retains location, affected extent and use status. Keep that detailed procedure there; link its reference into the acceptance decision. For a version mismatch or a missing inspection basis without observed damage, retain the open status in this acceptance record rather than presenting it as a damage case.

Return a usable decision to the packing team

Write the disposition for a named grouping and the requirements actually reviewed. An entry such as "continued hold pending inspection of the remaining identified cartons" tells the next team what remains open. A generic "supplier says fine" does not identify either the evidence or the person authorized to decide.

Before packing uses accepted goods, communicate their identities and the applicable decision. Keep rejected or held goods distinguishable under the project’s agreed handling process. This is a project-specific acceptance record, not a certification or a claim that an accepted lot contains no defects.

The downloadable receiving worksheet provides separate fields for receipt facts, inspection basis, observed findings and disposition. Replace the hypothetical examples with actual records; the worksheet does not choose your sampling plan or authorize production.

Download the receiving acceptance worksheet (CSV)

Blank template. Enter actual project records; no sample size or acceptance limit is prescribed.

Attach one located view without extending it to the delivery

A photograph should identify the unit and state it actually shows. Keep a wider view locating the component within carton C1 and a closer view of the same unit U1. A close crop alone can lose the item-to-carton relationship.

Fictional record field Teaching entry Scope limit
Reference U1 from carton C1; requirement A-03 Actual lot, item and requirement references would need confirmation
Located observation Corner mark at the indicated position; no actual photo taken A mark is not automatically a classified nonconformity
Evidence extent Only the illustrated unit view No whole-delivery count or defect rate established
Next decision Responsible owner applies the agreed requirement and method Continue the unresolved scope; do not infer all good or all defective

The diagram is an AI teaching example, not an H1 photograph of real goods. For actual work, retain the original view, date, sample identity and the conditions relevant to the check. Record whether the observation covers artwork, surface condition or another feature; one view may leave the others open.

If the photo instead shows superseded A-02 against required A-03, keep that mismatch located on the identified unit and apply the actual disposition rule. Do not turn the revision label into evidence about every unexamined piece or use a new convenient acceptance rule after seeing the result.
